papers.abstract: Data attribution methods for Language Models (LMs) are typically evaluated using downstream tasks like fact retrieval. However, existing evaluations vary multiple dataset properties simultaneously, making it impossible to isolate exactly why an attribution algorithm fails. To diagnose these failures, we explore the design space of LLM data attribution, with a primary focus on evaluation. We introduce the Controlled Attribution Benchmark (CATT) for fact tracing, in which we fine-tune LLMs on entirely fictitious knowledge, providing unambiguous ground truth for attribution. This synthetic setup allows us to systematically alter one dataset configuration at a time, such as document redundancy and lexical distractors. With this configurable evaluation, we demonstrate that redundancy and distractors consistently degrade attribution performance. Rather than proposing a new estimator, we examine two design choices that are underexplored: the loss used to compute gradients and how per-token attribution scores are aggregated into a document score. We find that the true causal evidence within a training document is highly localized, but standard methods dilute this evidence into noise by averaging attribution scores across the entire document. We find that replacing standard cross-entropy loss gradients with the negative log-odds gradients surfaces the critical tokens from other uninformative ones. We can then aggregate only the top token scores to improve ground truth recall by 35 to 72 percentage points across multiple baselines on our diagnostic benchmark. The negative log-odds correction also generalizes to FTRACE-TREX, improving counterfactual retraining performance for every method we test, by up to 4.9x.
authors: Steven Yu, Sheng-Yu Wang, Kimia Hamidieh, Antonio Torralba, David Bau
bullets: Introduces CATT, a synthetic fact-tracing benchmark with unambiguous attribution ground truth and independently configurable dataset properties.
Shows that document redundancy and lexical distractors consistently degrade attribution performance.
Finds that causal evidence is localized to a few tokens, but document-wide averaging dilutes it with noise.
Uses negative log-odds gradients and top-token aggregation to recover critical evidence.
Improves ground-truth recall by 35–72 percentage points across baselines and counterfactual retraining performance by up to 4.9× on FTRACE-TREX.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Upweighting more influential tokens with log-odds improves Recall across token budgets. Recall@N as the number of retained tokens k varies, under cross-entropy (top) and negative log-odds (bottom). Columns show the three CATT settings. The yellow regions mark full-document scoring (“all”), with the upper-right endpoint in each column corresponding to the prior-work loss and aggregation choices. Negative log-odds with small token budgets substantially improve several methods, especially with distractors. Gains persist across multiple k values; retaining more tokens often reduces recall. Results are averaged over all dataset configurations and model seeds at |F| = 50 with error bars showing ±2 standard errors.

Figure 2: CATT: fact tracing tasks with controlled datasets. We fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B models on fictitious knowledge, which ensures our dataset is the sole causal source of its predictions. Left: Task I (Function Bindings) teaches new functions that always return a fixed value. Right: Task II (Routing Rules) teaches rules that sort objects based on their properties. Given a query phrased unlike any training document, we test whether attribution methods can correctly rank ground-truth documents. Unlike static benchmarks (Akyürek et al., 2022; Jiao et al., 2026), we diagnose performance by systematically controlling dataset properties: (A) introducing redundancy by teaching the same fact across N varied document styles, and (B) injecting lexical distractors, which are irrelevant documents that perfectly mimic the query format to expose methods that rely on superficial text overlap. Task II omits distractors because each fact uses a disjoint set of attribute words, making it difficult to construct clear lexical overlaps. Browse the datasets on our project page.

Figure 5: The loss determines what type of tokens occupy the top positions. (a) Per-token attributions for one query on one of its ground-truth Rule Routings documents, under cross-entropy (top) and negative log-odds (bottom). Boxes mark the ten highest-scoring positions. Negative logodds moves the document from rank 1499 to rank 12 of 1500. (b) Each token type’s share of the top-10 positions divided by its share of all positions. Cross-entropy favors item names. Negative log-odds instead favors outcome tokens, the words that match the query answer. Appendix D.4 shows the same pattern on Function Bindings tasks. Explore per-token attributions for other queries and methods in our demo.

Figure 4: Token selection and negative log-odds loss help isolate ground truth. Document scores for ground-truth (red) and other (gray) documents. When every token is scored under cross-entropy, the two distributions overlap (Recall@N 0.01). Keeping only each document’s top 10 tokens (0.30) or switching to negative log-odds (0.35) partly separates them, and combining both separates them completely (1.00). This result is from Grad-Dot on a model trained on Function Bindings dataset with distractors (N=50, |F| = 50). View these plots for each dataset, method, and model seed on our project page.

Figure 8: Fine-tuned models at |F| = 50. (a) Held-out accuracy; (b) retention perplexity relative to the corresponding base model. Lines show the mean over seeds 1001–1003 and shading shows the range. The hollow Rule Routings point at N = 1 lies outside the attribution grid. (c–e) Training loss of seed 1002. ∗The published runs with distractors left no loss log, so (d) shows the checkpointed retrain used by the trajectory methods.

Figure 9: Compute cost of the attribution methods. (a) Wall-clock hours per trained model against the number of candidate documents M , at |F| = 50 and |Q| = 200, for jobs run on one A100-80GB. Points are individual jobs and lines join medians. Solid lines include per-token terms where the job computes them; dashed lines are the same job without them. (b) Total recorded GPU-hours over the whole sweep, stacked by |F| and pooled over tasks, on a mix of A100, H100 and H200 GPUs. Each job produces every method in its group (Table 7).

Figure 3: Existing attribution methods struggle with redundancy and distractors. We evaluate attribution methods on CATT. Recall@N of each method’s attribution scores as the number of training documents per fact, N , increases, at |F| = 50 facts. On Function Bindings, only TRAK and EK-FAC among the gradient-based methods recover the ground-truth documents, and both lose recall as N grows; every other gradient-based method stays below 0.35. Distractors drive TRAK to 0 at every N and lower EK-FAC. On Rule Routings, no gradient-based method exceeds 0.32. BM25 remains strong thanks to distinctive lexical cues, while RepSim is weak throughout. Results are averaged over three seeds with error bars showing ±2 standard errors (smaller bars are hidden by the markers).

Figure 10: Recall@N with log-odds top-10 scoring. The counterpart of Figure 3. Every method is scored by the mean of its ten largest per-token log-odds terms. Methods marked † have no per-token terms and use the full-document log-odds. Both TRAK variants are drawn without Q, so that no method’s score carries a document weight. With Q, TRAK falls to about 0 on the distractor task at every N : the decoys are fit poorly (Q ≈ 0.17–0.20) and the ground-truth documents are memorized (Q ≈ 0.007–0.009), so Q ranks a decoy first for every query. The panel titles and method names follow the main-text figures.

Figure 1: The right loss focuses attribution on relevant tokens. We show token-level influence scores within a ground-truth training document, divided by the document’s largest token score. Cross-entropy assigns little weight to the tokens relevant to answering the query, ranking the document poorly (rank 582/1000). Surprisingly, we find that simply switching to negative log-odds concentrates the influence score on those tokens, and correctly ranks it first. Result is from our Controlled Attribution Benchmark.

Figure 7: Generalization to external FTRACETREX benchmarks. Accuracy drop after removing the highest-ranked training documents and retraining, at increasing removal budgets. Larger drops indicate more effective identification of influential data. In each panel, dashed: prior work; light: with negative log-odds; dark: negative logodds over the top 10 tokens (TRAK’s dense projection has no per-token scores); dotted: BM25. Mean over eight retrain seeds (Appendix E), error bars ±2 standard errors.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnostic benchmark and analysis of LM data attribution; relevant to understanding LLM training data influence.
papers.title: Elucidating the Design Space of LM Data Attribution
papers.tldr: A controlled benchmark reveals that document redundancy and distractors hinder LM data attribution, while localized token scoring with negative log-odds gradients substantially improves tracing accuracy.

papers.abstract: The Neural Thickets hypothesis posits that pretrained language models lie in dense neighborhoods of task-specific experts in weight space, which random Gaussian perturbations can uncover. We reproduce the reported gains, but show that they do not require this geometric explanation. Perturbing a single decoder block already recovers much of the improvement, while keeping the model entirely frozen and adding a random bias to its output logits matches or exceeds full-weight perturbations on most reasoning tasks. This suggests an alternative explanation based on output diversity, validation-based selection, and voting. We formalize this view as Perturb-Select-Vote (PSV), a general procedure that generates perturbed predictors, selects high-performing members on a small validation set, and aggregates their predictions. This interpretation connects Neural Thickets to established inference-time methods, including sampling, self-consistency, and verifier-guided selection. A first-order analysis further shows that small weight perturbations act primarily through their induced logit shifts. We extend this analysis to vision, where logit PSV substantially improves performance under domain shift, including on Earth observation, while full-weight perturbations provide little additional benefit. Together, these results suggest that the gains attributed to nearby weight-space experts can instead be obtained through output diversity, selection, and voting. Logit PSV realizes these benefits with a fully frozen model, providing a simple, training-free alternative to full-weight perturbation ensembles across language and vision.
authors: Nicolas Dufour, Elouan Gard\`es, Amil Dravid, Patrick P\'erez, Loic Landrieu
bullets: Single-block perturbations recover much of the reported improvement, while random output-logit biases often match or exceed full-weight perturbations on reasoning tasks.
The authors propose Perturb-Select-Vote (PSV): generate perturbed predictors, select strong ones on a small validation set, and aggregate their predictions.
A first-order analysis suggests small weight perturbations mainly matter through the logit shifts they induce.
Logit PSV improves vision performance under domain shift, including Earth observation, without modifying model weights.
The approach connects Neural Thickets to sampling, self-consistency, and verifier-guided selection, but its scope is limited to the tasks and settings evaluated.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Full-weight PSV versus logit PSV. Both methods share the same selection and voting stages (right), but differ in the perturbation (left). Neural Thickets (top) perturb the full dθdimensional parameter vector, producing N distinct networks. Logit PSV (bottom) keeps one frozen network and adds a V -dimensional bias to the output logits, fixed across decoding steps and inputs.

Figure 4: Logit PSV matches full-weight PSV across tasks and model scales. (a) On OLMo-37B-Instruct, logit PSV matches or exceeds full-weight PSV on all evaluated tasks. (b) Across model scales and tasks, logit PSV closely tracks full-weight PSV.

Figure 5: Temperature-tuned majority voting versus full-weight PSV. (a) On MATH-500 with a strong model, tuned TT-MV matches or exceeds full-weight PSV. (b) On USPTO with a weaker model, TT-MV remains far below PSV, showing the value of validation-based selection; both remain below the majority-class baseline. (c) Across tasks and model scales, TT-MV at T=0.7 closely tracks full-weight PSV, with larger gaps for weaker models and harder tasks.

Figure 7: Single-component perturbations transfer across architectures. Gain over base, in accuracy points, when perturbing one component of the first decoder block of Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on GSM8K (K=50; base 44.3%, full-block gain +11.8). Every component improves over base, with the largest gains from the value, up, and output projections. Qwen2.5 uses pre-norm blocks and includes QKV biases, unlike OLMo.

Figure 3: Single-component perturbations within a decoder block. Fraction of the full-weight PSV gain recovered by perturbing one component of the first decoder block of OLMo-3-7B-Instruct on Countdown with K = 50. All components recover at least 85% of the full-weight gain (base 66.6%, full-weight PSV 90.8%).

Figure 6: Performance as a function of ensemble size. Gain over the greedy base, in accuracy points, as a function of K for full-weight PSV and logit PSV on Qwen2.5-0.5B, 1.5B, and 3BInstruct (N=1000, N=2000 for full-weight Countdown; σ fixed per model as in Table 5). Countdown and USPTO are omitted at 0.5B because the base model cannot perform these tasks.

Figure 12: Peak accuracy of stacked perturbations versus individual methods and a logit-only control. Full-weight PSV stacked on logit PSV is compared against (a) the stronger individual method and (b) the same-mechanism control, which stacks two logit biases. The dashed diagonal indicates equal accuracy. Most points lie on or below it. Above it are 3B and 7B MATH-500 (+1.3, +1.0) and 7B GSM8K (+0.2) in (a), and 7B Countdown (+0.9), 7B MATH-500 (+0.3), and 3B Countdown (+0.2) in (b); only 7B MATH-500 is above it in both.

Figure 11: Accuracy gains from individual and stacked perturbation mechanisms. Peak gain over greedy decoding across ensemble sizes K, comparing full-weight PSV, logit PSV, their combination, and a same-mechanism control that stacks two logit biases with a smaller noise range. The symbol “◦” denotes successive application of two perturbations. Combining weight and logit perturbations rarely improves upon the stronger individual method or the logit-only control, except on 7B MATH-500.
Figure 2: Effect of perturbing individual decoder blocks. Countdown accuracy with OLMo-37B-Instruct (K = 50), perturbing one block at a time while keeping all other weights fixed.

Figure 9: Accuracy as a function of ensemble size K. Plurality-vote accuracy for full-weight PSV, logit PSV, and TT-MV across model scales (rows) and tasks (columns). The dashed line indicates the greedy-base accuracy.

Figure 10: Gain over the greedy base as a function of ensemble size K. Same runs as Figure 9, shown as the accuracy gain ∆ over the greedy base, across model scales (rows) and tasks (columns). The dashed line marks zero gain.

Figure 8: Single-component perturbations remain effective at larger scales. Gain over base, in accuracy points, when perturbing one component of the first decoder block on Qwen2.5-1.5B and 3B-Instruct for Countdown (K=32). All components improve over base, with the output and value projections among the strongest at both scales.

Table 5: Cross-scale comparison of full-weight and output-space perturbations. Accuracy at K=50 (%) for the greedy base, full-weight PSV, logit PSV, and an input-embedding-bias variant on Qwen2.5 and OLMo-3-7B-Instruct. The input-embedding variant adds a Gaussian bias to token embeddings and is evaluated on Qwen2.5 only. The logit-bias scale is fixed per model rather than chosen per task (σ=0.5 for Qwen2.5-0.5B, 1.0 for 1.5B and 3B, 2.0 for OLMo-3-7B), and fullweight PSV uses σ=0.001. Every method uses N=1000, except full-weight PSV on Countdown (N=2000). Degenerate Qwen2.5-0.5B cells on Countdown and USPTO are omitted. †A constant predictor of the majority reaction class scores 31.9% on USPTO; these cells are at or below it and are not bolded. ‡Above that baseline, but with lower balanced accuracy than full-weight PSV (26.7% against 29.7%).

Table 3: Vision PSV under domain shift. We report improvements relative to linear probing on the frozen DINOv3-7B backbone using worst-region accuracy for FMoW, worst-group accuracy for Waterbirds, and balanced top-1 accuracy for ImageNet. PSV variants use validation-selected ensembles with K = 10; closed-form denotes a single deterministic output recalibration. Weightspace perturbations yield little improvement, whereas output-space methods produce substantial gains on FMow, Waterbirds, which present strong train-to-test shift.

Table 6: Component-wise gains and selection-reward variability across scales. For Qwen2.51.5B and 3B-Instruct on Countdown (K=32), we perturb one component of the first decoder block and report its gain over base and the standard deviation of member rewards on the selection set. Every component produces nonzero reward variability and improves the final vote, with the largest effects generally obtained from the value and output projections.

Table 7: Matched comparison under the original protocol (N=5000, K=50, authors’ released code). Accuracy (%) of the greedy base, full-weight PSV, logit PSV, and TT-MV (T=0.7), and the paired difference between logit and full-weight PSV with its 95% bootstrap confidence interval over test items; bold intervals exclude zero.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Perturb-Select-Vote (PSV), an inference-time method for improving model performance through output diversity and selection, applicable to both language and vision models.
papers.title: Rethinking Neural Thickets Without Weight Perturbations
papers.tldr: Neural Thickets gains can largely be explained by output diversity, validation-based selection, and voting rather than nearby weight-space experts.

papers.abstract: Pixel-space generative Transformers typically use one token per image patch, so capturing finer detail requires more tokens and makes global attention increasingly expensive. We observe that finer detail does not necessarily require more global communication: low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange, while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally. Based on this insight, we introduce SpecSlot, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer that decouples output detail from the length of the global attention sequence. SpecSlot expands each spatial anchor into multiple slots, each assigned a disjoint band of DCT coefficients; this separates anchor density from spectral subdivision. Only the lowest-frequency slot from each anchor participates in global attention, while all slots interact locally. This allows the model to increase spectral detail without enlarging the global sequence. A spatial head further adds a local correction to the spectral prediction, while the generative state, target, and loss remain in pixel space. On ImageNet-256, SpecSlot achieves a comparable final FID to a FLOPs-matched JiT control while converging faster. On ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over the control with 3.9% fewer FLOPs, and comes within only 0.69 FID of JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, SpecSlot surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost.
authors: Jiongfan Yang, Weichen Fan, Haiwen Diao, Zhongang Cai, Ziwei Liu
bullets: Global attention captures low-frequency structure, while high-frequency detail is modeled locally.
Each spatial anchor expands into DCT-band-specific slots; only the lowest-frequency slots use global attention.
A spatial head adds local corrections while generation, targets, and loss remain in pixel space.
On ImageNet-512, SpecSlot improves FID by 2.84 with 3.9% fewer FLOPs than a matched JiT control.
It also approaches JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost and surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench at 40.6% lower forward cost.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces SpecSlot, a tokenization strategy for pixel-space Transformers that decouples global attention length from detail, directly addressing efficiency in generative models.
papers.title: Read, Allocate, Route: Role-Coupled Tokenization for Pixel-Space Generative Transformers
papers.tldr: SpecSlot increases pixel-space image detail without lengthening the globally attended token sequence, improving quality–compute trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Robot manipulation in everyday environments inherently involves substantial tool usage. Seemingly simple household tasks, such as cooking pan-fried tofu, require forceful cutting, delicate brushing, and precise placement using different tools under contact-rich interaction. Thus, the ability to autonomously swap and use task-appropriate tools is important for tool-centric manipulation. We introduce SwapBot, a modular, tool-centric end effector system featuring low-cost adapters that quickly convert common household tools into robot end effectors. Rather than pursuing a single universal gripper, SwapBot adopts a unified design principle that combines a fixed robot-side coupling interface with low-cost, tool-side adapters, enabling compatibility with diverse tools, including articulated ones, and multiple robot platforms. Each adapter integrates compact tactile sensors, supports fast autonomous swapping, and interfaces with an intuitive teleoperation system for efficient demonstration collection. User studies show that, during teleoperation, SwapBot reduces task completion time and operator workload. Using collected demonstrations on the robot, we train imitation learning policies to successfully perform tool-centric tasks like cooking tofu, stirring salad, flipping meat. Our ablation study shows that using tactile-augmented demonstrations improves policy performance across contact-rich skills, increasing success rates by 15 to 25 percentage points over RGB-only policies. These results highlight modular, tactile-equipped tools as a practical and extensible pathway toward robust and capable robot manipulation. Project website https://personalrobotics.github.io/SwapBot.

papers.abstract: Extreme weather is forecast days ahead, yet its consequences for agriculture remain hard to predict: a forecast says where a storm will strike, not which crops will suffer or how much is at risk, and the records that could tell span many sources. We present WxCrop, the first agent that judges agricultural hazards from physically interpretable weather indices examined by causal analysis, and the first that combines weather and agricultural information to predict crop loss reliably for past and forecast dates. We demonstrate it in Florida on hurricanes, freezes and dry heat, with a loss model calibrated on insurance records for each, and the same procedure extends to other hazards and areas. Three checks show reliability: the hurricane index detects recorded cyclone days with an AUC of 0.98, recorded losses in held-out years are reproduced to within 2%, and independent production records confirm the county rankings (rank correlation 0.63). Users ask the agent for each crop group's loss as a fraction of expected season value, every number sourced, so that governments, growers and scientists respond to agricultural disasters quickly.
authors: Minghan Yu, Mengyu Dai, Yixin Wen, Haizhao Yang
bullets: Addresses the gap between forecasting weather hazards and predicting crop-specific agricultural losses.

papers.abstract: Recent progress in visual scene generation has extended beyond static 3D scenes toward the more challenging problem of generating dynamic 4D scenes from minimal input. However, sound, despite being intrinsically coupled with dynamic objects and events, remains largely unmodeled in prior work. We introduce Video-to-4DAVScene, a new task that turns a video into an explorable, time-varying 4D audio-visual scene, and present the SonoWorld4D framework for this task. Given a monocular video, our method generates a 360 static background, reconstructs explicit motion trajectories of dynamic, sound-emitting foreground objects, and synthesizes a physically-grounded sound field consistent across multiple sources through dual-space audio diffusion synchronization. The resulting 4D scene supports real-time novel-view visual and spatial audio rendering. Evaluation on real-world dynamic scenes and a user study demonstrates SonoWorld4D generates 4D audio-visual scenes with perceptually realistic, physically grounded spatial audio consistent with scene geometry and visual content.
authors: Derong Jin, Xiyi Chen, Ming C. Lin, Ruohan Gao
bullets: Introduces Video-to-4DAVScene, a task for generating time-varying audio-visual scenes from a single video.
Reconstructs a 360° static background and explicit motion trajectories for dynamic, sound-emitting objects.
Uses dual-space audio diffusion synchronization to synthesize physically grounded, multi-source sound fields.
Supports real-time novel-view visual and spatial-audio rendering.
Real-world evaluations and a user study indicate perceptually realistic audio consistent with scene geometry and visual content.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SONOWORLD4D. Given a monocular video, we extract depth maps, camera poses, foreground masks, and VLM-derived audio prompts. For visual scene generation (Sec. 4.2), the framework reconstructs per-object dynamic Gaussians, lifts an outpainted 360◦ panorama into background Gaussians, and aligns them into a common world frame via scale correction and local displacement correction. For dynamic sound field generation (Sec. 4.3), static sources are synthesized via text-to-audio and anchored to the background. Dynamic sources are generated via dual-space diffusion synchronization: at each sampling step, forward rendering (Ri) maps object-space predictions to camera space, while source separation and inverse rendering (Qi) map camera-space mixtures back to individual object spaces. The resulting scene enables real-time novel-pose visual and spatial audio rendering (Sec. 4.4).

Figure 4: STFT visualization of spatial audio rendered at a novel-listener position. The top two rows show input video frames and our novel-view renderings on a shared timeline. Highlighted intervals (a) and (b) indicate when the airplane is closest to the input camera and the novel listener, respectively. Correct spatialization should concentrate energy near (b) with a downward frequency shift due to the Doppler effect. Sonic4D retains strong energy near (a). Ours (V2A) responds near both (a) and (b). Ours (T2A) responds near (b) but lacks clear spectral structure. Our full method produces a dominant response with a visible Doppler shift around (b), correctly adapting both amplitude and frequency to the novel-listener position.

Figure 3: Time-azimuth RMS visualization of ambisonics. Top: mid-frame panoramas of each video rendered by our method at microphone poses in SONOSCENE4D with faces blurred to protect privacy. Remaining rows compare the reference FOA recordings with baselines and ours. Each map shows the peak-normalized directional RMS response over time and azimuth after spherical-areaweighted aggregation over elevation. Our method more closely follows the reference azimuthal trajectories and temporal structure, while the baselines exhibit directional mismatches or reduced spatiotemporal variation.

Figure 6: Motion-type-specific instantiations for dynamic foreground generation. Each branch combines object motion estimation with canonical Gaussian generation and a local deformation model: identity for rigid objects, linear blend skinning (Magnenat-Thalmann et al., 1989) for humans, and learned per-Gaussian center offsets (Litman et al., 2026) for non-rigid objects.

papers.abstract: World models can achieve strong control performance without faithfully capturing the dynamics of their environment, limiting their potential for mechanistic interpretability and scientific discovery. Here, we introduce world2vec to learn mechanistic world models without reward information directly from observations and actions. World2vec learns latent dynamics that faithfully reproduce the true system over long prediction horizons, with at least one order of magnitude fewer parameters than DreamerV3, TD-MPC2 and LeWM. This enables state of the art performance in controlling continuous environments from pixels and accurate system identification across a benchmark of 71 attractors, demonstrating how world models are amenable to scientific discovery.
authors: Tobias Schmidt, Rodrigo Gonzalez Laiz, Kriszti\'an Szuppinger, Steffen Schneider
bullets: Targets world models that control effectively but may not faithfully represent environment dynamics.

Uses at least an order of magnitude fewer parameters than DreamerV3, TD-MPC2, and LeWM.

papers.abstract: An observer sees only part of the surrounding world, yet must keep track of what lies beyond the current view. Spatial perception therefore involves more than recognizing individual images: it calls for a persistent spatial state that is updated under self-motion and used to guide action. Do visual foundation models provide representations that support such a state? We study this question through four levels of spatial capability---spatial structure, object persistence, predictive spatial update, and actionability---using frozen-feature probes on ten representations under streaming egocentric observations of static indoor environments. The resulting capability profiles vary across tasks, network layers, and prefix lengths: strong readout of the visible scene does not ensure accurate object persistence or future-feature retrieval. Matched controls separate readout accuracy from reliance on visual history and motion. Native future prediction retains recoverable spatial structure, but a spatial reader trained on real features does not transfer to predicted features unchanged. Finally, goal-dependent candidate selection does not establish reliable continuous action utility: predicted actions respond to goal changes, yet supplying the correct goal does not reliably improve progress. Across the four levels, object persistence and actionability build on camera-pose readout, whereas feature prediction builds on visible-scene readout. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial representations not only by what can be decoded from them, but by whether that information is maintained beyond observation, updated predictively, and used for goal-directed action.
authors: Baiqiao Yin, Zhongang Cai, Ruisi Wang, Qiwei Liang, Lei Yang, Ziwei Liu

papers.abstract: As robots and intelligent systems increasingly interact with humans, they must anticipate long sequences of future actions from only brief observations. While purely neural models typically require extensive observations to predict future actions and remain difficult to interpret and adjust, symbolic priors offer a structured alternative. To this end, we introduce SymAnt, a novel neuro-symbolic approach that unifies the expressiveness of neural networks with the structured reasoning of scene and knowledge graphs. Given a short video, SymAnt performs a joint-search over both graphs to construct a symbolic context, enabling unified reasoning over spatial relationships, object attributes, affordances, and associated actions. This symbolic context serves as a prior for an iterative refinement process that progressively generates and improves the sequence of future actions. By grounding predictions in symbolic context, SymAnt anticipates long-horizon actions from short observation windows in a parameter-efficient manner, while enabling users to directly edit the underlying knowledge to adjust predictions without further training. Through our experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of SymAnt, particularly when only short observation contexts are available, across five diverse datasets: Breakfast, 50 Salads, EPIC-KITCHENS, EGTEA Gaze+, and Assembly101.
authors: Fnu Aryan, Yaqi Xie, Joseph Campbell, Woojun Kim, Kwonjoon Lee, Hossein Nourkhiz Mahjoub, Ehsan Moradi-Pari, Katia Sycara, Simon Stepputtis

papers.abstract: Safety alignment has enabled large language models to reliably refuse harmful requests directly, yet the same request distributed across a multi-turn conversation still succeeds far too often. This brittleness has a mechanistic root: Alignment is shallow, with safety behavior concentrated in a model's first few output tokens, and existing defenses inherit the weakness, supervising the surface form of the response without ever giving the model an explicit safety decision to learn. We take the opposite view of shallowness: if a short span determines the trajectory of an entire response, that span is the highest-leverage place to intervene, and the defender can occupy it first. We propose Assess $\to$ Decide $\to$ Respond, a framework in which the defender assesses the user's intent, commits to an explicit, parseable safety decision, and only then generates a reply conditioned on it, with the commitment trained by reinforcement learning at the payload turn. Because the decision is a token span, the reward can be a rule: a self-verified reward checks the committed label against the conversation's known nature, requiring no judge and no annotation, while the same format also supports an LLM-as-judge reward over a graded decision space with safe redirection. Across two model families and fourteen benchmarks spanning safety, utility, and helpfulness, our defenders achieve the strongest multi-turn safety in a controlled comparison, maintaining their lead in safety while preserving utility at a modest cost to helpfulness. A per-token KL analysis and interventional probes confirm why this works: training concentrates its effect on the brief deliberation that sets a response's trajectory, and the decision committed there is a causal control point. The very shallowness attackers exploit becomes the mechanism of defense.
authors: Qiyao Ma, Xiaodong Liu, Weiwei Yang, Mingqian Feng, Chengquan Guo, Jialin Song, Carolyn Buractaon, Zhe Zhao, Junshan Zhang, Sandeep Atluri, Christopher White, Jianfeng Gao
bullets: Targets the brittleness of direct refusals when harmful requests are distributed across multiple conversation turns.

Across two model families and 14 benchmarks, achieves the strongest controlled multi-turn safety while preserving utility, with a modest helpfulness cost.
Per-token KL analysis and intervention probes indicate that the brief deliberation acts as a causal control point for response trajectories.

papers.abstract: Interactive world models generate visual content conditioned on user actions, yet maintaining spatial consistency over long-horizon exploration in real time remains challenging. Existing approaches rely on either temporal context or explicit 3D memory, both of which scale poorly because memory grows with the length of the generated stream. Moreover, explicit 3D memories condition latent video generators by re-encoding RGB renderings, which precludes real-time generation. In this paper, we introduce a Latent 3D Gaussian Memory (L3G) that combines the efficiency of feed-forward reconstruction with a compact, rapidly renderable scene representation. Building on this memory, we propose L3G-World, in which a memory updater and a video diffusion transformer (DiT) alternate autoregressively to generate spatially consistent worlds. The memory updater spawns Gaussians in newly observed regions and refines existing ones, so that the memory grows with scene extent rather than stream length. Each Gaussian further stores a VAE latent feature, allowing the memory to be rendered directly into the DiT's latent space without VAE re-encoding. Experiments show that L3G-World achieves state-of-the-art generation quality and long-horizon spatial consistency, with up to $38.6\times$ fewer 3D primitives, $3.2\times$ faster memory updates, and $359\times$ faster memory rendering relative to the most efficient prior 3D-memory baseline for each metric, enabling real-time world generation at 9 FPS.
authors: Jinhyeok Choi, JoungBin Lee, Jongmin Lee, Minkyeong Jeon, Jiyoung Kim, Kaeun Han, Yoonjin Yoon, Seungryong Kim
bullets: Addresses the poor scalability and slow rendering of temporal-context and explicit-3D-memory world models during long-horizon exploration.
Alternates a memory updater with a video diffusion transformer to autoregressively generate observations and maintain scene consistency.
Stores VAE latent features in Gaussians, avoiding RGB rendering and VAE re-encoding during conditioning.
Grows memory with newly explored scene extent rather than generated stream length, while refining previously observed regions.
Reports state-of-the-art quality and long-horizon consistency, reaching 9 FPS with substantially fewer primitives and faster memory updates and rendering than prior 3D-memory baselines.

papers.abstract: We present TextSeal2, a distortion-free watermark for large language models that keeps its signal under speculative decoding: tokens that replace rejected drafts remain watermarked with the same keys, and the acceptance rate is unchanged. It also preserves output diversity and adds no measurable inference latency. Its predecessor, TextSeal, restores diversity in the Gumbel-max scheme by routing each token to one of two keys via a coin flip. This is suboptimal because the detector averages the scores from both keys without knowing which key was used. TextSeal2 instead merges two or more keys into a single virtual key and couples it to fresh noise through AutoMark's Gaussian copula. Any number of keys, including publicly shared keys, can be merged this way without diluting detection. Under speculative decoding, TextSeal2 verifies keyed drafts with one more exponential race, run on the leftovers of the draft races. By memorylessness, this race reproduces block verification, so the output follows the target model exactly. We evaluate TextSeal2 on three LLMs. At equal output token diversity, TextSeal2 detects 8 to 22 percentage points more 100-token answers than TextSeal at a false-positive rate of $10^{-3}$, and is comparable to textGrain while requiring no post-logits optimization. Under speculative decoding, it detects 18 and 22 percentage points more 200-token answers than TextSeal and textGrain, respectively, at the same acceptance rate.
authors: Tom Sander, Pierre Fernandez, Itai Gat, Haiming Bao, Jiaxin Shi, Jason Park, Valeriu Lacatusu, Sylvestre-Alvise Rebuffi, Hongyan Chang, Hady Elsahar, Tom\'{a}\v{s} Sou\v{c}ek, Tuan Tran, Surya Parimi, Alexandre Mourachko

Uses an additional exponential race over draft-race leftovers to reproduce block verification under speculative decoding.
Across three LLMs, improves detection over TextSeal by 8–22 percentage points for 100-token outputs and 18–22 points for 200-token outputs at the stated false-positive rate and acceptance rate.

papers.abstract: Proactive assistants offer short, memory-grounded hints during a conversation, deciding when to assist and what to suggest. Current systems split this between a gate and a larger generator; we evaluate both together on 28,058 decision points. Stage-wise generation scores are oracle-gate ceilings: behind a real gate, end-to-end exact match is 0.2619 against a ceiling of 0.2971, and end-to-end precision is 0.2387, leaving substantial headroom. A gate pays off through precision and compute, whose saving falls from 4.39x with an 8B generator to 1.38x with a 1B one. The memory profile drives hint quality: removing it costs 24.7 exact-match points (rescaled BERTScore 0.57 to 0.35), while retrieval and a larger generator add nothing on exact match. One 1B decoder can do both, gating from an intermediate layer and generating in the same pass. At its final checkpoint it matches or exceeds the two-model pipelines on automatic end-to-end measures with 1.31-1.76x less wall-clock time than the matched 1B pipeline; across three seeds, its deeper exit ties the separate gate. A human evaluation (1,144 ratings over 32 dialogues) supports the memory effect and rates the single model level with the matched 1B pipeline and below the 8B one. Graded metrics and LlamaPIE's native judge track human ratings more closely than exact match, which we report as a strict lower bound.
authors: A. J. A. Jubayer Talukder, Mohammad Ariful Haque
bullets: The task combines assistance gating with short hint generation over 28,058 decision points.

The single model achieves 1.31–1.76× lower wall-clock time than the matched 1B pipeline and matches or exceeds it on automatic end-to-end measures.
Human ratings support the memory effect; graded metrics and LlamaPIE align more closely with human judgments than exact match.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a compact decoder for joint gating and memory-grounded hint generation, addressing memory mechanisms and inference-time decision making in LLMs.
papers.title: When to Assist and What to Suggest: Joint Gating and Memory-Grounded Hint Generation in One Compact Decoder

papers.abstract: A playable, programmable game world must maintain persistent state, enforce executable rules, and support extensible gameplay mechanics. Existing video world models can generate plausible combat, yet struggle to keep hit reactions and health updates consistent with game rules. We introduce Fight World Model (FWM), which separates rule-governed combat execution from video rendering. An executable engine maintains state and resolves interactions. A deterministic compiler encodes these outcomes and attempted actions in a spatially and temporally aligned interaction proxy. The proxy aligns action and skill windows, brief hit reactions, and persistent health by fighter identity and timing. These cues can be controlled separately to render interactions under modified rules. Identity-bound references preserve character appearance across side switches. We train FWM on FightWorld Corpus, spanning 52 skill effects, 187 character-appearance variants, and 15 arenas. Without retraining the renderer, FWM supports damage scaling, limited-hit immunity, lifesteal, and multi-stage skill mechanisms beyond the native game. It also allows character and arena customization. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of FWM, which outperforms existing game world models in action fidelity, hit reactions, health-state consistency, and character appearance preservation. Our project is available at https://fight-world-model.github.io.
authors: Jiahua Li, Zixu John, Tom Zhong, Fuping Wu, Tianhao Xu, Ruicheng Zhang, Jun Zhou, Zunnan Xu
bullets: Addresses inconsistent hit reactions and health updates in existing video world models.
Uses an executable engine for persistent state and interaction resolution, then encodes outcomes into aligned interaction proxies.
The proxy controls action and skill timing, hit reactions, persistent health, and identity-bound character references.
Supports modified combat rules—including damage scaling, limited-hit immunity, lifesteal, and multi-stage skills—without retraining the renderer.
Experiments report stronger action fidelity, hit-reaction quality, health consistency, and appearance preservation than existing game world models.

papers.abstract: The hair of stylized characters in games and avatars is built from hair cards: artist-placed ribbons whose geometry is the visible hair, animated by spring bones. Existing image-based methods produce realistic hair or a single fused mesh, while CHARM, the only generator of stylized hair cards, decodes a hairstyle autoregressively as a long sequence of control points. Observing that a card hairstyle is an unordered set of artist-defined primitives, we propose HairDeck, which generates it as one: each card is a single token, and a set diffusion transformer denoises all cards together. From a single image, HairDeck generates the cards and the spring-bone chains that drive them, yielding an animatable asset that exports to ready-to-use downstream formats. On CHARM's own test set, it lowers Chamfer distance by 44% and card-orientation error by more than half while running 33 times faster, and from single images it outperforms CHARM, image-to-3D pipelines and strand-based methods. Project page: https://hyzcluster.github.io/HairDeck
authors: Yuze He, Yixiang Wei, Wang Zhao, Chuhao Chen, Yanning Zhou, Yong-Jin Liu
bullets: Targets game- and avatar-ready stylized hair represented as artist-placed hair-card primitives.
Models each card as a token and jointly denoises the unordered card set with a diffusion transformer.
Also generates spring-bone chains and exports assets in downstream-ready formats.
On CHARM’s test set, reduces Chamfer distance by 44%, more than halves orientation error, and runs 33× faster.
Outperforms CHARM, image-to-3D pipelines, and strand-based methods from single images.

papers.abstract: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) models expand parameter capacity by activating a small subset of experts per token. Expert selection directly affects model capabilities under a fixed active-expert budget. Dense evaluation of all experts reveals weak agreement between single-router rankings and expert-utility evaluation rankings, especially in middle and deep layers. Richer signals for selection and computation incur additional cost: selection based on internal expert activations requires preliminary computation, while processing multiple full representations separately through the same expert repeats its computation. We propose Multi-View MoE to improve expert selection with multiple routers and reuse their preferences to modulate expert computation under a fixed expert budget. Its Multi-Router submodule aggregates sigmoid scores from independently initialized routers. These routers develop highly differentiated expert preferences during training, allowing experts strongly favored by one router or jointly supported by several routers to be selected. Multi-View further uses each selected expert's relative scores across routers to mix learned latent views into its input, reusing routing preferences for both selection and computation. Each selected expert executes one forward pass, preserving the active-expert count, expert FLOPs, and all-to-all communication volume. On a 24-layer 10B-A1B model trained on 708B tokens, full Multi-View MoE improves the nine-task downstream mean by 1.18 percentage points over the baseline. Multi-Router alone yields a 0.6-percentage-point gain and improves the rank correlation between router scores and evaluated expert utility, with relative increases of 8.1% globally and approximately 58% in the layer with the lowest single-router alignment. Controlled mixing interventions show the model uses input differences that depend on both the expert and the token.
authors: Zelin Zhao, Tianchi Ma, Junyuan Shang, Shuohuan Wang, Dianhai Yu

On a 24-layer 10B-A1B model trained on 708B tokens, full Multi-View MoE improves nine-task mean performance by 1.18 percentage points over baseline.
Multi-Router alone improves performance by 0.6 points and strengthens router–utility rank correlation; controlled interventions indicate token- and expert-dependent input modulation.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) is limited by sparse outcome-level feedback on hard reasoning tasks: when all rollouts in a group fail, rewards provide no learning signal. Stronger teachers can provide additional guidance, but this raises a central question: how can such signals be incorporated into RLVR to support successful rollouts while remaining learnable for the student? We distinguish two complementary mechanisms: trajectory-level intervention, which improves access to reward-bearing trajectories, and token-level supervision, which provides dense targets to guide student learning. Our controlled experiments show that either mechanism alone can remain insufficient, motivating their combination. We therefore introduce PIVOT, which inserts teacher-generated corrections into student rollouts and applies token-level KL supervision to these segments alongside the RLVR objective. Beyond their combination, we systematically analyze where to intervene and how to supervise, yielding a recipe for effective guidance. Across hard logic games and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, PIVOT consistently outperforms existing methods, nearly doubling mean avg@8 on logic games from 19.5% for the best-performing baseline to 35.6%.
authors: Zhihao Yang, Boyuan Zheng, Puhui Tan, Yukun Chen, Kuan Zhang, Longze Chen, Jiaming Li, Renke Shan, Lu Wang, Xianpei Han
bullets: RLVR can fail when every rollout receives zero outcome-level reward.
Trajectory interventions help expose students to successful paths, while token-level supervision provides dense learning targets.
PIVOT inserts teacher corrections into student trajectories and applies token-level KL supervision to the corrected segments alongside RLVR.
Experiments on hard logic games and mathematical reasoning show consistent improvements over existing methods.
On logic games, mean avg@8 nearly doubles from 19.5% for the best baseline to 35.6%.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of PIVOT. For each query, the policy model samples a group of rollouts, including teacher-assisted trajectories. In a teacher-assisted rollout, the student first generates a prefix, the teacher provides a correction segment, and the student then continues generation. The completed trajectory is optimized by the verifier-based GRPO objective, while the teacher-generated segment provides dense token-level supervision through a teacher-student KL loss.

Figure 8. Prefix versus middle intervention (continued). The student-conditioned middle state is completed by both models. All excerpts and counts refer to the same puzzle and the controlled continuations described on the preceding page.

Figure 5. Prefix vs. middle intervention. Guidance is more effective when the teacher can build on the student’s partial solution and correct errors along the way.

Right: the teacher corrects the error itself and continues from there, so its targets are unimodal whether it backtracks (“Wait”) or proceeds (“So”), and the trajectory reaches the reward.

papers.abstract: On-policy Self-distillation (OPSD) has proven effective for post-training large language models by constructing a teacher conditioned on privileged references. However, existing approaches keep the teacher fixed either throughout training by consistently exposing it to the full reference, or within each response by adaptively varying partial reference exposure only across responses. In this paper, we argue that neither of them is sufficient. Instead, every token needs its own teacher, as the teacher preference can vary token by token within the same response. Through a teacher-intervention pilot study, we validate that the teacher preference differs across tokens, and reveal that a preferred teacher can be identified for each token through majority voting and KL-based selection. Motivated by these findings, we propose Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-Distillation (MTA-OPSD), the first token-level adaptive OPSD method. Our method constructs a multi-teacher pool consisting of candidate teachers, and enables every token to adaptively select its preferred teacher during training. Experiments with Qwen3 models on mathematical reasoning tasks show that MTA-OPSD consistently outperforms existing OPSD approaches with an average gain of up to $+5.9$ over the base model, highlighting the importance of adapting teacher supervision at the token level. The code is available at https://github.com/xingzhejun/MTA-OPSD.
authors: Yifu Luo, Chuang Ma, Zeyu Chen, Enkelejda Kasneci, Qi Chen, Gjergji Kasneci
bullets: Existing OPSD methods use fixed or response-level adaptive teachers, overlooking token-level preference differences.
A teacher-intervention study finds that preferred teachers vary across tokens and can be identified via majority voting or KL-based selection.
MTA-OPSD builds a pool of candidate teachers and selects a preferred teacher independently for each token during training.
Experiments on Qwen3 models for mathematical reasoning report gains of up to +5.9 over the base model.
The method is evaluated within the studied Qwen3 mathematical-reasoning setting; broader scope is not established by the abstract.

papers.abstract: Realistic, fast robotics simulations could enable large-scale training of embodied AI models that transfer to the real world. However, despite decades of progress, available simulations cover only a narrow range of real-world tasks and physical phenomena. The core bottleneck is that creating better simulations requires significant expert effort and therefore does not scale. To address this, we introduce Gym-Anything for Robotics, a framework in which coding agents create realistic robotics simulations. Our core insight is that simulation creation is a coding agent task, so improvements in coding agents translate directly into richer and more faithful simulations. We select simulations based on U.S. GDP data to cover economically valuable physical work, define what makes a good simulation and a good task, and develop an adversarial creation-audit loop that checks each simulation and task against these definitions. Using this pipeline, we build RoboWorld, a set of 25 simulations with 25 test and 175 training RL environments of varying difficulty. Even the best frontier models fail on every RoboWorld test task, achieving an average reward of only 0.06. Building on RoboWorld, we introduce several new ways for frontier models to improve, including in-context learning across repeated attempts, a privileged teacher that reads the simulator state and teaches a student in context, self-assisted learning from the model's own privileged experience, and code policies that generate demonstrations across varied scenes to train vision-language-action models (VLAs) such as $\pi_{0.5}$. Each of these substantially improves performance. We release our pipeline, RL environments, and benchmark to facilitate future research. Code and data are available at https://gym-anything.github.io/robotics
authors: Pranjal Aggarwal, Sean Welleck
bullets: Existing robotics simulators cover limited tasks and phenomena because expert-driven creation is difficult to scale.
The framework selects economically relevant tasks, defines simulation-quality criteria, and uses a creation–audit loop to generate and verify environments.
It produces RoboWorld: 25 simulations containing 25 test and 175 training reinforcement-learning environments with varied difficulty.
Frontier models initially fail on all RoboWorld test tasks, but in-context attempts, privileged teaching, self-assisted learning, and code-generated demonstrations substantially improve performance.
The pipeline, environments, and benchmark are released for future research; its scope is the included simulated tasks and physical phenomena.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Gym-Anything for Robotics. Phase 3: A task creation agent proposes tasks of targeted difficulty, which six audit agents check, and each task runs with many robots and variations. Phase 4: Models learn from privileged simulation state through incontext learning, coaching, and code policies that train VLAs.

papers.abstract: Foundation models are typically trained in stages: pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL), with changes in both data and learning algorithms. We show that this algorithmic separation is not fundamental. By deriving suitable RL objectives as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated target distributions, we place all of these stages under a single likelihood-based training algorithm, unified training. This perspective turns the foundation-model training lifecycle into a problem of choosing which data to train on, in what proportions, and when, with conventional staged training as a special case. We instantiate this framework in a unified training system that mixes static data and RL generations within a single trainer. Across controlled and real-world experiments, unified training improves the accuracy-compute tradeoff and task coverage while preserving broader capabilities, and provides a stronger starting point for continual learning. This work lays the groundwork for a unified science of foundation-model training, connecting mathematical principles, training infrastructure, and the development of model capabilities.
authors: Yuda Song, Alvin Zhang, Fahim Tajwar, Daman Arora, Jeff Schneider, Daniel Khashabi, Ruslan Salakhutdinov, J. Andrew Bagnell, Aarti Singh, Andrea Zanette
bullets: Reframes staged training as a data-selection and data-mixing problem rather than requiring distinct algorithms.
Derives RL objectives as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated target distributions.
Implements a trainer combining static datasets with reinforcement-learning generations.
Reports improved accuracy–compute tradeoffs and task coverage while preserving broader capabilities.
Provides a stronger starting point for continual learning, though the abstract does not specify experimental scope or limitations.

papers.abstract: In robotics, shape control (or shape servoing) refers to the automatic manipulation of a deformable object to achieve a desired shape. It involves a feedback loop that exploits the relation between robot motion and changes in the measured shape. This relation, known as the interaction Jacobian or, in this context, the deformation Jacobian, depends on the object's mechanical properties, geometry, and boundary conditions (e.g., where the object is grasped). Because these factors are often difficult to model accurately, the deformation Jacobian can be estimated locally from observed shape changes produced by commanded robot motions, without requiring a fine-tuned mechanical model. This article is the first of a two-part tutorial on data-driven Jacobian-based shape control of deformable objects. It introduces the central elements of the approach: the formulation of the shape-control problem, shape representation, estimation and online update of the deformation Jacobian, and a standard control law from the literature. It then assembles these elements into a complete shape-servoing loop, derives a local stability condition for this loop, and illustrates why some target shapes cannot be reached. Part II covers more advanced topics. Throughout both parts, a simulated planar example in which two robot arms manipulate an elastic rod observed by a camera illustrates the concepts.

Covers foundational concepts; more advanced topics are deferred to Part II.

papers.abstract: Predicting how many tokens a large language model (LLM) will decode, using only prefill-phase hidden states, is a key primitive for inference scheduling. We show that current benchmarks conflate predictor quality with task hardness: when the target model, dataset, or sampling configuration changes, reported accuracy collapses even though the predictor is unchanged. We trace this instability to an overlooked error source---the inherent stochasticity of autoregressive decoding---and derive bounds that every prefill-side method must obey. Our analysis treats decoding as a stopped stochastic process. The per-step stopping probability of a response is not constant but ramps up over hundreds of steps, so the decode length inherits a central limit theorem from the many local decisions that determine where a response ends; this yields per-prompt normality with an explicit error term, together with an affine variance law $\sigma=\alpha\mu+b$ whose slope is the coefficient of variation of the number of response segments. Empirically, the normal law reproduces the per-prompt MAE and the central mass of the decode-length distribution to within a few percent, and the residual departures from normality (mild right skew, slight excess kurtosis) are the ones predicted by the sampling-noise correction. Under fixed model, data, and sampling conditions, a broad design space of predictors (MLP, EGTP, FiLM, soft-label, and Mixture-of-Experts variants) converges to similar performance close to the bound, confirming that \emph{system error dominates model error}. We argue for a benchmarking protocol that fixes the model, data, and sampling parameters and that reports relative-error metrics alongside absolute ones. Code and analysis tools are available at https://github.com/ShwStone/DecodingPredict.
authors: Haowen Shi, Xuzhe Yan, Fahao Chen, Peng Li
bullets: Existing benchmarks mix predictor quality with task difficulty: changing the model, dataset, or sampling setup can sharply change accuracy.

Experiments find the predicted distribution matches empirical MAE and central mass within a few percent, with expected mild skew and kurtosis.
Under fixed conditions, diverse predictors perform similarly near the bound, indicating system error dominates model error; relative-error metrics are recommended alongside absolute ones.

papers.abstract: Mobile robots must open doors and drawers, yet their scene maps record what each object is and whether it has moved, not how it will respond to a pull. This paper proposes PhysVLMM, a method that maintains a physical belief for every articulated part of a Vision-Language-Motion Map and answers a planner's queries about it, with two algorithms: a map update and a query. Watching a part move provably cannot identify its dynamics, and a measured pull identifies only the pulled part, up to one direction. PhysVLMM therefore (i) keeps that direction as a posterior instead of a point estimate, (ii) passes the evidence of each pull in closed form to the untouched look-alike parts of the map, and (iii) answers whether an action will succeed at a stated risk, or abstains. On real doors and drawers in 18 homes, it identifies the joint type in 86% of held-out pulls (48% for a learned single-view method) and predicts the response to a pull with 41% lower error than differentiable simulation (CRPS 0.323 vs. 0.544), four orders of magnitude faster (13 ms vs. 230 s per case). The posterior lowers the final-position error from 0.460 to 0.270, sharing lowers the force error of untouched parts from 56% to 42%, and at every stated risk from 0.02 to 0.30 the false-safe answers stay within it. Pooling all measured parts of a home does as well as the look-alike groups, and simpler variants predict where a pulled part stops at least as well.

papers.abstract: We present DAWN (Diffusion-based Alignment and unfastening Workflow Network), a hierarchical robotic framework designed to perform real-world, unfastening tasks through multi-modal sensory integration. Autonomous robotic unfastening is crucial for improving recycling processes, enhancing safety, and reducing operational costs; yet, it remains predominantly manual due to inherent challenges in precise screwdriver engagement with fasteners, detailed force execution, and robustness to environmental variability. To address the complexity of learning long-horizon, contact-rich manipulation tasks, we subdivide the unfastening task procedure into two sequential stages: (1) alignment & insertion, and (2) unfastening. DAWN consists of three key components: AlignNet, a diffusion-based policy ensuring precise screwdriver tip engagement; LatchNet, a multi-modal classifier reliably detecting successful stage transitions; and UnfastNet, which achieves stable, force-controlled screw removal. Experimental validation on a Franka Emika robot demonstrates that DAWN achieves alignment & insertion success rates comparable to trained human operators, robustly transitions between stages, and attains an impressive success rate in unfastening across various unseen scenarios. Ablation studies further elucidate critical input modalities and effective training strategies, highlighting DAWN's scalability, robustness, and data efficiency.
authors: Hemant Kumar, Piyush Goenka, Nikhil Chopra
bullets: Targets autonomous unfastening to reduce manual effort and improve recycling safety and efficiency.

Ablations identify important sensory modalities and training strategies, supporting the framework’s robustness and data efficiency.

papers.abstract: Images reveal appearances, but counting often asks about physical objects. A single entity may be visible directly, in several reflections, or through glass, so detecting every visible occurrence does not determine how many entities are present. Existing visual counting benchmarks rarely separate these two operations. We introduce PhysCount, a benchmark for evaluating whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can distinguish what appears in an image from what physically exists in the scene. PhysCount contains 546 real-world images and 4,595 human-written questions organized into 651 target-specific groups. For each group, annotators locate the relevant appearances, label how each is observed, and identify appearances of the same entity. Four complementary question families test the enumeration of appearances, the enumeration of physical entities, image-formation-specific counting, and appearance--entity correspondence. We measure both accuracy on each family and the proportion of groups answered entirely correctly. Across 40 MLLMs, counting visible appearances is substantially easier than recovering the identities that connect them. Even the strongest model answers every question correctly in only 13.36\% of groups. Performance declines when one entity produces many appearances or when its appearances cross observation modes. Higher image resolution improves access to visual evidence but brings limited gains in complete-group accuracy, whereas answering related questions jointly produces a marked improvement. These results expose a gap between recognizing what is visible and correctly recovering the physical entities behind those observations.
authors: Lidong Lu, Jiaxin Lv, Liangrui Dong, Xinyi Mao, Lidong Zou, Zhenquan Li, Tong Lu, Guo Chen
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 546 real-world images and 4,595 questions across 651 target-specific groups.
Tests appearance counting, physical-entity counting, image-formation-specific counting, and appearance–entity correspondence.

Performance worsens when one entity creates multiple appearances or appearances span different observation modes.
Higher resolution offers limited gains in complete-group accuracy, while jointly answering related questions helps substantially.

papers.abstract: Cross-modal scene and instance retrieval aims to retrieve a corresponding 3D environment or object given query 2D images, serving as a foundational mechanism for spatial reasoning in robotics and AR/VR. Existing methods achieve this by learning alignment only at the level of whole scenes or objects, which provides no supervision for the fine-grained local structure within them. In this work, we show that supervision on a set of sparse 2D-3D correspondences, without scene- or instance-level contrastive objectives, is sufficient to train a single model for both scene- and instance-level retrieval. Specifically, we propose $\textbf{CrossWeave}$, a novel framework for cross-modal retrieval that learns sparse patch-point alignment, which alone outperforms existing methods. An optimal transport-based aggregator over the aligned features gives further gains by clustering structurally redundant regions, freeing descriptor capacity for semantically distinct local features. CrossWeave achieves state-of-the-art performance on both scene- and instance-level retrieval on ScanNet and 3RScan with a $\textit{single model}$, whereas existing methods require separate models for each task. Our results suggest that whole-scene encoding is unnecessary for cross-modal retrieval and that sparse local correspondence supervision is a more effective and flexible alternative.
authors: Aadith Warrier, Gnana Prakash Punnavajhala, Siddharth Tourani, Muhammad Haris Khan, Avinash Sharma, Madhava Krishna
bullets: Targets cross-modal retrieval of 3D scenes or objects from 2D image queries for robotics and AR/VR.
Learns fine-grained sparse patch–point alignment without scene- or instance-level contrastive objectives.
Aggregates aligned features with optimal transport to cluster redundant regions and preserve capacity for distinct local features.
Reports state-of-the-art scene- and instance-level retrieval on ScanNet and 3RScan using a single model.
Suggests sparse local correspondence supervision can replace whole-scene encoding, though the abstract does not specify broader limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of CrossWeave. CrossWeave learns cross-modal retrieval representations from sparse image patch-3D point correspondences rather than scene- or instance-level labels. Scene Sampling: Given calibrated RGB-D observations and a reconstructed 3D map, visible patchpoint pairs are obtained by projecting 3D points into the image plane, filtering occluded points using rendered depth, quantizing valid pixels into DINOv2 patch tokens, and selecting a compact semantically diverse subset using feature-space farthest point sampling. Feature Extraction: Frozen encoders extract local patch and point features, which are projected by learnable projection matrices W patch and W point into a shared embedding space. Feature Aggregation: A shared SALAD aggregator then maps variable-sized sets of local features into fixed-dimensional descriptors. Training combines a local patch-point Lp2p contrastive loss with an aggregated image-point-cloud contrastive loss Li2pc, preserving fine-grained alignment while organizing local evidence into retrieval-ready descriptors. At inference, the same encoders and projection heads serve both tasks: SALAD descriptors are used for scene retrieval and mean-pooled local features for instance retrieval.

Figure 2: Qualitative comparison of cross-modal scene retrieval on ScanNet. Given a set of query RGB images, each model retrieves the most similar 3D scenes from the database. The groundtruth scene is shown on the left, and retrieved scenes are ordered by similarity from left to right. CrossOver and CrossOver (Updated) fail to retrieve the correct scene within the top five results, while CrossWeave retrieves it at rank 1. The remaining retrieved scenes are also semantically consistent, indicating that CrossWeave learns descriptors that capture both local cross-modal correspondences and global scene context.

Figure 7: Comparisons of Top-5 retrievals on a ScanNet room scene. Retrievals are ordered from most to least similar moving left to right, with correct matches highlighted in green. CrossWeave successfully retrieves the correct scene at rank 1, while CrossOver (Updated) retrieves it at rank 2, and the base model of CrossOver fails within the top 5.

Figure 9: Qualitative results on a 3RScan dining area scene. CrossWeave successfully retrieves the ground truth point cloud as its top match, while CrossOver (Updated) ranks it fourth and the base CrossOver model fails to retrieve it within the top 5.

Figure 10: Retrieval results on a 3RScan kitchen and dining scene. CrossWeave demonstrates superior discriminative ability by retrieving the exact scene at rank 1 from highly localized query images, whereas both baseline models completely fail to place the correct match within their top 5 retrievals.

Figure 3: Qualitative instance retrieval on ScanNet. For each query view with its instance mask (left), CrossWeave ranks the instances of the same scene (middle) by cosine similarity. The Top-3 retrievals are shown with their similarity scores, and the correct match is outlined in green.

Figure 13: Failure case on a 3RScan living room scene. All three models miss the ground-truth scene in the top 5, as the retrieved scenes are visually and structurally similar to the query (a brown sectional sofa with a wooden coffee table). CrossWeave’s top matches still share the furniture arrangement (sofas and central coffee tables), whereas CrossOver (Updated) retrieves structurally different scenes.

Figure 6: Visualizations for the effect of FPS sampling. Images with red dots denote random sampling. Images with blue dots denote FPS sampled points. It can clearly be observed that FPS enables us to avoid over-sampling on the often visually dominant but geometrically uninformative areas in the images such as walls, floors and other flat surfaces, thereby boosting feature diversity within each training batch. Note: We have visualized a large number of pixel-point pairs in these images; in our training framework we only use 32 patch-point pairs. Refer to Section 3.1 for more details.

Figure 8: Additional qualitative results on a ScanNet office scene. CrossWeave retrieves the ground truth point cloud as its top match, whereas both CrossOver (Updated) and CrossOver only identify the correct scene at rank 5.

Figure 11: Additional results on a 3RScan kitchen scene. CrossWeave correctly identifies the target environment at rank 1, outperforming CrossOver, which places the match at rank 4, and CrossOver (Updated), which misses it entirely.

Figure 12: Qualitative instance retrieval on 3RScan. For each query view with its instance mask (left), CrossWeave ranks the instances of the same scene (middle) by cosine similarity. The Top-3 retrievals are shown with their similarity scores, and the correct match is outlined in green.

Figure 14: Instance retrieval failures on ScanNet and 3RScan. In both cases the query is a chair and the Top-1 retrieval (red) is another chair of the same type in the same scene, while the correct instance (green) is ranked second with a similar score.

Figure 4: Scene retrieval performance (Top-1 recall) on ScanNet and 3RScan as a function of training data volume. Performance is stable across data regimes, with even 10% of the full training set sufficient to outperform the previous state of the art.
Figure 5: Scene retrieval performance (Top-1 recall) as a function of the number of query camera views. The main results use 10 views.

papers.abstract: Safety alignment for Large Language Models is heavily focused on English with limited multilingual representation, particularly damaging low-resource language performance. Related open training datasets are often limited in size or do not follow region-localized harmful topics to broaden the scope of alignment beyond cultures. We propose a scalable template-based augmentation pipeline to produce massive multilingual refusal and benign corpora, extracting safe templates from harmful prompts, translating them and then filling in the slots with culturally authentic entities, both harmful and benign. As a result, we release MSafeTemp, a validated corpus spanning 60 languages useful for multilingual safety alignment and evaluation. Using the dataset, we show that English-only evaluation misjudges multilingual safety: for several models, attacks that fail in English succeed once translated, while culturally localized variants expose further failures that translation alone misses. We also confirm that augmenting safety training data through templates allows for higher diversity and quality of alignment, resulting in improved safety performance beyond English. MSafeTemp and the respective pipeline are aimed at facilitating research and development of safer and more responsible models for less-represented cultures.
authors: Max Neuwinger, Hanna Yukhymenko, Imanol Schlag
bullets: Multilingual safety alignment is underdeveloped, especially for low-resource languages and region-specific harmful topics.
The pipeline extracts safe templates from harmful prompts, translates them, and fills slots with culturally authentic harmful and benign entities.
MSafeTemp is a validated corpus covering 60 languages for multilingual safety alignment and evaluation.
Experiments find that translated and culturally localized attacks can bypass models that appear safe in English.
Template-based augmentation increases alignment-data diversity and quality, improving safety performance beyond English.

papers.title: How I Aligned Your Model: Scaling Up Multilingual Safety Training with Templates
