papers.abstract: AI has made remarkable progress in mathematics, solving challenging problems with machine-checkable proofs in Lean, yet typically relying on predefined mathematical definitions and formal specifications. This raises a natural question: can it reason rigorously about an unknown world? We introduce the Algebraic World Model (AWM), a framework that turns interaction with unfamiliar environments into explicit mathematical models supporting formal reasoning. AWM explores the environment and develops executable Python hypotheses, continually testing and revising them against observations. It then structures these hypotheses into typed objects and shared rules, simplifies their structure through category-theory-guided transformations, and formalizes the resulting model in Lean 4 to prove reachability and impossibility. AWM can formally prove that a goal is unreachable, even beyond explored trajectories. On two impossible game levels, it constructs closed, kernel-checked Lean proofs excluding every legal winning sequence in all six runs, while Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, equipped with coding tools, produce none in twelve baseline runs. Four of AWM's six initial bounds are correct, compared with one for Opus 5.5 and none for GPT-6 Astra; given only feedback that a cheaper win exists, AWM revises its rules and constructs new proofs, reaching six of six correct bounds. Moreover, AWM produces interpretable mathematical models whose rules can be inspected and tested step by step. Across all 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, these models enable Lean to replay the winning trajectories of all 183 levels and generalize beyond observed play, predicting unseen transitions and detecting changes in game mechanics. With Claude Opus 5, AWM clears all levels with a score of 99.9, while its certified winning trajectories use only 43% of the human baseline's actions.
authors: Guancheng Pan, Qixin Tan, Yang Yuan, Andrew Chi-Chih Yao
bullets: Addresses the challenge of rigorous reasoning when mathematical definitions and specifications are initially unknown.
Explores environments, proposes and tests executable Python hypotheses, then organizes them into typed objects and shared rules.
Uses category-theory-guided simplification and Lean 4 formalization to certify reachability, impossibility, and generalization beyond observed trajectories.
On two impossible game levels, it produced kernel-checked proofs excluding every legal winning sequence, while baseline models produced none.

Across 25 ARC-AGI-3 games, its models replayed all 183 winning trajectories, predicted unseen transitions, and detected changing mechanics; with Claude Opus 5, it achieved a 99.9 score using 43% of human-baseline actions.

figures.caption: Figure 1: AWM’s three-stage pipeline: interactive exploration builds a provisional executable model, algebraic transformations reveal and simplify its structure, and Lean 4 formalization enables certified proofs of reachability or impossibility.

Figure 4: Sealed sc25 level 4. AWM proves in Lean that the minimum winning cost under its learned model is 19, one unit above the budget, and verifies a route at that cost; GPT-6 Astra claims 22 without a proof.

Figure 3: From shared structure to formal proofs in lp85. (a) Eleven concepts describing four button mechanisms are generalized into a shared permutation rule. Each before/after pair shows a recorded press, with the pressed button circled and changed tiles outlined. (b) A five-click sequence witnesses reachability. (c) Recoloring the only yellow tile makes the goal unreachable, since every press preserves color counts. Both conclusions are formally proved in Lean 4.

Figure 5: An executable concept in lp85. (a) Scope, evidence and abridged code for a click on an arrow pointing against its belt’s order; helper names are simplified. (b) On the first click of the certified level-1 run, the checker returns TRUE and the prediction matches all 20 tiles.

Figure 6: Testing a merge on lp85. (a) A recorded press and three of the five diagnostic constructions. (b) On the same 120 diagnostic transitions, press_permutes preserves all 55 rejections of its eleven source concepts and adds 21. Lack of unique rejections alone does not justify deletion: dead_click, board_static and bar_never_drops are retained based on further tests.

Figure 7: The complete algebraic world model of an ARC-AGI-3 game. (a) Level 1 of lp85: 20 colored tiles form a closed belt, and each click on an arrow moves every tile one place around the belt, counterclockwise for the left arrow and clockwise for the right; the level is won when a yellow tile stands in the slot marked by yellow corners. (b) All objects and rules of the model, with the form each takes in Lean; the two rules about the budget bar stay in Python. (c) Excerpts: one rule as its Python check, the same rule as a Lean definition, and the Lean step, which only dispatches to rule definitions. Lean replays every recorded transition of the game with no mismatch. (d) On the original level, Lean checks a winning witness, the certified run. (e) With the only yellow tile recolored, the conservation law of press_permutes shows that no click sequence wins. Both statements are theorems about the model.

Figure 9: Why the level-4 model needed revision. (a) The opening. (b) Walking checks only the large block’s top-left quarter for fuel, whereas growing checks its full footprint and can collect fuel under the bottom-left quarter, refunding 10. Missing this distinction led one AWM run to report 20. (c) The cheaper witness uses 27 actions and requires 19. It is replayed at cap 19; at the sealed cap 18, action 26 ends the game. All frames come from the engine.

Figure 2: Four transformations guided by projective and inductive limits, applied to object types and rules. Dashed boxes mark removed components and bold boxes mark introduced components; arrows indicate relationships between components. Generalization uses r(θ), and an instance is written r(θi); specialization makes distinctions explicit through case-specific types or parameters.

Figure 8: The three introductory levels and two sealed evaluation levels of sc25, rendered from the engine in the official palette. Panels (a–c) isolate resizing, teleportation and shooting; panels (d–e) combine them. The annotations show each objective and the main stages of a minimum-budget winning route. The sealed caps, 18 and 35, are one unit below the required 19 and 36.

Concepts: concepts written during play, with those withdrawn in brackets. Rules (Lean): rules translated into Lean. AWM’s certified clears follow uncertified sessions of the same run in 22 games. The actions for Rodionov’s agent are from its ARC Prize scorecard and Memento 3’s as reported in (Zhao et al., 2026).

The text specifies the timing and cost-accounting conventions.

papers.abstract: We present LucidLyra, a framework that makes generatively reconstructed 3D scenes directly queryable for semantics and instances in a feed-forward manner from video latents. While generative 3D reconstruction can synthesize virtual environments from a single image, downstream applications in robotics and physical AI require not only visual realism but also access to scene semantics and object identities. Existing 3D understanding approaches, however, require captured multi-view scenes, have limited generalization capabilities, or rely on expensive per-scene processing and optimization. To bridge this gap, our method distills complementary knowledge from a camera-controlled video diffusion model and frozen 2D vision foundation models into a unified model to jointly infer 3D Gaussians encoding geometry, appearance, open-vocabulary semantics, and class-agnostic instance cues. The resulting scenes support novel-view rendering, open-vocabulary segmentation, and object grouping without per-scene optimization, while training requires neither manual 3D annotations nor captured multi-view data. Our method outperforms baselines combining state-of-the-art 3DGS segmentation approaches with generative 3D scene reconstruction on curated synthetic and real-image-conditioned benchmarks, while preserving reconstruction quality. Furthermore, our latent formulation naturally extends to monocular video, reconstructing structured dynamic 3D scenes across time. By turning renderable but unstructured outputs into queryable 3D worlds, LucidLyra enables downstream applications including 3D scene editing, 3D asset mining, and robotic simulation.
authors: Oliver Hahn, Rodrigo Marcuzzi, Sangeetha Grama Srinivasan, Alessandro Burzio, Sherwin Bahmani, Jiahui Huang, Stefan Roth, Shengyu Huang, Qunjie Zhou, Laura Leal-Taix\'e
bullets: Addresses the gap between visually realistic generative 3D reconstruction and the semantic, instance-level understanding needed for robotics and physical AI.
Jointly predicts 3D Gaussians encoding geometry, appearance, open-vocabulary semantics, and class-agnostic instance cues from video latents.
Requires neither captured multi-view data, manual 3D annotations, nor per-scene optimization.
Supports novel-view rendering, open-vocabulary segmentation, object grouping, and extension to structured dynamic scenes from monocular video.
Outperforms combined reconstruction and 3DGS-segmentation baselines on curated synthetic and real-image-conditioned benchmarks while preserving reconstruction quality.

papers.title: LucidLyra: Feed-Forward Generative 3D Scene Reconstruction and Joint Understanding via Multi-Task Distillation

papers.abstract: Unlearning concerns the task of removing the influence of a sensitive portion of the training data, such as protected, copyrighted or private text, from a model without retraining it from scratch. While unlearning requests happen continuously during a model's lifetime, the vast majority of LLM unlearning methods are ill-suited for iterated removal, yielding steep decay in forgetting and utility upon sequential unlearning. This decay stems from interference between successive updates, as each new deletion can undo earlier ones or push the model further along directions already degraded by them. To address this, we introduce Continual Orthogonal Projection (COP), a gradient-projection scheme that restricts each update to the orthogonal complement of activation subspaces cached from prior forget sets. This approach provably guarantees first-order non-interference with earlier deletions. COP stores only a low-rank basis per layer, requiring neither past gradients nor previous forget sets, and plugs into unlearning methods that update the model through gradient steps on a differentiable loss without modifying its objective. Experiments on standard LLM unlearning benchmarks (TOFU and RWKU) show that COP preserves utility across sequential requests without weakening forgetting, preventing the collapse of standard objectives and forgetting more effectively than continual-specific baselines.
authors: Juan Belieni, Ana Carolina Erthal, Eliezer de Souza da Silva, Diego Mesquita
bullets: Sequential unlearning can degrade both forgetting and model utility because updates interfere with prior deletions.
COP projects each update onto the orthogonal complement of activation subspaces cached from earlier forget sets.
The method provides a first-order guarantee of non-interference with previous deletions.
It stores only a low-rank basis per layer and does not require past gradients or previous forget data.
On TOFU and RWKU, COP preserves utility across sequential requests without weakening forgetting and outperforms continual-unlearning baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of COP for one linear layer with weights W . The input activations of earlier forget sets are summarized by a compact basis Vk−1, which marks the directions where earlier forgetting lives. At request k, the gradient of the unlearning objective on Fk, optionally combined with a retain term onR, is projected away from these directions, so the update cannot change how the layer responds to earlier forget inputs. After training, the dominant new activation directions of Fk are compressed and added to the basis, giving Vk for the next request.

Figure 3: COP maintains higher utility on real-world knowledge unlearning. Model utility on RWKU with Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct after each forget request, for each base objective (dashed, hollow markers) and its COP-augmented variant (solid, filled markers). Utility under COP remains stable as requests accumulate, while base objectives fluctuate or degrade.

Table 1: TOFU results on Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct (forget05). After each task, forget metrics are computed over all requests seen so far, and model utility (MU) is measured on the retain set and general utility datasets. Bold marks the higher MU within each pair of a base objective and its COP-augmented variant. From the third request onward, every COP variant retains higher utility than its base objective. COP prevents the utility collapse of GA and IDK, whose base versions reach lower EM only as part of that collapse, while forget metrics for NPO and SimNPO remain comparable with and without COP. O3 attains the highest utility but forgets weakly, with EM close to that of the original model. ALKN’s forget metrics fall together with its utility, which collapses as requests accumulate.

Table 3: RWKU results on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. After each task, forget metrics are computed over all requests seen so far, and model utility (MU) is measured on the retained subjects and world facts. Bold marks the higher MU within each pair of a base objective and its COP-augmented variant. COP keeps utility stable across requests, while O3 forgets at the cost of most of its utility and ALKN retains much of the targeted knowledge.

Table 2: TOFU results on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct (forget05), with the same metrics and notation as Table 1. COP improves utility at every request for SimNPO and IDK, from the second request onward for GA, and from the third onward for NPO. Base GA and IDK drive forget ROUGE close to zero only as their utility collapses, while their COP variants remain stable at the cost of higher EM. O3 attains the highest utility but fails to forget effectively, with EM above 0.9 at every request. ALKN’s utility falls sharply as requests accumulate.

papers.title: Preserving Utility in Continual LLM Unlearning via Orthogonal Projections
papers.tldr: Continual Orthogonal Projection enables repeated LLM unlearning while preserving utility and avoiding interference with earlier deletions.

papers.abstract: Financial AI workflows that reuse investor knowledge need persistent memory that integrates observations across sources and periods without losing identity or provenance. In a knowledge graph, recurring observations may use different surface forms, fragmenting relationship histories and preventing evidence from accumulating. We introduce Fusion and Identity Registry for Memory Evolution (FIRME), a registry-anchored memory graph that reconciles incoming observations to persistent canonical relationships and retains their source, time, and context. Within periods, rule-based fusion links investor-call discussions to portfolio cash-flow signals, directly or through a fixed product-topic ontology. Across periods, canonical identities and persistent aliases direct recurring observations to the same relationship history; deterministic updates summarize reinforcement, inactivity, and reactivation. We evaluate FIRME on proprietary investor-call and cash-flow records and on S&P 500 earnings-call transcripts. Compared with a historical registry that retains canonical identities and semantic fallback but omits alias memory, FIRME increases final-period Correct Match Rate by 7.8-12.1 percentage points across four dataset-backend settings under a fixed-judge and fallback-review protocol. A blinded human audit of 200 incoming observations per setting finds Correct Match Rate gains of 9.0-16.5 points and reattachment-recall gains of 22.5-29.0 points, with higher observed merge precision in all four samples. A separate audit finds valid evidence paths for 293 of 300 outputs from full within-period fusion in the investor-call setting. Extraction-faithfulness and round-trip diagnostics assess source grounding and preservation of extractor-derived graph content.
authors: Yunbai Zhang, Yunyi Gao, Han-Tai Shiao
bullets: Addresses fragmented relationship histories caused by inconsistent surface forms in recurring investor observations.
Uses rule-based within-period fusion, a fixed product-topic ontology, canonical identities, and persistent alias memory for cross-period reconciliation.
Deterministically updates relationship histories to capture reinforcement, inactivity, and reactivation while retaining evidence paths.

Evaluated on proprietary investor records and S&P 500 earnings-call transcripts; it improves Correct Match Rate by 7.8–12.1 points and human-audited reattachment recall by 22.5–29.0 points across four settings.
Scope includes fixed-judge/fallback-review evaluation and audits of source grounding and graph-content preservation; results rely on proprietary records and a fixed ontology.

papers.abstract: Audio-visual instance segmentation (AVIS) segments and tracks individual sound-producing objects in videos. Existing benchmarks predominantly use monaural audio, which lacks inter-channel cues for spatially distinguishing concurrent sound sources. We introduce AVPS-360 (Audio-Visual Person Segmentation 360), a spatial audio-visual benchmark bridging AVIS and sound event localisation and detection (SELD). Built upon STARSS23, it pairs first-order Ambisonics audio with synchronised 360{\deg} video across 230 recordings totalling 10.5 hours. Recordings average 164.0 seconds. The dataset captures intermittent sound production in real-world interactions dominated by speech, alongside laughter, clapping, and footsteps. It provides 31,678 manually reviewed instance masks linked to source identities and sound-event labels. We also present a baseline that integrates spatial audio with visual features for frame-level segmentation and identity association across frames. Experiments on AVPS-360 show that existing AVIS methods struggle with detection and identity association in long recordings with intermittent sound production, while our baseline substantially improves performance in both aspects.
authors: Yifu Sun, Parthasaarathy Sudarsanam, Tuomas Virtanen, Archontis Politis
bullets: Addresses the limitations of monaural-audio AVIS benchmarks for distinguishing concurrent sound sources.
Pairs first-order Ambisonics audio with synchronized 360° video in 230 real-world recordings totaling 10.5 hours.
Includes 31,678 manually reviewed instance masks linked to source identities and sound-event labels.
Covers primarily speech, plus laughter, clapping, and footsteps during intermittent sound production.
Shows existing AVIS methods struggle with detection and identity association in long recordings, while the spatial-audio baseline improves both.

papers.title: AVPS-360: A Spatial Audio-Visual Benchmark for Instance Segmentation and Tracking of Sound-Producing Persons

papers.abstract: The rapid growth in the size of state-of-the-art machine-learning (ML) models has led to increasing compute demands, spurring the development of energy-efficient hardware accelerators. Physical systems trained to perform ML inference, known as physical neural networks, have been proposed as accelerators in part because of their potential to be highly energy efficient. However, the ML inference accuracies reported in most investigations of physical neural networks have been substantially below the state of the art for conventional digital neural networks. In this work, we show in simulation studies that by applying modern ML training practices, including model compression, various candidate physical neural networks based on nonlinear dynamical systems can achieve accuracies as high as 99.2% on MNIST handwritten-digit recognition. We also show for one dynamical system that using it as the core building block of a parameter-efficient ML architecture inspired by MLP-Mixers enables accuracies of up to 86.4% on CIFAR-10 image classification (92.2% with pretraining and knowledge distillation), compared with 64% for the same system without the mixer architecture. The mixer approach achieved its accuracy while using $>5\times$ fewer trainable parameters than the baseline. Finally, we present back-of-the-envelope estimates for inference energy efficiency and speed when using an example physical dynamical system, suggesting that orders of magnitude improvements may be possible over digital-electronic neural networks.
authors: Tyler King, Magnus Saebo, Jeremie Laydevant, Haoting Zhen, Maxwell G. Anderson, Tatsuhiro Onodera, Peter L. McMahon
bullets: Physical neural networks are explored as energy-efficient accelerators, addressing the computational cost of increasingly large ML models.
Simulated nonlinear dynamical systems achieve up to 99.2% accuracy on MNIST when combined with modern training practices and model compression.
An MLP-Mixer-inspired architecture raises CIFAR-10 accuracy to 86.4%, or 92.2% with pretraining and knowledge distillation, versus 64% without the mixer.
The mixer architecture uses more than five times fewer trainable parameters than the baseline.
Back-of-the-envelope estimates suggest possible orders-of-magnitude gains in inference energy efficiency and speed, though results are simulation-based and partly prospective.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Overview of machine learning based on the controllable evolution in time of nonlinear dynamical networks (DynNets). (A) depicts the pipeline for classifying a sample MNIST input. The input image is padded with zeros and encoded in the initial conditions of a dynamical system. The output is taken as the state of the dynamical system at some time T . The process of optimizing the controllable parameters θ of the physical system adjusts the dynamics such that the input is mapped to a useful feature vector by the evolution of the system ϕ. We show that a variety of controllable dynamical systems can perform competitively for this optimization task, including (B) an inductively coupled network of Chua Circuits—chaotic electronic circuits; (C) Kuramoto coupled oscillators—a canonical dynamical system for modeling synchronization; (D) the coherent Ising machine—a coupled network of optical oscillators (shown as ring resonators here); and (E) a crossbar oscillator architecture with a feedback loop—a network representing sigmoidal oscillator dynamics.

FIG. 2: Dynamics and test accuracy of KuraNN architecture during MNIST training. (A)-(C) Mean KuraNN oscillator dynamics and class histograms for MNIST at epochs 2, 20, and 150. (D) Log-linear plot of test accuracy during training, achieving a maximum test accuracy of 98.88%. (E) End-of-training log-scale confusion matrix on the MNIST test set. (F) Oscillators associated with classes 3 and 6, exhibiting class separation between the two groups over the time horizon.

FIG. 3: Visualization of the coupling connectivity of the KuraNN as it trains with pruning. (A) MNIST image of a “3” with all couplings connected to the oscillator at index (7, 6). (B) Density of couplings from all oscillators to the oscillator at (7, 6) for epochs 100, 250, and 400. (C) Test accuracy during training on MNIST; final accuracy of 98.96%. (D) Connection density per epoch; we geometrically decay the connection density until we reach a desired density level (in this case, 10%). (E) Magnitudes of coupling coefficients between all 196 image oscillators.

TABLE II: Test accuracy averages and standard deviations over 5 runs on CIFAR-10 with trainable parameter counts. The first section details our results, the second section details results from other physically plausible architectures, the third details other continuous-time architectures, and the last one details three convolutional frameworks that obtain ≈90%, ≈95%, ≈99% on CIFAR-10. Pru. indicates pruning, Dist. indicates knowledge distillation, and Pre. indicates ImageNet pretraining.

TABLE I: Test accuracy averages and standard deviations over 5 runs with and without pruning on MNIST along with trainable parameter counts. Bolded results are the best-performing architecture for the pruned and unpruned settings. Note that our models involve downsampling inputs while most other architectures leverage the full MNIST image. Additional comparisons from both simulated physical systems and continuous-time neural network architectures are also included.

TABLE III: Energy and time per single-image MNIST inference. Measured rows are taken from their respective works; KuraNN rows are theoretical predictions from the model of Sec. V and are fully calculated in Appendix F. Pruned KuraNN models retain 10% of couplings via locality-aware magnitude pruning. Each inference spans 15.9 oscillator periods.

papers.selection_reason: Physical nonlinear dynamical systems as neural-network accelerators for energy-efficient inference; directly relevant to efficient AI hardware.
papers.title: Nonlinear Dynamical Systems as Scalable and Efficient Physical Neural Networks
papers.tldr: Modern training and compression techniques can make nonlinear dynamical physical neural networks substantially more accurate and potentially far more energy-efficient than conventional digital implementations.

papers.abstract: Infant pose and shape estimation is essential for applications in childcare, developmental monitoring, and medical diagnosis. However, existing methods and datasets are largely designed for adults, and direct transfer to infants fails due to substantial differences in body proportions, articulation limits, and frequent self-occlusion. To address this gap, we introduce InfantNet, the largest real-image infant dataset to date, comprising 108,902 RGB images of infants aged 6-18 months. Each image is annotated with 2D keypoints, and a curated subset of 11,642 images additionally includes 3D pose and shape annotations with full SMIL parameters, verified through multi-view rendering and reprojection-error filtering. We use an iterative annotation pipeline to ensure high fidelity across both 2D and 3D labels. InfantNet establishes a large-scale, comprehensive benchmark for infant 2D keypoint detection and 3D pose-and-shape recovery. Baseline experiments demonstrate that state-of-the-art adult pose estimators do not generalize well to infants, whereas fine-tuning on InfantNet yields a consistent improvement. The gains are even more pronounced for 3D pose and shape estimation, where SMIL-based estimation demonstrates robust performance with accuracy comparable to results reported for SMPL-based models. By releasing the InfantNet dataset and benchmark, we provide a vital resource for advancing infant pose analysis and related healthcare applications.
authors: Zhipeng Hui, Jiahao Wang, Xun Dong, Guofeng Zhang, Xingrui Wang, Jiawei Peng, Qihao Liu, Xiaoding Yuan, Yi Zhang, Junjie Oscar Yin, Wufei Ma, Qinfan Lyu, Sara N. Lupolt, Keeve Edward Nachman, Adam Kortylewski, Alan Yuille
bullets: Contains 108,902 RGB images of infants aged 6–18 months with 2D keypoint annotations.
A curated subset of 11,642 images includes 3D pose and shape annotations with full SMIL parameters.
An iterative annotation pipeline uses multi-view rendering and reprojection-error filtering to improve label fidelity.
Adult state-of-the-art pose estimators generalize poorly, while fine-tuning on InfantNet consistently improves performance.
The dataset supports benchmarking infant pose analysis for childcare, developmental monitoring, and medical applications.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Annotation pipeline of our InfantNet Dataset. Frames from YouTube and HomeVisit recordings were annotated using a semiautomatic, inspector-guided workflow. For 2D labels, RTMO-L provided initial keypoints that were refined by annotators with iterative quality control, following the COCO format. For 3D labels, we applied an optimization-based method to fit SMIL to infant images, and annotators further filtered the results to ensure accurate pose and shape annotations.

Figure 6. Visualization of 3D pose and shape estimation. From left to right, the columns show the input image, direct inference with adult body model and data, and training with infant body model and data for HMR [22], PARE [25], and 4D-Humans [15], respectively.

Figure 5. papers.title: InfantNet: A Large Scale Dataset for Infant Body Pose and Shape Estimation
papers.tldr: InfantNet is a large-scale, carefully annotated infant image dataset and benchmark that addresses the poor transfer of adult pose models to infant 2D and 3D pose-and-shape estimation.

papers.abstract: Aerial imagery provides complementary spatial context for autonomous driving by exposing road structure beyond the immediate perception range of onboard sensors. Yet map construction from aerial imagery, aerial-assisted online HD mapping, and cross-view localization are typically studied on separate data and benchmarks. We introduce KITScenes Aerial, an extension of the KITScenes Multimodal dataset that augments synchronized onboard sensor data, vehicle poses, and rich Lanelet2 map annotations with spatially associated aerial imagery and higher-resolution neural representations, providing a common basis for a variety of research tasks. Our mapping evaluation focuses on all 53 KITScenes map classes across different model designs, spatial ranges, and aerial resolutions, while retaining compatibility with the widely used three-class setting. Representative baselines show that aerial context is particularly beneficial for fine-grained and extended-range mapping, more than doubling 53-class mAP at the larger mapping extent. Higher-resolution aerial imagery yields a further 4.3 mAP (+24 %) improvement, with gains extending to challenging map elements such as traffic lights. We additionally evaluate cross-view localization under geographically disjoint conditions, where an adapted fine-grained feature-matching baseline achieves a mean translation error of 5.13 m. KITScenes Aerial thus enables unified study of aerial and ground-level information across complementary mapping and localization tasks. Project page: https://kitscenes.com/aerial
authors: Daniel Lengerer, Richard Schwarzkopf, Jonas Merkert, Fabian Immel, Rupert Polley, Frank Bieder, Jan-Hendrik Pauls, J. Marius Z\"ollner, Klaus Bogenberger, Christoph Stiller, Carsten Markgraf

Supports aerial map construction, online HD mapping, and geographically disjoint cross-view localization in one benchmark.
Evaluates all 53 map classes across model designs, spatial ranges, and aerial resolutions while retaining the standard three-class setting.
Aerial context more than doubles 53-class mAP at larger mapping extents; higher-resolution imagery adds 4.3 mAP (+24%), including gains for traffic lights.
An adapted feature-matching baseline achieves 5.13 m mean translation error for cross-view localization.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation commonly serves separate models for reranking and answering, duplicating model residency and passage processing. We introduce Glance, which equips the generator with a lightweight decision adapter and pointer head to score candidate passages from a shared prefill. Short relevance probes branch from the cached context, producing one score per passage without separately prefilling each query-passage pair. A single resident 9B backbone supports generation, general decisions and reranking, with approximately 0.1 GiB of additional memory per decision skill. After 39 minutes of MS MARCO fine-tuning, Glance achieves nDCG@10 of 0.741 on SciFact and 0.345 on NFCorpus, compared with 0.721 and 0.326 for bge-reranker-v2-m3. On 300 HotpotQA questions, its selected context improves answer F1 by 0.045 over cross-encoder-selected context under the same base generator (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.014, 0.076]). In a scaling study, reranking quality keeps rising up to 200 candidates (43k tokens) scored from one shared prefill, where it exceeds the cross-encoder by 0.058 nDCG@10, and a probe-only activated adapter lets generation continue from the original passage cache. These initial results demonstrate generator-based reranking with one resident backbone; evaluation currently covers two retrieval datasets, one QA dataset and one backbone family.
authors: Adilet Metinov, Chingiz Arziev
bullets: Uses a lightweight decision adapter and pointer head to score passages from one shared prefilling of the cached context.
A single resident 9B backbone supports generation, decision-making, and reranking with about 0.1 GiB extra memory per decision skill.
After brief MS MARCO fine-tuning, it reports higher nDCG@10 than bge-reranker-v2-m3 on SciFact and NFCorpus.
On 300 HotpotQA questions, Glance-selected context improves answer F1 over cross-encoder-selected context under the same generator.
Reranking quality continues improving to 200 candidates, but evaluation is limited to two retrieval datasets, one QA dataset, and one backbone family.

papers.abstract: We present PhysInsert, a framework for physically plausible reference-based object insertion that jointly adapts objects and their surrounding scenes. Existing methods often rely on masked inputs, generation-based pairs, or training pairs with limited viewpoint variation, leaving pose and illumination adaptation and bidirectional object-scene interactions insufficiently constrained. We construct the Insert World dataset with strictly aligned Blender-rendered counterfactual pairs and object references across viewpoints and lighting conditions. Building on these data, Geometry-Guided Adaptation couples a VGGT geometry stream with image and text streams under target-scene feature supervision to guide spatially consistent insertion. Complementary 2D Object-Scene Spatial Supervision jointly supervises object occupancy and environmental changes while grounding spatial instructions in object regions through image-text attention. We introduce PhysInsert-Bench with dedicated cross-environment and cross-view cases requiring illumination and pose adaptation beyond appearance copying. Experiments on PhysInsert-Bench and DreamBooth demonstrate improved image fidelity; a user study further shows more accurate placement and improved lighting integration, perspective, and pose plausibility.
authors: Yue Gong, Le Zhang, Rui Chen, Song Chang, Xiaochao Qu, Luoqi Liu, Ting Liu, Yebin Liu
bullets: Addresses limitations of existing insertion methods in viewpoint variation, pose and illumination adaptation, and bidirectional object–scene interaction.
Introduces Insert World, a dataset of aligned Blender-rendered counterfactual object–scene pairs across viewpoints and lighting conditions.
Uses Geometry-Guided Adaptation to combine geometry, image, and text features for spatially consistent insertion.
Adds 2D Object-Scene Spatial Supervision to model object occupancy and environmental changes using image-text attention.
PhysInsert-Bench, DreamBooth experiments, and a user study report improved fidelity, placement, lighting integration, perspective, and pose plausibility.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained manipulation requires a robot policy to follow instructions, remain robust to visual variations, and translate predicted actions into precise robot control. We present Demonstration Expansion and Execution Design (DEED), a framework for adapting a pretrained vision-language-action policy to the five MetaFine tasks through structured demonstration expansion and execution design. DEED generates demonstrations for different instructions from the same initial scene and renders each physical trajectory under different camera positions and lighting conditions while preserving its original states and action targets. A hierarchical sampling strategy balances instructions, trajectories, and visual conditions during supervised adaptation. At deployment, DEED converts predicted action chunks into robot commands using inverse kinematics, gripper mappings selected for each task, and closed-loop replanning. DEED achieves an official Overall score of 85.55%. Fixed-policy evaluations show that performance varies with execution horizon, denoising budget, and gripper mapping.
authors: Jingxu Gu, Dongze Lian
bullets: Targets instruction following, visual robustness, and precise action execution in five MetaFine tasks.
Expands demonstrations across instructions, camera positions, and lighting while preserving states and action targets.
Uses hierarchical sampling for supervised adaptation of a pretrained vision-language-action policy.
Executes action chunks with inverse kinematics, task-specific gripper mappings, and closed-loop replanning.
Achieves an official Overall score of 85.55%; performance depends on execution horizon, denoising budget, and gripper mapping.

papers.title: Improving Fine-Grained Manipulation through Demonstration Expansion and Execution Design

papers.abstract: Complex questions in retrieval-augmented generation require evidence spread over several documents, and an answer is reliable only when the retriever finds all of it. Chain embedding retrievers collect such evidence step by step, re-encoding the question together with the passages retrieved so far, and we find that they are already strong: trained only on gold histories, a small chain embedding retriever that calls no language model outperforms graph-based systems and is competitive with a search agent. This training, however, leaves a gap. At test time the retriever conditions on its own retrievals, which soon contain mistakes: by the third step, about half or more of the states it visits hold a wrong passage, and these passages lower its chance of retrieving a missing gold passage well beyond what the difficulty of the states explains. We propose on-policy state training, which trains the encoder on the states it reaches itself. At every epoch the current encoder retrieves chains for the training questions; each state it visits, including those built on its own mistakes, is labeled with the earliest gold passage still missing while the other missing gold passages are masked, so that no correct continuation is penalized; and the encoder is updated contrastively on these states mixed with teacher-forced ones, so that its training distribution follows it as it learns. The resulting retriever retrieves complete evidence more often than teacher-forced training and the systems we compare, and it transfers without further training to harder long-chain variants of HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA that we construct. On the same states, it recovers from its own mistakes far more often, and controlled comparisons attribute the gain to training on the states the encoder currently reaches.
authors: Chenjie Qiu, Zixuan Zeng, Shaobin Shi, Bingfeng Chen, Dongsheng Luo, Boyan Xu
bullets: Multi-hop questions require retrieving all relevant evidence across several documents.
Teacher-forced training performs well but fails to prepare retrievers for erroneous passages encountered at test time.
The method trains on states reached by the current retriever, labeling the earliest missing gold passage while masking other missing evidence.
On-policy and teacher-forced states are combined in contrastive training, allowing the training distribution to track the model’s behavior.
The resulting retriever improves evidence completion, mistake recovery, and transfer to harder long-chain variants of HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA.

papers.title: Retrieving from Your Own Mistakes: On-Policy Training of Embedding Models for Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves language-model reasoning by scoring sampled responses with a rule-based verifier and reinforcing those that pass. Where a classifier's training couples predicted probability to labels, nothing ties an RLVR policy's confidence in a response to its reward: aligned training would drive responses with the same advantage toward equal confidence, yet the advantage is blind to confidence. Under this sequence-confidence misalignment, a success the policy barely found earns the same update as one it produces with near certainty, and a confident error is corrected no harder than an exploratory one. We propose SCARL (Sequence Confidence-Aligned Reinforcement Learning), which reshapes, but never re-signs, each advantage with the alignment gap between the response's group-relative confidence and the outcome its advantage certifies, normalized into shares of each class's advantage budget. Misaligned samples absorb the force, responses with the same advantage are driven toward equal confidence, and repairing the misalignment doubles as a remedy for the entropy collapse that erodes exploration. SCARL provably reduces to its base estimator when a class's confidences agree, adds no extra passes and one hyperparameter. On Qwen3-4B-Base it lifts average Pass@32 by 2.4 points over DAPO and is best among nine compute-matched methods on both coverage and per-draw accuracy; applied unchanged across four estimators and four backbones, it improves 14 of 16 settings while preserving policy entropy and widening the confidence-correctness separation. Our code is available at https://github.com/kezhh163/scarl.
authors: Zhenghong Ke, Jingbo Zhou, Hua Wu
bullets: RLVR advantages reward correctness but ignore how confidently a response was produced, causing confidence–reward misalignment and entropy collapse.
SCARL reshapes each advantage using the gap between group-relative confidence and the verified outcome, without changing reward signs.
It reduces to the base estimator when class confidences agree, adds one hyperparameter, and requires no extra passes.
On Qwen3-4B-Base, SCARL improves average Pass@32 by 2.4 points over DAPO and performs best among nine compute-matched methods on coverage and per-draw accuracy.
Across four estimators and four backbones, it improves 14 of 16 settings while preserving entropy and increasing confidence–correctness separation.

papers.abstract: We introduce Continuous-Action World Models (CoAWM), a framework for learning cross-embodiment spatiotemporal dynamics priors that support robot action generation across embodiments and execution frequencies. At its core is a shared latent function space that captures the spatial and temporal structure of robot actions. We learn this space through two stages. First, function pretraining brings trajectories from different embodiments and sampling frequencies into a common representation, learning shared dynamics priors through action reconstruction and consistency across temporal sampling views. By accommodating heterogeneous robot trajectories, this stage broadens the range of data sources available for pretraining and facilitates scaling to larger and more diverse datasets. Second, we connect the pretrained function space to a world-model backbone, enabling observations, language instructions, and the current robot state to condition the prediction of a latent action function. A single decoder takes any query time and returns the corresponding end-effector action. By separating shared dynamics priors from task-conditioned action selection and temporal sampling, our approach provides a unified foundation for transferring robot experience across embodiments and control frequencies.

bullets: Addresses the challenge of transferring robot experience across heterogeneous embodiments and execution frequencies.

papers.abstract: Mathematical supervision for language models is typically flattened into isolated problem-solution pairs, discarding the curricular organization and evidential structure of the original sources. We introduce TOME-Math (Textbook-Oriented Mathematical Evidence), a large-scale corpus that converts 2,118 textbooks spanning the core areas of university-level mathematics subjects into approximately 380K structured proof-supervision records while preserving chapter order, proposition-proof links, dependency references, and source provenance. Leveraging these structural signals, we explore curriculum learning across multiple mathematical subjects and characterize scaling patterns with supervision volume and source breadth. At full scale, fine-tuning on TOME-Math raises the unweighted mean score across our held-out evaluations and established public benchmarks by 16.7 percentage points over the base model, while exceeding all three public instruction-data baselines evaluated in aggregate. Our findings highlight structured textbooks as both a scalable source of mathematical supervision and an empirical framework for studying the impact of data organization on mathematical reasoning. We will release the corpus to facilitate further research on structured mathematical supervision.
authors: Youqing Fang, Zhouqi Hua, Yinhao Tang, Yuzhe Gu, Lingkai Kong, Bin Liu, Weiming Zhang, Kai Chen, Yanan Sun, Wenwei Zhang

papers.abstract: Diffusion models have become the leading paradigm in generative modeling, yet many applications require sampling from distributions that are not those of any single pretrained model, but are instead defined through combinations of several models, possibly tilted toward high values of a downstream reward. Naively combining the scores of the models yields incorrect samples, while existing corrections are restricted to specific families of targets. In this work, we introduce the generalized Feynman-Kac correctors (GFKC), a principled framework for sampling from an arbitrary target function of several pretrained diffusion models. We show that the geometric interpolation between an arbitrary initial function and the target function of the models satisfies a Feynman--Kac partial differential equation, and derive its potential in closed form. To evaluate this potential during generation, we further generalize the log-probability ODE to track the density of each model along trajectories driven by a different velocity field. The resulting algorithm operates entirely in the log domain, incorporates reward-based steering at no additional conceptual cost, and corrects the generation on the fly, without retraining or fine-tuning the models. We validate the method on analytic Gaussian models, where it closely matches the ground-truth targets, and on diffusion models trained on MNIST, where it samples from non-trivial combinations of the models and enables effective steering.
authors: Wael Mattar, Daniel Freedman
bullets: Naively combining diffusion-model scores produces incorrect samples, and prior corrections support only limited target families.
The method uses a generalized Feynman–Kac formulation to derive closed-form correction potentials for arbitrary functions of multiple models.
A generalized log-probability ODE tracks each model’s density along trajectories driven by another velocity field.
Corrections and reward-based steering are applied during generation in the log domain, without retraining or fine-tuning.
Experiments on analytic Gaussian targets and MNIST show close agreement with ground truth and effective sampling of non-trivial combinations.

papers.abstract: The last year has seen a shift in AI-assisted mathematics, with frontier language models producing proofs of and counterexamples to long-standing open conjectures. However, studying only the current set of major breakthroughs provides an incomplete picture of LLM capabilities and the computational resources needed to achieve reported results. To address this, we introduce a new dataset, OpenConjecture, which collects conjectures from mathematics papers published on the arXiv since February 2026. We use these conjectures as a source of open mathematical problems, and apply frontier GPT models to a random sample of 200 of these conjectures over three passes using a reproducible protocol without problem-specific mathematical guidance. Rather than attempt expert verification of these candidate solutions, we analyze the types of problems for which LLMs produce solutions and the characteristics of these solutions. The models we test produce candidate solutions for roughly 60% of the conjectures, with counterexamples about 1.3 times more common than proofs. We estimate solution novelty, assess how solutions cite and relate to existing literature, and analyze whether the proposed resolution relies on either an error in or underspecification of the conjecture. We find that models sometimes propose resolutions that are outside the authors' intent (e.g., proposing the trivial group as a counterexample) and that a number of proofs follow closely from existing results, but that some resolutions exhibit at least moderate novelty. Our findings underscore the need for evaluations that go beyond correctness to assess fidelity to the intended statement, attribution, and the nature of the mathematical contribution.
authors: Helen Jenne, Davis Brown, Jesse He, Henry Kvinge

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated promising capabilities in robotic manipulation by integrating visual perception, language understanding, and action generation. Recent advances have further incorporated future prediction to enhance the understanding of environmental dynamics and task progression. However, existing methods often model short-term dynamics and long-term task objectives separately, while directly incorporating predicted futures into action policies without sufficiently considering their relevance to current action requirements. To address these limitations, we propose HiFOR, a hierarchical foresight framework with action-guided world retrieval. Specifically, Hierarchical Foresight Prediction jointly predicts short-term state evolution, semantic milestones, and final goal states through a Hierarchical Dependency Mask (HDM), establishing dependencies across temporal horizons. Building upon these predictions, Structure-Aware Latent World Modeling organizes future latent representations along the horizon, view, and spatial dimensions to facilitate fine-grained retrieval. Furthermore, Action-Guided Factorized World Retrieval adaptively retrieves relevant future information from the structured latent world based on evolving action representations during denoising, providing targeted guidance for action generation. Extensive experiments on two simulation benchmarks and six real-world robotic manipulation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.
authors: Rongxing Ding, Hongyu Qu, Kehong Wu, Xudong Wang, Fan Zhang, Xinguang Xiang, Xiangbo Shu
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between short-term dynamics, long-term goals, and their relevance to current actions in VLA models.

papers.abstract: Unsupervised environment design (UED) methods such as PLR, ACCEL, SFL and PAIRED are compared mostly on 2D mazes, grid worlds and BipedalWalker, while terrain curricula for legged robots are hand-designed and evaluated against a few baselines. We present a benchmark that runs fourteen UED, domain-randomisation and robotics curricula under one protocol on five 3D quadrupeds in MuJoCo MJX: the closed-chain W01-TEK and the open-chain Unitree Go1 and Go2, Google Barkour vB and Boston Dynamics Spot. Levels are vectors of eight interpretable terrain parameters, and all curricula drive the same PPO student at matched environment-step budgets. The evaluation reports success on random and held-out structured terrains, interquartile means with stratified bootstrap intervals, capability envelopes and a level-by-level domination comparison. We compare methods within each robot and report, per level set, the top group of methods not significantly below the best. No method is in the top group on every robot and level set. Methods with easy or low-difficulty training levels, curated or not, fill the top groups on in-distribution random levels of Go1 and Barkour, and of W01-TEK apart from PAIRED+BiBC. The success-driven terrain curriculum from legged-robot practice is in a top group most often, domain randomisation on uniform levels in none, and PAIRED in none outside Spot, where the fourteen methods lie within 3.8 points on random levels of difficulty 0.25. On three robots the leader on in-distribution random levels is not the leader on held-out terrain. We collect the results into a per-robot guide to choosing a curriculum.

On three robots, the in-distribution leader differs from the held-out-terrain leader, highlighting limited cross-robot and generalization consistency.

papers.abstract: In-context imitation learning (ICIL) adapts robot policies through test-time demonstrations, but long multimodal trajectories constrain how many examples fit in context. We ask what a compressed demonstration should preserve. We propose JEDI, which compresses demonstrations into latent slots trained to predict the query episode's next-stage keyframe in a frozen video-JEPA space. Task and process counterfactuals help the slots preserve execution details, while the predictor selects demonstrations from a bank. Post-training with keypoint tokens enables human-hand conditioning on robots. Experiments on LIBERO and real robots show that JEDI supports many-shot context; LIBERO objective controls show improved success and demonstration following over action-only compression. These findings support query-future prediction as a training objective for preserving execution-relevant information in compressed demonstrations.
authors: Jiazhao Liang, Zhewen He, Shuaihang Yuan, Hao Huang, Yi Fang
bullets: Addresses limited context length when adapting robot policies from long multimodal demonstrations.
Trains latent slots to predict the query episode’s next-stage keyframe in a frozen video-JEPA representation.
Uses task and process counterfactuals to retain task identity and execution information, then selects demonstrations from a bank.
Keypoint-token post-training supports conditioning on human-hand demonstrations for robot control.
Experiments on LIBERO and real robots show many-shot support and improved success and demonstration following over action-only compression in LIBERO controls.

papers.abstract: Agents powered by large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable progress in solving complex reasoning tasks. However, LLM agents often falter on long-horizon tasks due to cognitive overload, as their working memory becomes cluttered with expanding and irrelevant information, which dilutes their attention and hinders effective planning and reasoning. To mitigate this challenge, we introduce Cognitive Resource Self-Allocation (CORAL), a novel reasoning paradigm that empowers agents to proactively optimize their context. Implemented as an agent-callable working memory management toolset, CORAL allows an agent to checkpoint its task progress and verified facts, and adaptively initiate a new problem-solving episode by resetting cluttered context while preserving only the checkpointed information, enabling it to resume reasoning from a clean state. We further enhance the agent's checkpointing capabilities using a Multi-episode Agentic Reinforced Policy Optimization algorithm. On the GAIA benchmark, CORAL with an 8B model achieves 42.8% average accuracy, with particularly strong gains on the most challenging long-horizon tasks (Level 2 and Level 3). Crucially, these gains come at a substantially lower inference cost: CORAL consumes 6-7$\times$ fewer input tokens than a ReAct agent. It also generalizes to multi-hop Knowledge QA benchmarks and to the considerably harder BrowseComp, where it improves a strong proprietary agent by 8.0 points.
authors: Zheng Zhu, Xiaozhuan Liang, Xi Chen, Bei Yu, Jiaya Jia
bullets: Long-horizon agents can suffer from cognitive overload as irrelevant context accumulates and disrupts planning.
CORAL provides an agent-callable working-memory toolkit for checkpointing progress and verified facts, then starting fresh reasoning episodes with only that information retained.
A Multi-episode Agentic Reinforced Policy Optimization algorithm improves the agent’s checkpointing decisions.
On GAIA, an 8B model with CORAL reaches 42.8% average accuracy, with especially strong gains on difficult Level 2 and Level 3 tasks.
CORAL uses 6–7× fewer input tokens than ReAct and also improves performance on multi-hop Knowledge QA and BrowseComp.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Comparison of the ReAct and CORAL frameworks; both rows read left to right as the context grows. Top (ReAct). One context accumulates N ReAct blocks (thought, action, observation) above the system prompt and user task, and nothing is ever removed. Bottom (CORAL). The same blocks are interleaved with two agent-callable tools. Memory Management (MM) writes into the persistent MEMORY panel below the trace, holding task progress (the plan, each sub-goal pending or completed) and verified facts, so that panel evolves while the raw trace only grows. Context Optimization (CO), the vertical bar, ends the current episode: everything to its left is discarded and the next episode restarts from only the system prompt, the user task, and the current panel. A trajectory is thus a sequence of episodes (here 0–3).

Figure 2: Multi-episode ARPO. The reward is computed from a trajectory’s final episode (which contains the answer) and propagated to all preceding ones; episodes from all sampled trajectories are then pooled for group-based advantage estimation, enabling credit assignment across episode boundaries.

papers.abstract: Human demonstrations offer an efficient and scalable source of data for dexterous robot manipulation, but differences in sensing and hand morphology complicate the transfer of contact-rich interactions. We present TouchBridge, a hardware--software co-designed framework for human-to-robot data transformation. A wearable human demonstration interface and a corresponding robot interface establish cross-embodiment correspondence in visual and fingertip tactile sensing. We introduce Tac-Retarget, a tactile-conditioned retargeting method that uses measured contact to align fingertip contact patches and preserve their spatial relations within and across hands. Unlike object-aware or simulation-based transfer pipelines, Tac-Retarget requires no object mesh, object-pose estimate, or physics simulation for retargeting, enabling direct and scalable conversion of human demonstrations into robot-domain training data. Combined with visual synthesis and camera-anchored action conversion, TouchBridge produces robot-domain demonstrations for fine-tuning a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) model. Across four real-world contact-rich tasks, policies fine-tuned solely on TouchBridge-converted human demonstrations achieve a 72.5% average success rate, compared with 77.5% using an equal number of teleoperated robot demonstrations, while human demonstration collection is 7.0x faster. Under the same policy and training setup, Tac-Retarget outperforms DexPilot and UniDex by 25.0 and 42.5 percentage points, respectively.
authors: Haozhe Zhang, Gu Zhang, Zirui Zou, Yuzheng Chen, Jinlong Wu, Zixuan Hu, Jianke Zhang, Yucheng Hu, Zhecheng Yuan, Huazhe Xu

Combines matched human–robot visual and fingertip-tactile interfaces with Tac-Retarget, which preserves contact-patch relationships without object meshes, pose estimates, or simulation.
Adds visual synthesis and camera-anchored action conversion to fine-tune a pretrained vision-language-action model.
Across four real-world tasks, converted demonstrations reached 72.5% average success versus 77.5% for equally sized teleoperated datasets.
Tac-Retarget exceeded DexPilot and UniDex by 25.0 and 42.5 percentage points, respectively.

papers.abstract: Low-bit quantization enables efficient deployment of large language models by reducing memory footprint and computational cost. Achieving high accuracy at low precision requires selecting quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding decisions. Existing approaches typically optimize these components independently using local reconstruction objectives, which fail to account for the varying impact of quantization errors on downstream predictions. Direct optimization of task-level metrics would provide a more faithful objective, but is challenging due to the discontinuous nature of quantization operations and the high computational cost of evaluating their downstream effects. In this work, we derive a Hessian-guided approximation of the output change induced by joint weight and activation quantization. Based on a tractable Fisher approximation, we formulate a unified post-training quantization framework that enables the joint optimization of quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding under a common output-sensitivity objective. The resulting method remains practical for modern large language models and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art transformation and rounding methods across both channel-wise and block-wise quantization settings.
authors: Mads Toftrup, Marco Federici, Boris van Breugel, Paul Whatmough, Markus Nagel
bullets: Targets the limitations of independently optimized, local reconstruction objectives that overlook downstream prediction sensitivity.
Approximates output changes from joint weight and activation quantization using a Hessian and tractable Fisher approximation.
Jointly optimizes quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding under one output-sensitivity objective.
Designed to remain practical for modern large language models.
Consistently outperforms existing transformation and rounding methods across channel-wise and block-wise quantization settings.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Relationship between the KL divergence between the original and quantized model outputs and several layer-local error proxies across linear layers of Llama 3.2 1B Instruct under W4A4 quantization. Conventional reconstruction metrics, such as the output Frobenius norm, exhibit weak correlation with downstream output degradation. Fisher-weighted weight error fails to capture the effect of activation quantization. Output Fisher-weighted error correlates more strongly with the KL divergence, and our proposed Kronecker factorization of the Output Fisher retains this correlation.

Figure 2: WikiText perplexity obtained by several weight scale-setting objectives on Llama 3.2 1B inst. under W4 per-channel quantization, with and without Hadamard transformations. Weighting the quantization error using the proposed Fisher estimate consistently exceeds the best reconstruction objective without requiring hyperparameter tuning.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video world models have enabled the generation of increasingly realistic and interactive virtual environments, opening new possibilities for player-customizable gameplay. Agentic frameworks further advance this direction by decoupling explicit game logic and controllable world representations from visual generation. However, existing approaches support only simple game settings and predefined motion patterns, generalize poorly to unseen environments and characters, and offer limited real-time interactivity. In this paper, we introduce Wizard, an agentic game world model that enables real-time, precise control over character motions while generalizing zero-shot across novel scenes, characters, and actions. To achieve this, we construct a diverse dataset spanning 750 scenes and 178 characters, incorporating skeleton and geometry information as structured representations. We leverage these representations as intermediate proxies to condition a video generation model, together with an adaptive masking mechanism that improves alignment between the conditioning signals and generated video rollouts. Furthermore, we introduce an agentic framework that explicitly maintains and updates game states, allowing players to freely configure their virtual worlds and exercise fine-grained control over character motions while preserving visual quality and gameplay consistency. By combining agentic control with structured proxy-based generation, our framework unlocks new possibilities for player-driven game creation with real-time, generalizable, and mechanically consistent world simulation.
authors: Yuzhe Wu, Zijun Lin, Yeying Jin
bullets: Addresses limited generalization, motion control, and interactivity in existing video world models.
Uses skeleton and geometry representations as structured proxies to condition video generation.
Introduces adaptive masking to better align control signals with generated video rollouts.
Maintains and updates game states through an agentic framework for consistent, configurable gameplay.
Targets real-time, visually coherent world simulation with player-driven character control.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of Wizard. Our method supports diverse gameplay experiences, including world exploration, character summoning, character transformation, and scene manipulation. By combining agentic control with geometric scene proxies and articulated character skeletons, Wizard achieves fine-grained control, zero-shot generalization, and mechanics-consistent gameplay with real-time interaction at 24 FPS.

Figure 2. Dataset Overview and Processing Pipeline. We construct 50.3 hours of data spanning 750 scenes and 178 characters from four complementary sources. Scene geometry and character skeletons are jointly encoded into unified visual proxies, followed by filtering and captioning to produce aligned proxy–video training pairs.

Figure 3. Inference Pipeline of Wizard. (a) Character animation is driven by motions retrieved from a high-quality library and retargeted from compatible source skeletons to the target character’s skeleton. (b) Scene manipulation is performed by a world agent that edits 3D scene geometry and renders visual proxies using OpenGL. (c) State-aware combat control adapts boss behavior to the current game state and enforces rule-based combat mechanics. (d) Real-time video generation is conditioned on visual proxies, reference images, and previously generated frames.

Figure 4. Video Generator Architecture and Character-Aware Adaptive Masking. (a) Visual proxy latents are concatenated with noisy video latents along channels, then combined with first-frame and character-reference tokens along the sequence dimension for DiT processing. (b) Skeleton-derived spatial masks restrict reference attention to the corresponding character regions, binding appearance guidance to character locations.

Figure 5. Visualization of Zero-Shot Generalization and Mechanics-Consistent Gameplay Enabled by Wizard. For each example, reference images are shown on the left, with visual proxies in the top row and the corresponding video rollouts in the bottom row.

papers.abstract: High-quality articulated assets are essential for embodied perception, simulation, and manipulation, yet constructing them at scale remains difficult. Manual annotation and procedural modeling require substantial human effort. Recent agentic systems automate asset construction through program synthesis, but repeat costly reasoning and refinement for every new asset. Our key observation is that assets within a category can share construction logic despite variations in structure and appearance. Agentic synthesis and procedural generation are therefore complementary: agents can construct reusable programs, while procedural execution reuses the resulting logic across many samples. We therefore present RFW-A, which combines the two in a new articulated-asset generation paradigm. Starting from existing articulated programs, RFW-A organizes reusable components and their dependencies into category-level generators. Agents test and refine these generators across sampled configurations and motion states. Once constructed and validated, the generators produce diverse assets through procedural execution with no further model calls or token charges. The estimated API cost of generator authoring averages $10.62, amortizing to $0.05 per asset over 200 assets, versus $1.24 for the sampled per-asset agentic synthesis baseline. Using RFW-A, we built RFW-A-400K, containing over 400K sim-ready articulated assets across more than 500 categories. Experiments show high structural and kinematic validity and stable execution across physics simulators. Beyond asset validity, training with RFW-A-400K improves part-level articulation estimation on seen and unseen categories, while policies trained in simulation with retrieved and program-edited assets transfer zero-shot to real articulated objects.

papers.abstract: Language models often need to maintain multiple contextual variables that evolve independently within a document. Prior work has identified structured representations of individual temporal or contextual quantities, but their joint organization remains less understood. We study this question using controlled documents with independently phased language-switch and topic-change timers. Across ten pretrained checkpoints, both timers are linearly decodable from the same hidden states. Removing a timer-associated centroid plane substantially reduces access to its associated variable while having little effect on the concurrent timer, although the planes are nonorthogonal and contain cross-timer information. Separate timer contributions also explain most reproducible variation among joint-state centroids. These signatures persist from 3 to 51 timer values and across Qwen3 checkpoints from 0.6B to 14B. Schedule position affects continuation probabilities, but the tested centroid displacement produces no consistent timer-specific output effect. Together, these results support approximate factorization based on selective accessibility and approximately additive joint-state geometry in overlapping subspaces.
authors: Xinhe Zhang, Arnau Marin-Llobet
bullets: Both language-switch and topic-change timers are linearly decodable from the same hidden states across ten checkpoints.
Removing one timer’s centroid plane sharply reduces access to that timer while largely preserving access to the other.
Timer planes are nonorthogonal and contain cross-timer information, yet separate timer contributions explain most variation in joint-state centroids.
The findings persist across 3–51 timer values and Qwen3 models ranging from 0.6B to 14B parameters.
Centroid displacement did not consistently produce timer-specific output effects, limiting evidence about causal behavioral influence.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes internal factorization and selective accessibility of concurrent variables in pretrained LLMs; relevant to LLM representation structure.
papers.title: Factorized Representations of Concurrent Temporal Variables in Pretrained Language Models
papers.tldr: Pretrained language models approximately factorize independently evolving temporal variables into selectively accessible, additive representations, even when those representations overlap.

papers.abstract: Looping in transformer models reuses weights by repeatedly applying the same transformer, or parts of it, making the model deeper without increasing its parameter count. Whether looping is useful depends on which constraint dominates: model size, training compute, or autoregressive inference efficiency. We study these trade-offs jointly in dense decoder-only transformers trained from scratch, varying which parts of the model are looped, how many loops are applied, and how information is passed between loops. Our experiments span models with up to 1B parameters, trained on up to 155B tokens with up to $1.07\times10^{21}$ FLOPs and 32 loops. We find that looping the full transformer generally gives the strongest quality at a fixed parameter budget, whereas looping a middle block of layers gives a better return when training FLOPs are constrained. Adding loops is not uniformly beneficial: gains eventually saturate, reverse, or become unstable. This motivates asking whether forcing every loop to use the same weights limits the benefit of deeper looping. We address this by adding small loop-specific low-rank adapters that improve quality, with larger gains as more loops are added. Looped transformers also suffer a decoding slowdown proportional to the number of loops. Parallel Loop Transformers address this by passing hidden states between loops across adjacent token positions, allowing loop stages to run concurrently. However, in our experiments the original formulation does not consistently retain the quality gains of ordinary looping. We find that preserving the current-token embedding and separately normalizing it and the previous-token hidden state before combining them recovers strong performance across model scales and training budgets. Together, these results show that effective looping requires matching the design to the resource constraint and inference setting.
authors: Chanakya Ekbote, Artidoro Pagnoni, Devendra Singh Sachan, Shruti Bhosale, Mike Lewis, Maryam Fazel-Zarandi, Shashank Rajput, Sujan Kumar Gonugondla
bullets: Full-model looping generally gives the best quality at a fixed parameter budget, while looping a middle layer block is more compute-efficient during training.
Increasing the number of loops eventually yields diminishing, reversed, or unstable gains.
Small loop-specific low-rank adapters improve quality, with larger benefits as more loops are added.

Looping slows autoregressive decoding; Parallel Loop Transformers enable concurrent loop execution but need separate normalization and preservation of the current-token embedding to recover strong performance.
The study evaluates dense decoder-only transformers across model sizes, training budgets, and up to 32 loops.

papers.selection_reason: Studies looping in decoder-only transformer architectures, a novel LLM architecture with explicit parameter, compute, and inference efficiency trade-offs.
papers.title: How to Loop Your Transformer: Loop Scaling, Specialization, and Parallel Inference
papers.tldr: Looped transformers can improve quality without adding parameters, but their benefits depend on the resource constraint and require specialized designs for efficient inference.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong zero-shot generalization but remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Existing adversarial fine-tuning methods often use pre-trained model guidance to preserve image--text alignment while improving robustness. Our analysis of visual representation drift reveals complementary limitations of two representative forms of guidance. Matching visual features provides broad coverage by constraining all directions equally, but lacks semantic emphasis. Matching prediction distributions prioritizes semantically relevant directions, but remains limited by the candidate texts and prediction probabilities. These limitations can hinder preservation of pre-trained image--text relationships and degrade zero-shot performance. To address these issues, we propose Textual Response-Aware Guidance (TRAG), which constrains visual representation drift using the pre-trained text encoder's responses to local variations in input embeddings. Specifically, TRAG constructs anchor-level constraints from the response directions and magnitudes around semantic anchors, then aggregates them using pre-trained image--anchor relevance, yielding an image-adaptive constraint. Extensive experiments across architectures and tasks demonstrate state-of-the-art clean and robust performance. Further analysis shows that TRAG helps preserve pre-trained image--text relationships.
authors: Yubo Cui, Xianchao Guan, Zheng Zhang
bullets: VLMs are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, while robustness fine-tuning can damage pretrained image–text alignment and zero-shot performance.
Feature matching covers visual directions broadly but lacks semantic focus; prediction matching is semantic but limited by candidate texts and probabilities.
TRAG builds anchor-level constraints from the text encoder’s response directions and magnitudes to local embedding variations.
These constraints are aggregated using image–anchor relevance, producing image-adaptive guidance.
Experiments across architectures and tasks report state-of-the-art clean and robust performance, with better preservation of pretrained image–text relationships.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of TRAG. We construct anchor-level constraints Wj from the text encoder’s local response directions and magnitudes under a fixed-budget criterion. Pre-trained image–anchor relevance on clean images weights their aggregation. After global trace normalization, Mx constrains visual representation drift during adversarial fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Large language model serving is limited by facility power. Energy per token determines how many tokens a datacenter can serve, while a latency target bounds how quickly each user receives them. During decode, every weight is read from memory for every generated token. Batching amortizes this read across users but makes no individual user faster. Speculative decoding does: a drafter proposes several future tokens, and the target model verifies them in a single forward pass that reuses the same weight read. Because every drafted token must be verified whether or not it is accepted, the energy speculation saves depends on how many drafted tokens are accepted. This saving is hard to pin down. It varies across target models from different attention families and across drafting schemes, and it depends on the text being served. Every drafter we evaluate accepts fewer tokens on conversation than on code, and every trained drafter accepts fewer on Romansh, a low-resource language, than on English. We measure speculative decoding under production serving conditions (SGLang, CUDA graphs enabled) on H100 and H200 GPUs, at batch sizes up to 64 across 5 corpora. On dense models, verification, not drafting, dominates the energy cost. The saving shrinks as the batch grows, because batching has already shared the weight read that speculation would divide among the accepted tokens. At large batch sizes, block drafters push verification past the balance point between arithmetic and memory traffic into the compute-bound regime, where the saving becomes a loss, and a drafter with low acceptance raises energy per token. Meeting a tighter latency target with speculation then costs additional energy. Larger batches lower energy per token without speculation. Speculation adds to that saving only when acceptance is high, and on the model we tested it leaves little headroom for latency-preserving DVFS.
authors: Bole Ma, Ayesha Afzal, Jan Eitzinger, Harald Koestler, Gerhard Wellein
bullets: Energy savings depend on accepted drafted tokens because every proposal still requires verification.
Acceptance varies by model, drafting scheme, and text: it is lower for conversation than code and for Romansh than English.
Measurements on H100/H200 GPUs with SGLang show verification dominates energy for dense models.
Larger batches already amortize weight reads, shrinking speculation’s benefit; aggressive drafting can make verification compute-bound and energy-inefficient.
Speculation provides little room for latency-preserving DVFS on the evaluated model.

papers.title: Only Accepted Tokens Count: An Energy Accounting of Speculative Decoding Under Latency Targets
