papers.abstract: Building general game agents requires both high-level task reasoning and low-latency action control in rapidly changing visual environments. These capabilities favor models with substantially different computational profiles, making them difficult to realize within a single model. In this work, we present TaskFrame, a hierarchical planner-controller framework that connects task-level planning with frame-level keyboard-and-mouse control. A vision-language task planner decomposes a high-level goal into an ordered sequence of atomic instructions and is optimized through supervised learning and dependency-aware GRPO. The hidden states of special goal tokens that terminate each atomic instruction provide continuous goal embeddings that are cached and reused across control steps. A causal Transformer controller combines the embedding of the active goal with recent observations to predict discrete keyboard and mouse-button actions and continuous camera motion at every game step. We train the system in three stages: planner training, controller pretraining, and joint alignment. Experiments in Minecraft show that TaskFrame is competitive with general-purpose vision-language models on instruction decomposition, and that in closed-loop evaluation the agent achieves a higher combat success rate than the evaluated baselines.
authors: Guangzhi Wang, Junfu Pu, Yiran Wang, Xingyilang Yin, Honghao Chen, Cheng Cheng, Lingen Li, Yinan Zhou, Jiarui Wu, Yinuo Jiang, Hongbo Jin, Xiaodong Cun, Ying Shan
bullets: Uses a vision-language planner to decompose goals into ordered atomic instructions.
Caches hidden states from goal-ending tokens as continuous embeddings for downstream control.
A causal Transformer controller predicts keyboard, mouse-button, and camera actions from goals and recent observations.
Trained through planner training, controller pretraining, and joint alignment.
In Minecraft, it is competitive on instruction decomposition and achieves higher closed-loop combat success than evaluated baselines.

papers.abstract: Flow policies are among the strongest robot controllers and are well suited to modelling multimodal action distributions. Our analysis shows that the continuous-action distributions of the studied flow policies are well approximated by Gaussians. We propose the Gaussian Action Readout (GAR), which replaces a flow policy's final layer with a Gaussian readout trained on just 0.02% of eligible states, while keeping the rest of the network frozen. It samples with one action-network pass, gives closed-form likelihoods, and achieves near-teacher task success at up to twice the inference speed.

GAR replaces only the final layer with a Gaussian readout and freezes the rest of the network.
Training uses just 0.02% of eligible states.
One action-network pass enables faster sampling and closed-form likelihoods.
The method retains near-teacher task success while reaching up to twice the inference speed.

papers.abstract: Autonomous highway driving for heavy-duty trucks is a challenging control problem. The greater mass, dimensions and intricate dynamics increase the requirements for cooperation from surrounding traffic in critical maneuvers, requiring a careful balance between safety constraints and efficient long-horizon decision making. Model Predictive Control (MPC) provides rigorous constraint satisfaction but relies on terminal cost which can limit its effectiveness at short, computationally affordable horizons. Reinforcement Learning (RL) captures long-term driving behavior but offers no constraint guarantees and tends toward overly conservative policies when trained under sparse collision penalties. In this paper, we propose a hybrid MPC and RL framework for highway driving in autonomous trucks, where a finite-horizon MPC, solved via dynamic programming, uses a pre-trained RL model for terminal cost estimation. We evaluate the framework in a simulation environment with reactive surrounding traffic and compare it against pure MPC with zero terminal cost, rollout with terminal cost estimation using a base policy, and pure RL. Results show that the hybrid approach achieves zero collisions with the lowest cost of any configuration.
authors: Hooman Hamze, Benjamin Houshmand, Deepthi Pathare, Erik B\"orve, Morteza Haghir Chehreghani, Nikolce Murgovski
bullets: Targets the challenge of balancing safety constraints with efficient long-horizon decisions for heavy-duty trucks.
Combines finite-horizon MPC, solved via dynamic programming, with a pre-trained RL model that estimates terminal costs.
Evaluated in simulation with reactive surrounding traffic against zero-terminal-cost MPC, base-policy rollouts, and pure RL.
The hybrid approach achieved zero collisions and the lowest cost among the evaluated configurations.

papers.abstract: We revisit advantage estimation in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and observe that any token-level advantage admits a two-stage factorization: a \emph{sample-level baselining} step that converts scalar verifier rewards into a comparable sequence-level signal, and a \emph{token-level credit assignment} step that distributes that signal over the trajectory. Existing estimators typically address only one of these stages: affine baselines preserve the shape of each task's reward law, so heavy tails and binary cliffs propagate into the gradient, while token-level credit rules tie the size of each token's update to raw confidence scales and need not conserve the total credit issued by the verifier. We propose \textbf{TACE} (Two-stage Advantage and Credit Estimation), a two-stage estimator that addresses both stages. At stage~(S1), we replace linear standardization with a one-dimensional optimal-transport map to a standard normal, which gives a common population reward law across tasks and caps finite-sample outliers deterministically. At stage~(S2), we rank-calibrate a stop-gradient evidence contrast within each trajectory and renormalize the clipped token weights to have mean one, so credit is redistributed across tokens while its total mass and sign are conserved. We prove population-level inter-task moment equity, a deterministic tail bound, and mass-conservation, boundedness, and sign-anchoring properties that affine baselines and unnormalized token weights do not satisfy. On a multimodal reasoning suite, TACE obtains the strongest results on a majority of the benchmarks but does not dominate every setting.
authors: Lang Chen, Zongxin Xu, Borui Wang, Anran Liu, Shitong Chen
bullets: Existing GRPO advantage estimators can propagate heavy-tailed or binary reward scales across tasks.
TACE uses optimal transport to map scalar rewards to a standard normal, aligning reward distributions and deterministically capping finite-sample outliers.
It rank-calibrates within-trajectory evidence contrasts and normalizes clipped token weights to conserve total credit.
The method provides inter-task moment equity, tail bounds, mass conservation, boundedness, and sign anchoring.
On a multimodal reasoning suite, TACE performs best on most benchmarks but not in every setting.

Stage (S2), ours (starting from the evidence ratio of Yang et al., 2026): runs πθ under non-privileged (PS) and privileged (PT ) contexts, rank-calibrates the per-token log-evidence within the trajectory, and applies a sign-anchored, mean-one (mass-preserving) magnitude weight wi,t. The composed token advantage Âi,t = Ai · wi,t plugs into the standard GRPO clipped surrogate.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are now used as zero-shot judges of image quality, but their color judgments are rarely tested with colorimetric ground truth. We present a five-task benchmark based on the CIE colorimetric framework: AWB pair judgment, skin-tone bias direction, CCT estimation, CIE Delta E 2000 pair ordering, and color naming under changing illuminants. We test eight MLLM endpoints, including four Qwen3-VL variants, GLM-4.5V, GPT-5.4, Claude-Opus-4.7, and Gemini-3.1-Pro. The models often solve coarse binary AWB judgments, but they remain weak on numeric CCT estimation and on some fine color-difference judgments. On ColorChecker-24 stimuli, the three closed-weight frontier models reach CCT MAE of 715-1056 K, compared with 1358-2133 K for the five open-weight models. A non-ColorChecker control shows that this advantage is partly template-dependent. The results suggest that current MLLMs have useful color words and coarse visual priors, but their color judgments are not reliably calibrated to CIE-computable color differences.

bullets: Introduces five tasks covering white-balance judgment, skin-tone bias, CCT estimation, Delta E 2000 ordering, and color naming under changing illuminants.

Models often succeed on coarse binary AWB judgments but struggle with CCT estimation and fine color-difference comparisons.
Closed-weight frontier models show lower CCT errors than open-weight models on ColorChecker-24, though the advantage is partly template-dependent.
Overall, useful color vocabulary and visual priors do not ensure reliable calibration to CIE-computable color differences.

papers.abstract: Bimanual dexterous manipulation requires continuous coordination of wrist motion, finger contact, and object motion. Human videos provide rich manipulation experience. Using this experience for robot control requires aligning human poses with robot commands and accounting for embodiment-specific kinematics and contact dynamics. We present AcrossDEX 1.0, a learning system that connects human motion pretraining, simulation-based expert learning, robot demonstration collection, and visual closed-loop execution. Pretraining on HOT3D Aria predicts one second of bimanual motion from five images and thirty annotated hand states over the preceding second. Robot adaptation preserves the visual encoder, temporal backbone, and wrist parameters. Shared wrist representations, separate finger fields, and validity masks support both six-channel Inspire hands and sixteen-joint Allegro hands. The robot policy predicts sixty control targets from frontal images, command history, and task conditions. It executes a prefix and replans from updated observations. We compare direct regression, diffusion, and flow matching on lid opening and return and closed-lid object reorientation. Direct regression achieves success rates of 40.6\% for opening and return, 100.0\% for Inspire reorientation, and 93.3\% for Allegro reorientation. Flow matching achieves 90.0\% on Allegro reorientation. Paired comparisons further show that constraining replanning with the previous plan improves the continuous execution of generative policies. These results demonstrate a common adaptation pipeline for two hand embodiments and highlight the roles of contact coordination and action-chunk continuity.
authors: Xiaoyu Yang, Nan Wu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of aligning human motion with robot commands while handling embodiment-specific kinematics and contact dynamics.

Evaluates direct regression, diffusion, and flow matching on lid manipulation and object reorientation tasks.

Reports up to 100.0% success on Inspire reorientation and 93.3% with direct regression or 90.0% with flow matching on Allegro reorientation; prior-plan-constrained replanning improves generative-policy continuity.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained action annotations can support skill reuse and compositional generalization in robot policies. However, robot datasets typically provide task-level instructions without subtask annotations. Although some include subtask labels, inconsistent formats and conventions hinder cross-source joint training. We propose RoboAtom-Data, which adds unified, time-aligned atomic-action annotations to existing data from multiple sources, covering 1.45 million trajectories, 6.88 million skill-labeled segments, and 16,882.1 hours. Our pipeline combines a unified protocol, large-scale manual annotation, propagation across repeated executions with the same ordered skill sequence, and multi-stage quality control. We evaluate the dataset through automatic atomic-action annotation and robot control. We construct RoboAtom-Bench to standardize evaluation of skill recognition and temporal boundary localization. Trained on the annotated data, RoboAtom-Anno achieves better automatic annotation performance than all evaluated open- and closed-source models on both RoboAtom-Bench and the external WGO-Bench. For robot control, atomic-action supervision paired with hierarchical execution improves task success over task-level baselines on LIBERO-Long, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin. We will release the data, benchmark, model, and construction pipeline to support further research on skill-level robot learning.

papers.abstract: Monocular RGB tracking is useful for robots operating near people, but perception errors affect binary stop/proceed decisions in ways that geometric accuracy metrics do not capture. We examine how much decision error arises from the safety rule versus perception. We prove that lateral-only distance is a lower bound on planar distance: with accurate positions, it cannot miss dangers identified by the planar rule, but it produces unnecessary stops. We introduce a two-factor Shapley attribution separating rule and perception contributions, and further distinguish missed detections from localization errors. Experiments use ETH and UCY pedestrian videos with simulated stationary robots, disjoint calibration and evaluation pedestrians, and time-block bootstrap intervals. Across 898 pedestrians in three scenes, the lateral rule missed no dangers on annotated positions but achieved only 5.6-31.9% stop precision. In two scenes with RGB perception, calibrated ground-plane localization achieved 0.59 m and 0.51 m planar RMSE, compared with 1.72 m and 1.39 m for a geometric baseline and 0.81 m and 0.68 m for calibrated Depth Anything V2. Detection recall of 0.43 and 0.26 made missed detections the leading source of missed danger. A two-standard-deviation safety margin with ground-plane localization matched or improved on the lateral rule's missed-danger rate in all eight scene-threshold settings and reduced unnecessary stops in seven. All robot interactions are simulated, and outcomes are offline decision classifications, not demonstrations of collision avoidance.
authors: Abdulahi Taiwo, Chijioke Cyriacus Ekechi
bullets: Lateral-only distance is a conservative lower bound on planar distance: it missed no dangers with accurate positions but caused many unnecessary stops.
A two-factor Shapley framework attributes decision errors to the safety rule versus perception, separating missed detections from localization errors.

Low detection recall was the leading contributor to missed dangers in RGB-perception experiments.
A two-standard-deviation safety margin matched or improved missed-danger rates in all tested settings and reduced unnecessary stops in seven of eight.

papers.abstract: Video generation is shifting from end-to-end synthesis toward agentic generation, where planning, tool use, and feedback enable coherent, controllable multi-shot videos. In parallel, video world models provide action-conditioned observations and predicted futures, serving as interactive environments for agents. We study their intersection through the agent harness: an executable runtime that constructs context, exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and manages budgets around video models. This report examines three directions. First, agentic video generation, where harnesses coordinate scripting, shot planning, asset management, production, and editing, alongside the evaluation challenges of these systems. Second, agentic world modeling, where harnesses mediate observation, control, execution, and state. We discuss hybrid designs in which game engines or agent-written programs maintain world state while video models render observations, and how agents and world models can mutually evaluate and improve one another. Third, recursive self-improvement (RSI) in video model development, distinguishing output revisions, updates to harness state, generator parameters, and evaluators, and changes to the improvement procedure itself. We identify how these improvements feed back into subsequent development. Across these directions, we analyze essential agent capabilities, including audiovisual perception, long-horizon planning, memory, code-based interaction, feedback-guided control, skill reuse, and multi-agent coordination. We conclude with challenges in autonomous video production, lifelong memory, programmable hybrid control, autonomous model development, provenance, cost accounting, and evaluation linking video quality and task performance to sustained improvements in models and harnesses.
authors: Liaoyuan Fan, Yuhao Zheng, Dongxing Mao, Hangyu Ran, Siyuan Hu, Weijia Mao, Rui Zhao, Weijia Wu, Guian Fang, Yanzhe Chen, Zeyu Zhu, Yuxin Jiang, Yiren Song, Yuchao Gu, Junchao Yi, Qi Hu, Dan Kong, Alex Jinpeng Wang, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Mike Zheng Shou, Wei Liu

Key open challenges include long-horizon planning, memory, provenance, cost accounting, hybrid control, and evaluation tied to sustained improvement.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) increasingly rely on axial attention mechanisms, but despite their empirical success, the theoretical properties of axial attention remain largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we extend the Single Location Regression framework introduced in Marion et al. [2025] to 2D structured data, in order to study sparse information settings where a target depends on a small number of tokens. We formulate an analytically tractable axial attention-type predictor and rigorously analyze its statistical properties and training dynamics. We prove that under a specific asymptotic regime and with knowledge of the underlying oracle parameters, our predictor achieves Bayes optimality, whereas a class of semi-linear simplifications strictly fails to do so, underlining the role of the inner non-linearity. We prove that for a specific temperature scaling, Projected Gradient Descent converges globally to the optimal oracle parameters. Extensive numerical experiments validate our theoretical findings and highlight the critical role of inverse temperature scheduling in empirical convergence.
authors: Andrei-Tiberiu Pantea, Aymeric Dieuleveut
bullets: Extends Single Location Regression to 2D structured data for analyzing sparse-information settings.

Proves global convergence of Projected Gradient Descent under a specific temperature scaling; experiments support the theory and the role of inverse-temperature scheduling.

papers.abstract: Given a set of procedural steps, Video Step Grounding (VSG) aims to identify which steps occur in a video and localize when they are performed. Existing methods are either offline, requiring access to the full video before making predictions, or online, but relying on fixed-length video segments producing noisy, over-segmented outputs. In this work, we propose Hierarchical Step Decomposition (HSD), a training-free framework for online VSG that leverages the semantic understanding capabilities of Large Multimodal Models. HSD addresses two central challenges in online grounding: constructing semantically coherent temporal segments from a streaming video, and bridging the semantic gap between coarse procedural step descriptions and visual observations. To construct elementary temporal units, HSD incrementally groups incoming segments into semantically consistent events, using an anchor caption that is continuously validated against the visual stream. Based on these events, we perform zero-shot procedural step classification and selectively refine uncertain predictions by decomposing candidate steps into finegrained substeps that capture more nuanced visual evidence. By operating on semantically coherent events rather than every fixed-length segment, HSD reduces redundant computation and produces more stable predictions. Experiments on HT-Step, Ego4D Goal-Step, and CrossTask show that HSD substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods, overall achieving better step recognition, more accurate temporal localization, and faster inference.
authors: Long Zhou, Luca Zanella, Paolo Rota, Massimiliano Mancini, Elisa Ricci
bullets: Targets online grounding without requiring the full video in advance.
Incrementally groups incoming segments into semantically consistent events using continuously validated anchor captions.
Performs zero-shot classification of procedural steps with Large Multimodal Models.
Decomposes uncertain candidate steps into fine-grained substeps for better visual alignment.
On HT-Step, Ego4D Goal-Step, and CrossTask, it improves recognition, temporal localization, and inference speed over prior methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of HSD. Given an input video V , the Online Semantic Event Construction module incrementally builds each event Ej from fixed-duration segments using a frozen LMM ΦLMM. The first segment of Ej is captioned as γanc, and each arriving segment is appended to Ej if its continuity score ϵsame exceeds ϵnew ; otherwise, Ej is terminated and a new event is initialized. For each completed event Ej , the Zero-Shot Event-to-Step Grounding module predicts a probability distribution pj over procedural steps. If its entropy Hj falls below threshold η, the most likely step is predicted. Otherwise, Hierarchical Step Refinement decomposes the top-k steps into substeps, re-evaluates Ej , aggregates substep scores into psubj , and outputs the final prediction âj .

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can now process hour-long videos, making extended multi-turn dialogue over a single video a natural mode of use. Sustaining such a dialogue requires more than answering each question in isolation: the model must retrieve and reuse information established earlier in the conversation, both what it has seen and what it has said, an ability we term in-context video memory. Existing video QA benchmarks leave this ability unmeasured: their questions are mutually independent, never reference one another, and each is answerable from the video alone, so nothing ever requires carrying information across turns. We introduce VideoMemBench, in which each sample pairs a single video with a long multi-turn dialogue, whose turns are connected by typed cross-turn dependencies: an Episodic Dependency refers back to a visual episode described in an earlier turn, probing memory of what the model has seen, while an Answer Dependency builds on the model's own earlier answer, probing memory of what the model has said. Every dependency is verified considering two properties: 1) necessity, meaning the question cannot be answered without its earlier turns, and 2) non-leakage, meaning the question does not restate the information from its earlier turns. To enforce these properties, we design a construction pipeline with three LLM roles: a planner, a generator, and a judger, with each dialogue reviewed by human experts. VideoMemBench comprises 326 videos with 2,476 turns, of which 1,387 depend on earlier turns, including multi-parent dependencies and long-range call-back. Among over 20 evaluated open- and closed-source MLLMs, Claude Opus 5 performs the best with an overall score of only 45.7\%, highlighting the challenge of in-context video memory. Our dataset and evaluation are released.
authors: Zhengdong Hu, Chao Wang, Kaituo Feng, Huanjin Yao, Mingfei Lu, Hehe Fan, Yi Yang
bullets: Evaluates in-context video memory rather than independent video question answering.
Tests two dependency types: recall of earlier visual episodes and reuse of the model’s own prior answers.
Ensures dependencies are necessary and non-leaking, using planner, generator, and judger roles plus human review.
Contains 326 videos and 2,476 dialogue turns, with 1,387 turns dependent on earlier turns.
Across 20+ open- and closed-source MLLMs, the best reported overall score is only 45.7%, underscoring the difficulty.

figures.caption: Figure 2 The VideoMemBench construction pipeline. Starting from a curated video pool, a planner specifies turn intents and a typed dependency graph. A generator constructs the dialogue turn by turn, while a judger checks necessity, non-leakage, and visual grounding, returning failed turns for regeneration. Completed dialogues are checked against the plan and reviewed by human experts.

Figure 1 Example of VideoMemBench with cross-turn dependencies: Independent turns (e.g., T1, T8) establish visually grounded facts; dependent turns refer back to earlier turns through expressions such as “the scene from T1” or “the target from T1”, without restating earlier content. An Answer Dependency (e.g., T3, T4) requires recalling what the model has said : each builds on the answer produced at an earlier turn.

papers.abstract: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning remains challenging in stochastic long-horizon settings, where compounding value estimation errors hinder reliable goal reaching. While prior methods have sought to address this challenge through various approaches, a key challenge remains path mirage, where agents overcommit to spuriously successful trajectories in offline datasets induced by stochasticity, often leading to failure on difficult tasks. To address this issue, we propose Branch-aware Graph Planning (BGP), which captures stochastic branching structures by identifying high-variability points as graph nodes and designing goal-conditioned edges with segmented learning to avoid unreliable branches and reduce unnecessary stochasticity along paths. As a result, BGP enables reliable goal reaching even in highly stochastic long-horizon environments, and experiments on diverse OGBench tasks show that it substantially outperforms prior state-of-the-art offline goal-conditioned RL methods. Our implementation is available at https://umlic.github.io/papers/BGP/.
authors: Junhyeon Bae, Jaebak Hwang, Gwanwoo Choi, Minung Kim, Seungyul Han
bullets: Targets path mirages: spurious successes in offline data that cause agents to commit to unreliable routes.
Represents high-variability points as nodes in a branching graph.
Learns goal-conditioned graph edges with segmentation to avoid unreliable branches and reduce unnecessary stochasticity.
Experiments on diverse OGBench tasks show reliable goal reaching and substantial improvements over prior methods.
Scope: designed for stochastic, long-horizon offline goal-conditioned environments.

papers.abstract: Vision--language models (VLMs) are tested for fine-grained understanding with image--text matching probes, a model must prefer the correct image or caption over handcrafted negative. In retrieval, the correct item must beat thousands of alternatives. We measure how these two evaluation methods relate by using two probing benchmarks, \svo{} and SugarCrepe, for retrieval tasks. For 100 image and caption queries we judge the top-10 retrievals from full dataset of six VLMs, with human annotators and an LLM assessor. We than compare how well models rank pool of items on the same queries, while changing only where the negatives comes from: the benchmark, a random draw, or the judged-incorrect retrievals of other models. On \svo{} the accuracy of retrieving a positive over handcrafted negatives is significantly higher than for retrieved ones (the correct item is preferred in 85\% against 77\% of the time). Using pool of ten retrieved negatives leads to same accuracy as when one uses pool of 200 to 430 random negatives. On SugarCrepe the order is reversed: its handcrafted negatives are harder than the retrieved ones. Incomplete relevance labels explain most of the low retrieval scores on \svo{}, where the top-ranked item is correct for 54--90\% of the queries under human labels against 6--21\% under the benchmark's labels. However, we detect no association between passing the probe for a query and retrieving a correct item first. The LLM assessor o3 agrees with individual annotators ($\kappa$ 0.57--0.61) slightly less than they agree with each other (0.64--0.68).
authors: Ivana Be\v{n}ov\'a, Michal Gregor, Mari\'an \v{S}imko
bullets: The study compares two probing benchmarks, SVO and SugarCrepe, with retrieval over full datasets for six vision–language models and 100 image/caption queries.
On SVO, handcrafted-negative accuracy is higher than accuracy against retrieved negatives (85% vs. 77%); ten retrieved negatives are as challenging as 200–430 random negatives.
On SugarCrepe, handcrafted negatives are harder than retrieved negatives, showing that probe difficulty depends on negative construction.
Incomplete SVO relevance labels substantially depress retrieval scores: human labels identify the top result as correct for 54–90% of queries, versus 6–21% under benchmark labels.
Passing a probe does not predict retrieving the correct item first; the LLM assessor shows moderate agreement with human annotators.

papers.title: It Takes Two to Probe, Thousands to Retrieve: Putting Vision--Language Probes to the Retrieval Test

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models can both generate and understand images within a single set of weights, offering an opportunity to use image synthesis as training supervision for visual comprehension. However, existing visual chain-of-thought methods rely on human-annotated helper images during training and require slow image generation at test time. We present SelfThinker, the first self-evolving framework that turns a unified model's self-generated visual thoughts into stronger understanding without human image annotations. Given a visual problem, SelfThinker samples candidate helper images from its generation pathway and uses its frozen understanding pathway to score each candidate via conditional pointwise mutual information. High-utility visual thoughts then refine the generator via flow matching and serve as privileged teacher context for on-policy self-distillation. At inference, SelfThinker reasons directly from the original image in text without generating intermediate images. Although trained only on small synthetic visual-search and navigation datasets, SelfThinker transfers broadly to natural-image and spatial benchmarks, raising the seven-benchmark average of ThinkMorph-7B from 52.7 to 64.0 (+11.3 points). Controlled image-perturbation probes further show that SelfThinker surpasses ThinkMorph-7B by up to 40.4 points and its pretrained BAGEL-7B backbone by up to 23.2 points across fine-grained and spatial perception tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhangquanchen/SelfThinker.
authors: Zhangquan Chen, Ruqi Huang
bullets: Addresses reliance on human-annotated helper images and costly image generation at test time.
Samples candidate visual thoughts and scores them with the frozen understanding pathway using conditional pointwise mutual information.
Uses high-utility thoughts for flow-matching generator refinement and on-policy self-distillation.
Trained on small synthetic visual-search and navigation datasets, it transfers to natural-image and spatial benchmarks.
Raises ThinkMorph-7B’s seven-benchmark average from 52.7 to 64.0, while inference avoids intermediate image generation.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of SelfThinker . Verify: the frozen Understanding pathway scores each candidate by its log-likelihood utility, calibrates the acceptance threshold against thoughts from other problems, and selects the top verified thought under the ground-truth answer or majority vote. Evolve: the verified thought is distilled into the Student Understanding pathway via on-policy token-level JSD distillation from the EMA Teacher (SelfThinker), supported by flow-matching generator refinement (SelfThinker -Gen). No human image annotation is used

papers.abstract: Tumor delineation is required for radiotherapy planning, yet automatic segmentation is limited by errors, predominantly false positives, that distort dose and increase editing time. The radiology report accompanies the scan and localizes disease at the suborgan level, but existing text-promptable models condition on short referring phrases, and most operate in 2D. We present RepConTUR, a single native-3D early-fusion multimodal model that conditions volumetric abdominal tumor segmentation on the narrative report. We extend AbdomenAtlas 3.0 to a suborgan-level promptable segmentation dataset and generate report-based VQA pairs, yielding four report-derived tasks on the same annotations: referring segmentation (RES), report-grounded segmentation (GSEG), report generation (RRG), and visual question answering (VQA). We train RepConTUR, comprising a 3D CT encoder, an early-fusion language model, and a native-3D segmentation module, jointly on the four tasks. Across liver, kidney and pancreas, RepConTUR attains the highest Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), instance-wise precision, and detection F1 among the text-promptable baselines, and adding the report raises mean precision while leaving recall comparable. Against two vision-only specialists, nnU-Net and the report-supervised R-Super, RepConTUR attains the highest value on every in-domain metric for liver and pancreas and the highest mean DSC, recall, precision, and detection F1 over the four out-of-distribution public cohorts. Ablations indicate that conditioning on the narrative report raises detection F1 from 0.499 to 0.528 within the same model, that joint GSEG training raises RES F1 from 0.450 to 0.482, and that the native-3D segmentation module raises GSEG F1 from 0.139 to 0.528 over its 2D counterpart. Code is available at https://github.com/Oncosoft-Research/RepConTUR.
authors: Seunghwan Lee, Sangjoon Park, Jongmin Lee, Yoon Jo Kim, Wonyoung Cho, Jin Sung Kim, Han Joo Chae
bullets: Addresses false-positive tumor delineation errors that increase radiotherapy-planning dose distortion and editing time.
Combines a 3D CT encoder, early-fusion language model, and native-3D segmentation module, jointly trained on segmentation, report generation, and VQA-related tasks.
Extends AbdomenAtlas 3.0 with suborgan-level report-promptable annotations and four report-derived tasks: RES, GSEG, RRG, and VQA.
Outperforms text-promptable baselines on DSC, instance precision, and detection F1 across liver, kidney, and pancreas; report conditioning improves mean precision with comparable recall.
Ablations show gains from report conditioning, joint GSEG training, and native-3D segmentation; evaluation focuses on abdominal tumors and specified public cohorts.

papers.abstract: Effective multi-domain adaptation of large language models requires prioritizing relevant domain knowledge while minimizing interference from irrelevant domains. Existing approaches commonly use Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to train a separate adapter for each domain and combine these adapters within one model. However, they either weight adapters equally regardless of the input domain or dynamically weight adapters while still activating all of them including irrelevant ones. Additionally, while efficient, their low-rank structure limits performance. In contrast, upcycling is a model expansion method that adds experts and a router to a dense Transformer layer offering larger capacity than LoRA approaches. In this paper, we propose Domain-Specialized Upcycling (DS-Upcycling) for multi-domain adaptation. We introduce a new domain-aware supervision that allows the router to effectively learn to distinguish domains by selecting the appropriate experts. During fine-tuning on each new domain, we update only the corresponding expert and router while freezing all other parameters. Experiments show that our method achieves the highest average performance across the adapted domains compared to baselines while retaining general performance. With just 256 examples per domain for router supervision, DS-Upcycling achieves 90-98% routing accuracy after adaptation compared with 43-70% for routers trained without our approach.
authors: Mingzi Cao, Xi Wang, Nikolaos Aletras
bullets: Targets interference from irrelevant domains and limited capacity in LoRA-based multi-domain adaptation.
Expands Transformer layers with experts and a router rather than relying solely on low-rank adapters.
Uses domain-aware router supervision and updates only the relevant expert and router during each domain’s fine-tuning.
Achieves the highest average performance across adapted domains among the compared baselines while retaining general performance.
With 256 supervision examples per domain, routing accuracy reaches 90–98%, versus 43–70% without the proposed supervision.

papers.abstract: Robot foundation models increasingly rely on flow-based action generation for general-purpose manipulation, yet the generated actions are not guaranteed to satisfy physical constraints such as joint limits and collision avoidance. This problem is especially challenging when the feasible set cannot be described analytically and is accessible only through black-box feasibility oracles. We study this practical oracle-only setting and propose an oracle-guided differentiable safeguard for safe flow-matching robot policies. The safeguard uses binary feasibility queries to correct unsafe updates in the forward pass, while extracting local boundary information to provide constraint-aware learning signals in the backward pass. Combined with discrete-time flow matching, the same safeguard is used during training and inference, enabling forward--backward aligned policy learning without explicit or differentiable constraint models. Experiments on obstacle-aware robotic manipulation demonstrate 100% constraint satisfaction while preserving task performance.
authors: Jianming Ma, Rongjun Jin, Yizhi Chen, Yue Gao
bullets: Addresses unsafe action generation when feasibility is available only through binary black-box oracles.
Corrects unsafe forward updates and extracts local boundary information for constraint-aware backward learning.
Uses the same safeguard during training and inference with discrete-time flow matching.
Obstacle-aware manipulation experiments achieve 100% constraint satisfaction while preserving task performance.

papers.abstract: The way software gets built is changing dramatically. AI agents now create pull requests, select dependencies, refactor codebases, interpret test failures, and execute infrastructure changes across the entire Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). AI agents are autonomous team members, but unlike human engineers, they are ephemeral - their reasoning, decisions, and tool calls vanish the moment the session ends. Modern Security incidents involving intent mismatch or injection are becoming increasingly common - forcing us to address AI Agents as an insider threat. No widely adopted standard yet enables agentic provenance and governance and its obvious that you can't hold an ephemeral process accountable. The git log was designed for human commits. It shows what changed. It does not show what an AI agent did, which model it used, which tools it called, or whether anyone was accountable for the outcome. Every governance framework, every audit trail, every compliance control in the SDLC was built around one assumption: a human made the decision. That assumption no longer holds. This shift introduces 3 main procedural problems (not addressing scale) - Supply-chain vector - The agentic coder is software, so it is a supply-chain security risk. Policy guardrails - How to ensure the agentic coder is compliant with the policies of the organization. Task-alignment - How to align the agentic coder on its tasks and goals. We introduce Agentic Process Evidence (APE), a signed, tamper-evident, machine-readable attestation of agentic processes, linking the sessions to their outcome (process-aware logging). APE enables Policy-as-Code control over the agentic processes, allowing for human in the loop only when it's needed. We support the in-toto style attestation framework, and the protocol is aligned with the relevant regulations
authors: Yuval Kainan, Carmit Hershman
bullets: AI agents increasingly perform SDLC tasks, but their ephemeral reasoning, decisions, and tool calls disappear after sessions end.
Traditional Git history records code changes, not the agent, model, tools, policies, or accountability behind them.
APE addresses supply-chain risk, policy compliance, and task alignment for agentic coding processes.
The framework links agent sessions to outcomes through process-aware, machine-readable logging.
APE supports in-toto-style attestations and Policy-as-Code, with human intervention when needed; regulatory alignment is claimed but not detailed in the abstract.

papers.abstract: The HECKTOR 2026 challenge benchmarks machine learning for head and neck cancer, where teams delineate primary and nodal tumour volumes, perform TN staging, and predict recurrence-free survival (RFS). This report describes the submissions for the HECKTOR challenge of team nucli. As the three tasks span both dense and global information from multicentric PET/CT scans, we utilise self-supervised pre-trained encoders, training a 2D DINOv2 encoder (PET-DINOv2-MIPs) on HECKTOR 2026's PET scans. Our final test submission ensembles a DynUNet trained from scratch with a SwinUNETR whose Swin trunk was initialised from a SimMIM-pre-trained checkpoint for segmentation, reaching a mean Dice of 0.5409. For TN staging, GTVp/GTVn geometric features from the segmentation masks are fit to stage probabilities by logistic regression (LR) and fused with PET-DINOv2-MIPs deep features (PCA + LR) via a second-level LR, reaching balanced accuracies of 0.3962 (T-stage) and 0.6432 (N-stage). For the RFS prognosis task, we fine-tune the last two blocks of the PET-DINOv2-MIPs ViT-S encoder jointly with an MLP head under a CoxPH loss, concatenating clinical covariates with the imaging features, reaching a test Harrell's C-index of 0.6577 and a weighted challenge score of 0.5802. The prognosis result is comparable to the best entry of the previous edition and consistent with our internal cross-validation, while our segmentation result is well below it and limits the staging results that depend on it.
authors: Roxanne De Maeyer, Ine Dirks, Yannick Brackenier, Simon DeKeyser, Jef Vandemeulebroucke, Vicky De Ridder

papers.abstract: Understanding the internal routing of visual concepts is crucial for the safe and controllable adaptation of generative models. While concept localization has been widely studied in diffusion models, the emerging paradigm of next-scale visual autoregressive models remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce LoCo, the first model-agnostic framework to localize where and when specific concepts emerge within autoregressive models. Driven by the native coarse-to-fine nature of next-scale generation, our method precisely maps conceptual knowledge across three distinct dimensions: Layer, Scale, and Position. To systematically localize and evaluate concept routing without context bias, we propose LoCoBench, a comprehensive dataset spanning 10 diverse categories. Extensive probing on image and video autoregressive models like Infinity, HunyuanImage-3.0, and InfinityStar shows that the localized positions are both interpretable and causally related to concept emergence. Building on these insights, we apply our localization method to three key applications: concept erasure, model personalization, and adversarial concept injection. Experiments demonstrate that our targeted intervention achieves state-of-the-art performance, substantially reducing computational overhead while preserving benign utility. Overall, our findings offer insights into how conceptual knowledge is routed during autoregressive generation, introducing a practical pathway for more interpretable, efficient, and secure adaptation.
authors: Nanxiang Jiang, Yang Liu, Yuanhao Wang, Min Xu
bullets: Addresses the largely unexplored problem of concept localization in visual autoregressive models.
Maps concept routing across layer, generation scale, and spatial position using a model-agnostic framework.
Introduces LoCoBench, a 10-category dataset for systematic, context-bias-free localization and evaluation.
Probing image and video models finds localized positions that are interpretable and causally linked to concept emergence.

(c) Replacing their inputs with concept-agnostic prompts {pc-neutral

papers.tldr: LoCo localizes where and when concepts emerge in next-scale visual autoregressive models, enabling efficient and targeted model interventions.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used to train robust, adaptable systems across healthcare, e-commerce, and robotics. In these settings, legal, ethical, or logistical concerns may preclude certain key variables that drive decisions from being collected during deployment time. This gives rise to a setting known as runtime confounding: the logged data hold full observability, but deployment time lacks knowledge of certain variables, known as runtime confounders. Unlike single timepoint and non-adaptive settings, runtime confounding under reinforcement learning has the potential to propagate over time, as earlier decisions affect future states, observations, and action assignments, leading to biased learning. We address these problems with three contributions: we (1) develop policy learning algorithms under runtime-confounding, (2) develop semi-parametric efficient off-policy estimation procedures, and (3) provide diagnostics for understanding the price of runtime confounding.
authors: Raphael Kim, Michele Santacatterina, Ramin Zabih, Keith Barnatchez
bullets: Runtime confounding occurs when logged data fully observe key variables, but deployment does not.
In RL, missing confounders can propagate through future states, observations, and action assignments.
The paper develops policy-learning algorithms for runtime-confounded settings.
It proposes semiparametrically efficient procedures for off-policy estimation.
It introduces diagnostics to assess the cost of runtime confounding.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Problem setting. Ut is observed in the historical data, but unmeasured during deployment and in turn unavailable to the target policy.

papers.selection_reason: General RL policy learning and off-policy evaluation under runtime confounding, transferable to robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Reinforcement Learning Under Runtime Confounding: Policy Learning and Off-Policy Evaluation
papers.tldr: This work studies reinforcement learning when deployment omits decision-relevant variables and develops methods for policy learning, off-policy evaluation, and diagnosing the resulting temporal bias.

papers.abstract: Activation steering changes what a language model generates by editing its hidden states at inference time. Its most common form adds one vector, the difference of class means (DiM), to every hidden state. CHaRS (concept heterogeneity-aware representation steering) uses optimal transport instead: an entropic plan pairs the clusters of the two classes, and each hidden state moves along a mixture of the cluster displacements, weighted toward its nearest clusters. We study this family of clustered optimal-transport maps for toxicity mitigation in Gemma-2-2B and Granite-3.1-2B, and ask what the plan adds to DiM and whether that survives INT8 and NF4 quantization. We prove an identity: whatever the plan, the displacements averaged with the cluster sizes as weights equal DiM, so a clustered map can differ from DiM only for tokens whose routing weights depart from the cluster sizes. In the CHaRS protocol they stay close, and CHaRS is statistically equivalent to Mean-AcT, which adds DiM at every layer, in all eight pre-specified equivalence tests. A variant fitted on individual tokens, which routes each token mainly to its nearest clusters, leaves 37-39% less toxicity than DiM on Gemma and 51-61% less on Granite at steering strength 3 (toxic-bert), where DiM already removes 76-85% of it. Two other toxicity classifiers confirm the gain on Granite, but on Gemma only one does. At equal strength the variant has somewhat higher perplexity, but at matched toxicity it is slightly more fluent than DiM. Yet a nearly constant map from the same clusters also leaves about 30% less toxicity, so the role of treating tokens differently remains open. Under INT8 and NF4 the variant still leaves less toxicity than DiM, and transferring it from full precision to the NF4 model instead of refitting it adds no significant toxicity after correction for multiple tests.
authors: Illia Makarov
bullets: The study tests whether clustered transport maps add value beyond DiM for toxicity steering in Gemma-2-2B and Granite-3.1-2B.
A proven identity shows that clustered displacements average to DiM; differences arise only when token routing weights depart from cluster-size weights.
In the CHaRS protocol, routing stays close to cluster-size weighting, making it statistically equivalent to Mean-AcT across eight pre-specified tests.
A token-level routing variant leaves 37–39% less toxicity on Gemma and 51–61% less on Granite than DiM at steering strength 3, though it can have higher perplexity at equal strength.
The variant remains better than DiM under INT8 and NF4; however, a nearly constant map also improves toxicity, so the importance of treating tokens differently is unresolved.

papers.selection_reason: Studies inference-time activation steering for LLM toxicity mitigation, including quantization robustness, directly relevant to LLM behavior and control.
papers.title: One Vector or Many? Clustered Optimal-Transport Steering under Quantization
papers.tldr: Clustered optimal-transport steering can outperform a single mean-difference vector for toxicity mitigation, including under quantization, but the benefit of token-specific routing remains unclear.

papers.abstract: We report that allocating compute to synthetic pre-pretraining (PPT) never outperforms pure natural-language training in our compute-matched experiments. This holds across four PPT curricula (k-Dyck, neural cellular automata (NCA), declarative reference corpora, and code) and three training regimes: data-constrained, data-unconstrained, and a high token-to-parameter-ratio regime (881M parameters trained on 50B tokens). When natural language is scarce, repeated epochs over a 100M-token corpus beat every synthetic curriculum on natural-language validation loss, with no consistent downstream accuracy advantage from PPT. We find that PPT gains reported in prior work are sensitive to the weight initialization scheme. In an NCA reproduction, we recover a 5.4% perplexity improvement from PPT under the original initialization scheme. An alternative scheme improves both methods, but the no-PPT baseline more, closing the gap between them. However, when PPT receives additional compute rather than a share of the natural-language budget, gains persist at small natural-language budgets even with improved initialization, but disappear by 1B tokens. Finally, models forget what they learn during PPT in subsequent natural-language training; interleaving the same data throughout training prevents forgetting, but does not significantly improve natural-language performance. Our results suggest limited benefits of synthetic pre-pretraining as a distinct training stage and motivate rethinking how such data are used in language model training.
authors: Alexander Stern, Tim Rockt\"aschel, Acyr Locatelli, Laura Ruis
bullets: Across four synthetic curricula and three training regimes, PPT never outperformed pure natural-language training in compute-matched experiments.
Repeating scarce natural-language data yielded better validation loss than every tested synthetic curriculum, without consistent downstream accuracy gains.
An NCA reproduction recovered a 5.4% perplexity improvement only under the original initialization; an alternative initialization largely eliminated the gap.
PPT benefits persisted with extra compute at small natural-language budgets but disappeared by 1B tokens.
Models largely forgot PPT-learned information during later natural-language training; interleaving data prevented forgetting without significantly improving performance.

figures.caption: Figure 4: PPT is useful at 50M–100M natural-language tokens, but its gain at 1B disappears under spectral-based initialization. In the additive-compute regime with a 336M-parameter model, NCA and k-Dyck, each at its lowest-loss configuration, improve on the optimal no-PPT baseline at 50M and 100M natural-language tokens. Under spectral-based initialization this gain disappears by 1B tokens, but under the other initializations it persists at every budget (Appendix E.1 shows the full breakdown). Because spectral-based initialization yields the lowest loss for every method at this largest budget, we use it in all compute-matched experiments, which run at comparable FLOP budgets.

The model size here is 336M parameters. Within each panel the leftmost point is that configuration’s own baseline with no PPT, marked by the gray dashed line. The green dashed line and band mark the lowest-loss no-PPT baseline across the three initialization schemes, providing a reference for comparisons across initializations. Solid lines with filled markers are Muon PPT and dashed lines with open markers are AdamW PPT. AdamW performs better than Muon for the PPT methods at the lower natural-language budgets; at 1B tokens, however, the two are indistinguishable under spectral-based initialization. Importantly, if one is to train with the alternative initializations, the PPT benefit would still exist even at this larger budget.

The axis is broken above 0.992, where the early exploratory trials of both searches sit.

In the example shown, a reference inside the opened scope retrieves the value of a name declared in that scope, and after the scope closes a reference retrieves the value of a name declared before the scope. Generation and tokenization details are given in Section 2 and Appendix A.

Figure 9: No PPT method scales better than the baseline. Here we plot FineWeb validation BPB against training compute for the data-unconstrained experiments. Each line is a separate power law, BPB = AC−α (Kaplan et al., 2020), fitted by least squares on log BPB against logC over that method’s nine runs (three seeds per scale), with C in units of 1018 FLOPs, so A is the fitted BPB at 1018 FLOPs. The table gives A and α with their standard errors. The baseline has the lowest A, and no method’s exponent is significantly larger than the baseline’s (within standard error). Raising PPT from 1% to 5% raises A for every method. However, its effect on the exponent is unclear as at 5% every exponent is within standard error of the baseline’s. Every synthetic PPT method remains above the baseline at every budget, while C4, independent of percentage, is the same as the baseline. Since we only have three budgets per method, and three seeds, we do not fit an irreducible-loss term as in Hoffmann et al. (2022).

Figure 5: Uniformly distributing the PPT data across training, rather than front-loading it, prevents forgetting on the PPT distribution. In the interleaved runs, 5% of every batch consists of NCA, k-Dyck, or code throughout training. In the PPT runs, the same 5% of compute is instead spent up front, at 2.7 × 1019 FLOPs. Left: FineWeb validation BPB at the end of training. Right: validation BPB on the PPT corpus itself across the whole run, one panel per corpus on its own scale, with the gray dotted line marking 5% of total compute. Under the PPT schedule the models lose this ability at the PPT-to-PT boundary; under interleaving they keep it and continue to improve on it. Elsewhere in this work the vocabulary is replaced at the phase boundary for the synthetic PPT distributions, which means the PPT corpus cannot be scored after the PPT phase. Every run here instead shares a single vocabulary, extended to hold the NCA and k-Dyck tokens, so the corpus can be tracked throughout training. These runs are not hyperparameter-tuned (configurations in Appendix D.5, Table 7), so the FineWeb panel is included only to show that the interleaved runs sit in a similar range to their PPT counterparts.

papers.selection_reason: Directly investigates LLM training curricula and compute allocation for synthetic pre-pretraining, relevant to large language model training methodology.
papers.title: Rethinking Pre-pretraining
papers.tldr: Compute-matched synthetic pre-pretraining provides little consistent benefit over training directly on natural language, and its reported gains depend on initialization and extra compute.

papers.abstract: Efficient crowd navigation requires anticipating dynamic collision-free space without relying on fragile object tracking. We propose the Don't Risk It Planner (DRIP), an end-to-end LiDAR-only planning framework that couples occupancy forecasting with trajectory-conditioned clearance and uncertainty estimation. Operating directly on LiDAR-derived occupancy grid histories, DRIP predicts a distribution over minimum robot-obstacle clearance for candidate control sequences to evaluate collision risk. The model is trained using a risk cost that grounds predictive uncertainty directly in empirical collision outcomes rather than geometric regression alone. In closed-loop experiments with up to 45 pedestrians, DRIP achieves higher success rates with fewer collisions and reduced freezing behavior compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
authors: Mathai Mathew Pulicken, Laksh Nanwani, Basant Sharma, Phani Teja Singamaneni, Arun Kumar Singh, K. Madhava Krishna
bullets: Addresses safe, efficient navigation in dynamic crowds without relying on fragile object tracking.
Uses LiDAR-derived occupancy-grid histories to forecast occupancy and estimate clearance and uncertainty for candidate control sequences.
Trains risk predictions against empirical collision outcomes, rather than geometric clearance regression alone.
In closed-loop experiments with up to 45 pedestrians, it improves success rates while reducing collisions and freezing versus state-of-the-art baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of DRIP’s LiDAR-only prediction and trajectory-conditioned risk architecture. A history H of pose-warped BEV occupancy maps is encoded independently by a shared-weight spatial CNN, conditioned on ego velocity V through FiLM. Spatiotemporal Transformer blocks then reason over the temporal history and spatial BEV tokens to produce a shared scene representation zscene. Two branches use this representation: the occupancy decoder predicts the future evolution of the scene (Ôk) over a 20-step horizon, while the trajectory-conditioned Distance Head combines scene features with candidate trajectory queries qk to predict a stepwise clearance distribution (µk, σ 2 k) and a trajectory-specific kernel width λ. These predictions are subsequently used to compute the distributional MMD2 risk r̂θ(u) for each candidate trajectory u.

Fig. 3: Box plot of best-of-K clearance residuals relative to privileged ground truth across dynamic evaluation episodes. The risk-calibrated model ((18)) yields a lower median error and narrower spread than the NLL-only baseline without Lrisk , Lhaz), demonstrating well-calibrated predictive variance that tightly bounds actual obstacle encounters.

Fig. 4: Visualization of the occupancy forecasting. Top row: The first 5 steps of the predicted future occupancy maps (Ôk), visualized as thresholded binary maps, taken from the full 20-step planning horizon. Bottom row: The corresponding ground-truth future occupancy maps (Ogt k ). The network successfully anticipates the continuous motion of dynamic obstacles and maintains static boundary structures, closely matching the ground truth without relying on explicit pedestrian tracking.

papers.selection_reason: End-to-end LiDAR-only crowd navigation with trajectory-conditioned distributional collision risk and occupancy forecasting.
papers.title: Don't Risk It!: Trajectory-Conditioned Distributional Risk for LiDAR-Only Crowd Navigation
papers.tldr: DRIP enables LiDAR-only crowd navigation by predicting trajectory-specific clearance distributions to assess collision risk without object tracking.

papers.abstract: Language models handle text well, and rule engines give conclusions with proofs. Systems that combine the two are usually described by example, and the same coupling turns up under different names in agent frameworks, guardrail toolkits and neuro-symbolic research. This document defines thirteen patterns for coupling a language model with an executable rule language, in the catalogue form introduced for object-oriented design: intent, motivation, applicability, participants, collaborations, consequences, implementation, known uses and related patterns. Four patterns concern what crosses the boundary between model and rules, five who controls whom, three how the model takes part in the reasoning, and one how knowledge is kept over time. Five invariants hold for every combination, and five failure patterns name the couplings that break them. We relate the catalogue to published pattern catalogues and taxonomies of hybrid and neuro-symbolic systems and show where they overlap with it. A decision guide leads from a problem to a pattern. It rests on our measurements, including the cases in which a model alone did as well as the hybrid or better, and it reports what each design cost.
authors: Siegfried Handschuh, G\"otz-Henrik Wiegand, Lorena Raichle
bullets: Addresses the inconsistent naming and example-driven description of hybrid language-model/rule systems.
Classifies patterns by boundary crossing, control, reasoning participation, and knowledge persistence.
Defines five invariants for valid combinations and five failure patterns for broken couplings.
Connects the catalogue to existing hybrid and neuro-symbolic taxonomies and published pattern catalogues.
Provides a decision guide grounded in measurements, including cases where a language model alone matched or outperformed the hybrid and the costs of each design.

papers.abstract: Memory in reinforcement learning raises two problems. Attention finds the relevant item by scoring the whole store, which is costly for robots under latency and energy limits. When a retrieved memory pays off, credit for acquiring it must cross the whole sequence. We argue that both are governed by one quantity, the value of information, and propose to estimate it from archived rollouts with a learned world model. We obtain that, when read at the observation, it yields a provable lower bound on the optimal value of the acquiring action, which floors its TD target and attributes this floor to the observation that earned it. Read at the decision, it defines the optimal retrieval set. A pilot retrieval system, to be trained and improved with this signal, solves a memory task with reduced context.
authors: Daniel Strauss, Nikolaos Sotirakis, Zhenshan Bing, Alois Knoll
bullets: Targets costly attention over entire memory stores in latency- and energy-constrained reinforcement learning.
Estimates information value from archived rollouts using a learned world model.
At observation time, provides a provable lower bound on the acquiring action’s optimal value and credits the observation.
At decision time, defines the optimal retrieval set.
A pilot system solves a memory task with reduced context, though further training and improvement are needed.

papers.abstract: Medical image segmentation is crucial for clinical diagnosis and treatment planning, requiring both global contextual understanding and fine-grained structural precision. While the Segment Anything Model (SAM) demonstrates strong generalization capabilities, its direct application to medical images often lacks domain-specific adaptability. Meanwhile, State Space Models (SSMs)-based methods, such as Mamba, efficiently capture long-range dependencies but may struggle with preserving fine anatomical details. To address these challenges, we propose a segment anything model based context guided mamba unet, SAMBA-UNet, a novel framework that integrates SAM's context knowledge with Mamba's hierarchical feature learning to enhance both global representation and local detail refinement. Specifically, we introduce the Hierarchical Context Enhancement Module (HCEM), an attention-based fusion module that deeply incorporates the multi-level features of SAM and Mamba to improve detail perception and segmentation precision. Additionally, we employ LoRA and Adapter-based fine-tuning to adapt SAM to medical imaging tasks, further enhancing its domain-specific segmentation capability and robustness. We conducted a comprehensive study on several medical segmentation datasets, including Synapse, ISIC17, and ISIC18, evaluating our method across multiple metrics. Experimental results demonstrate that SAMBA-UNet achieves state-of-the-art performance, effectively balancing generalization, segmentation accuracy, and computational efficiency. Our code will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Chenchen Wang, You Zhou
bullets: Addresses SAM’s limited medical-domain adaptability and Mamba-based methods’ difficulty preserving fine anatomical details.
Introduces the Hierarchical Context Enhancement Module to fuse multi-level SAM and Mamba features for improved context and detail perception.
Uses LoRA- and Adapter-based fine-tuning to adapt SAM to medical imaging tasks.
Evaluated on Synapse, ISIC17, and ISIC18 across multiple metrics, with reported state-of-the-art performance and improved balance between accuracy, generalization, and efficiency.

papers.abstract: Choosing a robot action model requires evidence about task capability, adaptation cost, deployment requirements, and the reliability of reported conclusions. Success rates alone offer limited guidance to researchers with different computing budgets and goals. We propose RoboSeed, a multidimensional evaluation framework for vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAM), within a continuing program to train, evaluate, and openly release robot models with verifiable evidence for model selection. The framework defines five dimensions: capability, downstream training affordability, deployment affordability, locally verified research value, and reproduction evidence. It maps empirical measurements and audit criteria to 0-100 profiles using fixed normalization anchors, with balanced, training-constrained, and deployment-constrained preference settings. Interface and protocol checks establish when comparisons are appropriate. Missing measurements remain explicit, incomplete aggregate scores are withheld, and weighted input coverage identifies evidence gaps. We apply the framework to representative VLA and WAM models, drawing on local training, released-weight evaluation, task-level audits, and an evaluation-system study. The results reveal budget-dependent backbone choices, sensitivity to adaptation recipes, and differences between language and visual task interfaces. Reproducible scoring code and machine-readable evidence support extension to additional models. The study provides dimension-level assessments and priorities for further measurement, while incomplete serving traces and heterogeneous protocols preclude overall numerical rankings.
authors: Xin Ma, Furong Chen, Xinlong Man, Bo Zhang, Yalong Guo, Haolan Lei, Chaochen Cui, Hongyuan Zhang, Mulin Chen, Yi Wang, Lap-pui Chau, Chuang Yang
bullets: Assesses five dimensions: capability, downstream training affordability, deployment affordability, locally verified research value, and reproduction evidence.
Uses fixed normalization anchors, multiple budget preferences, and interface/protocol checks to make comparisons more reliable.
Applies the framework to representative vision-language-action and world-action models using local evaluations, audits, and released weights.
Finds budget-dependent backbone choices, sensitivity to adaptation recipes, and differences between language- and visual-task interfaces.
Provides reproducible scoring code and machine-readable evidence, but does not produce overall rankings because serving traces and protocols are incomplete or heterogeneous.

papers.abstract: Automatic operator design (AOD) has increasingly adopted large language models (LLMs) to generate problem-specific search and variation operators for multi-objective combinatorial optimization (MOCO). Yet most methods evolve the operators while leaving the process that discovers them fixed. This limits adaptation as new Pareto trade-offs and operator interactions change where and how the search should proceed. We introduce HEMO, which makes the AOD harness itself a self-evolving optimization target. HEMO maintains a persistent harness state and updates one module at a time, revising the logic that determines which experience to retrieve, which operators to improve, which parents to select, and how to formulate the orchestration of search steps. Downstream solution quality and runtime guide these updates, while a discounted UCB scheduler directs adaptation toward promising modules as their utility changes. A persistent memory filesystem preserves candidate outcomes and diagnostic feedback across harness states, enabling successive states to build on accumulated optimization experience. Experiments across eight MOCO tasks and two structurally distinct evolutionary backbones demonstrate strong performance against conventional evolutionary, neural, and LLM-based AOD baselines, together with effective transfer to related tasks. HEMO extends automatic operator design beyond evolving individual operators to improving the search process that discovers them.
authors: Jianghan Zhu, Cong Zhang, Ni Zhang, Yifan Yang, Yew Soon Ong, Zhiguang Cao
bullets: Targets a limitation of LLM-based automatic operator design: fixed discovery and orchestration processes cannot adapt to changing Pareto trade-offs and operator interactions.
Maintains a persistent harness state and revises modules for experience retrieval, operator improvement, parent selection, and search-step orchestration.
Uses downstream solution quality and runtime as feedback, with discounted UCB scheduling to prioritize promising modules.
A persistent memory filesystem retains candidate outcomes and diagnostic feedback across successive harness states.
Evaluations on eight MOCO tasks and two evolutionary backbones show strong performance against evolutionary, neural, and LLM-based baselines, plus transfer to related tasks.

papers.abstract: DINO (self-DIstillation with NO labels) has become a stan- dard for self-supervised pre-training, producing features that generalise across datasets and downstream tasks. In medical imaging it has been adopted mainly for radiology (X-ray, CT and MRI), where even natural- image DINO features transfer well. In the literature, these features have been reported to transfer worse to functional imaging such as PET. Yet PET-specific DINO models have barely been introduced, and even less validated across multiple tasks and datasets. We present PET-DINOv2-2D, the first DINOv2 model pre-trained on 2D PET, and benchmark it against open-source encoders: the origi- nal DINOv2 (pre-trained on the LVD-142M natural-image dataset) and OmniRad (pre-trained on CT, MRI and ultrasound). Using the same lightweight heads for every backbone, and despite far less pre-training data, PET-DINOv2-2D matches or outperforms both on three down- stream PET tasks: normal/abnormal classification, lesion segmentation and recurrence-free survival prognosis. Its advantage is largest when few labels are available, suggesting that PET pre-training gives more transferable, label-efficient features. Code is made available at https://github.com/nuclivision/pet-dinov2-2d/.

bullets: Introduces the first DINOv2 model pre-trained on 2D PET.
Benchmarks it against original DINOv2 and OmniRad using identical lightweight task heads.
Evaluates normal/abnormal classification, lesion segmentation, and recurrence-free survival prognosis.
Shows the largest benefit in low-label settings, indicating improved label efficiency and transferability.
Code is publicly available on GitHub.

papers.abstract: Agentic robots must turn a high-level goal into actions while keeping the physical conditions needed for future steps valid. A completed action does not ensure that its effects will persist: a later disturbance can invalidate support that the remaining plan still assumes. We present LOGIV, a graph engineering framework for agentic robot execution that uses an explicit task graph to connect symbolic planning, observation-based verification, and embodied action. LOGIV compiles a validated plan into condition-support and resource-ordering edges, checks their physical validity during execution, and uses dependency tracing to determine what must be restored after a failure. Repair is constrained by retained unfinished actions, and the combined continuation is symbolically validated before execution resumes. The framework operates above existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and World Action Model (WAM) policies without adding trainable components. Across 20 dual-arm tasks from RoboTwin~V2 and BiCoord with three execution backbones, LOGIV improves mean task success without injected disturbances by 10.67 and 15.33 percentage points, respectively. Under predefined perturbations, it achieves higher task completion and condition restoration than three adapted recovery baselines for every backbone on both benchmarks. On three real-robot tasks, successful trials increase from 12/30 to 17/30. These results support explicit, continuously checked task dependencies as a practical interface for reliable agentic robot execution.
authors: Enqiao Lu, Yuxiang Xie, Xingrui Yu, Yuyang Wang, Yipeng Gu, Zhenglin Wan, Pengfei Zhou, Wangbo Zhao, Yang You, Yuxiang Gao, Ivor Tsang
bullets: Addresses the problem that later disturbances can invalidate conditions required by unfinished actions.
Compiles validated plans into task-graph edges for condition support and resource ordering, then checks them during execution.
Uses dependency tracing to identify what must be restored while retaining unfinished actions; symbolically validates the repaired continuation before resuming.
Works above existing VLA and WAM policies without adding trainable components.
Improves task success across simulated benchmarks and increases successful real-robot trials from 12/30 to 17/30.

papers.abstract: AI assistants are increasingly embedded in computational notebooks, scientific workflows, software engineering tools, and learning systems, yet human-AI interactions are often treated as transient prompt-response exchanges rather than durable data products, hindering reproducibility, explainability, replay, behavioral analysis, and adaptive AI support. We argue that these interactions form a new data class requiring formal representation and introduce the Human-AI Interaction Description Language (HAIDL), a formal interaction model with a Backus-Naur Form-inspired concrete syntax. HAIDL encodes each interaction as a structured object capturing computational context, user request, prompt payload, AI response, feedback, problem context, provenance, and model metadata. We integrate this vision into HAIDL-X, a middleware for JupyterLab that instantiates HAIDL by capturing user-bot state, building contextualized prompts, interfacing with AI providers, collecting feedback, and storing interactions in a repository. We add a learning layer over HAIDL that maps interaction objects and notebook execution traces into reproducible measures of user behavior, including engagement, performance, help-seeking, error-oriented use, and learning personas. HAIDL-X provides a foundation for treating human-AI collaboration as structured, queryable, replayable, analyzable data.
authors: Michela Taufer, Kin Ng, Ian Lumsden, Aashish Pandey, Rajasi Gore, Angelina Ju, Sukanya Moudgalya, Ewa Deelman, Sai Swaminathan
bullets: Addresses the problem of treating AI interactions as transient prompt–response exchanges, which limits reproducibility, replay, and behavioral analysis.
Introduces HAIDL, a formal language for representing context, requests, prompts, responses, feedback, provenance, and model metadata.
Implements HAIDL-X, a JupyterLab middleware that captures interaction state, builds prompts, interfaces with AI providers, collects feedback, and stores records.
Adds a learning layer that derives measures of engagement, performance, help-seeking, error-oriented use, and learning personas from interactions and notebook traces.
Provides a foundation for structured, queryable, replayable, and analyzable human–AI collaboration data.
