papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence for science (AI4S) is extending from interpretation of existing data to the design and execution of experiments. Space offers distinctive scientific opportunities while restricting physical support. Microgravity and extraterrestrial environments expose phenomena that terrestrial experiments cannot fully reproduce; finite samples, constrained resources, and limited opportunities for intervention complicate sustained investigation. This critical review examines orbital laboratories and planetary in situ science across biology, materials, fluid and thermal physics, and adaptive exploration. We distinguish learning from space-derived data, selecting scientific actions, executing them, and preserving experimental validity. Terrestrial self-driving laboratories provide complementary evidence on optimization, dedicated automation, robotic manipulation, and the support needed for unattended operation. The synthesis connects scientific gains already demonstrated by bounded AI systems to gaps in observation, executable actions, and continuity of valid evidence. Space robots can expand the attainable scope of autonomous science when necessary interventions exceed validated instrument capabilities and timely human support is unavailable. Their value must be established against dedicated mechanisms, redundancy, and human-supported operation. We develop a framework connecting sample history, scientific decisions, physical execution, and claim-specific validity. A worked orbital design, a planetary extension, and matched evaluation schemes separate the contributions of sensing, decision policies, and physical actions. The resulting agenda measures autonomy through valid scientific return, task coverage, intervention costs, and evidence integrity across complete campaigns.
authors: Zizhe Wang, Jia Deng, Xin Lu, Zehao Jia, Yi Huang, Yao Zhu, Jianing Li
bullets: Space environments enable experiments unavailable on Earth but impose severe limits on samples, resources, interventions, and human support.
The review covers orbital laboratories and planetary fieldwork across biology, materials, fluid and thermal physics, and adaptive exploration.
It distinguishes learning from space data, selecting scientific actions, executing them, and preserving valid evidence.
Drawing on terrestrial self-driving laboratories, it identifies gaps in observation, executable actions, and continuity of valid evidence.

It proposes evaluating autonomy by valid scientific return, task coverage, intervention costs, and evidence integrity, while comparing robots with dedicated mechanisms, redundancy, and human-supported operation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Complementary terrestrial routes toward experimental autonomy. Clio combined adaptive formulation with dedicated fluidics; its 42 physical experiments and simulated search-efficiency comparison are distinct results [110]. eVOLVER illustrates dedicated automation with residual vial replacement [111]. Ada reported different replenishment intervals in two configurations and workflows, not a controlled before–after comparison [112, 113]; Kanda et al. demonstrated a long robotic optimization campaign with specified human preparation, imaging and validation [114]. The lower panel is an original, proposed space-transfer strategy; the case annotations are not a common acceleration metric.

Fault responses distinguish inspection, restart, replacement and restored function. Sources correspond to GLARE [37]; wet foams [14, 69]; FBCE [15, 59, 60]; MOBP [23]; CAL [73, 74]; AEGIS [8, 80]; PIXL [9]; ISAAC [101]; and Curiosity recovery [24]. For foams, ? denotes the unreported 2023 analysis location; G(i) denotes inferred ground reanalysis in the 2024 software study, based on its offline labeled-image workflow. MOBP resumed part of a predefined schedule; missing experimental history remained unresolved. CAL module replacement was performed by crew; fault recovery was not established. Cited cases establish the bottlenecks; candidate pathways and acceptance conditions are proposed here for evaluation. Dedicated automation and human assistance remain explicit comparators.

papers.abstract: Event cameras offer microsecond temporal resolution, high dynamic range and no motion blur, but referring video object segmentation (RVOS) lacks event-stream datasets and models. We introduce Event-SAMA-239K, a synthetic-event conversion of the SAMA-239K grounded video-chat corpus and all additional SAMA training data: 30,650 video clips and 392,162 images. Optical-flow, FILM or saccade upsampling followed by a linear event generator preserves all mask, referring-expression and dialogue annotations. We also introduce Event-SAMA, adapting SAMA-4B with a two-channel polarity patch embedding initialised from pretrained RGB weights and a zero-initialised event adapter. End-to-end training yields 24.37 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ on MeViS valid_u and 22.33 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ on the converted ReVOS valid subset, establishing the first event-native RVOS baseline (RGB SAMA-4B: 55.4 on MeViS). Frozen RGB SAMA-4B with pseudo-RGB renderings or E2VID reconstructions of the same events scores 13.23 and 15.94 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$. Without retraining, Event-SAMA works on real event-camera recordings when the accumulation window matches their event density. A seed-controlled ablation with a measured noise floor of 0.47 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ finds gains from diverse training sources over MeViS alone (+4.99), RGB-mean event-stem initialisation (+4.33), and a trainable SAM2 mask decoder (+2.76); the event adapter, partial ViT unfreezing and event polarity are within noise at this budget. An earlier, partially converted corpus snapshot trained with the identical recipe scores 1.38 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ higher on MeViS and 1.12 higher on ReVOS. Both are single runs that also differ in schedule length, so we draw no conclusion about corpus scale.
authors: Sergei Fedorchenko, Max Zehnder, Nikola Zubi\'c, Rong Zou, Davide Scaramuzza
bullets: Builds Event-SAMA-239K by converting 30,650 videos and 392,162 images from SAMA data into synthetic event streams while preserving masks, referring expressions, and dialogue annotations.
Adapts SAMA-4B with two-channel event-polarity input embeddings and an event adapter for end-to-end RVOS training.
Achieves 24.37 J&F on MeViS valid_u and 22.33 J&F on converted ReVOS, compared with 55.4 for RGB SAMA-4B on MeViS.
Pseudo-RGB and E2VID reconstructions score lower at 13.23 and 15.94 J&F, supporting direct event-stream processing.

Performance transfers to real event-camera recordings when the accumulation window matches event density; ablations identify data diversity, initialization, and decoder training as useful under the tested budget.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) draw on parametric knowledge and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to solve knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet problem solving in unfamiliar domains calls for tightly coupled knowledge acquisition and reasoning, beyond factual retrieval and aggregation or learning solely from a preassembled context. We study self-learning -- autonomously retrieving, studying, and applying knowledge from long-form reference materials on the fly. To investigate this capability, we formulate a textbook-based mathematical problem-solving task. LLMs must navigate textbook exposition, learn and apply relevant principles, and construct proofs for exercises, with reference solutions withheld. We introduce a BookNavigator interface to support this human-inspired study process and incentivize self-learning through reinforcement learning (RL) with fine-grained rewards. Experiments show that our method improves performance across in-domain and out-of-domain textbooks and subjects, raising Intern-S2-Preview-35B's overall proof accuracy from 51.5% to 79.5% and outperforming RL-trained textbook-free and fixed-retrieval baselines. These gains extend to complex long-context benchmarks involving different task types, with improvements over the base model of 1.7 and 2.3 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus and CL-bench, respectively. Together, these findings suggest that RL can foster a domain-agnostic self-learning strategy, highlighting the potential of self-learning from long-form corpora to strengthen broader problem-solving capabilities on complex, long-context tasks.
authors: Lingkai Kong, Yuzhe Gu, Haiteng Zhao, Zijian Wu, Youqing Fang, Zhouqi Hua, Yanan Sun, Kai Chen, Wenwei Zhang
bullets: Targets self-learning in unfamiliar domains, beyond factual retrieval or reasoning over preassembled context.
Introduces BookNavigator for retrieving, studying, and applying information from long-form textbooks while solving problems.
Uses reinforcement learning with fine-grained rewards to incentivize the study-and-reason process.
Improves Intern-S2-Preview-35B proof accuracy from 51.5% to 79.5% across in-domain and out-of-domain textbooks and subjects.
Also improves performance on BrowseComp-Plus and CL-bench, suggesting transfer to diverse long-context tasks.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers generate high-quality videos, but the quadratic cost of 3D full attention dominates their inference. Dynamic block-sparse attention reduces this cost by computing exact attention only on key/value blocks selected from current activations. However, its fidelity degrades under aggressive sparsity: blocks are scored from coarse summaries or formed by costly global clustering, pruned blocks vanish from the softmax, and whole tiles are kept or dropped even when only a few of their keys matter. To address these limitations, we propose Accurate Block Attention (AB-Attention), a training-free method that accurately approximates dense attention at high sparsity. Its Intra-Block Clustering Selector (IBCS) estimates block importance faithfully yet cheaply by clustering queries only within each query block, without permuting tokens. Sampling with Inclusion-Probability Weighting (SIP) then samples blocks in proportion to these estimates and reweights them by inverse inclusion probability, so that one pass estimates dense attention rather than truncating it. Finally, its kernel gathers key/value blocks much smaller than a tile into full tensor-core tiles, refining selection at no extra tensor-core cost. On Wan2.1 and HunyuanVideo, AB-Attention skips 89--92\% of attention, whereas the baselines compute 1.8--3.6$\times$ as much, yet it still improves PSNR by up to 4.4~dB over the strongest baseline and achieves up to 2.23$\times$ end-to-end speedup. Our code is available at https://github.com/InfRec-Cardinal/AB-Attention.
authors: Bin Xu, Mo Zhang, Zhengfeiyang Zhang, Xinfeng Yang, Yixing Ma, Wei Wang, HeXin Wang, Pengfei Zhou, Wangbo Zhao
bullets: Targets the quadratic inference cost of 3D full attention and fidelity loss under aggressive block sparsity.
Uses Intra-Block Clustering Selector (IBCS) to estimate block importance from queries within each query block.
Applies Sampling with Inclusion-Probability Weighting (SIP) to estimate dense attention instead of simply dropping unselected blocks.
Gathers smaller key/value blocks into tensor-core tiles for finer-grained selection without extra tensor-core cost.
On Wan2.1 and HunyuanVideo, skips 89–92% of attention, improves PSNR by up to 4.4 dB over the strongest baseline, and reaches up to 2.23× end-to-end speedup.

(a) IBCS clusters each query block 𝑄𝑖 into centroids ?̄?𝑖 with weights 𝑤𝑖, and scores every key/value block by the weighted attention of the centroids to its pooled keys. (b) SIP samples each block with probability 𝜋𝑖 𝑗 proportional to its score 𝑆𝑖 𝑗, so no block is excluded, and weights it by 1/𝜋𝑖 𝑗 to estimate full attention. (c) The kernel gathers the sampled blocks into full tensor-core tiles and attends to them with logits shifted by − log𝜋𝑖 𝑗.

papers.abstract: Thinking vision-language models reason for thousands of tokens, yet still miss small details in high-resolution images. Zooming methods pay for extra inference passes, and outcome rewards never tell the model where to look at. In Qwen3.5-4B, we find that the bottleneck is selection, not seeing: a few attention heads, which we call localization heads, pick the evidence out of thousands of visual tokens; ablating four of them costs 13.2 points more than ablating four random heads, and their focus fades as the reasoning grows. We therefore propose Localization-Head Alignment (LHA), which makes attention a training signal: whenever the reasoning states a visual fact, these heads learn to look at the focal region rather than the background, as an auxiliary loss in both SFT and RL training. On benchmarks of V*, HR-Bench 4K and TreeBench, LHA lifts Qwen3.5-4B from 74.1% to 76.6% accuracy, the best single-pass 4B result we evaluate, ahead of multi-pass zooming and released 7B models. Alignment alone adds 1.8 points over otherwise identical training while shortening reasoning by 20%, and the gains carry over to Qwen2.5-VL-3B.
authors: Yuan Wang, Wei Wu, Hongning Wang
bullets: The main bottleneck is selecting visual evidence, not processing high-resolution images.
A small set of localization heads identifies relevant regions; disrupting four causes a 13.2-point larger accuracy loss than disrupting random heads.
LHA uses an auxiliary attention-alignment loss whenever reasoning states a visual fact, and supports both supervised and reinforcement learning.
On V*, HR-Bench 4K, and TreeBench, LHA improves Qwen3.5-4B from 74.1% to 76.6% accuracy and reduces reasoning by 20%.
The approach also transfers to Qwen2.5-VL-3B, but its scope is evaluated on the reported benchmarks and models.

papers.abstract: Colonoscopy is inherently comparative: reliable visual assessment of polyps often depends on complementary views acquired under different viewpoints and imaging conditions. Retrieving such views requires polyp tracklet representations, which recent contrastive methods learn from temporal cues but still build from manually annotated bounding boxes. We propose an annotation-free framework that constructs tracklet views directly from raw colonoscopy videos, enabling temporal self-supervised learning on full-procedure videos, including frames without visible polyps. On REAL-Colon, our method achieves state-of-the-art results on tracklet retrieval and re-identification, outperforming both self-supervised and supervised baselines. We then introduce few-shot polyp retrieval, a task closer to clinical use, where a few observations of a target polyp are used to retrieve its remaining tracklets: with only two examples, our method surpasses most competing methods given ten. Finally, we show that a modest number of unlabeled procedures suffices for competitive performance, making on-site model development more practical. Code is available at https://github.com/lparolari/freerep.
authors: Luca Parolari, Lamberto Ballan, Carlo Biffi, Loic Le Folgoc
bullets: Addresses the need to retrieve complementary polyp views across viewpoints and imaging conditions without manual bounding-box annotations.
Builds tracklet views directly from full-procedure videos, including frames without visible polyps, for temporal self-supervised learning.
Achieves state-of-the-art tracklet retrieval and re-identification on REAL-Colon against supervised and self-supervised baselines.
In few-shot retrieval, two target-polyp examples outperform most competing methods using ten examples.
Competitive performance requires only a modest number of unlabeled procedures, supporting more practical on-site development.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models can get individual judgments right while struggling to recover and consistently use the exact properties of a 3D object. To characterize this gap, we introduce BedBench, a controlled benchmark of thirteen procedurally generated tasks spanning individual judgments and composite answers. Across twelve open-weight and four frontier models, per-color counting exposes a pronounced weakness: humans achieve 93.3% accuracy, compared with 7.2% for the best model. Targeted fine-tuning raises one model's accuracy from 3.0% to 68.6%, but reveals a further difficulty: its answers about the most common colors remain inconsistent with its own per-color counts. Supplying those counts as text improves its judgments, showing that recovering a property does not mean using it consistently. Reasoning, scaling, and added visual cues each improve individual judgments, but none makes exact answers reliable. To locate the difficulty, we probe Qwen3.5-27B: exact per-color counts remain recoverable at the language model's input, yet the model's answers rarely recover them (65.0% for the probe vs. 3.0% for the model). Image-removal controls further show that some apparent successes require no visual evidence. These findings motivate evaluating 3D reasoning by exact correctness, consistent use, and image dependence, rather than accuracy alone. Code and dataset are publicly available: https://github.com/leduckhai/BedBench
authors: Khai Le-Duc, Nguyen Kim Hai Bui, An Ngo, Nam D. Hoang, Yueqi Song, Jiarui Liu, Thai Quoc Hoang, Fang Wu, Chris Ngo, Terry Jingchen Zhang, Mona T. Diab, Ran Xu, Silvio Savarese, Xiao-Ming Wu
bullets: Introduces BedBench, a controlled benchmark with 13 procedurally generated tasks covering individual and composite 3D judgments.
Per-color counting exposes a major gap: humans reach 93.3% accuracy, while the best evaluated model reaches 7.2%.
Fine-tuning improves one model from 3.0% to 68.6%, but its answers about the most common colors remain inconsistent with its own counts.
Providing counts as text improves judgments, indicating that recovering a property does not ensure its consistent use.
Probing Qwen3.5-27B finds counts recoverable at the language-model input (65.0%) despite only 3.0% model accuracy; image-removal controls also reveal image-independent successes.

papers.abstract: One-step and few-step text-to-image generation must accurately render the details specified in the prompt despite limited opportunities for refinement. Distribution matching distillation (DMD) uses score differences to bring the generated distribution closer to a reference distribution. Following prior work, we estimate this difference with internal velocity branches, avoiding a separate fake-score network. We ask whether an explicit moment constraint improves this learned score supervision. A decomposition of the reverse-KL field into a Gaussian moment component and a non-Gaussian residual identifies statistics that can be constrained explicitly. We introduce Intrinsic Distribution Matching (IDM), which retains the full DMD correction and matches feature means and per-coordinate standard deviations using the generator's exponential-moving-average (EMA) copy, requiring no external feature encoder. Experiments use full-parameter and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) tuning on Z-Image-Turbo 6B and Qwen-Image 20B. At two network evaluations, IDM reaches 94.25% and 90.20% on Chinese and English LongText-Bench, the highest scores among the compared methods at this budget. Controlled ablations show gains from the added moment loss, while generator EMA features perform competitively with an external DINOv2 encoder across the five reported metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/inclusionAI/IDM.
authors: Deyuan Liu, Yansen Han, Kaiwen Zheng, Jun Xie, Jiacheng Liu, Zhenglin Cheng, Peng Sun, Jintao Zhang, Jianguo Li, Tao Lin
bullets: Targets accurate prompt-detail rendering when only a few denoising steps are available.
Decomposes the reverse-KL field to motivate matching feature means and per-coordinate standard deviations.
Uses the generator’s EMA copy for feature statistics, avoiding an external feature encoder.
Evaluated with full-parameter and LoRA tuning on Z-Image-Turbo 6B and Qwen-Image 20B.
At two network evaluations, reports 94.25% on Chinese and 90.20% on English LongText-Bench; ablations attribute gains to the moment loss.

papers.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into agentic architectures has substantially increased token consumption, raising concerns about their energy footprint. Yet, estimating the energy consumption of proprietary API-based models remains challenging, and existing approaches focus primarily on generated output tokens while overlooking the impact of the large input contexts characteristic of agentic workflows. To address this gap, we systematically profile compute time and energy consumption across a wide range of prefill (input) and decode (output) token lengths. Using generalized linear models, we show that decode compute time and energy scale linearly with output length, whereas prefill compute time and energy exhibit both linear and quadratic scaling with input length. These findings demonstrate that input context becomes a relevant factor for large-context workloads. Furthermore, we show that compute time serves as a reliable proxy for energy consumption when direct energy measurements are unavailable. Our mapping framework enables precise energy estimation and supports more sustainable deployment decisions for agentic AI.
authors: Lars Krupp, Daniel Gei{\ss}ler, Francisco M. Calatrava-Nicolas, Stefan Gerd Fritsch, Paul Lukowicz, Jakob Karolus
bullets: Agentic LLM workflows increase token usage, but prior estimates often overlook input-context costs.
Decode time and energy scale linearly with output-token length.
Prefill time and energy show both linear and quadratic scaling with input-token length.
Compute time is a reliable proxy for energy when direct energy measurements are unavailable.
The framework supports energy estimation and more sustainable deployment decisions for agentic AI.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models aim to follow user actions while maintaining scene consistency over extended interactions. History-based methods reuse generated latents to preserve scene content, but three limitations of this reuse contribute to error recirculation. 1) The latent generated at each interaction is retained as history, potentially containing blurred details, geometric distortions, or semantic drift. 2) Although retrieved historical content matches the current scene, it can still contain errors that are carried into the next chunk. 3) New outputs then become history for later interactions, potentially reinforcing the same errors through repeated reuse. To limit this cycle, we aim to predict the future scene state from the current generated latent and the next action before generating the next interaction's video chunk. This future-state prior provides guidance for the next chunk, with the aim of reducing the errors carried forward from history. To this end, we propose a plug-and-play Causal Next-Chunk Predictor (C-NCP) with cross-model adaptability and prediction-guided modulation. We integrate C-NCP into four base generators and evaluate the augmented models across three benchmarks for interactive long-video generation and action-conditioned world modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate reduced error accumulation and improved long-horizon consistency across diverse generation settings. The project page is at https://GuangYuanKK.github.io/futureworld.
authors: Guangyuan Li, Kelu Yao, Shuolin Xu, Xinlei Yu, Wei Xing, Lei Zhao, Peng-Tao Jiang, Xiaogang Xu, Xiaobin Hu
bullets: History-based interactive video models can recycle blur, distortions, semantic drift, and prior errors across interactions.
The proposed plug-and-play Causal Next-Chunk Predictor forecasts a future scene state from the current latent and next action.
This prediction guides generation of the next video chunk through prediction-guided modulation.
C-NCP adapts across models and is integrated into four base generators.
Experiments on three interactive video and action-conditioned world-modeling benchmarks report reduced error accumulation and improved long-horizon consistency.

Panel c shows autoregressive inference, where the predicted future state guides a frozen autoregressive video DiT through modulation to generate the next latent chunk.

papers.abstract: We show that the transformer architecture emerges as the score of last-token laws in a natural statistical model of language, where sentences are empirical measures of tokens, a language is a law on $P(S^d)$, and our prior belief is that sentences carry no structure at all. By the maximum-entropy principle, we select the law closest to this prior in relative entropy among those reproducing an observed sentence-level statistic. We discuss the relevance of the statistic in the posterior interaction between tokens and we build a statistic, able to capture that interaction, with Luce's choice axiom truncated at the lowest relational order. This procedure gives the softmax choice rule, with the attention cross-moment as its mean parameter. The query--key matrix is then the Lagrange multiplier of a maximum-entropy problem inside each sentence, and the value matrix the multiplier of the constraint over the language, so that the two are untied. Under the optimal entropic law we then show that a transformer head appears in the score of the last-token law. For ordered sentences, causal masking follows from the masked reference choice rule, and with a next-token cross-moment the score equals one causally masked attention head. We also discuss multi-head attention, weight-tied unembedding, and a heuristic reading of residual blocks as projected Langevin steps.
authors: Giacomo Greco
bullets: Models sentences as empirical token measures and languages as probability laws over sentences, with an unstructured prior.
Uses maximum entropy under interaction constraints based on a lowest-order truncation of Luce’s choice axiom.
Derives the softmax choice rule, with the attention cross-moment as its mean parameter.
Interprets query–key and value matrices as distinct Lagrange multipliers at sentence and language levels.
For ordered sentences, a next-token cross-moment yields exactly one causally masked attention head; multi-head attention and residual blocks are also discussed.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Transformer architecture as a three-step procedure. In the first step an embedding operator maps each token, represented by a one-hot vector in R|V|, to a vector of Rd+1 through a learned matrix E ∈ R(d+1)×|V|, possibly combined with normalization and with a positional encoding which keeps track of token order. Then, in the second step the sequence of vectors x1, . . . , xn goes through a stack of L identical layers. Each layer consists of a residual attention sub-layer, in which every token updates its representation by attending to the other tokens of the sentence, and a residual MLP which acts on each token separately. The output is then projected back to Sd via LN. Finally, an unembedding matrix Wout ∈ R|V|×(d+1) maps the output representation of the last token to a vector of logits, one per element of the vocabulary. Their softmax is the law of the next token, from which a token is sampled and appended to the text.

Figure 2. Causal version of the pipeline of Figure 1. Two things change. First, each token is recorded together with its position, so that the sentence becomes the ordered measure → µ = 1 n ∑ i δ(xi,i) ∈ P(Sd×N). Second, the attention sub-layer is causally masked: the additive mask M sets to zero the weight of every key coming after the query (j > i), so that each token only reads itself and the tokens before it.

Figure 3. Multi-head version of the causal transformer block of Figure 2. The single masked head is replaced by H heads, each with its own query, key and value matrices Qh,Kh, Vh, all sharing the same causal mask M . The head outputs are summed before the residual connection and the normalization. In our model each head corresponds to a different choice rule, with attention matrix Λh = Q⊤ h Kh, and Vh is the Lagrange multiplier of the corresponding cross-moment.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical derivation of transformer/attention architecture from maximum-entropy principles, relevant to LLM architecture understanding.
papers.title: Emergence of the transformer architecture as the score of entropic laws of random measures
papers.tldr: A maximum-entropy model of token interactions derives a causally masked transformer attention head as the score of the next-token distribution.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) jointly support visual understanding and image generation, yet information flow between these two capabilities remains largely asymmetric: understanding representations routinely condition generation, whereas generative representations are rarely reused for multimodal reasoning. In this work, we investigate whether intermediate representations from a UMM's native diffusion branch can enhance spatial reasoning without compromising general multimodal understanding. We propose DiFuse, which selectively incorporates intermediate diffusion representations into the understanding pathway of UMMs. Through systematic layer-wise analysis, we identify which diffusion representations are most informative and where they can be integrated with minimal interference to semantic processing. Guided by these findings, DiFuse spatially aligns diffusion features with visual tokens and injects them into selected multimodal decoder layers via residual fusion. Extensive experiments on UniWorld-V1 show that, DiFuse consistently improves spatial reasoning over a matched SFT baseline while maintaining broadly comparable performance on general multimodal benchmarks. Further analyses show that these gains depend critically on the choice of diffusion representations, injection positions, and the preservation of spatial correspondence between diffusion features and visual tokens. Results on OmniGen2 further demonstrate the transferability of DiFuse across unified multimodal architectures. Overall, our findings show that native diffusion representations can provide complementary spatial cues for multimodal reasoning when selectively integrated in a structure-preserving manner.
authors: Ruixin Fan, Weining Wang, Jiahui Sun, Tailai Chen, Jing Liu
bullets: UMMs typically use understanding features to condition generation, but rarely reuse diffusion representations for reasoning.
DiFuse identifies informative diffusion layers and injects their spatially aligned features into selected multimodal decoder layers through residual fusion.
Experiments on UniWorld-V1 show improved spatial reasoning over a matched SFT baseline while preserving broadly comparable general multimodal performance.
Results on OmniGen2 indicate that the approach transfers across unified multimodal architectures.
Performance depends on selecting suitable diffusion representations, injection locations, and preserving visual-token spatial correspondence.

figures.caption: Figure 3: DiFuse architecture. (a) Overall pipeline. Given an input image and a question, the UMM’s understanding branch processes the visual and text tokens, while its native generation branch receives the same image and a fixed generation prompt “Generate the depth map of this image.” DiFuse extracts an intermediate spatial representation from the frozen DiT at a selected layer and denoising timestep, without decoding a final image. (b) DiFuse module. The extracted feature is spatially pooled and compressed with PCA, then normalized and projected through a convolutional adapter. Bilinear resizing aligns the resulting feature map with the visual-token grid. DiFuse adds the aligned features to visual-token states at selected decoder layers through residual connections; text-token states receive no direct residual update.

Figure 1: Overview of DiFuse and its impact on unified multimodal models. (a) DiFuse establishes a generation-to-understanding pathway by reusing intermediate representations from the native Diffusion Transformer (DiT) branch and integrating them into the visual understanding pathway of a unified multimodal model. (b) General–spatial capability landscape. Models are positioned by their average general-understanding (Avg-G) and spatial-reasoning (Avg-S) scores. Marker shapes distinguish general-purpose MLLMs, UMMs, spatially enhanced models, and DiFuse. (c) Gains relative to Qwen2.5-VL-7B. We compare four Qwen2.5-VL-7B-based models against the same baseline. Blue and green bars show changes in Avg-G and Avg-S, respectively. UniWorld-V1 + DiFuse improves Avg-S by 2.60 points while leaving Avg-G nearly unchanged (+0.02 points).

Figure 2: Paradigms for generation-assisted and structure-enhanced multimodal understanding. Existing methods use diffusion objectives, explicit visual states, external diffusion features, or dedicated geometry branches, whereas DiFuse directly reuses spatially aligned representations from the UMM’s native DiT branch.

Figure 4: Diffusion responses across timesteps at fixed layer g18. Response maps are shown at t ∈ {50, 100, 200, 300} for three representative images. Spatial organization is retained across timesteps, while the response granularity varies.

Figure 5: Diffusion responses across candidate layers at fixed timestep t = 100. Response maps are shown for the vital-layer candidates identified following Stable Flow (Avrahami et al., 2025). The spatial responses vary substantially across diffusion depth despite using the same image and timestep.

Figure 6: Qualitative comparison between SFT and DiFuse. Examples cover spatial relations, depth and 3D reasoning, and general and fine-grained visual understanding. Compared with the matched SFT baseline, DiFuse corrects several errors involving spatial relations and depth reasoning while largely preserving predictions on general visual understanding examples. Red and green responses denote incorrect and correct predictions, respectively.

papers.abstract: Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs) frequently fail to recognize culture-specific concepts, especially from underrepresented regions. Effectively injecting this long-tail knowledge into existing models remains a challenge. In this work, we investigate knowledge editing as a targeted alternative by introducing CulturalBind, a benchmark comprising 3.2K images of 1K concepts from 6 domains, designed to evaluate culture-aware cross-modal knowledge as well as concept-level knowledge editing in VLMs. Pre-edit evaluation reveals that textual and visual knowledge is decoupled: models often demonstrate text-based knowledge of cultural concepts but fail to identify them from images. We then evaluate editing methods in single and sequential scenarios. Although current methods successfully correct individual visual recognition errors, they exhibit low cross-modal portability, failing to integrate edits into the model's broader parametric knowledge. Furthermore, performance degrades rapidly under sequential editing, highlighting the need for comprehensive adaptation approaches that better consolidate multimodal knowledge over time.
authors: Malvina Nikandrou, Georgios Pantazopoulos, Ioannis Konstas, Alessandro Suglia
bullets: Cultural knowledge from underrepresented regions is often poorly recognized in images despite being known textually.
CulturalBind benchmarks 3.2K images covering 1K concepts across 6 domains for cross-modal knowledge and editing evaluation.
Current editing methods can fix individual visual recognition errors but have limited cross-modal portability.
Sequential editing causes rapid performance degradation, revealing weak knowledge consolidation.
The findings motivate more comprehensive methods for sustained multimodal adaptation.

papers.abstract: Understanding how humans interact with the world requires a representation of physical interactions at the hand surface. Tactile sensing captures these interactions, but collecting tactile data at scale requires specialized hardware. We introduce TactoHand, a model that predicts three dense hand-surface interaction fields---contact, proximity, and 3D force---from monocular video. We derive geometry-based contact and proximity labels and motion-derived force labels from eligible training data within a curated collection spanning approximately 50 million source frames. TactoHand uses a temporal transformer to aggregate visual evidence across frames, while three learned queries decode the corresponding hand-surface fields. A differentiable physics layer further constrains force predictions using observed object motion. Across in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, TactoHand improves contact and proximity estimation over prior methods. In addition, physics supervision reduces position and rotation errors in motion rollouts, and the predicted contact and proximity fields improve downstream hand-object reconstruction. Together, these results show a scalable, low-cost path to learning hand-surface interaction fields without collecting tactile measurements. Code will be released at https://github.com/zhenqis123/Tactohand.
authors: Ziheng Xi, Weibo Li, Jiayi Yu, Sipeng Zheng, Wanpeng Zhang, Haiweng Xu, Hao Luo, Chuan Mao, Zongqing Lu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of scaling tactile-data collection for modeling physical hand-object interactions.
Derives geometry- and motion-based supervision from eligible video data and aggregates temporal evidence with a transformer.
Uses separate learned queries to decode contact, proximity, and force fields, with differentiable physics constraints on force predictions.
Improves contact and proximity estimation across in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks.
Physics supervision benefits motion rollouts, while contact and proximity predictions improve downstream hand-object reconstruction.

Contact, proximity, force, and pose losses are applied according to the supervision available for each sample.

Lower right: the penalty weight (q(s)2 + ϵ)−1 rises toward the relaxed 20 mm candidate cut-off.

papers.abstract: Human demonstrations provide a natural and scalable source of data for learning dexterous manipulation policies. However, existing retargeting methods primarily transfer human kinematics, while the tactile information underlying physical interaction is rarely preserved across embodiments. To address this limitation, we present a hierarchical three-stage framework for kinematic-tactile aligned dexterous retargeting. We use object-centric contact wrench space as a physical representation for tactile alignment between human and robot hands. The framework first aligns hand kinematics and contact geometry, and then constructs a human wrench support profile from tactile forces and contact geometry. Robot fingertip force targets are subsequently optimized to cover the human wrench support and converted into joint position corrections, yielding directly replayable robot hand trajectories. We evaluate the framework in simulation and real robot experiments across three pouring conditions. In the real robot experiments, our method achieves a 96.7\% replay success rate and higher wrench transfer fidelity than representative retargeting baselines. The framework enables physically grounded transfer of kinematic and tactile information from human demonstrations to robot hands, providing a path toward scalable learning of contact-rich dexterous manipulation.
authors: Xinyuan He, Ziheng Xu, Yueyuan Chen, Yufan Ye, Yuanshuo Tan, Huiming Pan, Jianjun Meng, Shuo Jiang, Peter B. Shull
bullets: Addresses the loss of tactile and physical interaction information in kinematics-only retargeting.
Aligns hand kinematics and contact geometry before modeling the human contact wrench support profile.
Optimizes robot fingertip force targets to cover the human wrench support, then converts them into replayable joint corrections.
Evaluated in simulation and on a real robot across three pouring conditions.
Reports higher wrench-transfer fidelity than representative baselines in addition to the 96.7% real-robot replay success rate.

(b) Physics-aware contact alignment refines the hand– object configuration. (c) Object-centric wrench space alignment optimizes robot normal force targets to cover the human wrench support profile along the demonstrated manipulation trajectory and converts them into joint position corrections.
Fig. 4. Qualitative visualization of a representative pouring sequence. (a) Human demonstration and (b) the corresponding robot replay across four task phases: grasp and lift, tilt, pour, and hold.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a retargeting framework for dexterous manipulation that transfers kinematic and tactile information from human demonstrations.
papers.title: Kinematic-Tactile Aligned Dexterous Retargeting with Contact Wrench Space Alignment
papers.tldr: A three-stage retargeting framework transfers both human hand motion and tactile contact forces to robot hands through contact wrench-space alignment, achieving 96.7% replay success in real-robot pouring experiments.

papers.abstract: For a time-homogeneous Markov process, the fixed-lag solution operator \( (T_\tau f)(x)=\mathbb E[f(X_{t+\tau})\mid X_t=x] \) of the Kolmogorov backward equation evolves observables linearly and deterministically, even when the dynamics are stochastic. We approximate this operator using a two-stage method where we first approximate this operator directly from data, without knowledge of the governing equation (e.g., Fourier Neural Operator), and then compress the Galerkin projection onto a finite-dimensional observable space that is fixed in advance or selected variationally. The error analysis traces the learning error of the estimator, the sampling error of the Galerkin inner products, and the invariance and reconstruction properties of the observable space to the computed spectra and forecasts. The sampling error enters only through a multiplicative factor. Near an isolated spectral cluster, the invariance defect of a subspace controls its distance from the target invariant subspace. The forecast error is controlled by the one-step error of the reduced model and the projection error of the observable; when the measure is invariant and the reduced model preserves constants and is stable on mean-zero observables, the bound is uniform in the horizon. For deterministic dynamics, a learning rate for Fourier neural operators (FNOs) gives one explicit bound for the learning error. Numerical experiments illustrate spectral approximation and forecasting, including long-rollout stability and a comparison with extended dynamic mode decomposition (EDMD) when fewer transition pairs than basis functions are observed.
authors: Yuanchao Xu, Claire Valva, Ben Gao, Isao Ishikawa
bullets: Approximates the fixed-lag Markov transition operator directly from data, potentially using Fourier Neural Operators.
Compresses the learned operator into a finite-dimensional observable space chosen in advance or variationally.
Provides error analysis linking learning, sampling, subspace invariance, and reconstruction errors to spectral and forecast accuracy.
Under invariant-measure and stability conditions, forecast-error bounds remain uniform over the forecasting horizon.
Numerical experiments demonstrate spectral approximation, long-rollout stability, and performance when transition pairs are fewer than basis functions, compared with EDMD.

papers.abstract: Multi-turn conversations with multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reuse input context, but long multimodal inputs increase time to first token (TTFT). Query-aware hard pruning reduces prefill tokens but permanently excludes information that later questions may require. We propose Raincheck, a framework for deferred multimodal prefill that decouples initial token selection from later information availability. An existing pruning method selects tokens for initial prefill; Raincheck preserves and progressively prefills unselected tokens in source order using unused compute capacity during decode. Unfinished prefill continues after answer return during available scheduling gaps. Attention visibility control and affine state mapping enable context updates after generation begins in full-attention and hybrid recurrent models. Prefill-decode fusion reduces repeated weight reads. We evaluate Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3.5-9B with 30% initial multimodal-token retention. Across both models and four pruning methods, Raincheck recovers on average 77.7% and 60.4% of the quality lost to matched hard pruning on MultiVerse and ConvBench, respectively. On MultiVerse, the SGLang implementation reduces mean first-turn TTFT by up to 24.1% relative to full prefill, with less than 0.5% increase in mean time per output token (TPOT).

papers.abstract: Recent advances in test-time optimization have shown that the multimodal reasoning performance of large multimodal language models (MLLMs) can be improved during inference without modifying backbone model parameters. However, existing approaches primarily operate at the prompt or output level, leaving the latent reasoning process largely uncontrolled and insufficient to prevent error accumulation during autoregressive generation. To address this limitation, we propose LatentWeave, a test-time framework that treats multimodal reasoning as a controllable latent trajectory. LatentWeave performs structured Latent Weaving, progressively refining intermediate hidden states segment-wise to correct emerging deviations, and further introduces Reasoning Anchors via lightweight WEAVE tokens to stabilize reasoning structure and guide answer-oriented generation. These mechanisms are designed to enable fine-grained, step-aware intervention in the latent reasoning process while keeping the main MLLM backbone parameters fixed. Extensive experiments across diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks report improvements over the evaluated baselines; the contribution of latent optimization, anchor training, and additional test-time computation is analyzed separately in the ablation and efficiency studies. Our code is available at https://github.com/jins7/LatentWeave.

papers.abstract: In segmentation-based continuous sign language recognition, an untrimmed video is first partitioned into lexical units; segmentation is therefore a means to an end---downstream recognition. However, segmenters are usually judged by local boundary detection rather than by the quality of the lexical segments and the recognition they enable. We present BEACON, a begin/end-aware segmenter that combines four-class Outside/Begin/Inside/End (BIOE) labeling, constrained Viterbi decoding over eight legal transitions, and boundary knowledge distilled from a binary teacher into a shared student. Under strict no-cut evaluation with validation-based model selection, BEACON improves segment-F1 by 14.58/14.59 points and boundary-F1 by 2.17/1.22 points, and reduces the downstream word error rate (WER) by 9.10/4.15 points relative to the state-of-the-art in the PHOENIX-14/BSL Corpus. To examine which segmentation metric better reflects downstream recognition, we evaluated five distinct architecture families. Segment-F1 aligns more consistently with lower WER than boundary-F1 in both corpora (Spearman $\rho=-1.0/-0.9$ versus $-0.9/-0.8$). These results support evaluating sign language segmentation in terms of segment quality and downstream recognition utility rather than local boundary accuracy alone.

During training only, a separately trained, frozen binary teacher (shown dashed, with its own encoder, and discarded after training) distills boundary evidence into this student IO branch via a KL loss; inference uses a single 5M-parameter model with one encoder. papers.abstract: Reasoning informs decision-making by connecting intended actions with their expected consequences. Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models incorporate embodied chains of thought (ECoTs) to guide action generation. However, such guidance remains implicit, as actions are conditioned on ECoTs rather than explicitly optimized to align with them. We introduce CoRAct, a consequence-grounded reasoning-to-action alignment framework that explicitly aligns reasoning and action through reward-guided optimization in action noise space. CoRAct formulates two physically grounded ECoT components as verifiable signals: movement specifies intended motion, while waypoints encode expected spatial consequences. A unified Mixture-of-Transformers jointly models ECoT reasoning, action generation, and action-conditioned future prediction. For candidate actions generated from sampled noise, CoRAct computes alignment rewards based on movement consistency and agreement between predicted outcomes and specified waypoints. These rewards guide group-relative optimization of the initial noise distribution, steering action generation toward consistency with intended actions and expected consequences. Experiments across RoboCasa, VLABench, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate improvements in task success, generalization, and reasoning-execution alignment over strong ECoT-based VLA baselines. CoRAct also grounds externally provided ECoTs in executable behavior, enabling zero-shot adaptation to novel scenarios by leveraging knowledge from powerful vision-language models. Project page and dataset: https://onlyxingxingzyx.github.io/CoRAct/
authors: Yixue Zhang, Wenke Xia, Kun Wu, Wenbo Yu, Pei Ren, Junnan Nie, Di Hu, Zhengping Che, Chang Liu

papers.abstract: One-step distillation turns pretrained diffusion models into fast generators, but strong results often require substantial training machinery and compute. Pure adversarial distillation offers a simpler route, yet has struggled at modern text-to-image scale. To address this limitation, we propose ROAD (Representation-grounded One-step Adversarial Distillation), a one-stage framework that distills text-to-image models with one adversarial objective and a lightweight representation-space critic. First, we replace the classical convolutional head with a Lipschitz-controlled Transformer head with token-level text conditioning, which matches the semantic tokens of modern visual encoders. Second, we observed a fixed random feature mixing leads to long-horizon degradation. We attribute it to generator-critic co-adaptation around one realization-specific view, and periodically re-draw the mixing to keep the randomization effective. Third, for our dense and vector-valued logits, we introduce Jacobian R1 which penalizes the full input-logit Jacobian, overcoming pooled R1's limitation of neglecting most of logit sensitivities. A single adversarial objective then suffices: in one step, ROAD reaches 11.03 FID on SDXL and 13.73 on SD3.5-M on COCO-10K, surpassing the multi-step teachers at a fraction of distribution matching's training compute.
authors: Xiaoou Li, Shan You, Tao Huang
bullets: Targets the high training complexity and compute traditionally required for one-step distillation at text-to-image scale.

Introduces Jacobian R1 regularization to capture sensitivities across dense, vector-valued logits.
Reports 11.03 FID on SDXL and 13.73 on SD3.5-M on COCO-10K, with a fraction of distribution-matching training compute.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agent skills enable AI agents to accumulate and refine reusable procedural knowledge from interaction experience without updating model parameters. However, since such skills are typically represented as textual documents and executed through LLM reasoning, even previously learned procedures must be repeatedly interpreted and regenerated, introducing avoidable uncertainty into every execution. In contrast, program execution is deterministic and independently verifiable. Intuitively, transforming well-specified operations into executable programs can reduce reliance on LLM reasoning and, consequently, reduce execution uncertainty. Motivated by this intuition, we introduce SKillCompiler, a self-evolving skill framework that integrates programmatic compilation into the skill evolution process. Specifically, SkillCompiler adopts an executability-aware skill compilation strategy that decomposes skills into fine-grained operations, analyzes their executability, and constructs hybrid skill skeletons that retain LLM reasoning for context-dependent operations while compiling well-specified ones into validated programs. To avoid redundant program synthesis and enable executable knowledge to accumulate across evolving skills, we further design a program asset reuse mechanism that organizes validated programs as reusable assets, retrieves existing implementations whenever applicable, and synthesizes and verifies new programs only when necessary. Extensive experiments on five benchmarks and six model families demonstrate that SkillCompiler consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving up to 32.33\% improvement in task performance.

Experiments across five benchmarks and six model families report up to 32.33% higher task performance than existing methods.

papers.abstract: Progress toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) has largely relied on scaling a resource-intensive executive, System-2, through larger models, more data and compute, longer reasoning, and more agents. We ask whether the next stage may come instead from co-designing it with System-1, a lightweight, semantically aware predictor that evaluates candidate interactions before execution, so that System-2 acts only on those worth their cost. Our answer is a qualified yes. We study \textit{conditional interaction}, a predict--gate--execute--update loop: System-1 estimates each candidate's utility, System-2 executes those admitted by an adaptive threshold, and the outcomes update System-1. The loop spans training, test-time reasoning, adaptive decision-making, and agentic tool use, with utility and cost defined by the application. Under ideal screening and equal execution costs, execution compute falls by a factor approaching $1/\rho_u$, where $\rho_u$ is the density of utility-relevant interactions (cost-weighted when costs differ); prediction errors, exploration, and distribution shift reduce the saving. We bound selection regret by predictor error and the utility margin. These results motivate our central hypothesis: $\rho_u$ is a measurable coordinate of scaling efficiency and makes informative compute a better description of scaling than total compute.
authors: Qi Wang, Yun Qu, Lizhou Cai, Heming Zou, Haoang Chi, Yiqin Lv, Xiang Li, Haiyan Feng, Mengyu Ge, Yize Geng, Yuhang Jiang, Yixiu Mao, Xiangyang Ji
bullets: Introduces conditional interaction: predict utility, gate candidates, execute selected actions, and update the predictor.
Applies the framework to training, test-time reasoning, adaptive decisions, and agentic tool use.
Under ideal screening, execution compute can decrease roughly with the inverse density of utility-relevant interactions.
Prediction errors, exploration, and distribution shift limit compute savings.
Proposes utility-relevant interaction density as a scaling-efficiency measure beyond total compute.

Figure 1 An Illustrative Roadmap to AGI and its Beyond. As AI development progresses, broad capability resembles a summit that systems approach but may hit diminishing returns due to constraints in data, compute, and parameters. In Era 1 (2012–2020) progress came mainly from scaling model capacity, and in Era 2 (2020–2025) from scaling data and computation. For Era 3 (2026+), this work emphasizes a next-scaling lens: co-designing a cost-effective System-1 that prioritizes interactions by expected utility and a resource-intensive System-2 for complicated tasks. This emphasis becomes increasingly consequential for foundation models and embodied agents as they depend on generation, computation, tool use, and environmental interaction, and thus on the cost of each.

As AI increasingly produces the data and feedback it learns from (AI for AI), deciding which self-generated interactions are worth executing becomes a central efficiency problem.

papers.abstract: Compositional motion transfer requires a model to extract motions from multiple reference videos, and apply each motion to a user-specified object in one target scene. Existing methods normally struggle to reliably assign different reference motions to the correct target objects, thus a motion intended for one object may affect another. Meanwhile, some motion-specific tuning approaches are still facing another issue: they must run a new optimization whenever the reference video changes, making repeated transfers inefficient. To address these limitations, we propose RART, a framework that unifies object-wise motion extraction, target-region anchoring, and frame-aligned injection into a frozen video Diffusion Transformer for multi-object motion transfer. For each reference motion, RART extracts temporally ordered features from the masked reference video, and then conditions them on the target first-frame mask to form mask-anchored motion tokens. Frame-aligned motion cross-attention allows each generated frame to read only the motion tokens at the corresponding time slots, composing all object motions in one denoising process. During training, a motion-attention routing loss encourages each target region to attend to its corresponding motion tokens and reduces interference between objects. Therefore, RART can handle novel reference-target combinations without per-video optimization. Experiments show that RART achieves accurate motion preservation, efficient inference, and strong compositional generalization.

The abstract reports accurate motion preservation, efficient inference, and strong compositional generalization to novel reference-target combinations.

papers.abstract: AI coding agents now do long, multi-step and multi-session software work with little supervision. When a developer comes back to that work, the useful question is not what the model said but what was actually done, by whom, and whether it is finished. We study this in three parts. First, we verify Agenttrail, an open-source local observability tool for coding agents, against its source at commit e4ba2da: nine documented constants and mechanisms hold at file-and-line level, two event pipelines are never unified, and its Map service has an unauthenticated local mutation surface. Second, we run a prototype of our system on 45 real coding-agent sessions (102,233 records, 20,577 tool executions, 2,336 human-to-agent episodes). With a blind-audited classifier (precision 83.3% and 96.7%) we estimate that 23.4% (95% CI 17.1 to 35.7) of code-editing episodes end with no independent check after the last edit, and that 57.8% of to-dos the agent marked complete after editing had no proof in between. A 10-minute timing heuristic for session hand-offs recovers 6 of the 24 session pairs that content lineage links. 42% of sessions run longer than 24 hours, 48.1% of transcript bytes lie past a 2 MiB replay bound, and 1,326 records in 16 sessions contain credential-like strings. Third, we propose Soei (Structured Observability of Evidence and Intent): an acknowledgement-aware event schema, a hash-chained local ledger, a W3C PROV-aligned graph, calibrated inference for attribution and lineage, and a verification layer that keeps a claim of completion apart from proof. On the same corpus the ledger is 20% of raw size, holds no content or credentials, verifies at about 126k events/s, detects tampering and replays deterministically. We position the work against concurrent 2026 proposals and define autonomy levels with evidence gates and harness metrics baselined on our data.

papers.abstract: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) enable powerful multi-image synthesis but incur substantial computation from long visual contexts. While token pruning offers a direct route to accelerating inference, existing methods are primarily adapted from understanding tasks, suffering from insufficient reference image exploration, confused conditional guidance, and pooling-induced ambiguity that degrades generation quality. To address these issues, we propose CATP, the first training-free context-compression method tailored to UMM generation, which \textbf{C}alibrates the discrepancies of general \textbf{A}ttention-based \textbf{T}oken \textbf{P}runing for better quality-efficiency trade-off. Concretely, building on independent layer-wise pruning during denoising, we introduce Guidance-Consistent Pruning (GCP) to synchronize pruning decisions across conditioning branches, and a Taylor-Calibrated Attention Metric (TCAM) that derives a theoretically grounded second-order correction for pooling-induced bias. In addition, a Fast Scoring Operator (FSO) fuses the calibration into tiled online Softmax to reduce pruning cost. Extensive experiments across representative UMMs and benchmarks demonstrate that CATP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art token-reduction methods, achieving up to 2.09$\times$ attention-core speedup.

papers.abstract: View- and target-specific echocardiography AI models capture useful but complementary information and may not achieve sufficient predictive performance in isolation. A learned ensemble is a natural way to combine these outputs, but heterogeneous models typically require each output to be converted into a binary decision, probability, confidence score, or fixed-length feature vector. We developed a supervised large language model (LLM)-based late-fusion module that directly aggregates view-specific predicted finding statements and predicted measurements in language space and learns a case-level fusion function. In patient-level three-fold cross-validation of 859 examinations from 646 patients, the proposed method integrated heterogeneous outputs within a single framework, performed comparably to the best-performing reference strategy evaluated, and outperformed a general-purpose LLM without task-specific training. These results suggest that a supervised LLM can combine multiple upstream models without model-specific output conversion or feature engineering that requires medical knowledge.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning has become a widely adopted approach for vision-based robot policies, owing to its conceptual simplicity, scalability, and ability to leverage large-scale datasets. As these policies have grown more capable, action chunking has become their standard interface. At each decision step the policy outputs several future actions at once. Backbones from diffusion policies to large vision-language-action models all share it. Whatever backbone produces the chunk, its temporal structure is learned only implicitly. The commanded trajectory is therefore jerky both within a chunk and between successive chunks. On real hardware this appears as visible vibration and as repeated saturation of the follower's velocity limit. We address this issue by incorporating a movement-primitive-based trajectory representation into action chunking. Specifically, a trajectory segment is represented as a linear combination of smooth basis functions, yielding smooth trajectories by construction while leaving the policy architecture, training objective, and inference procedure unchanged. The same representation also yields a closed-form, inference-time correction for the second source of jerk. We condition the predicted coefficients so that the new chunk passes through a via-point at the previous chunk's last commanded action. This correction needs no retraining and, unlike asynchronous Real-Time Chunking, applies to policies queried in one shot. We instantiate it on a one-shot (ACT) and an iterative (DiT) backbone and evaluate in simulation and on a real bimanual ALOHA platform. The representation lowers within-chunk jerk by an order of magnitude on the one-shot backbone and by 2.4 times on the iterative one, with task success statistically non-inferior. The conditioning then removes 73-84% of the boundary discontinuity, at negligible per-step cost.
authors: Shota Nomura, Takayuki Osa, Yasuhiro Kato, Kazuki Ota, Naoki Shitanda, Tatsuya Harada

papers.abstract: Softmax routing in mixture-of-experts models can concentrate probability on a subset of experts, suppressing access to the others. We study how this concentration forms, why it persists, and how suppressed probabilities recover. For fixed experts, a stationary-loss barrier identifies the face supporting the optimal routed output. In a common-target square-loss model with freely trainable expert outputs, slow adaptation tracks fixed-expert dynamics on finite horizons, while every fixed positive adaptation rate yields an interior routing limit. An exact normal-velocity decomposition separates complementary-expert covariance from relative gradient advantage. Under positive two-sided power bounds along recovery paths, uniform over initial masses, the resulting coefficient's order of vanishing gives logarithmic or power-law recovery times. Integrations of constructed fields reproduce these orders. An exact discrete log-odds identity relates neural updates to threshold crossing. In paired Transformer-MoE training, removing a class-conditional router-gradient contrast delays confirmed recovery and reduces accumulated log-odds on fixed tokens, both with and without capacity constraints.
authors: Shengze Xu, Maolin Deng, Tieyong Zeng
bullets: Identifies a stationary-loss barrier determining the expert subset that supports the optimal routed output.
Shows that slow expert adaptation follows fixed-expert routing dynamics over finite horizons, while any positive adaptation rate leads to an interior routing limit.
Decomposes recovery motion into complementary-expert covariance and relative gradient advantage.
Derives logarithmic or power-law recovery times from the vanishing order of a recovery coefficient, with matching constructed-field examples.
In paired Transformer-MoE experiments, removing class-conditional router-gradient contrast delays recovery and lowers accumulated log-odds, with or without capacity constraints.

papers.abstract: Label-free test-time reinforcement learning adapts vision--language models using rewards derived from their own predictions. However, misinterpreted visual evidence and sensitivity to textual formulation can produce a consistent but incorrect consensus that majority voting reinforces. Cross-view aggregation can expose such errors, but image and text transformations may themselves degrade task-relevant evidence to different extents. We introduce \method, a reliability-aware harmonic consensus framework for multimodal test-time reinforcement learning. \method constructs a $2\times2$ grid combining original and perturbed images with direct-solving and reframing modes, selects pseudo-labels through weighted harmonic aggregation, and adapts modality-level weights using batch-averaged, temporally smoothed shifts in pseudo-label confidence as a heuristic reliability signal. We formulate consensus as a weighted $\chi^2$-barycenter problem whose unique minimizer is the normalized weighted harmonic aggregate, without requiring correct-answer invariance. An exact support--dispersion decomposition characterizes when harmonic aggregation preserves or corrects arithmetic rankings, while a sensitivity analysis establishes how modality reweighting changes pairwise ranking margins, informing interpretation of the heuristic updates. Across six benchmarks and three Qwen3-VL model scales, \method outperforms TTRV in 16 of 18 benchmark--model settings on adaptation instances and 17 of 18 settings on held-out instances under matched estimation and optimization rollout counts. These results demonstrate improved target-task adaptation and transfer to unseen instances without further updates.
authors: Haotian Lyu, Haoyu Wang, Ru Wang, Feng Ji, Ziwen Li, Jiaxian Guo, Mingming Gong
bullets: Addresses self-reinforcing errors caused by consistent but incorrect prediction consensus and unreliable image/text transformations.
Uses a 2×2 grid of original/perturbed images and direct-solving/reframing prompts.
Selects pseudo-labels with weighted harmonic aggregation and adapts modality weights using smoothed confidence shifts.
Provides a χ²-barycenter formulation, support–dispersion analysis, and ranking-sensitivity analysis for the aggregation method.
Outperforms TTRV in 16/18 adaptation and 17/18 held-out benchmark–model settings across six benchmarks and three Qwen3-VL scales.

For each instance, rollout rewards are pooled and jointly normalized to compute GRPO advantages.

Curves are smoothed using a time-weighted exponential moving average for visualization. Ground-truth answers are used only for post-hoc evaluation and are unavailable during adaptation. papers.abstract: Multi-arm robot platforms, including bimanual and humanoid robots, have the capability to complete tasks with lower cycle times than single-arm systems, but they are more difficult to safely control due to the presence of multi-arm constraints. The paradigm of training generalist robot policies from massive datasets is a promising approach to address general-purpose multi-arm manipulation, but the acquisition of large multi-arm manipulation datasets remains a bottleneck. Automated demonstration generation can alleviate this burden by synthesizing new demonstrations from a handful of source demonstrations, but existing algorithms ignore multi-arm constraints and as a result often induce unsafe and unsuccessful behaviors. We address this limitation by introducing ScheduleGen, an integrated planning & scheduling algorithm for multi-arm demonstration generation. We evaluate ScheduleGen on 28 simulation task variants, including seven externally authored RoboDojo tasks and settings inaccessible to prior systems; it achieves 79.6% mean data-generation success and trains policies with 65.5% mean success. ScheduleGen policies outperform those trained on a state-of-the-art data generation baseline, and achieve 50-80% success across eight real-world variants through zero-shot sim-to-real and real-to-sim-to-real transfer. Videos and more at: https://schedulegen.github.io/
authors: Neel Jawale, Stephan Pleines, Soha Pouya, Yuke Zhu, Ajay Mandlekar, Caelan Garrett
bullets: Multi-arm manipulation can be faster but is difficult to control safely because of coordination constraints.
Large multi-arm demonstration datasets are costly to collect; prior automated generation methods often ignore these constraints.
ScheduleGen integrates planning and scheduling to synthesize demonstrations from a small number of source examples.
Across 28 simulation variants, it achieved 79.6% mean data-generation success and trained policies reached 65.5% mean success.
Policies transferred zero-shot across simulation and real-world settings, achieving 50–80% success on eight real-world variants.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models can recognize visual content yet struggle to reason reliably over it across multiple steps. In counting, a model may see all objects but lose track of which ones it has counted. We argue that such failures, commonly attributed to perception, reveal a reference gap: the failure to bind language to the relevant visual entities, regions, or locations. Motivated by the theory of visual routines, we test whether external references such as numbering can narrow this gap. We introduce ReGap-Bench, a paired benchmark of five visual reasoning tasks in which the scene, question, and answer are fixed and only the reference varies. Results show that task-matched references improve accuracy by up to 25\%, while mismatched references provide little benefit or even hurt performance. These findings identify the reference gap as a bottleneck distinct from visual perception and show that constructing task-appropriate visual references can serve as a training-free visual skill for improving multimodal reasoning.
authors: Guizhen Chen, Weiwen Xu, Wotao Yin, Anh Tuan Luu, Hou Pong Chan
bullets: Identifies a “reference gap”: failures to link language with relevant visual entities, regions, or locations, even when objects are perceived.
Introduces ReGap-Bench, a paired benchmark covering five visual reasoning tasks where only the reference varies.
Tests external visual scaffolds such as numbering, motivated by visual routines theory.
Task-matched references improve accuracy by up to 25%; mismatched references offer little benefit or can reduce performance.
Shows that constructing suitable references is a training-free visual skill, distinct from perception.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the 'reference gap' in multimodal reasoning, identifying a bottleneck in binding language to visual entities. This directly addresses Multimodal Foundation Models and Spatial Intelligence.
papers.title: Diagnosing the Reference Gap: What Visual Scaffolds Can and Cannot Fix in Multimodal Reasoning

papers.abstract: Linear recurrences are emerging as practical alternatives to softmax attention in large language models, appearing in both standalone and hybrid architectures. However, despite their rapid emergence, low-precision inference remains much less developed for these models than for softmax attention. During prefill, chunkwise-parallel algorithms cast much of the recurrence as dense matrix multiplications, suggesting a natural path to low-precision execution. Simply quantizing these operations in their native form, however, can be fragile. In this work, we identify functional invariances that preserve the full-precision computation while making the operands more amenable to quantization. Building on this observation, we introduce LinQuant, a framework for low-precision recurrent prefill based on seven such invariances, including rotations, diagonal rescalings, and alternative placements of recurrent decay and write factors. We derive when these transformations remain valid across common recurrence families spanning linear, gated, and delta-rule updates, and show that they provide complementary degrees of freedom for improving low-precision accuracy. Finally, we translate this framework to production by augmenting SSDi8, an existing low-precision prefill pipeline for Mamba-2, with the applicable invariances. LinQuant improves perplexity at matched latency on Mamba-2 1.3B, 2.7B, and 8B and Nemotron-H 8B, demonstrating the practical utility of invariance-based quantization for recurrent models.
authors: Neehal Tumma, Philipp Nazari, Rohan Cherukuri, Daniela Rus, T. Konstantin Rusch
bullets: Targets the underdeveloped problem of low-precision inference for linear recurrences, especially during chunkwise-parallel prefill.
Introduces seven functional invariances, including rotations, diagonal rescaling, and alternative placements of decay and write factors.
Characterizes when these transformations preserve computation across linear, gated, and delta-rule recurrence families.
Extends the SSDi8 Mamba-2 low-precision prefill pipeline with applicable invariances.
Improves perplexity at matched latency across Mamba-2 1.3B, 2.7B, 8B and Nemotron-H 8B models.

papers.tldr: LinQuant improves low-precision recurrent-model prefill by exploiting computation-preserving invariances to make recurrence operations easier to quantize accurately.

papers.abstract: Predicting where to grasp and how to move is fundamentally a geometry problem. Vision-language models treat it as language generation instead. They tokenize spatial coordinates into text and decode them autoregressively. This mechanism ignores spatial structure and truncates continuous precision. Errors compound across coordinate tokens during decoding. In this paper, we show that compact off-the-shelf VLMs with 0.5-2B parameters already encode rich spatial information in their intermediate hidden states. Autoregressive decoding is the dominant bottleneck for trajectory prediction, while affordance prediction depends additionally on feature depth and decoder architecture. We expose the latent spatial information with a lightweight, geometry-compatible prediction head that attaches to a frozen backbone. It reads features from an intermediate hidden layer, conditions a learned query on the task instruction and refines it via cross-attention over the visual tokens to regress affordance boxes and trajectory waypoints directly as continuous values, without modifying the backbone. We evaluate on ShareRobot-Bench and AGD20K. Our 2B variant reduces trajectory error by over 60% and improves ShareRobot-Bench affordance mAP by 85% relative to the autoregressive baseline. It approaches RoboBrain on trajectory prediction (0.251 vs 0.191 DFD) at 3.8x higher throughput. These results demonstrate a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off for instruction-conditioned 2D geometric prediction.
authors: Akila Ayanthi, Darshana Priyasad, Tharindu Fernando, Dimity Miller, Sridha Sridharan, Clinton Fookes, Peyman Moghadam
bullets: Problem: Tokenizing coordinates as text loses continuous spatial precision and causes autoregressive error accumulation.
Method: Attach a lightweight head to a frozen VLM, using intermediate features, instruction-conditioned queries, and cross-attention to regress boxes and waypoints directly.
Contribution: Separates geometric prediction from language decoding without modifying the VLM backbone.

Results: On ShareRobot-Bench and AGD20K, the 2B model reduces trajectory error by over 60%, improves affordance mAP by 85% relative to the autoregressive baseline, and achieves 3.8× higher throughput than RoboBrain while approaching its trajectory performance.
Scope: Affordance prediction also depends on feature depth and decoder architecture.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Architecture overview. A frozen VLM processes an RGB image and task instruction; hidden states from an intermediate layer are passed to a lightweight geometric prediction head. A DETR-style transformer decoder, conditioned on the instruction via the final text token hidden state, refines a learned query against the visual memory tokens. Two independent FFNs decode the query into continuous outputs: affordance boxes (L1+GIoU loss) and trajectory waypoints (L1+startpoint+endpoint loss). No gradient flows into the VLM.

Figure 7. Predicted waypoint heatmaps over the test set, visualizing how endpoint supervision shapes the spatial distribution of trajectory predictions. (a) Ground-truth distribution: waypoints are broadly spread, reflecting the spatial diversity of manipulation trajectories in the dataset. (b) Zero-shot Qwen2-VL-2B baseline: predictions collapse to the image boundaries, confirming that vanilla autoregressive generation fails to produce spatially meaningful trajectories. (c) Geometry head without endpoint supervision: predictions collapse to a single central region, as the uniform L1 objective is minimised by regressing toward the dataset mean. (d) Geometry head with endpoint supervision: the distribution recovers spatial diversity matching the ground truth, demonstrating that boundary supervision forces input-specific localization rather than dataset-level averaging.
