papers.selection_reason: Decodes geometry directly from VLM hidden states for robot affordance and trajectory prediction, avoiding autoregressive tokenization.
papers.title: Decoding Geometry, Not Tokens: Efficient VLMs for Robot Affordance and Trajectory Prediction
papers.tldr: A lightweight geometry-aware head unlocks spatial information already present in compact VLMs, enabling faster and more accurate continuous robot affordance and trajectory prediction than autoregressive coordinate decoding.

papers.abstract: Training language models whose parameters and optimizer state exceed a single node's memory requires sharding these tensors across devices. Under tensor parallelism (TP) or fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP), matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon introduce communication to perform global matrix operations across shards. We propose Dobb (Distributed Optimizer with Block-diagonal Eigenbases), a matrix-aware optimizer designed to compute updates locally within parameter shards. Dobb approximates the input-activation second moment with diagonal blocks and tracks a complete basis within each block. It projects momentum into these bases, applies sign normalization to the coefficients, and reconstructs the update. When each block lies within one shard under TP or FSDP, Dobb applies its matrix update locally, requiring no communication beyond data-parallel synchronization of the activation second moments. We benchmark Dobb against Dion, a distributed matrix-aware optimizer designed to retain the benefits of orthonormalized updates while reducing communication. On GPT-2 XL (1.56B parameters), Dobb with 16 blocks reaches a validation loss of 2.476, compared with 2.511 for Dion at rank fraction 1/16. Under FSDP on 32 H100 GPUs, Dobb reduces the amortized optimizer-call time from 124.1 ms for Dion to 9.2 ms.
authors: Shi-Yuk Fong, Shuhua Yu, Jiawei Zhang
bullets: Targets matrix-aware optimization for models whose parameters and optimizer states are sharded across devices.
Approximates activation second moments with diagonal blocks, tracks blockwise eigenbases, sign-normalizes momentum coefficients, and reconstructs updates locally.
Requires no communication for matrix updates when blocks fit within shards; only activation-second-moment synchronization remains.
On GPT-2 XL, Dobb with 16 blocks achieves 2.476 validation loss versus Dion’s 2.511 at rank fraction 1/16.
Under FSDP on 32 H100 GPUs, optimizer-call time decreases from 124.1 ms with Dion to 9.2 ms with Dobb.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Effective rank of the second moments from GPT-2 Small runs on OpenWebText. Within each plot, four panels show transformer layer depth at the indicated fraction of training completed; curves distinguish weight-matrix types. From 50% to 100% of training, the effective-rank distribution remains stable. Effective rank is exp(− ∑ i pi log pi) as a percentage of the factor dimension, n for At and m for Gt, where pi is the ith normalized eigenvalue. The second-moment matrices are averaged over accumulated mini-batches. The output-gradient plot separates the query, key, and value blocks of the fused attention projection.

Figure 1: GPT-2 XL (1.56B parameters) validation loss and optimizer-specific cross-shard payload. Losses are measured under the shared update-scale protocol (Table 4). Labels give block count B or rank fraction ρ. For a weight matrix of size m × n, optimizer-specific cross-shard payload is the logical number of scalar entries exchanged between devices holding different shards of that matrix during one optimizer step; collective factors and bytes per entry are omitted. We express this derived count relative to Muon’s dense count mn. At Dion rank r, the per-matrix ratio is r(m+ n)/(mn); the aggregate ratio for the plotted GPT-2 XL matrices is 1.5ρ. Payloads are derived for FSDP with FS = 4, where each Dobb block lies within one shard; Dobb and AdamW then have zero payload under this definition. The count excludes forward-backward communication and Dobb’s separately counted data-parallel synchronization of activation second moments (Section 5).

Figure 3: Learning-rate scaling. (a) Final validation loss relative to the fitted per-size minimum, with the shared-curvature parabolas of Equation 8; ticks at zero mark the fitted optima. Filled points are the per-size optima of Table 10 with 68% intervals, and the line and band are the fitted law of Equation 11 with its 68% bootstrap band. Each 68% interval and band spans the 16th to 84th percentiles of its bootstrap distribution, which equals ±1 standard deviation for a normal distribution. The open circles are the extrapolated optima at 772M and 1.56B, and the diamonds mark the learning rate used for both, γ = 2.5×10−3 (j = −2). The shaded region lies beyond the largest swept size.

Optimizer call is the mean duration of optimizer.step(); Dobb’s is averaged over one refresh cycle, (Refresh + 8 · Non-refresh)/9. Iteration is the pooled iteration time defined in Appendix G.1. Dion uses rank r = 400 on Large; rank fraction ρ = 1/3 on XL (A5000), 6B, and 8B; ρ = 1/4 on XL (H100) and 3B; and on Qwen3, a rank fraction matched to the block width 1024/FS (Appendix G.5). For GPT-2 XL on H100, Table 23 also reports Dion at ρ = 1/16, the rank fraction of the loss comparison in the abstract, with an optimizer call of 124.1 ms. Dashes mark methods not run on Qwen3. Appendix G gives Dobb’s step() times on refresh and non-refresh iterations and all other configurations.

Table 4: Final validation loss under the shared update-scale protocol, with common learning rate and weight decay within each model scale. Small, Medium, Large, and XL train for 10,000, 20,000, 30,000, and 40,000 steps. Dion ranks are fractions of each weight matrix’s full rank.

Table 22: GPT-2 optimizer-call times and pooled iteration times on A5000 GPUs, in milliseconds. The GPT-2 XL runs use activation checkpointing. Refresh and Non-refresh give Dobb’s mean optimizer-call time on iterations with and without an eigenbasis refresh, over three refresh iterations per run and two at 2× 16× 1. Amortized is the mean optimizer-call time, for Dobb averaged over one refresh cycle (Appendix G.1); the other methods perform the same update on every iteration, so their split entries are empty. Optimizer-call means cover 30 timed iterations, and 15 at 2 × 16 × 1. Pooled iteration times are derived from the measured means (Appendix G.1). Dion’s label gives its rank r or rank fraction ρ.

Table 8: Training protocol for the principal quality comparison. Table 10 gives the architecture, step count, training token budget, and AdamW grid at each size. Grid indices j refer to Equation 7. Validation loss is computed on a fixed set of held-out sequences.

Table 1: Orthogonality of updates on synthetic 768 × 768 gradients. (a) A matrix Y with prescribed effective rank and its sign. (b) Sign normalization (Dobb) and column normalization in the same eigenbasis of the full activation second moment (a single block), on gradients DX⊤ whose output-gradient second moment G has the stated effective rank, with the effective rank of the activation second moment fixed at 15%. Effective rank is the entropy-based measure of Figure 2 as a percentage of the dimension, computed from the singular values of Y in (a). Orthogonality is ∥O∥∗/( √ min(m,n) ∥O∥F ) for a nonzero m × n matrix O, where ∥ · ∥∗ and ∥ · ∥F denote the nuclear and Frobenius norms; it equals 1 exactly when all singular values are equal. Appendix D describes the construction.
Table 6: Notation. Parenthesized values are the principal settings.

Table 10: Model sizes and learning-rate sweeps. Nparam is the parameter count, including token embeddings and excluding position embeddings, andD is the training token budget. Sweeps use the grid of Equation 7, and grid ranges are inclusive. For swept sizes, γ̂⋆ is the optimum of a quadratic in j fitted to the five grid points centered on the sweep’s best run, with both seeds at 62M; its 68% interval comes from a parametric bootstrap at the measured seed noise. For 772M and 1.56B, γ̂⋆ is the extrapolation of Equation 11 with a 68% residual-bootstrap interval; both models are trained at γ = 2.5× 10−3 (j = −2).

Table 21: Dependence of optimizer operations on the current gradient, the mini-batch gradient of a weight matrix after its reduction across data-parallel ranks. Step: the operation reads the gradient and runs in the optimizer call. Fwd/bwd: it reads activations or output gradients and runs during forward-backward. Movable: it reads no gradient and can run before the optimizer call of the same iteration, once its inputs exist. Lagged: it reads statistics or momentum that include gradients, so it can leave the optimizer call only by using values from earlier steps. The first Dion row describes the standard algorithm used in our experiments. Decoupled weight decay reads only the weights and is omitted. aOur GPT-2 implementation launches the reduction behind the backward pass and runs the refresh inside the optimizer call.

The counts exclude the dataparallel synchronization of Dobb’s block second moments, n2/B entries per matrix at each refresh.

papers.selection_reason: Distributed optimizer with shard-local preconditioning; reduces communication and memory in LLM training.
papers.title: Dobb: Shard-Local Preconditioning in Block-Diagonal Eigenbases
papers.tldr: Dobb enables communication-efficient, shard-local matrix-aware optimization by using block-diagonal eigenbases, substantially reducing optimizer-call time while achieving lower reported validation loss than Dion.

papers.abstract: Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) devices allow human experts to demonstrate tasks for robot learning without teleoperating physical robots. Using these demonstrations as training data still requires a consistent hardware setup, calibration, and data processing. We present UMI-Live, a full-stack open-source bimanual UMI system for in-the-wild data collection. We design our custom UMI-Live hardware to integrate camera and LiDAR--inertial sensing, onboard compute, and power, without external tracking equipment or calibration within the collection environment. We implement a simple user interface for recording data while an asynchronous pipeline performs parallel SLAM reconstruction and publishes training-ready datasets. We also release software that supports dual-YAM teleoperation and VLA policy training and inference. We validate UMI-Live data quality by fine-tuning $\pi_{0.5}$ and MolmoAct2, achieving success rates of 10/10 and 8/10, respectively on a bimanual pick-and-place task. Furthermore, we release 40 hours of UMI-Live data across three tasks, and complete hardware designs, software, and reproduction guides at our $\href{https://umi-live.github.io/}{\text{project website}}$.
authors: Govind Velamoor, Adrian Lin, Sam Jung, Spencer Mateega, Brandon Y. Yang, Amish Sethi
bullets: Integrates cameras, LiDAR-inertial sensing, onboard compute, and power into custom wearable hardware.
Provides a simple recording interface with asynchronous SLAM reconstruction and dataset generation.
Supports dual-YAM teleoperation plus VLA policy training and inference.
Validated on a bimanual pick-and-place task with 10/10 success for π₀.₅ and 8/10 for MolmoAct2.
Releases 40 hours of data across three tasks, alongside hardware, software, and reproduction guides.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) can condition robot actions on generated visual futures, but this additional context is neither cost-free nor uniformly beneficial. We examine what a predicted future actually changes: the action delta $\Delta a$ between the future-conditioned and future-free execution paths of the same model. Under a shared WAM checkpoint, this delta barely shifts average benchmark success ($+0.8$ points on LIBERO, $-0.8$ on RoboTwin~2.0), while generating visual futures increases inference latency by 1.7--1.9$\times$. These aggregate metrics conceal a concentrated failure mode that we term \emph{future-induced negative transfer}: while predictive deltas benefit long-horizon tasks ($+2.4$ points on LIBERO-Long) and remain negligible on most routine manipulations, they induce severe degradation on precision tasks---with \emph{Press Stapler} and \emph{Place Can Basket} losing 54.0 and 34.0 points, recurring as top failure modes across independently trained WAM variants. We introduce \textbf{Utility-WAM} for in-place correction of future-conditioned control. Its primary learning component is a residual adapter that repairs future-induced velocity deltas under a frozen shared WAM by aligning them with ground-truth dynamic guidance and penalizing excess error beyond the future-free baseline. The adapter selectively eliminates the majority of severe task drops (reducing losses to 6.0 and 14.0 points) while preserving long-horizon foresight. To eliminate superfluous video computation, a lightweight pre-generation gate reuses counterfactual action outcomes to selectively bypass video generation on 75.5\% of RoboTwin queries, cutting latency by 38\% while improving average success to 93.3\% on RoboTwin~2.0 and 98.9\% on LIBERO. On physical bimanual manipulation across three real-world tasks, Utility-WAM succeeds in 53 of 60 trials, compared to 43 for FAST-WAM.
authors: Feihong Zhang, Xi Lin, Yulong Shi, Zuxing Lu, Yanghong Mei, Zhaopeng Gu, Tingyu Yuan, Zihao Liang, Yinuo Wang, Zhaowen Li
bullets: Future-induced action changes provide little average benefit and can severely hurt precision tasks, despite helping long-horizon tasks.
A residual adapter repairs future-conditioned velocity changes against dynamic guidance while preserving the shared WAM and its foresight.
A lightweight gate bypasses video generation for 75.5% of RoboTwin queries, reducing latency by 38%.
Utility-WAM reduces major task losses, reaches 93.3% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and 98.9% on LIBERO, and succeeds in 53/60 real-world trials versus 43/60 for FAST-WAM.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Utility-WAM repairs future-induced action changes before allocating future-generation compute. Stage 1 trains a shared WAM with matched future-free and future-visible action paths. Stage 2 freezes the WAM and trains a residual adapter on self-generated future features, using beneficial ground-truthfuture velocity deltas and the future-free path as supervision. These two stages establish the core correction method. Stage 3 reuses the adapter’s paired final-action outcomes to train a gate. At inference, the gate runs before video generation: it either executes the future-free path and skips that compute, or invokes future generation and the corrected future-conditioned path. Solid arrows denote inference data flow; dashed orange arrows denote training-only supervision.

Figure 4: Representative successful real-world evaluation sequences. Keyframes for Place Empty Cup, Insert Can, and Stack Three Blocks are shown from top to bottom and progress from left to right, illustrating the main manipulation stages and the final task configurations after gripper withdrawal. These examples are qualitative and are not used for method attribution.

Figure 2: Accuracy–compute frontier of selective routing. Success rate versus effective video generation steps on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0; moving left saves video generation. Neff denotes the average number of video generation steps per action query. Red stars mark the validation-calibrated operating points; the remaining points form a test-time threshold sweep. The selective configuration is compared with two compute-matched baselines. The correction-only curve is a static schedule that updates the future video only during the first n of the ten denoising steps of every query, so that Neff = n. The dashed Random Gate curve routes each query to the corrected future-conditioned path with probability Neff/10.
Figure 3: Real-world platform and tasks. (a) Bimanual platform (image: AgileX Robotics). (b–d) Initial task configurations.

Table 2: Controlled diagnosis and mitigation of future-induced negative transfer. All entries are success rates (%) under a shared Stage-1 checkpoint. The fixed w-versus-wo comparison measures the aggregate effect of future conditioning. Utility-WAM (Correction) isolates the core correction method with future generation always enabled; Utility-WAM (Selective) adds the adapter-derived gate. papers.abstract: This letter proposes MulClip, a lightweight activation function for reservoir computing (RC) on microcontrollers (MCUs). In a ring reservoir, a representative sparse RC topology, multiply-accumulate operations are few, and evaluating tanh accounted for 75% of the state-update time on a Cortex-M4. MulClip introduces curvature into the response using only comparison, absolute value, multiplication, and subtraction, and places its clipping threshold not at the extremum but at the point where the response returns to zero after passing the extremum. As a result, a single function has both a monotonic regime and a nonmonotonic folding regime that increases the expressiveness of a single unit. Which regime is used is determined by the usual hyperparameter search, e.g., over the input scale, so no task-specific threshold tuning is required. The state-update time measured on hardware was 0.34 times that of tanh and shorter than that of any of the 11 evaluated tanh approximations. In PC-based evaluation, third-order MulClip achieved a 22% lower NMSE than tanh on NARMA-20, where the pre-activations remained in the monotonic regime, and on 8-bit parity it raised the accuracy from 0.76-0.78 for the monotonic-clip variant without folding to 0.97-0.98. For these two tasks, on-device inference yielded nearly the same values as on the PC.
authors: Guren Matsumura, Masato Takemoto, Shinzo Koyama
bullets: Targets the high cost of tanh evaluation in microcontroller reservoir computing.
Uses comparisons, absolute value, multiplication, and subtraction, avoiding lookup tables.
Provides monotonic and nonmonotonic folding regimes within one activation; input scaling selects the regime.
Hardware state updates took 0.34× the time of tanh and were faster than 11 evaluated tanh approximations.
Third-order MulClip reduced NARMA-20 NMSE by 22% and improved 8-bit parity accuracy to 0.97–0.98; PC and device results were nearly identical.

papers.abstract: We present SONIC-K1, to our knowledge the first open-weights whole-body motion tracker for the Booster K1 humanoid, obtained by adapting the SONIC framework to this smaller robot. The policy is trained from scratch on a single shared GPU with a small fraction of the compute reported for SONIC. In MuJoCo simulation, it tracks nearly all held-out motion clips and performs well on external benchmarks under SONIC's success criterion. On the real K1, it tracks upper-body and slow motions, while stepping and turning remain less reliable, and simulation experiments show a sensitivity to action latency. These results show broad motion-tracking capability on a modest training budget and point to quantitative hardware evaluation as the main next step. Code, policy weights and evaluation tools are publicly available.
authors: Kyrylo Kolesnichenko, Jong-Hoon Kim
bullets: Targets whole-body motion tracking on the smaller Booster K1 humanoid.
Trains the policy from scratch using a single shared GPU and substantially less compute than the original SONIC work.
Tracks nearly all held-out motion clips in MuJoCo and performs well on external benchmarks under SONIC’s criterion.
On the real robot, upper-body and slow motions work reliably, while stepping and turning are less reliable.
Simulation reveals sensitivity to action latency; code, weights, and evaluation tools are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems provide critical computation services in the Manufacturing Industrial Internet (MII), and their resilience depends on timely diagnosis of hazards across the data, AI pipeline, and cyber-physical layers. During operation, new hazard types keep emerging with only a few samples each, hazards co-occur, and the diagnosis model runs on memory-constrained computation nodes. Replay-based class-incremental learning (CIL) can learn new hazard classes while revisiting a small memory of past samples, but existing methods assume single-label, balanced streams, store high-dimensional raw samples, and select them independently of the classifier. We propose Class-aware Latent Attention Replay (CLAR), which combines a dual buffer that stores mostly compact latent representations with a few raw samples, an Attention Leverage Score (ALS) that upper-bounds the classifier logit and guides class-balanced reservoir sampling, and an exponential-moving-average teacher that slows latent-space drift. For an idealized buffer model, we prove that the buffer is class-balanced and follows an ALS-weighted class distribution, and that below a critical per-class capacity, ALS-guided replay has a lower replay-gradient error than class-balanced uniform replay. In the case study, On hazard diagnosis data from an MII testbed, CLAR achieves the highest mean average weighted F1 score among the evaluated replay methods with the same buffer size
authors: Avranshu Mahanty, Ran Jin, Yingyan Zeng
bullets: Targets emerging, co-occurring hazards with few samples in the Manufacturing Industrial Internet.
Uses a dual replay buffer containing mostly compact latent features and a small number of raw samples.
Introduces Attention Leverage Scores to guide class-balanced reservoir sampling based on classifier importance.
Uses an exponential-moving-average teacher to reduce latent-space drift during incremental learning.
Theory supports balanced, ALS-weighted replay; an MII testbed study reports the highest mean average weighted F1 among evaluated methods at equal buffer size.

papers.abstract: Learning-based traffic signal control (TSC) has achieved promising performance, but most methods rely on structured traffic states that must be estimated from sensor observations in real deployments. Visual TSC learns signal decisions directly from images, yet existing methods depend on fixed roadside cameras and remain tied to specific intersection configurations and visual domains. UAVs offer on-demand bird's-eye-view (BEV) observations that jointly capture intersection topology and traffic dynamics, making them a promising sensing platform for visual TSC. We present BEVLight, a generalizable TSC framework that directly maps BEV observations to signal actions. BEVLight grounds visual features onto individual lanes and composes them along the junction topology into movement and phase representations, allowing a shared policy to score candidate phases across heterogeneous intersection layouts and signal plans. To train the policy, we develop a web-based virtual teleoperation platform and collect over 5K human control decisions together with their underlying traffic states. Simulator-provided traffic states first supervise lane- and movement-level representations, after which human phase selections and rankings supervise the phase scorer. Re-rendering the recorded trajectories under diverse appearances preserves both forms of supervision and encourages robustness to visual changes. Closed-loop experiments demonstrate zero-shot generalization across traffic demands, signal plans, and intersections: BEVLight reduces average waiting time by 7--9\% relative to perception-to-control visual baselines and matches or outperforms structured-state RL controllers that receive ground-truth traffic states, achieving the lowest waiting time in 12 of 16 scenarios. An offline study further shows that BEVLight transfers to real UAV observations without target-domain adaptation.
authors: Maonan Wang, Yuxin Cai, Junming Liu, Zhengyan Huang, Yi Yu, Ding Wang, Yifeng Zhang, Yirong Chen
bullets: Addresses the dependence of existing visual traffic signal controllers on fixed cameras and specific intersection layouts.
Maps visual features to lanes, movements, and phases, then uses a shared policy to rank candidate signal phases across layouts and plans.
Trains with over 5K human control decisions, simulator traffic-state supervision, and appearance-diverse trajectory re-rendering.
Closed-loop tests show 7–9% lower average waiting time than visual baselines and the lowest waiting time in 12 of 16 scenarios.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic tasks are commonly decomposed into semantic subgoals to simplify planning. However, subgoal progress in LLM-based planning is typically inferred implicitly from interaction histories. Inaccurate estimates can misguide execution and allow local errors to propagate. To address this, we propose ProLoop, a Progress-Aware Closed-Loop framework that derives explicit subgoal progress from structured relations between desired and execution states. A learned State-Relation Monitor assesses these relations, which are then aggregated into subgoal progress as ongoing, deviated, or completed. The resulting progress guides execution adaptation, enabling reliable progress-aware control throughout execution. Experiments on AgentBoard ALFWorld and a real-world robotic platform show that ProLoop improves success rate by 12.94% overall and by 15.46% on Hard tasks, while reducing environment interactions by 32.3%.
authors: Runxin Zou, Qingmiao Liang, Jiatao Zhang, Xinyan Lv, Liangyu Qie, Meiyi Bu, Wei Song, Shiqiang Zhu
bullets: Implicit progress estimates from interaction histories can cause planning errors to propagate.
A learned State-Relation Monitor compares desired and execution states to classify subgoals as ongoing, deviated, or completed.
These progress assessments guide execution adaptation throughout task completion.
Experiments in ALFWorld and on a real-world robotic platform report 12.94% higher overall success, 15.46% higher success on Hard tasks, and 32.3% fewer environment interactions.

Structured State Construction derives comparable desired and execution states, the State-Relation Monitor infers subgoal progress from their structured relations, and Progress-Guided Adaptation regulates continuation, targeted correction, or subgoal transition, with memory updated upon completion.
Fig. 5. Real-world execution of a breakfast preparation task with ProLoop on the dual-arm mobile robot.

Fig. 4. Representative ALFWorld executions with ProLoop. Ongoing progress allows execution to continue without additional intervention, deviated progress triggers targeted correction, and completed progress enables subgoal transition and memory update.

Fig. 1. Compared with existing approaches, ProLoop explicitly derives subgoal progress from the relation between desired and execution states, distinguishes ongoing, deviated, and completed execution, and uses the resulting progress to support timely closed-loop adaptation.

papers.abstract: Fine manipulation requires robots to recognize when a grasped object makes or changes contact with its environment, yet such extrinsic contact is not always directly observable from vision or local contact geometry. Force and torque signals carry this information, but also vary with object weight, grasp configuration, and robot motion, leaving it unclear whether they can provide a reusable representation of physical state. Here we show that bilateral six-axis force/torque histories can be pretrained as a semantically structured physical representation by aligning them with a frozen language space using supervision generated from simulated pick-and-place interactions. On unseen objects in simulation, the learned representation supports text-prototype readout of robot action, object weight, and grasp interaction. In real-world placement, unlabeled calibration enables contact and support-state recognition without updating the encoder, outperforming a vertical-force sign-reversal rule baseline. For connector insertion, an event absent from pretraining, low-rank adaptation improves data-efficient learning over training from scratch. These results show that force/torque histories can support both direct readout of known physical states and efficient adaptation to new extrinsic-contact events.
authors: Kazuki Takahashi, Hiroaki Murakami, Ryota Sakuma, Mitsuhiro Kamezaki, Matthew Ishige, Yoshihiro Kawahara
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of inferring environmental contact from vision or local geometry alone, given force/torque variation from weight, grasp, and motion.
Pretrains six-axis force/torque histories by aligning them with a frozen language space using simulated pick-and-place supervision.
Supports text-prototype readout of robot action, object weight, and grasp interaction on unseen simulated objects.
Enables unlabeled real-world calibration for contact and support-state recognition, outperforming a vertical-force sign-reversal baseline.
Low-rank adaptation improves data-efficient learning for connector insertion, an event not included during pretraining.

papers.abstract: Unlimited OCR ushers the era of long-horizon parsing, substantially mitigating the growth of working memory as document lengthens. However, as document length scales to hundreds of pages, the visual context grows substantially, sharply increasing the computational cost of each decoding step and limiting the scalability of ultra-long document parsing. Inspired by human book transcription via localized focus without re-scanning preceding pages, we introduce Unlimited OCR 2, a document parsing model that looks only at what it transcribes. Building on Unlimited OCR, we upgrade all the decoder attention modules to Sparse Reference Sliding Window Attention (SR-SWA), bounding active reference tokens to a fixed capacity and thus sustaining constant computational costs across arbitrarily long documents. By combining SR-SWA with Unlimited-Horizon Decoding Paradigm, Unlimited OCR 2 enables document parsing over virtually unlimited lengths without prohibitive memory overhead. At the hundred-page scale, Unlimited OCR 2 achieves 7.0$\times$ and 5.6$\times$ per-step speedups over Full Attention and R-SWA, respectively. Furthermore, it delivers state-of-the-art end-to-end performance on both MPDocBench and MarathonDocBench, our newly proposed benchmark targeting hundred-page document parsing. Ultimately, the capacity for uninterrupted, one-shot document parsing signifies a fundamental paradigm shift into the OCR 3.0 era.
authors: Shu Wei, Jingjing Wu, Qunyi Xie, Lingshu Zhang, Xiangcheng Du, Yannian Fu, Mengjie Wang, Zuyi Wang, Zhichao Liu, Yangliu Xu, YY, Yi Yang
bullets: Addresses the rising per-step computation and memory costs of parsing documents hundreds of pages long.
Introduces Sparse Reference Sliding Window Attention (SR-SWA), which bounds active reference tokens to a fixed capacity.
Combines SR-SWA with Unlimited-Horizon Decoding for constant-cost decoding across document lengths.
At the hundred-page scale, reports 7.0× and 5.6× per-step speedups over Full Attention and R-SWA.
Achieves state-of-the-art end-to-end results on MPDocBench and the proposed MarathonDocBench.

figures.caption: Figure 5 | Performance comparison on multi-page benchmarks. Unlimited OCR 2 (Ours) consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluation categories.

Figure 3 | Inspired by the process of humans copying books, we propose Unlimited OCR 2. SRSWA combines Page Gate and Token Sieve to construct a fixed-length set of working reference visual tokens, substantially reducing computational and memory overhead while keeping both independent of document length throughout generation.

Figure 4 | Comparison of (a) standard decoding and (b) our Unlimited-Horizon Decoding paradigm. Standard decoding retains visual KV caches for all pages, causing GPU memory usage to grow linearly with document length and eventually overflow. Our paradigm divides long documents into manageable chunks and processes them sequentially, reusing the KV cache of shared boundary pages and releasing inactive caches to keep GPU memory usage bounded while preserving cross-chunk continuity.
Figure 2 | MarathonDocBench versus MPDocBench. MarathonDocBench extends document length from tens to hundreds of pages (a), with substantially richer cross-page structures as shown in (b) and (c).

Figure 6 | Performance and efficiency comparison across varying document lengths. UnlimitedOCR 2 demonstrates (a) robust parsing accuracy and (b) near-constant decoding latency (ms/step) as document length scaling.

Figure 1 | R-SWA vs SR-SWA. R-SWA computes attention over all visual tokens across pages, inducing extreme visual redundancy; SR-SWA sparsely attends to relevant visual regions, aligning machine decoding with human reading intuition.
Table 1 | Performance comparison on MPDocBench. All models in the table are end-to-end VLM-based architectures.

papers.abstract: Generating editable computer-aided design (CAD) models from text requires selecting operations that produce the intended changes to the geometry constructed so far. An incorrect operation can compromise subsequent steps, making reliable multi-step generation challenging. Existing methods based on large language models (LLMs) primarily learn to predict commands, without explicit supervision of the geometric states those commands should produce. Inspired by world-action models, we introduce CAD-WAM, which couples geometry-conditioned action generation with next-state prediction. We define complete modeling operations as actions in a CAD domain-specific language (DSL) and encode surface point clouds of intermediate solids into compact latent states using a pretrained variational autoencoder. An LLM backbone generates the next action from the target description and current geometric state, while an auxiliary head on the same backbone predicts the next state to provide geometric supervision during training. We construct step-wise training trajectories from parametric CAD models in the DeepCAD dataset, pairing each trajectory with an expert-level textual description. At inference, each generated action is executed by a CAD kernel, and the resulting solid is re-encoded to inform the next decision. On the DeepCAD test set, CAD-WAM outperforms the task-specific baselines in geometric accuracy and output validity, with larger gains on models requiring more operations, and produces more accurate geometry than general-purpose LLMs prompted with the same DSL. Ablations further show that next-state supervision reduces mean Chamfer distance by 13.2\% relative to an otherwise identical model trained only to predict actions. Code is available at https://github.com/Lzy-1037/CAD-WAM.
authors: Zhengyang Li, Weijie Zheng, Yuxin Cui, Sijie Wang, Wenjie Feng, Qiyu Kang
bullets: Represents complete CAD operations as actions in a domain-specific language and conditions generation on the current geometry.
Encodes intermediate solids as compact latent states from surface point clouds using a pretrained variational autoencoder.
Uses an auxiliary next-state prediction head to provide geometric supervision alongside action prediction.
Executes each generated action in a CAD kernel and re-encodes the resulting solid for subsequent decisions.
On DeepCAD, improves geometric accuracy and output validity; next-state supervision reduces mean Chamfer distance by 13.2% versus action-only training.

papers.abstract: Whether models trained on different modalities converge to the same representation of the world is central to AI. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) conjectures that they do as they scale, but without a proof it offers neither a guarantee nor a recipe. We turn the hypothesis into a theorem. First, we prove a \emph{Platonic Representation Theorem}: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) trained separately on any number of modalities learn the same representation up to one rotation whenever their positive pairs are two observations of one scene--\emph{good views}--and their misalignment is bounded otherwise. Second, we show that next-token prediction is a JEPA with \emph{bad views}, parts of a single document, which explains why language models align with vision only through scale. Third, we validate the theory from 145k captions to the texts of 940M web images, and uncover a scaling law of alignment that predicts unseen runs within seed noise. Good views need 42 times fewer training samples than next-token prediction on the same corpus to reach the same alignment, and a 109M-parameter text JEPA aligns with DINOv2 and CLIP's image encoders better than every language model we evaluated, up to 72B parameters, and than CLIP's text encoder: next-token prediction is a remarkably inefficient route to platonic representations. As a showcase, one rotation turns separately trained encoders into an image captioner (CIDEr .838 on COCO). Even that rotation needs no pair: on the latest pair-free benchmark, our text JEPA beats every zero-shot accuracy reported with language models up to 8B parameters, e.g., 64\% against at most 56\% top-5 on ImageNet-100. Positive views, and not scale alone, are thus the lever to build platonic representations.
authors: Randall Balestriero, Yann LeCun
bullets: Proves a Platonic Representation Theorem: separately trained JEPAs align up to a rotation when positive pairs are observations of the same scene and misalignment is bounded.
Frames next-token prediction as using “bad views,” helping explain its weaker vision–language alignment without large scale.
Finds that good-view training needs 42× fewer samples than next-token prediction to reach the same alignment on the studied corpus.
A 109M-parameter text JEPA aligned better with DINOv2 and CLIP image encoders than evaluated language models up to 72B parameters and CLIP’s text encoder.
A single learned rotation enabled image captioning, while the text JEPA also achieved strong pair-free zero-shot ImageNet-100 performance.

figures.caption: Figure 9. Good views scale. Left and middle: text JEPAs trained on the texts of 2.16M to 940M web images (Recap-DataComp), never on a Flickr or COCO caption, against frozen DINOv2 ViT-B on WIT-1024 (PRH-paper protocol) and on Flickr (R@1 through one rotation fitted on 30k pairs). Solid lines and circles: BERT-S (33M); dashed lines and diamonds: BERT-B (109M), trained with next-token prediction and bad views on the texts of 940M images only, hence single diamonds there. Lines are means over seeds and faint dots the seeds (one seed for the bad-view JEPA at 940M). Shaded: the language models we evaluated (Qwen2.5 0.5–72B, Llama-3-8B and -70B, Mistral-7B; left); grey dashed: CLIP’s text encoder and Qwen2.5-0.5B under the same protocol (middle). Right: image JEPAs trained from scratch (ViT-S on 2.16M and ViT-B on 10M Recap images, ViT-S on ImageNet-1k) and frozen DINOv2, each against the good-view, next-token and bad-view text JEPAs trained on the same texts of 50M web images (WIT; means of three seeds, dots: seeds). We clearly observe that good views beat bad views and next-token prediction at every scale and with every image encoder we compared, and that a 109M good-view JEPA on the texts of 940M images surpasses every language model we evaluated.

Figure 5. Good views align, bad views and next-token prediction do not. Alignment between a separately trained image JEPA and three text encoders on Flickr, at matched epochs (mean of three seeds, band: range; dashed: chance). All start at chance. We clearly observe that the good-view JEPA (caption views) aligns markedly better than the bad-view JEPA (masked spans) and next-token prediction, which nearly coincide, as predicted by Theorem 2 and Proposition 4.

Figure 3. What counts as a positive, and which observations it connects. Eight captions of two scenes (dots), joined as each objective’s positives join them. (a)Good views join every description of a scene and never another, so the world kernel they induce is the world’s own (Theorem 4). (b) Weak corruptions mostly pair a caption with itself, keeping its wording, and join other captions only where their corruptions overlap, which takes dense data. (c) Strong corruptions also coincide across scenes, so the induced kernel mixes scenes whatever the amount of data. (d) Next-token prediction pairs a prefix with its own continuation, and implicitly contexts followed by the same token (Proposition 4): narrow links within scenes, plus spill through frequent tokens. That is, good views fix the world kernel by design, while bad views and next-token prediction get it from the data.

Figure 4. Positives that join less of a scene need more data (Theorem 4). A synthetic world of five classes of six states (literal data, as in Figure 12): alignment of a text JEPA with the image side against the samples per state N and the reach ∆ of its bad views (means over three samplings; a state has width 1/6). White: the 0.9 contour, and ∆ ∝ log N/N (dashed, one fitted constant), the scale of the largest gap between a state’s samples. Reach large enough to cross classes caps alignment (.95), and good views (top strip) align exactly at any N. We observe that weaker positives need more data for the same alignment.

Figure 2. Kernel mismatch bounds misalignment (Theorem 2). Each point is one randomly generated finite world (8–39 states, random marginal, embedding dimension k from 1 to 5) with a pair of kernels on it: the world’s kernel, and a second kernel of the same marginal that mixes in an unrelated kernel with weight 10−4 to 1, as if a second modality had partly different positives. For each pair we compute the two spectral embeddings (Proposition 1) and plot their distance after the best rotation (vertical) against the bound of Theorem 2 (horizontal); of the 300 worlds, half are clustered, with small spectral gaps. We clearly observe that the error lies below the bound in every world (dashed: equality), at 18% of it at most.

Figure 7. Trimming is the knob that matters. One change at a time to the good-view text JEPA on Flickr: R@1 with frozen DINOv2 through one rotation, last epoch, three seeds where they exist (faint dots; large dot: mean of the seeds that do not collapse; black: default). Top: the two changes to trimming, with the change of their mean from the default’s; whole captions as views lose a quarter of the alignment. Dashed: the bad-view JEPA and next-token prediction with the default recipe. That is, trimming matters most, and every variant of the good-view JEPA that does not collapse stays far above both baselines; gradient clipping prevents most collapses.

Figure 8. Good views help on both sides. MSR-VTT, 1,000 test clips. Top: image JEPAs trained on different frames of a clip (good) or crops of one frame (bad), against text JEPAs trained on different captions (good) or spans of one caption (bad); dots are the three seeds, dashed is chance. Bottom: alignment of each with frozen DINOv2, whose own positives are crops. This demonstrates that good views on both sides align best in mutual 10-NN, and that DINOv2 prefers the image JEPA whose positives match its own.

Figure 6. Alignment lives in the leading spectral directions. Left: after the best rotation, correlation between image and text embeddings along the text embedding’s principal directions (good-view JEPA, at initialization and at epoch 199). Right: variance of the text embedding along the same directions. This suggests that alignment concentrates where the spectrum is well separated, consistent with Theorem 2, although noise in low-variance directions would produce the same trend.

Figure 11. A scaling law of alignment in good views and samples seen. Flickr test R@1 (DINOv2 ViT-B, 30k-pair rotation) of BERT-S text JEPAs trained on the texts of 10.2M web images, against the samples seen. Each point is a run, colored by its fraction q of training items with good views (black: q = 0, bad views only). Circles: the grid the law is fitted on; diamonds: runs predicted before training. Lines: the law at five values of q, dashed beyond the fitted range. We observe that R@1 grows linearly in the logarithm of the samples seen at every fraction of good views, faster with more of them, and that the law predicts unseen runs within seed noise up to twice its range.

Figure 12. Weak views need many data, the kind of data sets the ceiling, good views need neither (Theorem 4). A synthetic world of five classes of six states; the image side is a good-view JEPA whose world kernel links states of one class. The text side observes each state through samples on a line, one block per class, with gaps between blocks (left, literal data) or without (right, mixed data); its bad views join two samples with weight e−d2/2∆2 (weak ∆ = .005, medium .08, strong 1; a state has width 1/6). Alignment is the mean canonical correlation of the two spectral solutions over paired observations (k = 4; 1: equal up to a rotation); lines are means over five samplings, bands their range.

Figure 14. One rotation superimposes two separately trained encoders. Top: joint t-SNE of test images after the best rotation (blue) and their captions (orange), at initialization and after training (good-view JEPA); grey lines join 60 random true pairs. Bottom: independent t-SNEs of the image and text embeddings, colored by caption keywords used only for coloring. We clearly observe that after training, images and their captions share one geometry.

Figure 15. Retrieval through one rotation. Image→caption retrieval (good-view JEPA, epoch 199) for five Flickr test images, with the rank of the true caption among the 1,000 above each list (✓would mark it among the top three). We observe that misses are mostly semantically close.

Figure 13. The captioner’s noise and pairs are predicted, not tuned. Flickr test images. Top: CIDEr against the noise the decoder is trained with; dashed, the noise matched to the residual of the rotation (rotation from 1,014 pairs). Bottom: CIDEr against the number of pairs that fit the one linear map, with and without unpaired refinement, against retrieving the nearest caption through the same map; dashed, decoding the true caption embedding. We clearly observe that transfer peaks at the matched noise, and that a few pairs refined on unpaired data match caption retrieval from 1,014 pairs.

Table 4. A 109M good-view JEPA beats every pair-free zero-shot accuracy of Schnaus et al. [54]. The protocol and method of Schnaus et al. [54], unchanged: DINOv2 ViT-B/14 and a text encoder aligned with zero pairs on unpaired halves of COCO train2014, scored on the 40,504 val2014 pairs (FOSCTTM, lower is better) and by zero-shot top-1 on CIFAR-10 and top-5 on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-100 (%). Means over training seeds times the method’s five seeds (std in Section C). Their best: the best number of their paper for each metric over its 21 vision–language pairs, on these data and in any of its five settings (paper/data/schnaus2026_reported.csv); our reruns of their MPNet pair (all-mpnet-base-v2) reproduce their reported .04, 70, 46 and 45. Last row: the ceiling of Procrustes on all training pairs, range over all encoders. Our good-view JEPAs are trained on the texts of 940M and 100M web images. We clearly observe that a 109M good-view JEPA beats every zero-shot accuracy of Schnaus et al. [54], matches their best FOSCTTM on these data, and matches or significantly beats their 8B language model under identical conditions, while next-token prediction on the same texts fails; only CLIP’s text encoder, trained on 400M image–text pairs, aligns better on FOSCTTM and ImageNet-100.

Table 3. At scale, good views beat language models up to 72B parameters. Text encoders against frozen vision models under the PRH protocol: mutual 10-NN and unbiased linear CKA on WIT-1024 with DINOv2ViT-B,mutual 10-NNonWIT-1024with CLIPViT-H/14 and on the 5,000 COCO test pairs with DINOv2 ViT-B, and Flickr R@1 through one rotation fitted on 30k pairs. Our three encoders are BERT-B models (109M) trained with 900M samples from the texts of 940M web images (one seed for the bad-view JEPA); –: not measured. More models in Tables 16 to 18. We clearly observe that the good-view JEPA agrees with both vision models more than any other text encoder, while next-token prediction on the same texts falls far behind.

Table 2. Good-view JEPAs agree with DINOv2 more than the pretrained models we tested. Same protocol with a frozen DINOv2 ViTB/14. Top two rows and bottom two: pretrained models (last layer); the others are ours (BERT-S unless named). All entries use final checkpoints, except the early-stopped row (selected on a loss over the validation and test captions, which can only favor this baseline), with no selection on test data (mean ± half-range over three seeds where shown, seed 0 elsewhere). The last column fits the single map on all 30k Flickr train and validation pairs instead of 1k (–: we kept no epoch29 checkpoint to embed the training captions with). No network is trained on pairs in either case. For reference, our Flickr image JEPA vs. DINOv2 (image vs. image) reaches mutual 10-NN .101 and R@1 .217. The rows above the first rule are trained on Flickr (and COCO) captions, so this comparison is in-domain for them and out-of-domain for most pretrained models (all-mpnet-base-v2, trained on a billion sentence pairs, saw Flickr and COCO captions); the Recap rows never saw a Flickr or COCO caption. CLIP’s text encoder was trained with 400M images. Bold: best of ours. This demonstrates that good-view JEPAs have the neighborhoods closest to DINOv2’s and, trained on web text alone, match or exceed the retrieval of text encoders trained on pairs.

Table 1. Good views align across modalities. Image JEPA vs. each text encoder (epoch 199) on 1,000 Flickr test pairs (backbone features; mean± half-range over three seeds): good-view JEPA (caption views), bad-view JEPA (masked spans), next-token prediction, and next-token prediction on pairs of captions of one image; R@1 and R@5 use a single rotation fitted on validation pairs. We clearly observe that caption views beat masked spans and next-token prediction on every metric, even when next-token prediction is trained on pairs of captions of the same image.

Table 17. The ranking holds on COCO. PRH protocol on the 5,000 COCO Karpathy test pairs (first caption), seed 0 for our encoders except the 940M row, the mean of three seeds (each at or above all-mpnet-base-v2); chance mutual 10-NN is .002. We clearly observe that the 109M good-view JEPA aligns best on a second, five times larger benchmark, ahead of language models up to 72B parameters and of text encoders trained on pairs.

Table 18. Good views win with every vision family. WIT-1024 (PRH protocol) for frozen vision encoders trained by pixel reconstruction (MAE), latent prediction (I-JEPA), crops (DINOv2) or image–text contrast (CLIP’s image encoders, the vision models with which language models align best in Huh et al. [22]), against our text JEPAs (good / bad / next-token on the texts of 50M images, seed 0; the 109M good-view JEPA on the texts of 940M images, seed 0) and pretrained language models. We clearly observe that good views beat next-token prediction and bad views with every vision encoder, and that the 109M good-view JEPA beats the three language models with each of them. MAE and I-JEPA align alike, both below DINOv2, which saw far more curated images; we draw no conclusion on the vision objective. With CLIP’s image encoders, the 109M good-view JEPA’s three seeds average .215, .219 and .230, against .193, .203 and .210 for the best of all our language models up to 72B (Qwen2.5-72B), and its next-token and bad-view controls on the same texts .137–.146 and .108–.116 (runs/results/wit_clip.txt).

Table 16. No language model up to 72B parameters reaches the 109M good-view JEPA. PRH protocol (per-layer features, maximum over layer pairs) on WIT-1024 and on the 5,000 COCO test pairs, for base language models from 0.5B to 72B parameters and our 109M good-view text JEPA trained on the texts of 940M images (mean of three seeds). We clearly observe that scaling next-token prediction by 660 times in parameters does not reach the alignment that good views give.

Table 10. The captioner improves without pairs. Building the captioner up one change at a time: Flickr test (1,000 images) and COCO Karpathy test (5,000 images), beam 3 unless stated; consensus rows choose among the greedy caption and 32 samples. The text JEPA is BERT-S trained on the texts of 100M web images; the decoders are trained on its embeddings of Flickr and COCO training captions only, with noise matched to the alignment (σ = 1.9); the image encoders are frozen. The first row is the captioner of Table 9: on Flickr, the Flickr text JEPA and decoder (σ = 3); on COCO, the Flickr and COCO ones (σ = 2); it decodes greedily on Flickr and with beam 3 on COCO. Decoding the true caption embedding gives .694 and 1.305 (captions-as-written row), and .743 and 1.369 with the web-pretrained decoder. Only the rotation is fitted on image–caption pairs. Without consensus decoding, the best captioner reaches .496 and .806. This demonstrates that stronger frozen encoders, a pretrained language model and consensus decoding each add to the captioner, from CIDEr .668 to .838 on COCO, while a larger decoder does not.

Table 8. Cropping matters, the rest barely moves the mean, and clipping prevents most collapses. R@1 against frozen DINOv2 on Flickr test pairs with one rotation fitted on validation pairs (chance .001), last epoch, for three seeds where shown (one otherwise); a run collapses (×) when its last-epoch R@1 falls below .05. Default views: 2 global and 6 local spans of 50–100% and 15–50% of a caption. Mean: over the seeds that do not collapse (–: every seed collapses). ∗Best over checkpoints on the test pairs, for reference only; the other columns involve no selection. That is, every run that does not collapse stays far above the bad-view JEPA and next-token prediction, and without gradient clipping 3 of the 36 runs with the default SIGReg weight collapse. In stable-pretraining as we ran it, SIGReg is scaled by the number of embeddings it sees, so the batch and view rows also change its effective weight: ×2 for batch 512, × 1 2 for 2 + 2 views and ×1.5 for 2 + 10 views.

Table 6. Bad views spend their embedding on nuisance. Scene-explained fraction ρ( f ) = tr C1/2 f /k of each text encoder’s top-k whitened embedding (mean ± half-range over three seeds), the lower bound 2k(1− ρ( f )) of Theorem 3 on the best-rotation error against DINOv2 ViT-B, and that error (means over seeds; bounds from the unrounded fractions; uncorrelated embeddings give 2k, i.e., 64 and 256). We clearly observe that the bound holds for every encoder, and the scene-explained fraction ranks the encoders as their alignment does.

Table 7. The views and the data both set the alignment. BERT-S text JEPAs, one recipe per scale, three seeds (mean and range), scored on WIT-1024 with DINOv2 ViT-B and on Flickr through one rotation fitted on 30k pairs; scene-explained: ρ( f ) on Flickr captions (k = 32, seed 0, Table 6). The paraphrase is written from the alt-text alone by a text-only language model, so that row involves no image captioner. We observe that with the same bad views, LLaVA recaptions align far better than alt-texts, and with the same texts, good views double alignment (Theorem 4).

Table 11. Captions and retrieval for video, from photos alone. Top: zero-shot captioning of the MSR-VTT test clips (20 references each; CIDEr on a 0–1 scale) by our captioner, whose networks never saw a video, a video–caption pair or MSR-VTT text, and by captioners built on CLIP’s encoders without MSR-VTT text, with one trained on MSR-VTT captions for reference (–: not reported). Bottom: alignment (mutual 10-NN fits nothing) and retrieval through one map on the 1k-A split, against zero-shot CLIP. We observe that a rotation fitted on photos captions and retrieves videos, above captioners built on CLIP that use no MSR-VTT text, though CLIP’s jointly trained encoders retrieve better.

Table 14. Alignment keeps growing with the texts of 940M images. Checkpoints of our largest good-view JEPAs (seed 0 unless named; †: mean of three seeds at the end of training; ‡: another seed with twice the effective SIGReg weight, see text; next-token: the same encoder trained to predict the next token; bad views: two masked copies of one text, at the effective SIGReg weight of the first 940M run), scored on WIT-1024 with DINOv2 ViT-B and on Flickr through one rotation fitted on 30k pairs. We observe thatWIT alignment jumps between the texts of 200M and 940M images and rises again by 850M samples, while Flickr retrieval rises more slowly. Bold: best per column.

Table 12. Linear-evaluation features and concatenated encoders align best. Flickr test pairs, text JEPAs trained on Recap texts only (seed 0), each against a frozen self-supervised image encoder through one map with orthonormal rows fitted on the 30k Flickr train and validation pairs (chance: mutual 10-NN .01, R@1 .001). Bottom rows: the CLS + mean patch features of two encoders, each rescaled to unit root-mean-square per coordinate, concatenated. No network is trained on pairs. Notably, with DINOv3 ViT-7B, one rotation retrieves the true caption first for more than half of the test images.

Table 15. A 109M text JEPA beats language models on the PRH benchmark. PRH protocol of Huh et al. [22]: WIT-1024 pairs, per-layer features, clipping, normalization, maximum over layer pairs. For reference, DINOv2 ViT-B × BERT-base scores .111, all-mpnet-base-v2 .118 and CLIP’s text encoder .124 (.113–.137 across DINOv2 sizes for these two); our Flickr-trained text encoders (good / bad / next-token) score .029–.036 with every DINOv2 size and .023–.024 with our Flickr image JEPA; and our Flickr image JEPA × DINOv2 ViT-B (image vs. image) .241. nt: next-token prediction. Our 33M text JEPAs’ entries are means of three seeds, which differ by at most ±.009 with DINOv2 ViT-B; the 109M column is the mean of three seeds (each above every language model). At least 43 of the 1,024 WIT captions appear among the Recap-DataComp alt-texts; on the other 981 pairs, none of the nine text models we checked with DINOv2 ViT-B (ours, Qwen2.5-3B/7B, Mistral-7B) changes by more than .002. This demonstrates that the 109M good-view JEPA surpasses every language model we evaluated with every vision encoder it was scored with, including our image JEPAs trained from scratch.

Table 13. Good views help on both sides (numbers behind Figure 8). MSR-VTT, 1,000 test clips, final checkpoints, mean ± half-range over three seeds (chance: mutual 10-NN .01, R@1 .001). R@1 and R@5 use one rotation fitted on the 1,990 validation clips. Every seed ranks the four combinations the same way in mutual 10-NN; the image-side effect is small and reverses on R@5.

Table 9. Captioning from independently trained encoders. BLEU-4 [45], CIDEr [62] on Flickr test images. The decoder never sees an image; the image encoder never sees text; pairs only fit one linear map. BLEU-4 rewards generic n-grams, so the random map’s fluent but generic captions score above 1,014-pair retrieval on BLEU-4, not on CIDEr. We clearly observe that decoding through the rotation beats retrieving captions through it by a wide margin.

Table 5. Good views also make better text encoders. Text encoders alone (caption→caption retrieval among the 5,000 Flickr test captions: is the nearest caption one of the four others describing the same image?) and alignment measured on projector outputs (seed 0; –: no trained projector). We clearly observe that the bad-view JEPA learns little beyond word overlap (below TF-IDF), while the good-view JEPA goes well beyond it. The image JEPA reaches 78.5% 20-NN accuracy on Imagenette [21] (29.1% at initialization).

papers.selection_reason: Theoretically and empirically studies multimodal representation alignment in joint-embedding predictive architectures, relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Proving and Improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs
papers.tldr: The paper proves that JEPAs trained on well-matched views can converge to shared representations more efficiently than next-token prediction, challenging scale-only routes to multimodal alignment.

papers.abstract: We present Youtu-Parsing-Omni, an omni-modal parser that converts documents, images, audio, and video into structured records grounded in space and time, providing a perception layer for agents that read, locate, and cite evidence across modalities. Its design rests on one encoder for every modality and one schema for every task. Youtu-Omni-Encoder, initialized from a pre-trained language model to strengthen text reading, encodes all modalities with shared weights in a unified space-time coordinate system, and a few fusion layers let video frames attend to concurrent audio, bringing cross-modal fusion and temporal alignment into perception itself. OmniSchema unifies the outputs of all ten parsing tasks, allowing a single self-evolving post-training procedure, OmniSchema-Aware On-Policy Distillation (OSAD), to provide a shared token-role-based objective across tasks. In each round, the model is trained on its own rollouts against token-level targets from a reference-conditioned copy of itself, which is then refreshed with the trained weights, so that the parser and its supervision co-evolve. With a single 5 B-parameter checkpoint, Youtu-Parsing-Omni achieves state-of-the-art performance on OmniDocBench v1.6 (96.96 Overall) and leads all open-weight models on OmniParsingBench (75.08 Avg.), with its advantage concentrated on audio and video. It also achieves the best overall chart-parsing score (95.02) and the highest exact chemical-fingerprint agreement among compared systems, and matches a dedicated optical-music model in character-level transcription of typeset sheet music while staying far ahead of general-purpose systems. Code and model weights are publicly available.
authors: Yunhang Shen, Zhangquan Chen, Xiaotian Li, Zhongpeng Cai, Qing Zhou, Zekai Zhang, Kun Zhang, Zezhong Wu, Jian Hu, Haihan Gao, Heting Gao, Xin Li, Yinsong Liu, Deqian Jiang, Di Yin, Haoyu Cao, Xing Sun, Bing Liu, Yanqiu Qu, Yunfei Wu, Kun Yin, Zhixiang Wei, Yongxiang Hua, Qianyu Li, Xiaoxing Hu, Peiyuan Zhang, Lijiang Li, Dong Xu, Zhenchuan Yang, Yiliang Jiang
bullets: Unifies ten parsing tasks through OmniSchema and a shared token-role objective.
Youtu-Omni-Encoder represents all modalities in a common space-time coordinate system, with audio–video fusion layers.
OSAD uses self-generated rollouts and refreshed reference models for self-evolving post-training.
A single 5B-parameter checkpoint reports leading results on OmniDocBench v1.6 and among open-weight models on OmniParsingBench, especially for audio and video.
It also performs strongly on chart parsing, chemical fingerprints, and typeset sheet-music transcription; code and weights are public.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of omni-modal parsing architectures. We compare how visual and audio inputs are encoded before reaching the language model in the conventional design and in Youtu-Parsing-Omni. papers.abstract: Discounted regret measures the performance of an online learner by assigning exponentially decaying weights to past losses, reflecting the greater importance of recent losses in non-stationary online learning. While previous work obtains uniform discounted regret bounds over a continuous range of discount factors using a specialized meta-algorithm, its results are limited to convex functions. In this paper, we demonstrate that strongly adaptive regret bounds can directly imply uniform discounted regret guarantees for convex, strongly convex, and exp-concave loss functions. Our key observation is that discounted regret against a fixed comparator admits an exact decomposition into a convex combination of interval regrets. For convex functions, this reduction yields an $O(\sqrt{\log T/(1-\lambda)})$ discounted regret bound for all discount factors $\lambda\in(0,1)$, matching the previous rate over a broader range of discount factors. For strongly convex and exp-concave functions, we provide regret bounds of $O\left(\log T\left(1+\log\frac{1}{1-\lambda}\right)\right)$.
authors: Sifan Yang, Wenhao Yang, Lijun Zhang
bullets: Discounted regret emphasizes recent losses through exponentially decaying weights, making it useful for non-stationary online learning.
The paper shows that discounted regret against a fixed comparator exactly decomposes into a convex combination of interval regrets.
This reduction extends uniform discounted-regret guarantees beyond convex losses to strongly convex and exp-concave losses.
For convex losses, the bound is O(√(log T/(1−λ))) for every λ∈(0,1), while strongly convex and exp-concave losses achieve O(log T(1+log(1/(1−λ)))).

papers.title: Strongly Adaptive Online Learning Achieves Uniform Discounted Regret

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies increasingly learn from data collected across diverse tasks and embodiments, yet typically assume a single controller for each robot. This assumption limits transfer because different controllers can assign different physical meanings to the same action and may require different strategies to complete a task. We study how to transfer robot data across both embodiments and controllers without allowing conflicting action interpretations to interfere with learning. Our setting spans six controller types as well as variations in controller gains and compliance. We propose a framework that encodes behavioral interaction under a controller through examples of commanded actions and the resulting robot motions. A transformer context encoder summarizes these interactions, allowing a single policy to adapt in context. Across real-world experiments, our method improves average success by 33 percentage points over naive data pooling, achieves 50\% success on unseen controller modes and 52\% on unseen controller gains, and transfers to tasks with limited controller-specific data. On contact-rich tasks such as USB insertion and surface wiping, behavioral interaction context enables the policy to adapt not only its actions but also its strategy. Our results provide a path toward generalist robot policies that can leverage data collected across diverse action interpretations. For more information, visit \href{https://controller-transfer.github.io}{https://controller-transfer.github.io}.
authors: Jonathan Yang, Chelsea Finn, Dorsa Sadigh
bullets: Addresses conflicting action meanings across robot embodiments, controller types, gains, and compliance settings.
Uses a transformer context encoder to summarize commanded actions and resulting motions, enabling in-context policy adaptation.
Evaluated across six controller types and real-world tasks, including USB insertion and surface wiping.
Improves average success by 33 percentage points over naive data pooling; reaches 50% success on unseen controller modes and 52% on unseen gains.
Supports transfer with limited controller-specific data, including strategy adaptation on contact-rich tasks.

papers.abstract: Lattice-type modular reconfigurable robots rearrange standardized modules across tasks. Dedicated transport robots reduce module weight and cost by eliminating module level reconfiguration actuators. But existing systems use low capacity connections or internal fastening robots that occupy space for functional components. This paper presents CuBot-STT, which integrates module transport, interface locking, and release in one external robot. Cubic modules provide structural support and $24\,\mathrm{V}$ power distribution. On each face, a gear transmission converts one external input into motion of four helical locking points, preserving internal space. The robot uses alternating foot support, a gripper for module handling, and a tightening head for interface actuation. The controller coordinates two-foot support and module locking through continuous constraint transfers. The planner decomposes relocation costs into an analytical lower bound and a residual learned through expert-guided, goal conditioned Q-learning. Contact face $A^*$ search expands relocation sequences into robot primitives satisfying connectivity, asymmetric manipulation, and foot stance constraints. Experiments demonstrate normal and tangential interface capacities of $300\,\mathrm{N}$ and $490\,\mathrm{N}$, electrical continuity across six modules, and autonomous reconfiguration of an 11-module lattice. Planning benchmarks show superior search efficiency over analytical guidance and bidirectional heuristic search, with generalization beyond training lattice sizes without fine-tuning.

Demonstrations include 300 N normal capacity, 490 N tangential capacity, electrical continuity across six modules, and autonomous reconfiguration of an 11-module lattice; planning generalizes beyond training sizes without fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Predicting future physical states stands as a central challenge in embodied intelligence. Existing video world models leave 3D dynamics implicit, action-based formulations remain tied to specific robot configurations, and 3D motion prediction models use flow-only supervision, providing a limited learning signal for physical dynamics. To circumvent these limitations, we introduce \method{}, a generative world model that jointly predicts future video and query-based 3D trajectories. By parameterizing 3D motion as continuous displacement tokens aligned with the video grid, a unified Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) backbone jointly denoises both modalities under a rectified-flow objective. This formulation couples explicit geometric dynamics with visual evolution, effectively unlocking the physical commonsense embedded within pretrained video models. To empirically scale and validate this unified architecture, we train \method{} on a heterogeneous mixture of 1.44 million object-level samples spanning simulated and real-world domains. We further introduce WorldFlowBench, comprising 1,678 evaluation samples from 11 data sources across simulated and real-world interactions, including spatial reasoning tasks. Across all three evaluation sets, WorldFlow achieves the lowest average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) among the evaluated learning-based methods. Notably, on the challenging SpatialCog set, WorldFlow achieves an ADE of 0.060 m, a 54.2\% reduction compared with the strongest external baseline. It also reduces ADE and FDE by 55.9\% and 68.5\%, respectively, compared with its flow-only variant. Project page: https://worldflow-rbs.github.io/.
authors: Yuhao Lu, Jiongxu Chen, Hexiang Wei, Jiajin Wu, Juelin Li, Mingjian Liang, Fan Yang, Zhuowei Liang, Zihao Liu, Zhennan Wang, Sheng Wang, Lin Shao

papers.abstract: An effective agent memory system should adapt to a user's history and task requirements. Human-annotated supervision can guide this adaptation by providing feedback for evaluating and improving memory designs. Yet suitable labels are rarely available for new user histories, and manually constructing QA pairs and supporting evidence is costly. We introduce MemSteer, which turns unlabeled user histories into question-answer (QA) supervision with supporting evidence for memory-design optimization. MemSteer constructs an evidence-grounded answer plan that specifies how facts across related records jointly support a reference answer. The plan guides question generation, while source-grounded auditing and blind answer recovery check the resulting annotations. To study the utility of this supervision, we develop MemSteer-Opt, which combines QA-based design evaluation with evidence-guided failure diagnosis to revise memory store, retrieval, and context construction without updating model parameters. Experiments on ATM-Bench and RHELM show that this supervision is competitive with official-QA-guided optimization. Relative to Base-BM25, MemSteer-Opt improves ATM-Bench Question Score by 13.4 points and RHELM accuracy by 4.1 and 6.6 points without and with external data, respectively. The supervision also benefits two existing optimizers on ATM-Bench, while new-user experiments demonstrate continued design optimization using supervision generated from the target histories.
authors: Jie Huang, Cuiling Lan, Qize Yu, Xiulian Peng, Yan Lu
bullets: Addresses the scarcity and cost of manually annotated QA pairs and supporting evidence for new users.

Improves over Base-BM25 by 13.4 ATM-Bench Question Score points and 4.1/6.6 RHELM accuracy points without/with external data.
Supports continued optimization for new users and benefits two existing ATM-Bench optimizers.

papers.abstract: Engineering design frequently involves redesigning a prior solution to adapt to changes in context, such as material prices or system requirements. Redesign often leverages simulators too complex and/or computationally intensive for traditional numerical solvers, which lack engineering knowledge and context, to ensure global solution quality. Large language models (LLMs) can interpret semantic information, including engineering knowledge about the system and changes in context, to help guide search, and recent studies have shown that incorporating this knowledge into optimization can improve search performance. However, how best to combine LLMs with numerical solvers in redesign remains unclear. We develop and test an integrated LLM-optimization approach for redesign and compare three methods for leveraging LLMs (warm start, variable fixing and ReAct) and four black-box solvers (Bayesian optimization, genetic algorithms, mesh adaptive direct search and random search) on an electric vehicle battery pack cost minimization case study across four types of redesign scenarios. We find that the integrated approach can match feasible design discovery of the numerical-solver baselines with 80% fewer simulator evaluations while tripling the fraction of runs that find near-optimal solutions. We find that the best LLM-solver integration approach and the way the prior solution is leveraged depend on the structure of the design requirement change, and that the benefit of increasing LLM model size grows with the extent to which the LLM controls the search. These results show clear potential for LLMs in redesign tasks for guiding or replacing numerical solvers.
authors: Chan-Eui Song, Jeremy J. Michalek, Christopher McComb
bullets: Addresses redesign problems where expensive, complex simulators make conventional optimization inefficient and context-insensitive.

The best LLM–solver combination and use of the prior design depend on the type of requirement change.

papers.abstract: Legged robots have demonstrated advanced capabilities across a wide range of real-world tasks, yet much of this progress concerns the robot controlling only itself. Once the robot is coupled to an external object -- particularly an underactuated one -- the dynamics of the combined assembly become more complex. Towing a wagon is a common practical scenario, where coupled dynamics make reliable navigation challenging. This difficulty is amplified in confined spaces, where collision-free navigation requires finding a narrow set of feasible paths under strict real-time constraints. To address this, we propose a navigation framework that combines Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) with Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control over a learned Forward Dynamics Model (FDM). The CFM model mitigates the initialization problem of MPPI and accelerates its convergence, while MPPI with the FDM recovers feasible solutions beyond the CFM model's training distribution by iterative refinement. We integrate the framework into a full-stack navigation system for RAIBO-Wagon, a quadruped towing a custom wagon, and validate it in real-world outdoor experiments on 15 m-long courses through confined spaces, with all sensing and computation performed fully onboard. The system achieves an 85% success rate across 40 trials, towing a total load of up to 40 kg -- nearly 100% of RAIBO's body weight.
authors: Insung Yang, Eunchae Kim, Jungwoo Hur, Seunghun Jeon, Donghyuk Choi, Jemin Hwangbo

papers.abstract: While frontier vision-language models demonstrate strong capabilities in user interface (UI) navigation, their high inference costs prohibit everyday use. Conversely, smaller models trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or offline reinforcement learning often memorize static trajectories, leading to brittle execution and an inability to recover from errors. To address these limitations, we propose a novel online reinforcement learning framework that trains UI navigation agents directly on live iOS applications. Our framework decouples the agent into two specialized components: a Planning agent and a UI Grounding model. We rely on an LLM-as-a-Judge to provide comprehensive reward signals, combining dense, step-level feedback to evaluate intermediate progress with a terminal reward for overall task completion. To effectively leverage this dual reward structure, we optimize the agent using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with step-level advantage estimation. Furthermore, we introduce GiGPPO, a novel neighbor-conditioned value estimation method that improves critic stability by leveraging reward signals from visually similar states across concurrent trajectories. To support this online training paradigm at scale, we introduce an efficient infrastructure that orchestrates hundreds of concurrent virtual iOS devices. Evaluations on rigorous benchmarks, including UINavBench, iOSWorld, and AndroidWorld, demonstrate that our online RL trained agents substantially outperform both SFT and terminal-only RL baselines while accelerating training convergence. Notably, our 8B RL agents achieve nearly a sevenfold improvement over the SFT baseline in out-of-distribution generalization to Android environments, while outperforming Gemini-3.5-Flash and tying with Gemini-3.1-Pro on real iOS applications.
authors: Peitong Duan, Khashayar Gatmiry, Jeffrey Nichols, Samy Bengio, Emmanuel Abbe
bullets: Addresses brittle trajectory memorization and high inference costs in UI navigation.
Decouples navigation into a Planning agent and a UI Grounding model.
Uses LLM-based dense step rewards plus terminal task-completion rewards, optimized with PPO and step-level advantages.
Introduces GiGPPO, which stabilizes value estimation using rewards from visually similar states in concurrent trajectories.

Evaluations across UINavBench, iOSWorld, and AndroidWorld show stronger performance than SFT and terminal-only RL baselines, including nearly sevenfold OOD improvement for 8B agents on Android and competitive results on real iOS apps.

Figure 2: Example traces of the GiGPPO-trained planning agent and the SFT baseline on the UINavBench task: ”Find a route from Apple Park to the Santa Clara Caltrain Station.” Pink crosshairs indicate the agent’s tap and text-entry actions at each step. Because the Apple Maps workflow requires selecting the destination before the starting location, the agents are easily confused by the task prompt’s phrasing, which mentions the starting point first. The GiGPPO agent initially sets the destination as Apple Park, but it corrects itself by exiting the directions search and restarting with the Santa Clara Caltrain Station as the destination, demonstrating strong error recovery. In contrast, the SFT agent opens the wrong directions search page and gets stuck repeatedly trying to set the starting point of a custom route until it reaches the maximum step limit.
