papers.abstract: Trajectory-level GRPO is a common approach for training multi-step GUI agents, but repeatedly rolling out complete trajectories from the task root can be inefficient: task-level rewards provide coarse supervision over which intermediate decisions require improvement, while already-mastered prefixes are repeatedly re-executed before reaching difficult states. We introduce a two-stage adaptive training framework that jointly addresses where to learn and how far to roll out. We first construct reusable intermediate checkpoints from successful expert trajectories and select informative pivots using action disagreement, which measures uncertainty directly from sampled GUI actions. Stage I performs one-step RL at these pivots to improve uncertain local decisions. Stage II then progressively expands policy responsibility through adaptive Local, Suffix, and Root training according to task progress. Recoverable checkpoints enable repeated training from intermediate states without replaying the preceding trajectory. Across MobileGym and CUA-Gym-Hub, our method reduces environment interaction by 56-61% relative to Vanilla GRPO while improving task performance, demonstrating that jointly allocating training across states and rollout ranges can substantially improve GUI-agent RL efficiency.
authors: Yuxiang Chai, Quyu Kong, Panrong Tong, Steven Hoi, Yue Wang
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of replaying full trajectories from the task root and the coarse supervision of task-level rewards.

Recoverable intermediate states avoid replaying mastered prefixes during repeated training.
On MobileGym and CUA-Gym-Hub, it reduces environment interaction by 56–61% versus Vanilla GRPO while improving task performance.

papers.abstract: We introduce SocialArena, a benchmark for systematically defining and evaluating the social intelligence of large language models (LLMs). Although LLMs are increasingly deployed in socially interactive applications such as mental health counseling, companionship chatbots, and educational tutoring, existing evaluations remain fragmented focusing on isolated capabilities or single scenarios and evaluation reliability is largely unverified. This work makes three main contributions to address these limitations. (1) We first propose a unified three-tier framework that defines social intelligence along three capability dimensions: role-playing ability, mental state reasoning, and behavioral reasoning. To operationalize this definition, we design a role-playing dialogue paradigm with explicit character thinking for evaluation, enabling simultaneous assessment of these capabilities in a manner that mirrors realistic human interactions. (2) To ensure diversity across social scenarios and thereby prevent evaluation conclusions from being confined to specific scenarios, we introduce the U-TRIMF framework, which guides us in synthesizing social contexts with broad coverage. (3) To obtain reliable evaluation, we invest $132.4K to recruit and train human annotators and adopt a human-annotated arena-style protocol, where annotators compare model responses and provide preference labels along with natural-language critiques. We hope that SocialArena can provide valuable insights and guidance for future LLM improvements.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a powerful tool for improving multimodal reasoning. However, standard outcome supervision suffers from credit assignment ambiguity, as a model may receive positive rewards by exploiting language priors or dataset shortcuts rather than grounding its reasoning in the requisite visual evidence. This makes high-quality negative responses critical, since effective negatives should remain plausible under the current policy while exposing the shortcut that should be suppressed. In this paper, we propose EVAN, a multimodal reinforcement learning framework utilizing EVidence-Ablated Negatives to train LMMs against their own language-prior failures. EVAN first identifies highly visually dependent examples using a scaled image information gain metric and preserves data diversity with a mixed-ranking strategy. It then constructs evidence-ablated images by masking the most discriminative image patches, eliciting plausible but visually ungrounded responses from the current policy. During policy optimization, these negative responses are incorporated as bounded auxiliary signals under the clean image, penalizing shortcut learning while maintaining RL stability. Experiments across challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that EVAN mitigates modality imbalance and improves over strong RLVR baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/DawnLIU35/EVAN.git.
authors: Chenxi Liu, Tianyi Xiong, Yanshuo Chen, Heng Huang
bullets: RLVR outcome rewards can miss whether reasoning is grounded in images, allowing language-prior shortcuts.
EVAN identifies visually dependent examples and masks discriminative image patches to generate plausible, ungrounded negative responses.
These negatives are used as bounded auxiliary penalties during policy optimization to suppress shortcut learning while preserving stability.
Experiments on challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks show improved modality balance and performance over strong RLVR baselines.
Scope: the approach targets multimodal reasoning settings where visual evidence is necessary.

papers.abstract: Embodied world models should not only imagine plausible futures, but also perceive the geometric, semantic, and motion structure of the evolving world. We present GenSight, a unified embodied world model that brings future video generation and dense perception into a single pretrained video diffusion transformer. GenSight uses a unified spatiotemporal representation for video, depth, embodiment segmentation, and first-frame-relative 2D flow. Built on a shared DiT backbone, GenSight uses lightweight task modulation to predict all modalities within the same architecture. All tasks are jointly optimized within a unified velocity prediction space. At inference, GenSight supports two complementary modes: multi-step future video generation with aligned dense predictions and single-step dense perception from an observed video. By unifying modality representation, model architecture, and prediction space, GenSight avoids separate modality-specific pipelines and couples appearance, geometry, semantics, and motion in a shared representation. It promotes cross-modal consistency and allows dense perception to benefit from the spatiotemporal priors learned through video generation. Trained on embodied manipulation data spanning multiple robot embodiments and human-hand interactions, GenSight demonstrates strong performance in both video generation and dense 4D perception, highlighting the effectiveness of unifying seeing and imagining for embodied world modeling.
authors: Haitang Feng, Zhuoman Liu, Zhennan Wang, Sheng Wang, Juelin Li, Chengzhi Zhao, Hexiang Wei, Lin Shao
bullets: Addresses the need for world models that both imagine plausible futures and understand evolving geometry, semantics, and motion.
Uses a shared spatiotemporal representation and DiT backbone for video, depth, embodiment segmentation, and first-frame-relative 2D flow.
Jointly trains all modalities in a unified velocity-prediction space with lightweight task modulation.
Supports multi-step future generation with aligned dense predictions and single-step perception from observed video.
Trained on embodied manipulation data across robot embodiments and human-hand interactions, it shows strong performance in generation and dense 4D perception.

papers.abstract: Financial AI systems must support decision-bearing questions involving payments, collections, cash flow, and compliance while ensuring numerical accuracy, traceability, and auditability. Large language models (LLMs) enable natural language interaction but cannot independently guarantee reproducible calculations or evidence-grounded recommendations. We present a production-grounded architecture integrating three components: a financial knowledge graph for enterprise relationships, temporal context, and provenance; a deterministic optimization engine for financial calculations and decisions; and a multi-agent LLM layer for intent interpretation, task orchestration, explanation, and claim validation. A coordination layer, termed context engineering, selects, ranks, composes, and validates query-specific context across ERP systems, tools, and tenants. Based on observations from 15 deployments over approximately 11 months, single-agent pipelines exhibited hallucination rates of about 7-9% (5-10% across query types), including invented invoices and unsupported financial claims. Graph-backed multi-agent validation reduced observed rates to below 1%, although these findings are observational rather than causal. ERP data quality and tenant-specific schemas remained major implementation challenges. Reusable mappings, graph templates, and validation policies coincided with a reduction in deployment time from roughly six to two weeks. We argue that financial context engineering extends beyond text-centric retrieval-augmented generation by requiring structured relationships, temporal validity, exact numerical evidence, access controls, and validation against source records and solver outputs. We outline research challenges in evaluation, reproducibility, privacy, context quality, and cross-tenant generalization.
authors: Pradeep Kumar GS, Ravi Tanniru
bullets: Targets decision-bearing financial tasks such as payments, collections, cash flow, and compliance.
Uses context engineering to select, rank, compose, and validate query-specific information across ERP systems, tools, and tenants.
In 15 observational deployments, graph-backed multi-agent validation coincided with lower observed hallucination rates—from about 5–10% to below 1%.
Reusable mappings, graph templates, and validation policies coincided with deployment time falling from roughly six to two weeks.
Key challenges include ERP data quality, tenant-specific schemas, privacy, reproducibility, evaluation, and cross-tenant generalization.

papers.abstract: We present XLaw-JP-27B, an open-weight model specialized for Japanese law that runs on a single 48\,GB GPU under the Apache~2.0 licence. It adapts Qwen3.8-27B with hybrid retrieval over all current statutes and 31k case summaries, a light QLoRA fine-tune on its own verified answers to past bar-exam questions (self-distillation), a contract-specific LoRA adapter, and four-sample voting. We evaluate it on eight Japanese legal tasks---the multiple-choice section of the bar examination in 2024, 2025 and 2026, statement-level bar questions (JBE-QA), statute questions (LawQA-JP), the patent attorney exam, and contract review and drafting built from government model contracts---against open models of 12--33B under identical prompts and retrieval. XLaw-JP-27B ranks first on six tasks, ties on one and is third on one (mean rank 1.3 against 2.8--3.1 for the baselines). It is the only system that passes the bar exam in all three years (129, 120 and 130 of 175, meeting every subject minimum; no test-year material was used in training), while open Japanese 32--33B models fail at least one year. A controlled study of each component shows that retrieval, voting and self-distillation help, and that thinking mode, retrieval-grounded synthetic tuning, self-verification, per-statement decomposition and more self-distillation do not. The largest remaining gaps to frontier models are in contract review and patent law. The model is available as a free web service at https://x-law.jp/ with the weights available at https://huggingface.co/X-LawJapan/xlaw-jp-27b under Apache~2.0.
authors: Andrew Shin
bullets: Adapts Qwen3.8-27B with statute and case-summary retrieval, self-distillation via QLoRA, a contract LoRA adapter, and four-sample voting.
Ranks first on six of eight tasks, ties on one, and places third on one, outperforming the reported open-model baselines in mean rank.
Passes the Japanese bar exam in all three evaluated years while meeting every subject minimum; no test-year material was used for training.
Component analysis finds retrieval, voting, and self-distillation helpful, while several additional reasoning and tuning strategies do not improve results.
Remaining weaknesses are contract review and patent law; weights and a free web service are released under Apache 2.0.

papers.abstract: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) typically uses uniform coverage across Transformer layers despite heterogeneous positional requirements. Phase-off interventions reveal non-uniform, model-specific rotary-phase dependence, while coverage interventions relate it to coverage-upgrade benefits. We propose profiling-guided layer-wise RoPE allocation, assigning high/low coverage under a fixed budget using early coverage-benefit profiles. The framework supports fixed-width query/key representations and physical rotary-dimension allocation in Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA). Normalized-depth mapping transfers profiles within model families, enabling small-model measurements to guide larger-model allocations before pretraining. A brief analysis relates selection and transfer to score calibration and inter-layer interactions. From-scratch experiments demonstrate validation-loss improvements over available budget-matched baselines, while analytical resource accounting identifies favorable quality--storage--compute trade-offs for physical MLA. These results connect positional demand to transferable, efficient architecture design.

bullets: RoPE dependence varies across layers and models, motivating non-uniform allocation.

papers.abstract: We develop a fast method for the rigid alignment of voxelized three-dimensional density functions over $\mathsf{SO}(3)$ using sliced optimal transport. Our approach efficiently transforms each density map into a tensor of one-dimensional quantile functions, taken from central slices over the unit sphere, such that the Euclidean distance of the transformed volumes approximates the sliced 2-Wasserstein distance. Our formulation is therefore compatible with existing, fast, voxel-based Euclidean alignment algorithms. We provide theoretical analysis and numerical experiments demonstrating that the sliced 2-Wasserstein distance is a robust metric for comparing three-dimensional shapes and for computing their rigid alignment.
authors: Oscar Mickelin, Yunpeng Shi, Amit Singer, Eric J. Verbeke
bullets: Targets rigid rotational alignment of voxelized 3-D density functions over SO(3).
Transforms each volume into tensors of one-dimensional quantile functions from central spherical slices.
Enables use of existing fast voxel-based Euclidean alignment algorithms.

papers.abstract: Learning task progress from robot demonstrations provides a practical way to construct dense shaping rewards for robotic reinforcement learning. A common approach uses normalized demonstration time as progress labels, implicitly assuming monotonically increasing task progress. During policy exploration, however, actual task progress can stall or even regress. Such models may mistake regressions for progress, assigning positive shaping rewards to actions that cause progress loss. Real suboptimal and failed executions offer corrective experience, but assigning absolute progress values to their states is difficult. Our key observation is that stalls, regressions, and recoveries establish local relative progress relations even when absolute progress is unknown. We introduce Event2Reward, which uses normalized temporal labels to anchor the progress scale and these within-trajectory relations to constrain local changes, combining absolute and relative progress supervision. Its progress predictions serve as potentials for reward shaping. We curate an event-annotated dataset from approximately 100K raw real-robot execution records, covering successful, suboptimal, and failed executions, without requiring framewise absolute progress labels. Under the same training budgets, Event2Reward improves average policy success by 18.16 percentage points over a baseline using only sparse task rewards across 40 tasks in four LIBERO suites. On real robots, average success after 30 minutes of wall-clock training reaches 60.0% on three precise insertion tasks and 90.0% on three object manipulation tasks, exceeding the sparse-reward baseline under the same budget by 36.7 and 23.3 percentage points, respectively. Ablation studies further show that absolute progress supervision and relative progress relations are complementary, with joint supervision yielding better downstream policy learning.
authors: Junnan Nie, Zitian Fan, Jiachen Zhang, Junyi Lao, Likui Zhang, Chenghao Liu, Xiaoyang Lu, Yunbo Wang, Yixue Zhang, Linbo Zhai, Jiayi Li, Mengzhe Wang, Xichang Wu, Bin Wang, Chang Liu, Tianle Zhang, Songfang Huang
bullets: Addresses the problem that time-based progress labels can mistake regressions for genuine progress during exploration.
Uses normalized temporal labels to anchor progress and event-derived within-trajectory relations to constrain local progress changes.
Converts predicted progress into potential-based shaping rewards without requiring framewise absolute labels for failed or suboptimal executions.
Trains on an event-annotated collection of approximately 100K real-robot execution records spanning successful, suboptimal, and failed runs.
Improves policy success over sparse-reward training across LIBERO tasks and real-robot insertion and manipulation tasks under matched training budgets.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is increasingly explored as an input representation for 3D perception. Yet it remains unclear how current 3D architectures exploit heterogeneous Gaussian attributes. This ambiguity makes accuracy hard to interpret and limits principled architecture design for 3DGS perception. However, existing object-level 3DGS datasets lack the appearance variation or artifact control needed for systematic attribute-level analysis. We introduce COGS, a large-scale 3DGS dataset with 15,675 artifact-filtered and appearance-rich objects across 40 categories. Built on COGS, we establish COGS-Bench for object classification and attribute-usage diagnosis, complemented by external validation. Our benchmark shows that Gaussian attributes are not uniformly beneficial: selected subsets can outperform the full attribute set, and the effects of appearance, opacity, and covariance-related attribute combinations vary substantially across architectures. We further study this finding with HALO, a reference model that preserves attribute-specific evidence before hierarchical aggregation. Experiments on COGS-Bench and external 3DGS datasets demonstrate that COGS supports systematic diagnosis of 3DGS attribute usage, while HALO highlights the value of role-preserving attribute organization. Our dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/XiaoZhengCV/COGS.
authors: Zheng Xiao, Yifan Liu, Weijian Deng, Jiashu Li, Ziqin Liu, Zhenjun Han, Jianbin Jiao
bullets: Introduces 15,675 artifact-filtered, appearance-rich 3DGS objects spanning 40 categories.
Provides COGS-Bench for object classification and attribute-usage diagnosis, with external validation.
Finds that using all Gaussian attributes is not always optimal; selected subsets can perform better, with effects varying by architecture.
Presents HALO, a reference model that preserves attribute-specific evidence during hierarchical aggregation.
Experiments show COGS enables systematic attribute analysis and that role-preserving attribute organization is useful.

papers.abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly used to complete complex, long-horizon tasks without human intervention. To make progress toward the task goal, agents need to perform different duties, such as planning and verification, when needed. To understand how single agents manage these duties during long-horizon execution, we conduct a preliminary study. Our analysis shows that verification has the strongest association with task success, but often occurs late, leaving limited opportunities for correction. We also find that the proportion of duty-relevant information decreases as records from different duties accumulate in a shared context. These findings lead us to examine whether multi-agent systems (MAS) can address these problems by assigning duties to agents with separate contexts. Our analysis shows that this separation alone is insufficient. Agents can lose track of the overall goal and repeat prior investigations. They may also lack necessary background while receiving irrelevant information from others. To maintain goal awareness and coordinate collaboration as task needs change, we propose Goal-Aware Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration (GAD). It uses a growing execution graph to organize subtasks and their dependencies. To keep agents focused on their goals, each context retains the original instruction and the assigned task's goal and acceptance conditions. To adapt collaboration and information sharing during execution, agents can divide tasks into subtasks and specify dependencies based on execution evidence. These dependencies guide when agents work and which results they receive. Verification and recovery check subtask results and full task completion against their goals, providing feedback for repair when checks fail.
authors: Xu Shen, Lingyong Yan, Shuaiqiang Wang, Jianmin Wu, Zhikai Chen, Jiliang Tang, Jie Ren
bullets: Verification is strongly linked to success but often happens too late for effective correction.
Single-agent contexts become diluted as information from different duties accumulates.
Separating duties across agents can cause goal drift, repeated work, and missing or irrelevant context.
GAD uses a growing execution graph to organize subtasks, dependencies, and adaptive information sharing.
Verification and recovery checks provide feedback for repairing failed subtasks or incomplete overall tasks.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly described as acquiring "reasoning" skills after reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. However, whether these gains reflect genuine reasoning or more superficial adaptations remains underexplored. In this work, we probe LLMs trained in a finite and exhaustively analyzable logical domain, namely Tic-Tac-Toe, and trace how internal representations evolve across reinforcement learning (RL) with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Quantitatively, RL yields high accuracy and robustness across prompt variations, suggesting the emergence of game reasoning. Mechanistic interpretability, however, paints a different picture: features extracted with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) reveal that models primarily adapt to rely more heavily on information already explicit in the prompt, such as whose turn it is, game progression and board occupancy. In comparison, high-level concepts like board symmetries and strategic forks remain weakly represented, raising concerns that reasoning benchmarks overestimate model abilities. This suggests that RL-driven "reasoning" may conflate task-specific adaptations to input information with reasoning ability. We provide, for the first time: (i) a systematic interpretability pipeline tracing representation dynamics across RL training in small-scale LLMs; (ii) an extension of SAE-based feature discovery to hypothesis-driven testing in a finite logical domain; and (iii) an interpretability-based demonstration that RL post-training neither adds nor removes concept information but reorganizes which features dominate the representation, with causal interventions locating the decision downstream of it, in the late-layer state.
authors: Aishik Nagar, Cheston Tan
bullets: The study examines whether RL with GRPO produces genuine reasoning or task-specific pattern exploitation.
Across prompt variations, RL improves accuracy and robustness in the finite Tic-Tac-Toe domain.
Sparse autoencoder analysis finds stronger reliance on turn, game progression, and board occupancy information.
Board symmetries and strategic forks remain weakly represented despite behavioral gains.
Causal interventions place the decision process downstream in the late-layer state, where RL reorganizes feature dominance rather than adding or removing concepts.
papers.selection_reason: Uses mechanistic interpretability (SAEs) to analyze how RL training affects internal representations in LLMs, specifically distinguishing between genuine reasoning and pattern exploitation.
papers.title: Reasoning or Pattern Exploitation? Mechanistic Insights from RL-Trained Language Models
papers.tldr: In Tic-Tac-Toe, RL-trained LLMs appear robust and accurate largely by emphasizing prompt-explicit information rather than developing strong representations of higher-level strategic reasoning.

papers.abstract: Experience can help embodied agents turn high-level plans into grounded actions, but transferring it across tasks remains challenging: previously effective strategies may be inapplicable to the current state or fail to produce their intended outcomes. We present EmbodiExp, a framework for constructing transferable experiences and composing them online during embodied task execution. Our key observation is that tasks often share subgoals whose completion can be assessed independently of overall task success. We therefore introduce an outcome-grounded subgoal experience that specifies a subgoal, applicability conditions, an adaptable policy, and a verifiable outcome. During execution, applicable experiences guide action generation, while verified outcomes can establish the conditions required by subsequent experiences, enabling online composition. Subgoal-level outcome attribution further enables failure utilization: failed trajectories can still contribute verified local successes and condition-specific guidance on actions to avoid. Experiments on multiple embodied benchmarks under a fold-based protocol with frozen experience banks demonstrate the effectiveness of EmbodiExp.
authors: Zhifeng Gu, Ying Chen, Rui Jiang, Lei Yi, Bing Wang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of transferring strategies across tasks when applicability and outcomes vary by state.
Represents experiences with a subgoal, applicability conditions, an adaptable policy, and a verifiable outcome.
Composes experiences online by using verified subgoal outcomes to satisfy conditions for later experiences.
Uses subgoal-level outcome attribution to extract local successes and avoidable actions from failed trajectories.
Demonstrates effectiveness across multiple embodied benchmarks with frozen experience banks under a fold-based protocol.

papers.abstract: Edited endpoint images make the target of an image-to-video transition explicit and can improve transition completion, but also preserve context in the source image's layout. Full-frame endpoint conditioning turns this preserved context into requirements on the video's final state, potentially inducing temporal artifacts. We measure discontinuity with Hard-Cut (HC), late background reversal with Background Motion Reversal (BMR), and motion suppression with Dynamic Degree (DD). These artifacts appear across five video models spanning training-free and learned endpoint conditioning, in model-specific forms. We study Partial, a selective conditioning scheme that constrains only an edit-relevant region estimated from image-editor attention and leaves the remaining terminal content to the video model. Across three backbones on TC-Bench-I2V, Partial reduces temporal artifacts relative to full-frame conditioning, with no significant difference in Transition Completion Ratio (TCR); on Wan2.2-Turbo, uniformly weakening conditioning does not reproduce these reductions. A donor-context intervention keeps full-frame conditioning and replaces only the context outside the edit-relevant region with the final frame of a Partial video. It lowers HC and BMR on HunyuanVideo-1.5 and lowers BMR while restoring DD on Wan2.2-Turbo, with no significant difference in TCR, so constraint extent alone does not account for these artifacts. Together, these findings suggest that edited endpoints should serve as partial future goals, although edit relevance does not guarantee future validity. Code and data will be released at https://github.com/wannagetacat/Edited-Endpoints-I2V.
authors: Sihyun Kim, Sanghyun Jo, Kyungsu Kim
bullets: Full-frame endpoint conditioning can force preserved source context into the video’s final state, causing discontinuities, background reversals, and motion suppression.
The study evaluates these artifacts with Hard-Cut, Background Motion Reversal, and Dynamic Degree across five video models.
The proposed Partial scheme conditions only the edit-relevant region, estimated from image-editor attention, while leaving other terminal content unconstrained.
Across three backbones on TC-Bench-I2V, Partial reduces artifacts with no significant change in Transition Completion Ratio.
Donor-context experiments suggest artifact reductions are not explained solely by weakening or shrinking the conditioning constraint; edit relevance does not always ensure future validity.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video has emerged as one of the most scalable sources of data for learning generalizable manipulation priors. Yet, despite its growing use in pretraining robotic policies, it has been underutilized as a validation tool for physical intelligence, a key component of which is understanding where to make contact with an object to achieve an intended interaction. We present EgoContact, a large-scale egocentric dataset for evaluating the generalizability and precision of learned manipulation priors through future contact-point prediction. EgoContact contains 22.5K manually verified interaction events, each with a pre-contact observation, semantic intent, and pixel-precise contact locations. We find that current methods often struggle to predict precise interaction contacts and sometimes fail to localize the target object in diverse, in-the-wild scenes, even when allowed multiple predictions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the usefulness of EgoContact's annotated interactions for robotic manipulation: simply using EgoContact as the memory bank of an existing affordance-transfer policy improves grasp success from 14.2% to 31.2% in simulation and from 16% to 58% on a real robot.
authors: Adam Dery{\l}o, Alexey Gavryushin, Daniel Cremers, Marc Pollefeys, Xi Wang
bullets: Addresses the underuse of egocentric video for validating manipulation and contact-point understanding.
Introduces 22.5K manually verified interaction events with pre-contact observations, semantic intent, and pixel-precise contact locations.
Finds that existing methods struggle with precise contact prediction and target localization in diverse real-world scenes.
Using EgoContact as a memory bank improves grasp success for an existing affordance-transfer policy in both simulation and on a real robot.

papers.abstract: Aligning a partial, real-world 3D face scan to a canonical representation requires solving two coupled problems at once: estimating the rigid pose that brings the scan into a common frame, and completing the facial shape in regions the scan never observed. Existing pipelines typically decouple these steps, running a generic point-cloud registration front end followed by a separate non-rigid fitting or deformation stage. Building on the GeoTransformer superpoint-matching architecture, we propose a single network that predicts both a rigid pose and a shape-complete point cloud in one forward pass: a cross-attention regressor, conditioned on transformer point features and predicted coarse correspondences, maps a partial scan to per-patch coefficients of a 3D morphable face model learned offline from a corpus of 8,000 identities. The resulting morphed template is then used, in the same forward pass, as the target for fine-grained Sinkhorn matching and rigid pose estimation, supervised purely by geometric alignment to ground-truth morphed geometry, so no hand-labeled coefficients are required. Against six classical and learned non-rigid registration baselines on held-out identities, our method leads the strongest ones by 3-4 times on per-vertex error and baselines that collapse the head onto the visible region by more than an order of magnitude, and is simultaneously the most accurate and fastest method on ground-truth-free scans from two independent real-scan datasets, NoW and NPHM. Code will be made publicly available.
authors: Eli A. Underwood, Nicolas Rondan, Angel V. Peterchev, J. Matias Di Martino
bullets: Addresses the coupled problem of rigid pose estimation and completion of missing face regions in partial scans.
Builds on GeoTransformer features and coarse correspondences, then predicts local 3D morphable-model coefficients via cross-attention.
Uses the reconstructed morphed template for fine-grained Sinkhorn matching and pose estimation in one forward pass.
Trains using geometric alignment to ground-truth morphed geometry, without hand-labeled morphable-model coefficients.
Outperforms six classical and learned baselines by 3–4× or more in per-vertex error and is fastest and most accurate on NoW and NPHM real scans.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Pipeline overview. A shared KPConv (Kernel Point Convolution) backbone and GeoTransformer produce coarse superpoint correspondences between the mean-face template and a partial scan; a cross-attention regressor predicts per-patch morphable-basis coefficients z (conditioned on post-transformer features, pre-transformer backbone features, and the coarse correspondences), which are decoded into a morphed template that updates the reference positions used by Sinkhorn optimal-transport (OT) fine matching and local-to-global registration (LGR) to produce the estimated pose (R̂, t̂). Bottom: detail of the coefficient regressor, showing its various input feature sources and the per-patch decoding into z.

papers.abstract: The central bottleneck in visual generation and editing has migrated from achieving pixel-level fidelity to satisfying densely constrained user specifications through increasingly agentic workflows. Prevailing agentic generation pipelines remain shallow generate-verify-rewrite loops treating VLM judgments as coarse visual feedback, either discarding repair experience or admitting ungated updates that poison skill library. With memorize and govern periods left open, they degrade into ungoverned iterators of repeated trial-and-error rather than continual self-evolving harness. Towards this issue, we present \textbf{VEvo-Harness}, the first causally-guarded continual self-evolving harness system for agentic visual generation. VEvo-Harness introduces four coupled innovations: (1) \textit{a visual traceback} that densifies sparse judgments into root-cause attributions with a hierarchical verification tree; (2) \textit{a visual continual governance} that admits only causally valid skill patches through counterfactual dual-arm image generation replay; (3) \textit{a lifecycle-managed harness state} that hierarchically distills root-cause-anchored episodes across working, experience, and pattern tiers into a persistent skill library of routable and causally verified capabilities; (4) \textit{a heterogeneous sandbox policy} that orchestrates a diverse action space of repair primitives, dynamically routing cost-aware interventions based on root causes to select the most effective strategy. VEvo-Harness surpasses state-of-the-art agentic methods and rivals proprietary generators (\textit{e.g.}, GPT-Image, Nano-Pro) while maintaining the continual harness evolution and generalization.
authors: Yuan Wang, Yuhang Yu, Mengting Chen, Tianrun Xu, Zihao Pan, Xuetao Feng, Wei Li
bullets: Targets the gap between pixel fidelity and satisfying densely constrained visual specifications.
Uses visual traceback and hierarchical verification to identify root causes from sparse judgments.
Validates skill updates with counterfactual dual-arm replay, preventing harmful additions to the skill library.
Manages experience across working, experience, and pattern tiers for persistent, causally verified capabilities.
Routes cost-aware repair actions through a heterogeneous sandbox and reports performance surpassing existing agentic methods while rivaling proprietary generators.

papers.abstract: 4D perception models, which classify 3D point-cloud videos, are being built into robots, assistive monitoring and AR, yet before deploying one a practitioner cannot check which cue it relies on: how a body part moves, or what shape it has. 3D attribution is single-frame, video attribution is confined to RGB pixels, gradient maps need white-box access, attention is absent from state-space backbones, and point-level perturbations assume a point correspondence across frames that real depth and LiDAR data lack. We present Kinematic Causal Attribution (KCA), a black-box, interventional attribution method that queries only the model's outputs. Its freeze operator removes a region's motion while keeping its shape, and a shape-free proxy removes the shape while keeping the motion. Together they span a motion$\times$geometry cube for every tracked region, whose order-symmetric Shapley decomposition is complete and whose interaction is measured rather than assumed away. The operators rewrite per-frame point sets, so they need no correspondences, and a context-averaged estimator handles structures that span several regions. We validate KCA on the official PSTNet, P4Transformer and Mamba4D trained on MSR-Action3D. The decisive test is an audit: two binary tasks are built from real clips whose classes differ only in the motion or only in the shape of the same arm, and the motion share of the arm's importance follows the defining cue on all three backbones (0.83 vs. 0.60 on P4Transformer, 0.86 vs. 0.30 on PSTNet, 0.92 vs. 0.61 on Mamba4D), a distinction no single attribution map can make. The split costs no faithfulness: the necessity maps have the lowest deletion AUC on P4Transformer and PSTNet, tie with the best baseline on Mamba4D, and lose their correlation with the trained model's once the weights are randomised. Skeleton ground truth, re-sampling stability and cost complete the validation.
authors: Zerui Wang
bullets: Uses interventional operators to freeze a region’s motion while preserving shape, or remove shape while preserving motion.
Combines these interventions in a motion×geometry cube with an order-symmetric Shapley decomposition that captures interactions.
A context-averaged estimator supports structures spanning multiple tracked regions, and the operators rewrite per-frame point sets without requiring correspondences.
On MSR-Action3D audits across PSTNet, P4Transformer, and Mamba4D, motion attribution tracks whether the defining cue is motion or shape.
Necessity maps show strong faithfulness under deletion tests and lose correlation after model-weight randomization, supporting model-specific attribution.

A local or a context-averaged estimator turns the cube’s outputs into order-symmetric motion and geometry importance whose interaction is measured. Only outputs of f are used, so the same pipeline explains convolutional, attention and state-space backbones.

papers.title: Kinematic Causal Attribution: Black-Box Explanations of Motion versus Geometry for 4D Point-Cloud Video Models

papers.abstract: Operational strategies for long-horizon robotic tasks require reliable evaluation to determine whether execution is progressing, stalling, regressing, or recovering from errors. Yet real- world robot datasets that capture error recovery and provide frame-level error annotations remain scarce. To address this gap, we introduce and open-source ReSTEP, a dataset of 3,156 episodes across two manipulation tasks with semantic stage labels and frame-level er- ror annotations. ReSTEP supports training and benchmarking progress monitors through successful execution, mistakes, and recovery. Existing progress estimators can struggle to distinguish visually similar task stages and maintain temporally consistent predictions while responding to genuine setbacks. We therefore propose REMORA, an online progress esti- mator that combines recurrent visual memory, distributional prediction, and causal peak selection. Memory retains execution history to help resolve visual ambiguity, while distribu- tional prediction represents alternative progress hypotheses and causal peak selection tracks a supported hypothesis over time. Together, these components enable consistent progress tracking that remains responsive to errors and recovery. Experiments on both ReSTEP tasks demonstrate that REMORA outperforms the state-of-the-art SARM baseline in progress ac- curacy and temporal consistency.
authors: Chen Wang, Xinze Niu, Zihao Zhu, Keru Zhou, Yicheng Xu, Shihao Jin, Wenhao Wang, Bowen Jiang, Chang Zhou, Li Liu, Maoqing Yao
bullets: Addresses the lack of real-world robotic datasets with frame-level error and recovery annotations.
Introduces ReSTEP, an open-source dataset of 3,156 episodes across two manipulation tasks with semantic stage labels.
Proposes REMORA, an online progress estimator using recurrent visual memory, distributional prediction, and causal peak selection.
The method maintains alternative progress hypotheses while responding to setbacks and recovery.
Outperforms the SARM baseline in progress accuracy and temporal consistency on both ReSTEP tasks.

papers.abstract: As a representative form of embodied robotic interaction, aerial grasping requires close coordination between the aerial platform and manipulator. Most existing systems perform aerial grasping with static or slowly moving targets under fixed scenarios. Dynamic and precise grasping across different conditions introduces additional challenges, including target motion, localization drift, dynamic coupling, and external disturbances. In this work, we present CAPTURER, a dexterous aerial manipulator for centimeter-level grasping across diverse environments. To achieve the challenging goal, we first develop an onboard perception system for state estimation and target detection. Drift correction and global pose transformation are introduced to improve target localization during flight. A cooperative motion planner is proposed to coordinate the mobility of the aerial platform with the dexterity of the manipulator according to the relative target state. To maintain grasping accuracy under disturbances, we design a disturbance-rejection controller to compensate for dynamic coupling, model uncertainty, and external disturbances. The capability of CAPTURER is validated through indoor and outdoor experiments with both static and moving targets. The results demonstrate that CAPTURER achieves centimeter-level grasping accuracy for a marker pen measuring only 1.5 cm in diameter at flight speeds exceeding 1.5 m/s.
authors: Meng Wang, Jindou Jia, Sicheng Zhou, Zeshuai Chen, Kexin Guo, Xiang Yu, Lei Guo
bullets: Addresses target motion, localization drift, aerial–manipulator coupling, and external disturbances in dynamic aerial grasping.

Coordinates aerial-platform motion and manipulator dexterity through a cooperative motion planner.
Employs disturbance-rejection control to compensate for coupling, model uncertainty, and external disturbances.
Validated indoors and outdoors, grasping a 1.5 cm-diameter marker pen at speeds above 1.5 m/s.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of CAPTURER workflow. Body: CAPTURER integrates onboard perception, cooperative motion planning, and anti-disturbance control within a unified framework. Perception: The perception module combines visual–inertial state estimation, target detection, drift correction, global pose transformation, motion prediction, and active target search to provide consistent robot and target states. Planning: Based on the relative target state, the cooperative planner generates coordinated motion references for the aerial platform and manipulator while accounting for the predicted platform attitude and their different motion characteristics. Control: The dynamic controller reconstructs and compensates the strong coupling effects induced by manipulator motion and employs residual observers to handle model uncertainty and external disturbances. The resulting framework supports indoor and outdoor grasping of stationary and moving targets using onboard sensing and online replanning. More details, including CAD models and source code, are available on the Project Site.

papers.abstract: Learning from offline datasets is limited in scalability, as collecting new experience is often costly or unsafe in the real world. World models offer an alternative way to generate new experience through a learned dynamics model, yet learning policies in latent space is limited due to compounding errors in imagined rollouts. To this end, we propose using the world model as a local transition generator, leveraging critic guidance to choose actions inside that model to generate synthetic experiences. We study action refinement methodologies, introducing Critic-Guided Synthetic Experience (CGSE) generation in world models. Specifically, CGSE augments an existing offline dataset by sampling candidate actions using an offline policy and refining each to maximize a first-order approximation of the $Q$-function within a trust region. We then use a frozen latent world model to imagine the future state given each updated action, and use the critic to choose the best one, appending this synthetic transition to the replay buffer. Our method requires no additional real-environment interaction or test-time planner, as it generates synthetic experience offline using the world model. On three OGBench manipulation tasks, CGSE improves an offline policy by a relative improvement of $7.1\%$ on the average success rate.
authors: Jorge de Freitas, Christos Ziakas, Alessandra Russo
bullets: Addresses limited scalability and safety of collecting new offline experience, while reducing errors from long imagined rollouts.
Refines candidate actions from an offline policy to maximize a first-order Q-function approximation within a trust region.
Uses a frozen latent world model to predict each updated action’s transition and a critic to select the best synthetic experience.
Augments the replay buffer offline, requiring neither further environment interaction nor a test-time planner.
Improves average success rate by 7.1% relatively across three OGBench manipulation tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: CGSE transition generation in world model. Starting from an offline latent z0, the fixed BC-flow actor samples N candidate first actions and FMQ-style guidance applies a one-step trustregion critic-gradient refinement to each candidate. The refined candidates are rolled out under fψ, scored with Qϕ, and the best branch supplies only its first action a∗ and first model successor z′ψ = fψ(z0, a ∗). The resulting synthetic transition (z0, a ∗, z′ψ) is appended to the replay buffer.

papers.abstract: Collecting naturalistic human manipulation demonstrations with accurate contact force and hand pose is essential for robot dexterous manipulation policy and foundational world model learning - yet no existing wearable platform provides both calibrated fingertip force sensing and occlusion-resilient hand tracking in a form factor that preserves natural manipulation behavior. We present Tactus, a textile-integrated sensing glove that co-optimizes three design pillars: (1) a thin, conformal 3D-knit form factor (1.5 mm fingertip stackup) designed to minimize interference with natural manipulation, (2) strategically placed capacitive tactile sensors at manipulation-relevant regions informed by empirical contact studies, and (3) IMU-fused pose tracking that maintains accuracy through the hand-object occlusions where manipulation data is most valuable. Tactus includes a documented calibration pipeline for cross-glove consistency and per-session calibration for subject-dependent correction. To enable objective comparison, we introduce standardized benchmarking protocols for tactile force regression and hand pose estimation, and apply them to Tactus and two commercially available tactile gloves - to our knowledge the first quantitative cross-platform evaluation of this kind. Tactus resolves a minimum detectable force of 0.59 N at 95% confidence, 1.6 - 2.7x lower than the commercial baselines, and with 0.87 cross-participant consistency, while our pose tracking sustains 11.0 mm fingertip keypoint relative error during manipulation, when occlusion is heaviest. We show that these combined signals support object property estimation, slip detection, and representative recording of hand-object interaction - yielding demonstration data with the fidelity required for contact-aware manipulation policies and world models.

papers.abstract: Test-time compute mechanisms, such as retries, confidence-based escalation and non-local routing, are conventionally deployed as black-box additions to trained models. They typically add forward passes or halting heads, but give no structural account of what the extra compute buys or what it costs against the model's stability guarantees. We therefore propose a theoretical and empirical framework for test-time compute on a Latent Dynamics Model used as the memory. When an encoder's latent state $(q,p)$ is advanced by a damped symplectic (velocity-Verlet) step of a learned Hamiltonian, every mechanism that expands access has an exact phase-volume Jacobian, a bounded energy change and an exact latch-transport law. We split reachability failures into escape failures and reach failures. A Lorentz squeeze resolves escape failures by injecting bounded, re-absorbable energy. A gated canonical translation (a one-step channel across $C_T$) resolves reach failures at $\detJ=1$ exactly. We verify this certificate stack on a designed analytic testbed. Reaching just beyond $C_T$ with the squeeze requires energy that grows quadratically in the excess distance. The gated channel's energy cost equals the potential difference between its endpoints, which is zero on the matched channel measured here, and so does not grow with distance in this testbed. An untrained state-replacing map annihilates phase volume and erases stored charge, while the gated channel transports it. On a learned physics-structured memory, we show calibrated compute rationing and evaluate the scaling limits of non-local routing against a physics-free baseline. The main contribution is the formalization and verification of the certificate stack, not benchmark performance.
authors: Pratik Jawahar, Riccardo Maggioni, Jonas Petersen, Matteo Cozzi, Gian-Alessandro Lombardi, Marek Gajewski, Camilla Mazzoleni, Federico Martelli
bullets: Identifies two access failures: escape failures and reach failures.
Uses a Lorentz squeeze for bounded, re-absorbable energy injection in escape failures.
Uses a gated canonical translation that preserves phase volume exactly for reach failures.
Analytic tests show squeeze cost grows quadratically beyond the access boundary, while matched-channel translation has zero measured potential cost.
Demonstrates compute rationing and non-local routing limits on learned physics-structured memory; benchmark superiority is not the focus.

papers.selection_reason: Formalizes a theoretical framework for test-time compute on Latent Dynamics Models (physics-structured memory), providing certificates for stability and energy bounds. This bridges test-time learning and latent action models.
papers.title: Certified Access: Test-Time Compute on Conservative Physics-Structured AI Memory
papers.tldr: A physics-structured memory framework certifies test-time compute by controlling reachability, energy, phase volume, and stored-state transport.

papers.abstract: PhysicsNeMo-Mesh is the mesh module of the open-source PhysicsNeMo library. It provides mesh processing similar to PyVista, but on the GPU, in batches, and inside PyTorch's automatic differentiation. Like xarray for unstructured meshes, it attaches semantics to data: fields on points, cells, and whole meshes have names and shapes, and a simulation case keeps the complete PDE problem specification, including boundary conditions and their prescribed values. It addresses three problems that plague machine learning for physical simulation. First, GPU utilization is bottlenecked by I/O, because samples are very large relative to the compute per forward pass. Second, because traditional preprocessing is expensive, it is necessarily done once, during curation, rather than differently for each model and workflow at the point of use. Finally, advanced equivariant and mesh-native architectures require information that curation ordinarily discards. Fast GPU mesh processing makes it practical to preprocess at the point of use: on one GB200 GPU, mesh operations run $6.2\text{--}1{,}068\times$ faster than VTK with 72 threads, and loading a whole case is $8.0\text{--}88\times$ faster than reading its VTK files ($8.0\times$ when both read the same fields). Overlapped with training, this preprocessing costs $2.1\%$ of throughput for a $127\,\text{ms}$ Transolver step. So one dataset serves many models and workflows: in PhysicsNeMo's public recipe, one stored DrivAerML dataset feeds Transolver, GeoTransolver, and GLOBE. PhysicsNeMo-Mesh combines the speed of an intermediate array store with the flexibility of an archival format such as VTK. When shapes and wall conditions both vary, per-boundary conditions cut a heat-conduction error from $87\%$ to $6\text{--}9\%$. And by keeping field ranks and named boundaries, it retains the semantic structure that next-generation architectures will need.
authors: Peter D. Sharpe, Corey Adams, Negin Sobhani, Sanjay Choudhry
bullets: Processes batched meshes on GPUs within PyTorch autograd, with semantic fields on points, cells, and whole meshes.
Stores complete PDE specifications, including boundary conditions and prescribed values, while preserving field ranks and named boundaries.
Enables preprocessing at model-use time, reducing dependence on costly, one-time dataset curation and supporting multiple workflows from one dataset.
On a GB200, mesh operations are 6.2–1,068× faster than 72-thread VTK, and complete-case loading is 8.0–88× faster than reading VTK files.
Per-boundary conditions reduced heat-conduction error from 87% to 6–9% when shapes and wall conditions varied.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces PhysicsNeMo-Mesh, a GPU-native library for mesh processing and physics simulation. The technical contribution of efficient, differentiable mesh handling is transferable to 3D vision and embodied AI simulation.
papers.title: PhysicsNeMo-Mesh: GPU-Native Meshes and Simulation Cases for Physics AI

papers.abstract: LLM read-and-evaluate tasks include study screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, and critical appraisal in the evidence synthesis field. These task differ in the amount of LLM interpretation they require. Some tasks involve retrieving relatively simple information, such as an author name, sample size, or publication year. Others require the LLM to read source material, interpret it against predefined criteria, and make a judgement. Researchers should assess whether LLM judgements are accurate, supported by appropriate source evidence, and reproducible under specified conditions. A correct judgement does not necessarily indicate that the underlying evaluation process is reliable. We developed a taxonomy for identifying mechanisms that may compromise these properties and for informing the selection and reporting of appropriate evaluation methods. The taxonomy outlines potential ways that LLM judgments from read-and-evaluate tasks can fail, called TRAILS (Taxonomy of Reliability And Instability in LLM-assisted evidence Synthesis). The TRAILS taxonomy addresses two complementary questions. First, what mechanisms can cause the same read-and-evaluate task to produce different judgements across repeated LLM runs? Second, what mechanisms can systematically affect the judgement or required output in a way that is not apparent from the judgement itself? This study presents 38 mechanisms and identifies the deployment settings in which each can operate, approaches for testing them, and mitigation strategies. We also show why repeatability or accuracy does not rule out a hidden judgement failure and why human evaluation should assess whether a judgement is grounded in the supplied evidence, independent of inappropriate external influence, and produced through a process that can be examined and verified.

Distinguishes failures that cause different judgments across repeated runs from systematic influences hidden by the final judgment.

Argues that evaluation must assess evidence grounding, resistance to inappropriate external influence, and verifiability—not accuracy or repeatability alone.

papers.abstract: In transformer language models with gated multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), adjacent layers write partly against each other into the residual stream. Previous work interpreted this cancellation as layers proposing features and the next layer selectively rejecting the inappropriate ones. We decompose the cancellation by removing the previous layer's write from the input of the next MLP: what the next layer writes along that write splits into what it writes anyway and how much less its MLP writes because the write is present, which we call the damping, and we trace the damping to the neurons that carry it. In gated MLPs the damping is carried by neurons whose gates are closed. SiLU and GELU are slightly negative below zero, so a closed gate still passes a small negative multiple of what the neuron reads, and a neuron whose output weight points along its input weight then subtracts a fraction of the direction it read. Summed over such neurons, closed gates contract the average direction a gated MLP reads, and the previous layer's write is not singled out: the same layer's write at another token is damped as much or more, and the eigenvalue signature from which that work concluded that the correction is selective appears for another token's write as well. Over training the damping grows while what the next layer writes anyway stays flat, and cancellation begins when the damping overtakes it; annealing the negative side of the gate activation away in continued pretraining removes the damping and the cancellation. Adjacent-layer cancellation is therefore weak evidence about which features a model rejects: it is produced by a contraction that gated MLPs apply, on average over directions, to whatever they read.
authors: Harvey Dam, Ganesh Gopalakrishnan
bullets: Decomposes cancellation into the next layer’s baseline write and the reduction caused by the previous layer’s residual write.

Damping increases during training while baseline writing stays flat; cancellation begins once damping dominates.
Removing the gate activation’s negative side eliminates both damping and cancellation in continued pretraining.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement fine-tuning has become an effective post-training paradigm for improving the reasoning ability of large language models, but it remains sample-inefficient when the training distribution is mismatched to the model's current capability. In group-relative objectives such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), problems that are too hard often produce uniformly failed rollouts, while problems that are too easy provide little useful advantage signal. In this work, we introduce CLOSEDLOOPGAUSSIAN, a lightweight adaptive curriculum method for efficient reinforcement fine-tuning on ordered reasoning tasks. Instead of following a fixed easy-to-hard schedule, CLOSEDLOOPGAUSSIAN preserves the structure of an Easy-to-Hard Gaussian sampler while dynamically adjusting its pace and spread using periodic probe estimates of per-difficulty accuracy. The controller accelerates training when the model is ahead of a reference curriculum, slows down when the model falls behind, and broadens sampling when earlier difficulties regress. This feedback mechanism keeps training focused on tasks that are challenging but still learnable, without changing the reward function, model architecture, or underlying GRPO optimizer. Experiments on symbolic arithmetic reasoning task show that CLOSEDLOOPGAUSSIAN improves exact-match accuracy over vanilla GRPO and fixed open-loop curricula, with the strongest gains in intermediate-difficulty regimes where group-relative learning signals are most informative. Codes are available at https://github.com/yuvrajpant56/Closed_Loop_Curriculum.
authors: Yuv Raj Pant, Moshiur Rahman Tonmoy, Kaiqun Fu
bullets: Targets sample inefficiency caused by training on tasks that are too easy or too hard for GRPO.

Accelerates when learning outpaces a reference curriculum, slows when it lags, and broadens sampling after earlier-difficulty regressions.
On symbolic arithmetic reasoning, improves exact-match accuracy over vanilla GRPO and fixed open-loop curricula, especially at intermediate difficulty.
The evaluation is scoped to ordered reasoning tasks, with experiments reported on a symbolic arithmetic task.

papers.abstract: Controlling continuum robots' shape to operate in confined, enclosed environments is challenging, since it cannot rely on external observation. Existing embedded shape sensing methods, although they can provide shape reconstruction, are insufficient to enable real-time shape control due to limitations in reconstruction accuracy, computational speed, and compatibility with shape-state representation. In this work, we present an embedded shape-sensing framework that uses readily available IMU and actuator feedback to reconstruct the continuum-robot shape with a neural network, providing accurate shape feedback at $400~\mathrm{Hz}$ for physical closed-loop control. We systematically investigate four key reconstruction design choices: shape-state representation, network architecture, training objective, and sensing inputs, through more than $5{,}000$ trained models on one- and three-segment continuum robots. The selected framework achieves global shape errors of $0.9\%L$ and $1.7\%L$ (of the robot length) for the one- and three-segment systems, respectively. In closed-loop control, one-segment tip tracking achieves a $6.1\%L$ error and three-segment shape control achieves a $2.3\%L$ global shape error, whereas IMU--PCC reconstruction using the same uncompensated measurements fails. Enclosed-space experiments further demonstrate operation without external observation. These results provide a practical framework for translating readily available embedded sensing into high-rate feedback for continuum robot closed-loop control.
authors: Jiahe Wang, Sultan Haidar Ali, Eric Weissman, Jiefeng Sun
bullets: Addresses shape-control challenges when external observation is unavailable.

Demonstrates enclosed-space operation, while same-input IMU–PCC reconstruction fails in closed-loop control.

papers.abstract: Modern robot learning systems feed on high-quality demonstration data, and their performance hinges on coverage. Without good coverage, small errors compound and the policy can quickly go into out-of-distribution states from which it cannot recover. Yet there is no principled way of collecting high-coverage data, and data collection often relies on heuristic instructions to human operators. Purely online reinforcement learning (RL) explores at the cost of safety and sample efficiency, while DAgger-style interventions require the policy to fail by chance before a human can correct it. In this paper, we ask instead whether we can modify how the robot behaves during data collection to collect more useful data. We propose Data Inoculation (DI), a shared-control framework in which a human provide closed-loop teleoperation commands while a residual policy perturbs these commands. The residual policy is trained online, on the growing dataset, with the same reward-maximizing objective later used for policy extraction, so its perturbations steer data collection toward the deviations a policy trained on the data would make. These perturbations expose the robot to a wider range of states, while the human's continuous corrections provide recovery demonstrations, "inoculating" the dataset against the learner's future mistakes while the human remains in control. On three challenging real-world robotic tasks, DI consistently improves or matches the success rate of policies trained with both behavioral cloning and offline RL, showing DI as an effective data collection strategy for improving downstream policy performance.
authors: Qiyang Li, Zhiyuan Zhou, Charles Xu, Sergey Levine
bullets: Addresses poor state coverage and compounding errors in demonstration-based robot learning.
Uses shared control: a human teleoperates while an online-trained residual policy perturbs commands toward likely future mistakes.
Continuous human corrections provide recovery demonstrations while perturbations expand the collected state distribution.
Across three real-world tasks, policies trained with behavioral cloning and offline RL consistently improved or matched performance using DI-collected data.

papers.abstract: We ask when an AI trained on historical decisions should be allowed to recommend decisions, defer to human experts, or in other cases, flag concerning patterns in data and deviate from past practice. This can be challenging because past decisions record what was done rather than what should have been done, and where data is sparse, a model's predictions may be too uncertain to act on. We provide a framework for addressing this problem using a case study in deceased-donor kidney allocation. Nearly 30% of kidneys recovered from deceased donors in the United States are never transplanted, largely because they are hard to place through the standard waitlist sequence. One can use AI to flag kidneys at risk of delayed or failed placement for out-of-sequence (OOS) allocation, but this comes at the cost of bypassing candidates higher on the waitlist. Thus, OOS allocation should only be used when the organ is demonstrably at high risk of discard on the standard sequence. Using Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network match-run data from 2016-2019 and 2023-2025 (excluding COVID-19-disrupted years), we build the Arbitrator framework, which combines various interpretable models and acts only when the uncertainty in their predictions cannot change the preferred action. Our Arbitrator resolves 93.5% of organ placement decisions using explicit medical criteria learned from data, and defers the remaining 6.5% to a human or a more complex model. We show that the Arbitrator correctly identifies 70.1% of historically discarded low-KDPI kidneys as OOS candidates, projecting that up to 43.9% of historically discarded kidneys could be flagged for expedited placement and potentially transplanted. We then exploit the interpretability of the Arbitrator to create an agentic audit comparing the learned rules to published clinical literature in order to flag decision-making patterns that are contentious.
authors: Madeleine Pollack, Thomas Daillak, Mehmet Toner, Korkut Uygun, Heidi Yeh, Swati Gupta
bullets: Historical allocation decisions reflect what happened, not necessarily what should have happened, and sparse data can make predictions unreliable.

papers.tldr: The Arbitrator framework uses interpretable, uncertainty-aware AI to recommend, defer, or audit deceased-donor kidney allocation decisions, potentially reducing discard while limiting unjustified waitlist bypasses.

papers.abstract: Catching arbitrary objects requires generalization to novel projectiles and real-time adaptation to unpredictable contact dynamics under noisy visual observations. This paper presents Catch It All!, a sim-to-real catching framework for humanoid robots that generalizes and adapts to unseen objects with variable physical properties for underhand and overhand catches, using only one egocentric camera. We learn policies which generalize to unseen objects with varying geometry, deformability, elasticity, and physical properties. Effective grasps which adapt real-time to object poses and shapes are learned through careful grasp reward design. We provide safety-aware curricula which enable safe, high-frequency action execution near hardware limits, including wrist torque limits as low as 5 Nm. We validate our system by deploying zero-shot on a Unitree G1. With only one egocentric camera, Catch It All! successfully performs underhand and overhand catches on 9 unseen objects not seen during training, including low-rebound plushes, semi-deformable toys and chip bags, and rigid-elastic objects with high rebound on contact.
authors: Arth Shukla, Kehlani Fay, Huaze Liu, Darin Djapri, Alexiy Buynitsky, Nicklas Hansen

papers.abstract: In variable-step operator learning, agreement at observed step sizes does not by itself determine predictions at other temporal resolutions. We propose an operator whose step-size dependence is prescribed by a first-order Duhamel approximation of semilinear dynamics. It combines exact linear propagation with a local nonlinear function of the field and its derivatives, allowing evaluation below the observation interval without supervision densely sampled across step sizes. Under suitable conditions and at fixed spatial resolution, we prove that agreement between models at two step sizes controls their prediction differences throughout a prescribed range. We also give conditions for local identifiability of both components from two step sizes, supporting interpretation of the learned structure. A latent extension applies the same construction to learned fields. We evaluate the base model on two synthetic problems and the extension on two real datasets against several baselines.
authors: Jingye Li, Jinglai Li
bullets: Targets the ambiguity of predicting at unseen step sizes when models only agree at observed resolutions.
Uses a first-order Duhamel approximation: exact linear propagation plus a local nonlinear function of the field and its derivatives.
Proves that agreement at two step sizes bounds prediction differences across a prescribed range at fixed spatial resolution.
Provides conditions for locally identifying the linear and nonlinear components from two step sizes.
Evaluates the base and latent variants on synthetic and real datasets against several baselines.

papers.abstract: Recent generation methods produce 3D assets with detailed geometry and rich textures. However, these assets are non-emissive: they reflect light but emit none. We study a new task, emission generation: predicting spatially varying RGB emission over a 3D asset's surface from its geometry, non-emissive materials, and a rendered view. To support this task, we introduce LightGenBench. Our benchmark makes three contributions. First, we curate a dataset of 37k artist-authored emissive assets in UV, voxel, and multi-view form. Second, we establish baselines across four method families: UV-domain, sparse-voxel, multi-view, and segmentation-based generation. Third, we design an evaluation protocol that measures where an asset emits and how, complemented by user-study comparisons on renderings with varying emission strength. Across the four families, the sparse-voxel baseline TRELLIS.2-Emission performs best because generating emission natively in 3D avoids the failure modes of the other representations, such as the fracturing artifacts of UV space and the occluded emitters that multi-view generation cannot see. However, TRELLIS.2-Emission only reaches an IoU of 0.271, leaving the task far from solved. We hope LightGenBench establishes emission generation as a benchmarkable problem for 3D generation.
authors: Dongchen Yang, Xingguang Yan, Manolis Savva
bullets: Targets emission generation from geometry, non-emissive materials, and a rendered view.
Provides 37k artist-authored emissive assets in UV, voxel, and multi-view formats.
Benchmarks four method families: UV-domain, sparse-voxel, multi-view, and segmentation-based methods.
Uses spatial emission evaluation plus user studies across varying emission strengths.
TRELLIS.2-Emission performs best at IoU 0.271, while exposing representation-specific failures such as UV fracturing and unseen occluded emitters.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Overview of the four emission-generation methods in our benchmark. Each method takes the non-emissive materials M, the geometry g, and a rendered image I , and generates the emission Le in its own representation: an emission map on the input UV atlas (top), per-voxel emission on the o-voxel grid (middle), or multi-view emission images that are back-projected onto the mesh (bottom). TRELLIS.2-Emission and SegviGen-Emission share the same pipeline and differ in the target: continuous emission e, or a mask M that is thresholded and multiplied by the albedo (M ⊙ a); their initialization and decoders are detailed in Secs. 4.3 and 4.5.

Figure 3. Overview of our data filtering pipeline. (1) Metadata filtering (1st row) keeps assets with an emissive texture or a nonzero emission factor (left) and drops the rest (right). (2) Heuristic filtering (2nd row) removes any asset whose emission map is entirely black (left) or identical to its albedo map (middle), or that duplicates another asset (right). (3) VLM filtering (3rd row) rejects non-emissive assets and assets with other defects, e.g., the multi-object asset is rejected. It agrees with human annotations on 87% of 404 held-out shapes.

Figure 6. Qualitative comparison of the baselines. Each object is rendered in a dark room and lit only by its predicted emission; the leftmost column is the input image, and GT is rendered with ground truth emission. TRELLIS.2-Emission stays closest to the ground truth on all three assets, but still mislocates emissive surfaces or assigns inaccurate color (the ring’s emissive region is misplaced and it should glow yellow). The other baselines show their characteristic failures: TEXGen-Emission scatters emission across UV islands (spilled color on the helmet) and fails to keep non-emissive regions at exact zero (speckles on the helmet, faint glowing noise over the ring); Hunyuan3DEmission shifts the emission color (the red beam turns white) and lights up regions that should stay dark (the saber handle and the ring band); and SegviGen-Emission over-extends or misses emissive regions (the ring’s whole band glows, while the helmet’s stripes stay unlit).

Figure 2. Samples from our curated dataset. Each pair shows an object under standard lighting (top) and the same object rendered in a dark room, lit only by its own emission (bottom). Apart from illuminating the object’s surroundings (the lamps, the lit house), emission also decorates (the glowing cracks, the blade, the tree’s lights) and informs (the screen’s content).

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark and baselines for 3D emission generation, directly fitting 3D scene/asset generation.
papers.title: LightGenBench: A Benchmark for 3D Emission Generation
papers.tldr: LightGenBench introduces a benchmark for generating spatially varying RGB emission on 3D assets, showing that the task remains challenging despite the strongest baseline’s advantages.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is increasingly adopted in the post-training of large language models. However, a stronger teacher may fail to improve the student. Prior work attributes this to a lack of new knowledge, but what that knowledge is remains unclear. We show that OPD learns not only \textit{how to branch}, i.e., which candidate tokens to consider, but also \textit{where to branch}, i.e., where to keep reasoning paths open. The existing token-overlap metric captures only the former. We introduce the entropy shape, the sequence of next-token entropies, to characterize the latter, and propose the Entropy Shape Correlation (ESC) to measure student-teacher agreement in entropy shape. Tracking ESC throughout training and intervening on a teacher's entropy while preserving its token preferences, we empirically show that \textit{where to branch} causally drives OPD gains, independently of \textit{how to branch}. Finally, we formulate OPD outcome prediction as a teacher selection task and establish an evaluation protocol for it, under which pre-OPD ESC selects the best teacher for both students and outperforms existing predictors. Code is available at https://github.com/maybenotime/opd-esc.
authors: Shiping Yang, Chuanqi Tang, Hossein Hajimirsadeghi, Layla El Asri, Mohammad Amin Shabani, Angel X. Chang
bullets: Identifies two kinds of teacher knowledge: “how to branch” through token preferences and “where to branch” through locations of sustained uncertainty.
Introduces entropy shape—the sequence of next-token entropies—and Entropy Shape Correlation (ESC) to measure student–teacher agreement on branching locations.
Training analyses and entropy interventions suggest that where to branch causally drives OPD gains independently of token preferences.
Frames teacher selection as an OPD outcome-prediction task and proposes an evaluation protocol.
Pre-OPD ESC selects the best teacher for both students and outperforms existing predictors in the reported experiments.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Training dynamics of counterfactual teachers. Each row tracks one of the counterfactual runs of Figure 3. Right: six-benchmark average accuracy at saved checkpoints, with dashed lines marking the two source models. (b) Qwen3-1.7B distilled from q̃A←B , with preferences from Qwen3-4B-RL-Math and shape from Qwen3-4B. Where and how to branch can thus be learned either jointly or independently.

Shaded positions mark mismatches, where the teacher tends to branch (high entropy) while the student does not (low entropy). Right: how to branch.
