papers.selection_reason: Analyzes on-policy distillation for LLM post-training and introduces entropy-shape agreement as a causal metric, relevant to LLM training.
papers.title: Distilling the Shape of Uncertainty: What On-Policy Distillation Learns and How to Predict It
papers.tldr: On-policy distillation benefits from matching not just which tokens a teacher prefers, but where it preserves uncertainty for continued reasoning, and entropy-shape agreement can predict effective teachers.

papers.abstract: Compositional generalization remains a persistent limitation of transformer language models: even when a model learns to combine known facts correctly in-distribution (ID), the same compositional mechanism may fail when applied to out-of-distribution (OOD) knowledge. We investigate this compositionality gap in a controlled two-hop reasoning setting using a GPT-2-like transformer model trained from scratch. Building on prior work identifying a circuit associated with compositional generalization, we test whether the failure of OOD transfer is related to how atomic knowledge is structurally exposed during training. We modify the training distribution by presenting both ID and OOD atomic facts in a format positionally aligned with the second-hop retrieval step of the learned compositional circuit, without modifying the model architecture or adding OOD compositional supervision. Under this intervention, the model successfully transfers the learned ID compositional behaviour to held-out OOD atomic facts, closing the observed compositionality gap in the controlled setting. Our results provide evidence that the observed compositionality gap is not a fundamental architecture limitation and that it can be overcome through mechanistically informed training distribution design.
authors: Davide Venuto, Leonardo Venuto
bullets: Studies the compositionality gap in controlled two-hop reasoning.
Tests a GPT-2-like transformer trained from scratch without architectural changes or OOD compositional supervision.
Reformats ID and OOD atomic facts to align with the second-hop retrieval step of a learned circuit.
The intervention closes the observed OOD transfer gap in the controlled setting.
Suggests the gap may stem from training-distribution design rather than a fundamental architecture limitation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Generalization Performance Across Ablation Experiments. Comparison of ID and OOD test accuracy on the two-hop compositional task across three controlled ablations. (a) Removing ID atomic facts from the second-hop-compatible format prevents OOD compositional rule transfer. (b) Restricting the second-hop-compatible format to only a subset of OOD atomic facts results in partial OOD compositional generalization. (c) Removing two-hop compositional training examples prevents the model from learning the compositional task for both ID and OOD atomic facts.

Figure 4: Impact of Dataset Size-Density on OOD Compositional Generalization. (a) When trained on the full but less dense dataset, the model demonstrates delayed convergence in both training and testing metrics. As a result, the generalization effect driven by grokking does not achieve full accuracy within the performed training steps. (b) In contrast, training on a smaller but denser dataset leads to significantly improved generalization speed. The model reaches full accuracy on the OOD test set within the given optimization steps, highlighting the benefits of dataset density in accelerating generalization.

Figure 5: Ablation Analysis Results on the Full-Model for the experiments described in section 3.3. (a): ablation experiment (a) where no in-distribution (ID) atomic facts are provided in the new 2°hop format. Under this condition, the Full Model similarly fails to generalize to OOD examples, resembling the behaviour previously observed in the Smaller Model under the same setting. (b): ablation experiment (b) where out-of-distribution (OOD) facts are partially placed in the second-hop position. In the Full Model experiment, this partial OOD placement appears to completely hinder OOD generalization. This contrasts with the behaviour observed in the Smaller Model, where the same setting resulted in only a partial reduction in final accuracy (fig. 2b).

Figure 1: OOD Compositional Generalization under the Full Position-Aligned Intervention. ID and OOD test accuracy on the two-hop compositional task where both ID and OOD atomic facts are additionally presented in the second-hop-compatible format during training. OOD accuracy rises with delayed generalization in the grokking training regime, eventually reaching complete compositional generalization and closing the compositionality gap in the controlled experimental setting. The dashed gray curve shows OOD test accuracy under the original training distribution, without position-aligned atomic exposure, which remains near zero.

Figure 3: Identity-Bridge Control without Compositional Supervision. Accuracy under identity-bridge supervision after removing all two-hop compositional training examples. While training accuracy remains near perfect, both ID and OOD compositional test accuracy remain at zero, showing that identity-bridge supervision alone does not induce compositional generalization in our setting.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses compositional generalization and implicit reasoning in transformer language models, relevant to LLM reasoning research.
papers.title: Implicit Reasoning in Transformers: Bridging the Compositionality Gap in GPT-2-like Models
papers.tldr: Mechanistically aligning how atomic facts are presented during training enables GPT-2-like transformers to transfer two-hop reasoning from in-distribution to unseen out-of-distribution facts.

papers.abstract: Radio-frequency (RF) sensing enables robot ego-motion estimation in darkness, smoke, and fog, yet RF odometry remains challenging because multipath and moving reflectors make cross-frame matching highly ambiguous. Existing methods often rely on auxiliary inertial sensors or ground-truth pose supervision. We present RFWalk, a self-supervised, RF-only odometry framework that models dense correspondences across range-azimuth frames as random walks on a space-time graph and learns them from unlabeled sequences through temporal cycle consistency. To rule out correspondences that are cycle-consistent but physically implausible, we introduce a Doppler consistency loss that constrains correspondence-induced motion using radial velocity measured by the RF sensor itself. Ego-motion is then recovered through robust $\mathrm{SE}(2)$ registration that suppresses uncertain correspondences and those arising from independently moving objects. Without pose labels or auxiliary sensors, RFWalk remains competitive with supervised baselines in static scenes and reduces absolute trajectory error by 58% in dynamic scenes with moving pedestrians.
authors: Kunzhe Song, Jialuo Du, Jingkai Lin, Huacheng Zeng
bullets: Addresses ambiguous RF frame matching caused by multipath and moving reflectors.
Models dense range-azimuth correspondences as random walks on a space-time graph.
Uses temporal cycle consistency and a Doppler consistency loss without pose labels or auxiliary sensors.
Recovers ego-motion via robust SE(2) registration that downweights unreliable and independently moving-object correspondences.
Remains competitive with supervised baselines in static scenes and reduces absolute trajectory error by 58% in dynamic pedestrian scenes.

Figure 7: Effect of palindrome walk length K across speeds (m/s) and frame rates (Hz), measured by ATE Pos (m).

papers.abstract: Sparse-view computed tomography (CT) reduces the number of acquired projections, but conventional sampling strategies are designed primarily for image reconstruction rather than for downstream physical inference. Here, we investigate optimal task-aware projection selection for directly predicting hemodynamics from sparse CT angiography (CTA) measurements. Using computational fluid dynamics simulations of intracranial aneurysms, we generate synthetic fan-beam CTA projections and train a Fourier neural operator (FNO) to predict two targets: the spatially resolved time-averaged wall shear stress (TAWSS) field and the spatially averaged TAWSS. The FNO was coupled with optimal input selection for simultaneous optimal sampling and training. Our goal was to investigate if agentic AI could discover optimal sampling strategies that outperform current methods. We compared fixed uniform and golden-angle sampling with three task-aware optimal selection strategies: Gumbel-Softmax, a Soft top-K method, and an agentic AI selector. The methods were compared at different view selection budgets. A detailed analysis of the AI agent was performed to understand its reasoning and performance. For spatially resolved TAWSS, Agentic and Soft top-K achieve the lowest mean errors (Agentic performs slightly better) and substantially outperform fixed sampling under extreme sparsity. For spatially averaged TAWSS, optimized selection becomes important at extremely sparse acquisitions. Analysis of the selected masks reveals multiple distinct subsets concentrated around informative regions. Moreover, masks optimized for hemodynamic prediction yield poor image reconstructions, showing that task-optimal acquisition differs fundamentally from reconstruction-optimal acquisition. This work suggests the possibility of designing sparse acquisitions directly around downstream physical quantities.
authors: Mahmoud Elhadidy, Roshan M. D'Souza, Amirhossein Arzani
bullets: The study targets prediction of spatially resolved and spatially averaged time-averaged wall shear stress (TAWSS) from sparse-view CT angiography.
Synthetic intracranial aneurysm projections were generated from computational fluid dynamics simulations and processed with a Fourier neural operator.
Sampling and prediction were jointly optimized using Gumbel-Softmax, Soft top-K, and an agentic AI selector, alongside uniform and golden-angle baselines.
For spatially resolved TAWSS, Agentic and Soft top-K achieved the lowest mean errors, with Agentic slightly better and notably stronger than fixed sampling under extreme sparsity.
Task-optimized projection masks focused on informative regions and differed fundamentally from masks optimized for image reconstruction.

papers.selection_reason: Uses an agentic AI selector for task-aware projection selection in CT imaging, relevant to 3D perception and efficient sampling.
papers.title: Agentic AI Reasoning and Learned Sampling for Task-Aware Projection Selection in Sparse-View CT: Predicting Hemodynamics
papers.tldr: Agentic, task-aware projection selection can improve hemodynamic prediction from extremely sparse CTA acquisitions, even though its sampling patterns are poor for image reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Anticipating the motion of nearby objects is critical for safe and efficient robot navigation. Without a proper understanding of what may move, a robot may plan overly conservative, inefficient trajectories to guarantee safety, or it may be overly risky, resulting in unacceptable collisions. While tracking and predicting the motion of known objects has seen significant progress, little research addresses how a robot should adapt online to novel objects, including anticipating how one object may move another (e.g., a person operating a forklift to move a pallet). To enable this capability, we propose a meta-learned graph neural network that leverages a semantic, geometric, and relational history of objects to accurately predict, from a few online observations, when objects will begin to move in new environments. We demonstrate that our method, which is trained only in simulation, accurately anticipates the motion of objects unseen at training time, transfers to hardware without any fine-tuning, and outperforms a vision-language model and a class-frequency baseline in both simulation and hardware experiments. Our method's accurate prediction enables collision-free traversals in a closed-loop navigation simulation, while remaining within four seconds of the fastest, collision-prone planner.
authors: Mason Peterson, Gage MacLin, Camilla Tabasso, Jonathan P. How, Joshua Migdal, Tye Brady, Taskin Padir
bullets: Targets open-world motion anticipation, including one object causing another to move.
Uses semantic, geometric, and relational object histories in a graph neural network with meta-learning.
Trained only in simulation, it transfers to hardware and handles objects unseen during training without fine-tuning.
Outperforms a vision-language model and class-frequency baseline in simulation and hardware experiments.
Supports collision-free closed-loop navigation while staying within four seconds of the fastest collision-prone planner.

papers.abstract: In procedural videogame level design, many existing techniques combine hand-authored level chunks. Some existing analysis techniques also rely on a higher-level graph structure which abstracts the level design. In this paper, we explore techniques for computing both of these things automatically from an existing design. We introduce the concept of perceptual distance, based on analysis techniques from the architecture subfield of Space Syntax. We use this perceptual distance to segment level designs with hierarchical clustering. We compare with past work on StarCraft analysis, show results on rooms from Super Metroid, and also demonstrate a proof-of-concept level generation algorithm based on this segmentation method.
authors: Ross Mawhorter, Matthew Guzdial
bullets: Addresses automatic extraction of reusable level chunks and higher-level graph structures from existing videogame levels.
Defines perceptual distance to measure relationships within level layouts.
Applies hierarchical clustering to segment levels into structural regions.
Compares the approach with prior StarCraft analysis and evaluates it on Super Metroid rooms.
Demonstrates proof-of-concept level generation using the resulting segments.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The pipeline for computing the Perceptual Distance Segmentation shown on “Bubble Mountain” from Super Metroid. We begin by computing the probability of observing (angular area of) each visible surface (orange) from each point. The figure shows an example for a single point. Second, we use the Jensen-Shannon divergence of these probabilities to compute an approximate rate of change at each interior point (perceptual flux). We then find the minima of this field, and cluster the minima hierarchically based on the perceptual distance. Finally, the non-minima points are assigned to the cluster that they are closest to (in terms of perceptual distance).

Figure 11: A long hallway segmented with two different methods. In IJI, clusters below size 6 are also merged and the threshold value of 0.4 is chosen manually by the authors for best results. For PDS, the threshold value of 0.59 is the same as our other domains. papers.title: Syntactic Segmentation and Collage Generation for Videogame Levels with Perceptual Distance

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates autoregressive inference by leveraging the memory bound nature of decoding, verifying multiple draft tokens in a single forward pass. For mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, prior work predicts a concave speedup-batch size relationship, with gains peaking at intermediate batch sizes due to expert saturation. We evaluate this across 10 sparse MoE models (30B--1T parameters, 8--512 experts) and find recent fine-grained models break this trend, showing higher speedup at low batch size. We find verification cost is governed not only by activated-expert bytes, but also by temporal overlap across draft tokens and GPU execution dynamics. At low batch size, MoE layers in fine-grained models account for a much smaller share of runtime than of weights; on H100, kernel profiling attributes this mainly to higher bandwidth utilization of MoE kernels relative to attention, with L2 absorbing repeated reads of co-routed experts. Across draft tokens, routing overlap further reduces the unique experts activated during verification relative to independence assumptions. We model this effect using a maximum-entropy Iterative Proportional Fitting (IPF) framework that predicts unique expert counts from routing-overlap statistics with less than 4\% error, and substantially narrows the gap to real-model curves and captures the qualitative low-batch trend from synthetic routing.
authors: Ekagra Ranjan, Komal K. Teru, Bharat Venkitesh, Acyr Locatelli
bullets: Across 10 sparse MoE models spanning 30B–1T parameters and 8–512 experts, fine-grained models show greater speedup at low batch sizes rather than the expected intermediate-batch peak.
Verification cost depends on temporal overlap across draft tokens and GPU execution dynamics, not just activated-expert bytes.
At low batch sizes, MoE layers consume less runtime than their weight share; on H100, higher MoE-kernel bandwidth utilization and L2 reuse of co-routed experts help explain this.
Routing overlap across draft tokens reduces the number of unique experts activated during verification compared with independence assumptions.
An entropy-maximizing IPF model predicts unique expert counts with under 4% error and captures the qualitative low-batch trend in synthetic routing.

papers.selection_reason: Analysis and modeling of speculative decoding speedups on sparse MoE models, directly relevant to efficient inference.
papers.title: Why Speculative Decoding Works Better Than Predicted on Sparse MoE Models
papers.tldr: Speculative decoding can outperform predictions on fine-grained sparse MoE models because GPU execution, caching, and routing overlap make verification cheaper than expert-count estimates suggest.

papers.abstract: World models let observers explore and interact with generated worlds. Recent work shows that when observers revisit a region, current models often fail to regenerate it consistently. We view this as a context retrieval problem. LLM agents manage context retrieval at two layers of their stack. At the model layer, the KV cache design determines how much context fits in memory. At the agent harness layer, harnesses such as Claude Code pick the context sent to the LLM. Prior work on world models has mostly focused only on the model layer. In this paper, we make three contributions. First, we build a benchmark to measure world model context retrieval. It generates new worlds for every episode, preventing a model from recalling rooms using training data. It also separates context retrieval from guesses based on nearby frames. Second, we build an agent harness that performs context compaction for world models, which to our knowledge no prior work has studied. Third, we use our benchmark to study four world model designs. Context compaction lets our world models retrieve rooms up to 4 times beyond their context window without retraining. However, world models with sliding-window attention lose most of their context retrieval when dreaming. Therefore, a dreaming world agent benefits more from extending the reach of its world model using context compaction than switching to sliding window attention at the model layer.
authors: Hayder Tirmazi
bullets: Frames inconsistent regeneration of revisited regions as a context-retrieval problem spanning model and agent-harness layers.
Introduces a benchmark with newly generated worlds that separates true context retrieval from memorization and nearby-frame cues.
Presents an agent harness for compacting context, an approach not previously studied for world models.
Shows context compaction enables retrieval of rooms up to 4× beyond the context window without retraining.
Finds dreaming agents benefit more from harness-level context compaction than from switching to sliding-window attention.

figures.caption: Figure 3. The architecture of the four world models we train and evaluate on. Each world model has 8 transformer blocks. We show the KV cache corresponding to a transformer block to the right of each respective block. From left to right, each architecture changes one property of the model incrementally. Switching from Decoder-only to CED, the upper blocks compute their keys and values from the output z of the last lower block. From CED to CED-SWA, the lower blocks switch to using SWA so they only attend over the 2 most recent steps. Finally, from CED-SWA to DD, the 4 upper KV caches become one shared KV cache that is read by all the upper blocks.

Figure 1. Left: Impact of model architecture on context retrieval for our video game room generation world model. Decoder-only needs 28.3 MB of KV cache memory for a context window of 128 steps. In the same memory, DD fits a context of 1,020 steps. Middle: Context retrieval gain of each world model when it dreams (with context compaction enabled). DD, which saves its memory with SWA, loses most of its context retrieval. Right: Agent harness layer can improve context retrieval on top of model layer changes. Decoder-only retrieves a room revisited after 262 steps. The visit from 262 steps ago is no longer in Decoder-only’s 128-step context window. The model therefore cannot reproduce the room. However, context compaction allows the original visit to still be sent to the model.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces context compaction for world models to address context retrieval failures, a key challenge for video world models.
papers.title: Context Compaction for World Models
papers.tldr: Context compaction helps world models consistently retrieve revisited regions beyond their native context window, while sliding-window attention performs poorly during dreaming.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding speeds up large language model (LLM) serving only while the GPU has spare compute, so the best draft length, the number of tokens a small drafter guesses per step, shrinks as the batch grows. vLLM lets operators set the draft length for each batch size with a hand-written table, but nothing measures or corrects that table. We present TableTune. Its tuner times the decoding step for every batch size and draft length on vLLM's own serving path and computes, in minutes, the table that maximizes throughput. Its controller, a vLLM plugin, tracks how many guesses are accepted in live traffic and rebuilds the table while serving. We measure TableTune only against other ways to speculate. On an H100, the tuned table delivers at least 94% of the throughput of the best fixed draft length at every load in four of five drafter settings (88% in the fifth) without the operator having to know which length that is. Against reimplementations of TurboSpec- and Nightjar-style control on the same engine, its worst-case loss is never higher than theirs, and with the EAGLE-3 drafter it is 3% against 9% and 12%. On a mixture-of-experts model, vLLM's documented table loses up to 18% and the tuned table at most 3%. Starting from mistuned tables, the controller raises throughput by up to 58% (up to 45% on vLLM's default runner), and after a workload switch with the DFlash drafter it recovers 96% of a stale table's loss. In llm-d's optimized-baseline deployment as shipped, two Qwen3-32B replicas on four GPUs, the tuned table is up to 32% faster than a fixed draft length of 3 and up to 25% faster than vLLM's documented table at high load, and the controller raises the documented table's throughput by up to 29%.
authors: Abhishek Malvankar, Paul Castro, Nick Mitchell, Lionel Villard
bullets: Problem: Hand-written draft-length tables in vLLM can become inefficient as load, models, or workloads change.
Method: Benchmark decoding time across batch sizes and draft lengths, then build a throughput-maximizing table; a serving plugin refreshes it using live token-acceptance data.
Contribution: An automated tuner and self-correcting controller integrated with vLLM.

Results: The tuned table reaches at least 94% of the best fixed-length throughput in four of five drafter settings and improves throughput by up to 32% over fixed or documented tables in deployment tests.
Scope: Evaluated on H100 and mixture-of-experts settings, including vLLM and llm-d deployments; performance depends on the drafter and serving workload.

papers.selection_reason: Dynamic speculative decoding draft-length tuning directly targets inference latency and throughput, fitting Efficient AI.
papers.title: TableTune: Measured, Self-Correcting Draft-Length Tables for Dynamic Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: TableTune automatically measures and continuously updates speculative-decoding draft lengths, maintaining near-best throughput across changing batch sizes and workloads.

papers.abstract: Reliable obstacle avoidance is essential for safe quadrotor flight in unknown environments, yet conventional frame-based cameras remain challenged by motion blur, limited dynamic range, and latency under fast motion. Event cameras, with sub-millisecond latency, high dynamic range, and negligible motion blur, offer a promising alternative, but leveraging them for closed-loop control remains difficult. Existing approaches either adopt cascaded architectures that first estimate depth and then map it to control commands, introducing error propagation, or achieve end-to-end control through costly offline pretraining before online fine-tuning can even begin. We address these challenges with a CUDA-based event simulator that exploits GPU parallelism to render events efficiently within the training loop, integrated into a differentiable simulation pipeline that enables direct gradient backpropagation through the differentiable physics model, improving sample efficiency. This allows us to train an end-to-end policy that maps event frames directly to control commands, without intermediate depth estimation. We validate our approach through zero-shot real-world deployment on a quadrotor, achieving robust obstacle avoidance in both odometry-assisted and odometry-free settings, including under low-light conditions where conventional cameras typically fail.
authors: Chenlu Shou, Yunfan Ren, Jiaxu Xing, Davide Scaramuzza
bullets: Addresses motion blur, limited dynamic range, and latency in frame-based obstacle avoidance for fast quadrotor flight.
Uses a CUDA-based event simulator integrated with differentiable physics to backpropagate through the training loop.
Learns an end-to-end policy mapping event frames directly to control commands, avoiding cascaded depth estimation.
Demonstrates zero-shot real-world deployment in odometry-assisted and odometry-free settings, including low light.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: System Framework Overview. The simulator renders a grayscale frame from each quadrotor state, and two consecutive frames are used to compute the event frame. The event frame is fed into a differentiable policy consisting of a CNN and a GRU, which predicts an action. The differentiable point-mass dynamics model then propagates the current state forward using this action. A loss is computed based on the resulting state and action, and the corresponding gradients are propagated backward through the entire differentiable pipeline to update the policy.

papers.selection_reason: End-to-end event-based obstacle avoidance policy for quadrotors, directly relevant to learned robot navigation.
papers.title: Learning Event-based Obstacle Avoidance via Differentiable Simulation
papers.tldr: A differentiable event-camera simulation pipeline trains quadrotors for direct, robust obstacle avoidance without explicit depth estimation.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained audio-visual question answering (AVQA) requires models to resolve complex cross-modal correspondences and temporally grounding from sparsely distributed evidence. Omni-modal agents, which autonomously orchestrate perception tools to actively collect evidence, achieve strong performance, but it remains unclear whether active perception from both audio and visual modalities depends on broad specialized toolsets, especially audio or visual modality-specific tools. Such systems may also introduce long execution trajectories and substantial inference cost. We investigate whether comparable performance can be retained with a compact workflow exposing only essential perceptual capabilities. Starting from the specialized-tool OmniAgent, we conduct staged controlled experiments that prune the toolset and progressively consolidate modality-specific tools into omni-modal tools, motivating a two-tool agent comprising only Omni-modal captioning and Omni-modal QA. Across three widely used AVQA benchmarks, our compact agent achieves comparable or better accuracy than the specialized-tool agent while reducing inference cost by around 70%.
authors: Yi Wang, Tianzi Wang, Peter Bell
bullets: Targets the cost and long execution trajectories of broad tool-based audio-visual agents.
Uses staged tool-pruning experiments and progressively consolidates audio- and visual-specific tools.
The resulting workflow retains only omni-modal captioning and omni-modal question answering.
Evaluated on three widely used AVQA benchmarks with comparable or better accuracy than the specialized-tool agent.
Scope: focuses on compacting perception workflows while maintaining performance on benchmark AVQA tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses efficient agentic audio-visual question answering, focusing on spatial understanding and modality consolidation.
papers.title: Efficient Agentic Audio-Visual Question Answering through Toolset Pruning and Modality Consolidation
papers.tldr: A compact two-tool omni-modal agent preserves or improves AVQA accuracy while reducing inference cost by about 70%.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have led to significant progress in visual reasoning capabilities. However, existing benchmarks curate image-question pairs pertaining to object categories with few instances, enabling trivial object referencing and limited visual ambiguity. In this work, we introduce MIMO-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs in a Multi-Instance per Multi-Object categories (MIMO) setting. Each image-question pair in our benchmark pertains to instances belonging to object categories with multiple instances. The presence of such similar feature distractors causes hindrance in basic visual reasoning tasks, necessitating the referring expression to be composed of multiple visual subtasks to uniquely and unambiguously identify the target object. MIMO-Bench comprises 3,802 image-question pairs across attribute binding and numerical counting tasks. Despite impressive performances on existing benchmarks, both SOTA open-source (InternVL, QwenVL) and proprietary (Gemini, GPT-5) models exhibit substantially lower performance on MIMO-Bench, highlighting their limitations in the MIMO setting. The benchmark will be made publicly available.
authors: Saumya Mundra, Ajoy Mondal, Vineeth N Balasubramanian, C. V. Jawahar
bullets: Existing visual-reasoning benchmarks often contain few object instances, allowing relatively easy object reference.
MIMO-Bench introduces 3,802 image-question pairs involving multiple instances across multiple object categories.
Tasks cover attribute binding and numerical counting, requiring multi-step referring expressions to disambiguate targets.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting predicts a scene from a few images, but our predictor is less accurate than its own Gaussians optimized per scene on those images. This gap lies mostly in the shape of the Gaussians, their scale and rotation, since optimizing the shape alone recovers almost all of it and opacity and color recover less. Gradient steps on the input views correct this shape, and the model holds these views at inference. Log-anisotropy correction changes the axis ratios of each Gaussian in log space at constant volume, and in-forward gradient refinement renders the Gaussians into the input views and applies the gradient of the photometric loss with a learned recurrent update, first to opacity and color and then to the shape. GradSplat is a feed-forward model that refines its own Gaussians by learned gradient steps inside its forward pass, with no target view. On both complete six-view RealEstate10K protocols, it has the best PSNR and SSIM among nine methods and keeps its accuracy from $6$ to $42$ input views. Without fine-tuning, it is the most accurate on DL3DV and has the best PSNR and SSIM on ScanNet++. The code will be released at https://github.com/Jingong-Chen/GradSplat/.
authors: Jingong Chen, Linlian Jiang, Guangyuan Li, Xinxin Zuo, Yang Wang, Chulwoo Pack, Kyle Gao, Kwanghee Won
bullets: Addresses the accuracy gap between feed-forward predictions and per-scene Gaussian optimization, mainly caused by Gaussian shape, scale, and rotation.

Renders predicted Gaussians into input views and applies learned recurrent photometric-gradient updates, first to opacity and color, then to shape.
Requires no target view and preserves accuracy across 6–42 input views.
Reports best PSNR and SSIM among nine methods on complete six-view RealEstate10K protocols, and strong zero-shot results on DL3DV and ScanNet++.

papers.abstract: Lane-changing (LC) maneuvers are highly challenging vehicle interactions, with substantial implications for traffic safety and efficiency. Developing effective LC strategies for connected and automated vehicles in mixed traffic is complicated by the uncertainty associated with surrounding-vehicle behavior and the computational burden of embedding realistic prediction models within optimization schemes. To capture these complex interactions while retaining tractability, this study proposes a data-driven optimization framework that embeds neural network (NN) surrogates for safety and lateral comfort within a B\'ezier-curve-based trajectory planner. Specifically, the safety cost during the LC process is quantified via a surrogate composed of an input convex recurrent neural network (ICRNN) encoding the planned trajectory, a fully input convex neural network (FICNN) embedding the LC duration, and a partially input convex neural network (PICNN) decoder fusing them with historical traffic states; separately, another FICNN surrogate approximates the optimal lateral comfort cost as a function of the LC duration. Both surrogates are embedded via linear programming (LP) formulations, avoiding the binary variables required by conventional mixed-integer programming (MIP) approaches for NN-embedded optimization. We further theoretically establish their exactness at optimality and extend the framework to problems with additional analytical objective terms and multiple surrogates. Experiments on a hybrid dataset combining real-world and simulated trajectories demonstrate that the proposed method achieves surrogate accuracy competitive with unconstrained baselines while substantially improving optimization efficiency over conventional MIPs. Closed-loop simulations further show that the proposed planners markedly reduce the weighted planning cost and consistently outperform baseline methods.
authors: Yuanxiang Yang, Yu Liu, Fabricio Oliveira, Yu Han, Claudio Roncoli
bullets: Addresses safety, lateral comfort, uncertain surrounding-vehicle behavior, and the computational cost of NN-embedded optimization for connected automated vehicles.
Uses ICRNN, FICNN, and PICNN surrogates to model safety from planned trajectories, lane-change duration, and historical traffic states; a separate FICNN models lateral comfort.
Embeds the surrogates through linear programming, avoiding the binary variables required by conventional mixed-integer formulations.

Experiments show competitive surrogate accuracy, substantially better optimization efficiency than conventional MIPs, and lower weighted planning cost than baseline planners in closed-loop simulations.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly process multiple views of the same scene, but it remains unclear whether they integrate these observations into a coherent scene-level representation. Existing multi-image evaluations do not isolate this capability, as tasks may admit correct solutions through independent per-view processing without requiring cross-view correspondence. We introduce OneScene-Bench, a controlled benchmark designed to explicitly distinguish when cross-view integration is necessary. Our benchmark evaluates three complementary capabilities on real-world multi-view scenes: unique object counting, cross-view consistency, and spatial reasoning. For counting, we control object overlap across views to separate cases solvable by simple per-view aggregation from those requiring instance-level correspondence. For consistency, we introduce localized edits in shared and view-specific regions, testing whether models distinguish genuine scene contradictions from differences caused by viewpoint and visibility. For spatial reasoning, we construct object relations that require combining spatial evidence across viewpoints to compare physical proximity. We evaluate twelve state-of-the-art open-weight and proprietary VLMs and find that counting accuracy drops substantially on complementary views, ranging from 4.5-50.0%, compared with 45.5-81.5% on complete-overlap examples. Moreover, cross-view consistency remains around 50% across models, including recent proprietary VLMs, despite substantially stronger performance on spatial reasoning. Our results reveal a substantial gap between processing multiple images and integrating evidence across them, highlighting the need for evaluations that explicitly test scene-level multi-view understanding. Code and data are available at https://github.com/swathisuhas/OneScene-Bench.
authors: Swathi Suhas, Anurag Das, Bernt Schiele, Jonas Fischer
bullets: Introduces a controlled benchmark for testing cross-view integration in real-world multi-view scenes.
Evaluates unique object counting, cross-view consistency, and spatial reasoning.
Counting accuracy drops substantially on complementary views, reaching 4.5–50.0% versus 45.5–81.5% with complete overlap.
Cross-view consistency remains near 50% across models, including proprietary VLMs, while spatial reasoning is comparatively stronger.
Highlights a major gap between handling multiple images and combining evidence across views.

papers.abstract: Organisations keep decades of financial records as scanned PDFs on shared drives, and AI agents can now reach those drives through Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. Existing benchmarks do not mirror this production setting because they simplify the task. In some, the relevant documents are handed to the agent, so it never has to search. In others, the agent searches through documents with pre-extracted text, so it never has to read scanned images. We introduce TreasuryQA Bench, which requires both: 70 questions over 1,435 scanned U.S. Treasury publications, held in Veris's high-fidelity Dropbox twin. In each task the agent searches for the relevant file through Dropbox's MCP server, reads the pages it needs with Reducto's hosted OCR server or its own tools, and replies with one exact figure. A Python grader checks each answer against an accepted range around the correct value. In this paper we present results from ten agents. The best, Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, solves 64.8% of attempts and the worst, GPT-5.6 Terra in Codex, solves 16.7%, so the benchmark is far from saturated. We also test how scan quality affects performance: every agent solves fewer tasks on the blurriest scans. Most failed attempts reply with a wrong number rather than no number, and the most common cause is a digit misread from the scan. Three worked examples are included with their answer keys.
authors: Ritiz Tambi, Sahar Shayegan, Joshua Meyer, Sun Kim, Ali Khan, Victor Shih, Mehdi Jamei, Andi Partovi
bullets: Benchmarks 70 questions across 1,435 scanned U.S. Treasury publications in a Dropbox environment accessed through MCP.

Across ten agents, success ranged from 16.7% to 64.8%, indicating the benchmark is far from saturated.
Performance declined on blurrier scans, with digit misreads the most common failure cause.
Most failures produced an incorrect number rather than no answer.

papers.abstract: Predictive world-model objectives need not organize latent histories according to distinctions required for later control. With privileged simulator access during training, should response-derived structural information be predicted, decoded, or imposed directly on latent geometry--and how do these choices compare with structured belief distillation? We define posterior-marginalized structural tests whose response distributions induce a pseudometric over histories, then train quotient-preserving (QP) world models by aligning shared latent Euclidean distances to that metric. Across a fixed six-task diagnostic suite, the largest differences appear under held-out structural variation: QP improves planning success by 26.1 points $[21.5,30.7]$ over metric decoding and 6.4 points $[3.8,9.0]$ over structured belief distillation. On GridWorld, metric decoding accurately recovers held-out structural distances ($\rho=.91$) while its native latent geometry remains more distorted than QP's (paired IQD difference $.22$ $[.20,.24]$), showing that relational recoverability and direct geometric alignment can diverge.
authors: Todd Y. Zhou

On GridWorld, metric decoding recovers structural distances well ($\rho=.91$), but its latent geometry is more distorted than QP's, indicating recoverability and geometric alignment can diverge.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent debate systems require agents to retain and revisit arguments across multiple rounds, yet limited context windows and unstructured memories make relevant information increasingly difficult to recover. Existing flat and pairwise-graph memories also struggle to capture higher-order relations, including multi-agent agreement, conflicting evidence, and evolving consensus. We introduce HEDGE, a selective memory framework that represents debate trajectories as semantic hypergraphs. Hyperedges connect related claims across agents, while intra-hyperedge relational graphs preserve fine-grained argumentative structure. A learned memory selection module (MSM), trained through supervised learning and reinforcement learning, routes each memory candidate to STORE, BACKUP, or OMIT, retaining useful information while limiting redundancy. Across seven diverse benchmarks, HEDGE consistently outperforms strong single-agent, multi-agent, and memory baselines, improving accuracy by 5.0 points on average over the strongest multi-agent system with GPT-4o-mini. The gains reach 8.2 points on conflict-heavy tasks, while HEDGE reduces memory usage by 48% and the number of debate rounds by 34%.
authors: Amirhossein Abaskohi, Mahdi Mostajabdaveh, Zirui Zhou
bullets: Represents debate trajectories as semantic hypergraphs linking related claims across agents.
Uses intra-hyperedge relational graphs to capture agreement, conflicting evidence, and evolving consensus.
A learned memory selection module routes candidates to STORE, BACKUP, or OMIT to reduce redundancy.
Across seven benchmarks, it improves accuracy by 5.0 points on average over the strongest multi-agent baseline with GPT-4o-mini.
It achieves larger gains on conflict-heavy tasks while reducing memory usage by 48% and debate rounds by 34%.

papers.abstract: In reinforcement learning (RL), temporal reasoning is essential for estimating the density of future outcomes under a policy's occupancy measure. While self-predictive representations have been a dominant paradigm for occupancy density estimation, we find that they yield surprisingly poor estimates. On the other hand, generative occupancy models can produce remarkably accurate samples from the occupancy measure. Yet, they cannot easily recover occupancy densities, limiting their use for control despite their expressivity. In this paper, we propose Geometric Time Score Estimators (GTSE), a framework that bridges the two paradigms by learning occupancy density estimators along probability paths. We analyze how GTSE implicitly induces better occupancy estimators through improved representation learning and show how to directly extract self-predictive representations from this framework. Through experiments across several locomotion and manipulation tasks, we show that GTSE improves performance over state-of-the-art methods by $2\times$ to $6\times$ in goal-conditioned RL settings, and that the representations learned using our framework transfer effectively to downstream RL tasks. Website: https://aravindvenu7.github.io/website/gtse/
authors: Aravind Venugopal, Grace Liu, Jeff Schneider, Benjamin Eysenbach
bullets: Self-predictive representations can estimate future occupancy densities poorly, while generative models produce accurate samples but do not readily provide densities for control.
GTSE learns occupancy density estimators along probability paths, connecting the strengths of both paradigms.
The framework improves representation learning and enables direct extraction of self-predictive representations.
Experiments on locomotion and manipulation tasks report 2×–6× better performance than state-of-the-art methods in goal-conditioned RL.
Learned representations transfer effectively to downstream RL tasks.

papers.abstract: Autoresearch agents can now attempt long-horizon AI research end-to-end, i.e., self-improvement. However, best results are still obtained by research agents interacting with human researchers, and improving AI's ability to perform this co-research will only reinforce this effect---a process termed co-improvement (Weston and Foerster, 2025). Further, aligning with human expectations is likely a safer path for research agents, especially given recent agent reward hacking phenomena (OpenAI, 2026b). In this work we address these issues in four ways: (i) we empirically study the role of humans in directing autoresearch agents, focusing on the domain of benchmark creation, and find humans still play a pivotal role particularly in the ideation phase; (ii) we also develop a benchmark, HackBench, that shows current autoresearch agents are not aligned and are unable to achieve hack localization sufficiently; (iii) we present a method to train agents for improved human interaction by using human simulators as a proxy during reinforcement learning (RL); and finally (iv) we develop a method to improve model text generation, and hence agent communication, by RL with rubrics aligned with human experts. Together, our training and evaluation recipes provide a path toward more capable and aligned (co-)research agents.
authors: Tianjian Li, Chuanyang Jin, Seungone Kim, Tong Chen, John Hoffman, Yoram Bachrach amd Pedro Rodriguez, Ping Yu, Eryk Helenowski, Swarnadeep Saha, Jack Lanchantin, Weizhe Yuan, Ilia Kulikov, Jason Weston
bullets: Humans remain especially important for guiding research-agent ideation in benchmark creation.
HackBench evaluates reward-hack localization and finds current autoresearch agents insufficiently aligned and capable.
Human simulators are used as proxies during reinforcement learning to improve agent–human interaction.
Expert-aligned rubric rewards improve model text generation and agent communication.
The proposed evaluation and training recipes aim to support safer, more effective co-research.

figures.caption: Figure 8 AutoInteract is a two-phase framework for generating realistic, high-quality multi-turn interaction trajectories from verified tasks based on real user histories. In Phase 1, AutoInteract builds user models: modeling how users react by optimizing a history-conditioned user behavior prompt and building a diverse set of user profiles. In Phase 2, an agent combines verified source tasks with its user models to generate candidate tasks with multi-turn interaction trajectories, and selects them to be challenging, valid, realistic, coherent, and profile-consistent. If the checks fail, it revises the controller’s instruction until a task passes all checks or the retry budget is exhausted.

Figure 1 AutoBenchmark: evaluating the ability of autoresearch agents to create benchmarks. AutoBenchmark instructs an autoresearch agent to create a benchmark; we specifically target benchmarks that evaluate autoresearch agents themselves (i.e., benchmarking autoresearch). Within the benchmark creation loop, the autoresearch agent iteratively revises the benchmark via two main sources of feedback: one from the benchmark solvers (including the same model used as the benchmark creator) and the other from external verifiers of the benchmark (AI or human). We thus also study if having humans provide additional feedback on what benchmark to make and how to make it helps or not.
Figure 5 HackBench. Hack localization F1 per model. All monitors miss many hacks.

Figure 2 Performance of benchmark solvers and verdicts of benchmark judges across 10 iterations. A lower score means a harder benchmark. Muse Spark and Muse Glimmer are the solvers inside the loop, while Nemotron is held out. Filled markers passed all five quality judges and are eligible for selection; hollow markers were caught by at least one, and the star is the selected checkpoint, namely the eligible iteration with the lowest Muse Spark score. We display different levels of human feedback. The no-feedback curve is one autonomous run, in which the agent chooses the benchmark itself, shown in both rows as a reference. Feedback from humans improves over fully autonomous benchmark creation, with fine-grained feedback more useful than coarse-grained feedback.

Figure 6 HackBench. Given a full agent trajectory (left), an LLM monitor (center) reads the entire transcript and is scored on the hack localization task of returning the exact offending command(s) by command index (right).

Figure 4 Examples of critique fromLLM judges: Feedback from LLM judges (benchmark verifiers) gives the research agent insights that solver scores (i.e., trajectory feedback) alone cannot provide, and enables making a valid benchmark while keeping it challenging.

Figure 3 Execution feedback on SilentTrain Bench. Iterations 1 to 5 of a fine-grained proposal are run without extra human feedback, and then the experiment is forked at iteration 6: one continuation receives human guidance on how to instantiate the benchmark and the other continues unaided. The agent, the construct, and the grounding material are identical across the fork. Markers follow Figure 2 and ∆ is the gap between the two selected checkpoints on each solver. Extra expert human guidance helps.

Figure 7 Construction of a HackBench example with a synthetic hack through trajectory editing. Step 1: We begin with a real autoresearch trajectory. Step 2: We insert a synthetic reward-hacking command (red). Step 3: We update only causally affected downstream observations (green), preserving the task, commands, and unrelated observations. This produces a coherent example with command-level audited gold annotations.

Figure 9 The user-simulator prompt used to generate each user turn. It combines the learned user behavior prompt and a sampled user profile from Phase 1 with the interaction history and the privileged task context. After a failed attempt, the controller may also add revised role-playing guidance based on the trajectory evaluator’s feedback.

Figure 10 Training on AutoInteract tasks does not saturate as quickly as training on the source data. Training reward versus optimization step for Qwen3.5-4B RL runs on the source data (blue) and on AutoInteract tasks (orange). In the algorithmic domain (left), AutoInteract starts from a lower reward but continues improving and eventually reaches a higher reward than source-task training. In the SWE domain (right), AutoInteract also continues improving and reaches substantially higher reward, while source-task training saturates much earlier.

Right: validation absolute means—the gap increases from both directions, with the human’s score rising (3.4 → 5.0) as the model’s falls (7.6 → 2.7).

(optimizer Kimi-K2.6, judge and writer = Muse Spark 1.1); the meta-optimized rubrics are used for story and Wikipedia RL-XAR training. Each panel plots the mean expert-human−model gap by meta-prompt iteration for the train and validation splits (blind rubrics). Left (story): the validation gap rises from +0.16 and peaks around iteration 3 (+2.77). Right (Wikipedia): the validation gap peaks around iteration 3 at only +1.07 and stays small—consistent with the far more modest Wikipedia gains.

Mean human−model gap (writer = Muse Spark 1.1; positive = human favored) for each judge, with judges in decreasing capability order. On Story and Wikipedia, Qwen3.5-27B (red) is the only judge to turn negative, ranking the model above human writing (−0.55 story, −0.39 wiki); on Paper the four judges are close and all human-favoring. A weak grader is incapable of seeing the gap.

Figure 17 Online RL-XAR: Training the writer (via the current rubric generator) and the rubric generator (using the human-model gap) online simultaneously. While this is not the approach reported in our main experiments, it appears to work well also, and future work should explore this approach further.
Figure 15 Different Rubric Meta-Optimizers. Mean (human − model) gap per optimizer, averaged over three seeds.

Figure 11 AutoInteract makes challenging multi-turn interaction data through revisions. The source task, learned user behavior prompt, and sampled profile remain fixed. Stage 1 points directly to the likely code change, making the trajectory too easy: the weak solver scores 67%, above the 40% limit. Evaluator feedback leads Stage 2 to remove that clue, but the revision also omits the example file and expected behavior, leaving too little evidence: the strong solver scores 67%, below the 70% target. Stage 3 restores this evidence, identifies the relevant code area, and adds follow-up requirements without revealing the solution. The final trajectory is accepted with weak- and strong-solver scores of 25% and 100% and passes all validity, leakage, and realism checks.

Figure 12 Standard judgments (left, middle) rank themodel above the expert human—meta-optimizing the rubrics to be aligned with human experts reverses this (right). If AI slop is judged to be better than human writing by the LLM grader, then training will encourage more slop. On the academic paper section writing task, we find standard pairwise LLM judges or LLM-generated rubrics score GPT-5.6 or Opus-4.8 higher than high-quality human writing. Our RL-XAR (eXpert-Aligned Rubrics) approach instead meta-optimizes the rubrics on a training set of high-quality human-written sections, resulting in rubrics that reverse the result, and score the human writing higher on test papers.

Figure 16 Human−model gap by paper human writing-quality bin (low/medium/high, light to dark), comparing with two models (Muse Spark 1.1 and GPT-5.6). If the learned rubric is measuring genuine quality, the human-model gap should be larger for better-written human papers and shrink for weak ones, which is what we observe.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as cognitive interfaces that shape how users interpret evidence, communicate, and make decisions. As deployed systems become more multimodal, tool-using, and multi-agent, safety failures no longer arise only from isolated harmful outputs, but also from how agents update, store, and propagate epistemic commitments across retrieval, memory, tools, and peer communication. In this paper, we define belief as an engineering abstraction for evidence-based commitments that guide downstream action. Building on this view, we propose the Explicit Belief Multi-Agent System (EB-MAS), which externalizes belief states into a structured substrate, uses belief operators to propose candidate updates, and applies a Cognitive Firewall to bound or reject updates that are weakly evidenced but strongly driven by vulnerability cues. We also discuss the risk of group belief at the group level, including manufactured consensus, collusion, and cascading misinformation, and outline practical integration challenges around grounding, false positives, scalability, and ethical misuse. Therefore, scalable agent safety requires not only better output filtering or stronger base models, but also explicit interfaces for tracing, calibrating, and constraining belief revision at runtime.
authors: Zhuoyun Li, Boxuan Wang, Jinwei Hu, Xiaowei Huang, Yi Dong
bullets: Frames belief as an engineering abstraction for evidence-based commitments guiding agent actions.
Proposes EB-MAS, which externalizes belief states and uses belief operators to suggest updates.
Introduces a Cognitive Firewall to bound or reject weakly evidenced updates driven by vulnerability cues.
Highlights group-level risks including manufactured consensus, collusion, and cascading misinformation.
Identifies open challenges in grounding, false positives, scalability, and ethical misuse.

figures.caption: Figure 1: EB-MAS with an Explicit Belief Substrate (EBS). The framework spans three levels: Substrate Layer (Sec. 3.1) maintains a belief graph with attention-activated subgraphs; Individual Layer (Sec. 3.2) applies neuro-symbolic belief operators to update node attributes and evolve topology, guarded by a Cognitive Firewall against evidence–vulnerability mismatch; Group Layer (Sec. 3.3) couples agents via social priors to model consensus, polarization, and narrative collapse.

Figure 2: Monte Carlo simulations of belief-centric containment. (A,B) Under a belief-reframing attack, w/ EBS blocks risk-decoupling updates, reducing ASR and better preserving perceived risk. (C,D) w/ EBS lowers both the ASR of a coordinated sacrifice-based attack and attackers’ win rate, preventing post-attack trust surges.

Table 1: MM-DeceptionBench prototype results. Failure is the API-judged unsafe rate after defense. Benign false block is measured on 100 benign-control examples.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes an explicit belief system for LLM agents to manage epistemic commitments and safety, directly addressing agent memory and state management.
papers.title: Auditable Belief Updates as a Missing Safety Layer for LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Systems
papers.tldr: Safe multi-agent LLM systems need auditable runtime mechanisms to trace, calibrate, and constrain how agents form and propagate beliefs.

papers.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly adopted in long-horizon tasks and interact with diverse external environments. Despite their growing capabilities, these agents remain vulnerable to real-world attacks such as indirect prompt injections, which manipulate agents through malicious instructions embedded in external environments. While existing risk assessment work has primarily focused on the injection content, the effect of where an injection appears has not been systematically characterized. Studying injection placement requires agents to operate over longer-horizon tasks and interact with diverse environmental surfaces. Thus, we build three agentic testbeds spanning tool use, coding, and daily workflow domains with diverse injection surfaces. Holding the injection content fixed, we find that agent susceptibility varies across injection placements. We refer to this phenomenon as the trust region effect: agents implicitly assign different levels of trust to different regions of their environments. For example, an agent powered by GPT-5.4 follows an unsafe injection instruction placed in a repository documentation file (i.e., a README or TODO file) 2.6 times more often on average than the same instruction placed in a code or data file. Building upon this observation, we develop learning-based attackers that generate injection content and select better injection placements. Our approach demonstrates that both where an injection is placed and what content it contains can affect the strength of indirect prompt injection attacks. To the best of our knowledge, this work provides the first systematic characterization for the effectiveness of different injection placements, spanning both coarse-grained environmental surfaces and fine-grained positions. The uneven trust that agents implicitly place across their environments provides important insights for future attack and defense design.
authors: Chengquan Guo, Xiaodong Liu, Weiwei Yang, Mingqian Feng, Jialin Song, Qiyao Ma, Carolyn Buractaon, Christopher White, Bo Li, Jianfeng Gao
bullets: The study examines how injection placement affects agent susceptibility, beyond the injection’s content.
It evaluates three long-horizon testbeds covering tool use, coding, and daily workflows with diverse injection surfaces.
Holding content fixed, agents show different attack success rates depending on placement; repository documentation was especially influential compared with code or data files.
The authors develop learning-based attackers that jointly optimize injection content and placement.
Findings motivate defenses that account for implicit, location-dependent trust in agent environments.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the 'trust region effect' in LLM agents, characterizing how injection placement affects agent behavior, which relates to agent memory and learning about environment trust.
papers.title: Where You Inject Matters: The Trust Region Effect in LLM Agents
papers.tldr: LLM agents trust different parts of their environments unevenly, making indirect prompt injections substantially more effective in some locations than others.

papers.abstract: Contextual embeddings represent chunks of a document with respect to the document's global context. These models are typically trained and evaluated under the assumption that a relevant document contains only a single relevant chunk. In this work, we argue that in real-world use cases a retriever should not only find answers spread over several chunks but also surface the evidence needed to verify them. To address this, we introduce pplx-embed-v2-context, a family of contextual embedding models trained by distilling graded chunk-level relevance from a query-aware context compression model. This removes the need for gold-chunk labels and makes the training targets independent of the chunking. We utilize a vision-language backbone for training and release pplx-embed-v2-context in 9B and 0.6B sizes with compatible embedding spaces. On the evaluation side, we introduce two benchmarks that label both the chunks that answer a query and the evidence needed to verify the answer. Context-bench is a controlled diagnostic, and Q2D-Chunk is built from real-world search queries. To encourage further research, we also publish Q2D-Chunk as a public leaderboard. Our 9B model sets a new state of the art on both benchmarks and ConTEB. We find that the visual retrieval capabilities of our 9B model transfer from its vision-language base model and propose to extend chunking to image inputs. We demonstrate that our models achieve state-of-the-art performance among dense retrievers on visual ViDoRe-V3 and that performance improves with granular image chunking.
authors: Sedigheh Eslami, Markus Krimmel, William Barber, Antoine Chaffin, Maximilian Schall, Jonas Golde, Louis Milliken, Ekaterina Glazkova, Denis Bykov, Bo Wang
bullets: Targets graded chunk relevance distilled from a query-aware context compression model, making supervision independent of chunking.
Releases compatible 9B and 0.6B embedding models trained with a vision-language backbone.
Introduces Context-bench and Q2D-Chunk, which evaluate answer and verification evidence retrieval; Q2D-Chunk includes a public leaderboard.
The 9B model achieves state-of-the-art results on both benchmarks, ConTEB, and visual ViDoRe-V3 among dense retrievers.
Visual retrieval transfers from the backbone, and finer-grained image chunking improves performance.

papers.abstract: In many settings where LLM post-training is desirable, high-quality answers are recognizable but difficult to score with explicit rewards. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is limited to tasks where an explicit correctness signal is available. Prior adversarial approaches to training reasoning LLMs either complement verifiable rewards with co-trained critics or require reference reasoning traces. We ask whether a co-trained LLM judge can turn reference answers alone into the sole reward for on-policy post-training of reasoning LLMs. We call this method Reinforced Adversarial Learning (RAL). We first validate RAL on three verifiable tasks (integer multiplication, code-based arithmetic-expression synthesis, and SMILES-to-formula translation), using the verifiers only for evaluation. With sufficiently capable judges and enough training, RAL matches direct RLVR. We then apply RAL to scientific abstract generation in two settings. In the first setting, RAL guides the generator to produce abstracts in the scientific domain of the reference abstracts, even though the prompt leaves that domain unspecified. In the second setting, we generate abstracts for U.S. National Institutes of Health grant proposals conditioned on the grant title. Human scientists and an ensemble of LLM judges find our generations harder to distinguish from real abstracts than those of frontier-LLM baselines. These results suggest a path toward post-training reasoning models in scientific and other high-value domains, where increasingly capable judges infer hard-to-specify reward functions from example answers.
authors: Albert Bou, Javier Valdes-Aleman, Jon M. Laurent, Samuel G. Rodriques, Andrew D. White, Michaela Hinks, Siddharth Narayanan
bullets: Addresses settings where good answers are available but explicit reward functions are difficult to specify.
Trains a generator with rewards from an adversarially co-trained LLM judge, without requiring reference reasoning traces.
On three verifiable tasks, RAL matches direct RLVR when judges are sufficiently capable and training is adequate.
For scientific abstract generation, RAL captures reference domains and produces NIH grant abstracts judged more human-like than frontier-LLM baselines.
The approach depends on judge capability and training duration, and its strongest evidence is reported for the evaluated tasks and domains.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers increase computational capacity through the repeated application of shared blocks, but their recurrent depth makes conventional full-depth decoding expensive. While existing speculative pipelines accelerate generation by processing consecutive token positions at varying depths, they are typically limited by sequential decoding overheads. We introduce CopyLoop, a training-free decoding algorithm that combines low-cost context-copy proposals with shallow screening and continuous recurrent scheduling. Rather than step-by-step generation, CopyLoop proposes multi-token suffixes from repeated context. It then evaluates them early at a shallow recurrent depth to efficiently filter out incorrect branches, processing newer blocks concurrently while earlier blocks are still progressing toward full-depth verification. We evaluate CopyLoop across six model checkpoints from the Ouro, Raven, and Huginn families, covering code generation and multi-step mathematical reasoning. CopyLoop achieves decoding speedups of 2.98x--10.70x over full-depth autoregressive decoding on Base models and 2.74x--3.52x on Thinking models, consistently outperforming or closely matching all competing baselines across evaluation tasks. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm a strong synergy between shallow screening and continuous scheduling, while our analyses show that CopyLoop requires only lightweight model calibration and yields greater speedups on longer generations with reusable contexts.
authors: Wenyu Du, Stephen Chung
bullets: Targets the sequential overhead of conventional full-depth decoding in recurrent, looped Transformers.
Uses training-free multi-token context-copy proposals, shallow recurrent screening, and concurrent continuous scheduling.
Evaluated on six Ouro, Raven, and Huginn checkpoints for code generation and multi-step mathematical reasoning.
Reports 2.98×–10.70× speedups on Base models and 2.74×–3.52× on Thinking models, generally matching or outperforming baselines.
Ablations find shallow screening and continuous scheduling work synergistically; benefits increase for longer generations with reusable contexts.

papers.abstract: Agentic AI drives significant productivity gains across diverse domains, but concurrent long-context prefills from multiple agents can saturate GPU compute resources. Although CPUs offer a viable alternative, existing CPU attention kernels fall short in adapting to multi-tier cache hierarchies and lack effective thread scheduling. To address this, we introduce CACPU, a high-performance attention kernel featuring tiered cache blocking and an in-kernel task dispatching mechanism designed for causal full-sequence prefilling. CACPU achieves up to a 2.01x speedup over PyTorch SDPA, FlexAttention, and SGLang attention kernels. Integrated into SGLang, it reduces Time to First Token (TTFT) of Llama-3.1-8B by up to 1.74x while preserving model accuracy.
authors: Kwun Fung Lau, Frost Mitchell, Kanya Mo, Emani Ashok
bullets: Targets CPU attention bottlenecks caused by multi-tier cache hierarchies and inefficient thread scheduling.
Uses tiered cache blocking with in-kernel task dispatch for causal full-sequence prefilling.
Reports up to 2.01× speedup over PyTorch SDPA, FlexAttention, and SGLang attention kernels.
Integrated with SGLang, it reduces Llama-3.1-8B TTFT by up to 1.74× while preserving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Agents deployed at scale repeatedly encounter related problems, and it is natural to let them learn from each other's experience rather than starting over each time. Unfortunately, there is no single way to retain that experience that works well across settings, and no way to know in advance which future problems a given experience will help with. A global history preserves every detail but becomes expensive and mixes together experience that may not belong together; compressing that history into one fixed representation limits the cost but can throw away valuable details. We introduce Routed Continual Learning (Routed CL), an architecture that decides how to partition and retain experience. Past trajectories are grouped into clusters, each of which maintains state using one memory system from a fixed library. Before each run, an LLM-based router either reuses an existing cluster or creates a new one, basing its decision on the problem statement, memory system descriptions, and cluster summaries. We also introduce Context Memory Adapter, which mediates between the memory system and the agentic loop. We evaluate the architecture on a heterogeneous stream that interleaves 301 instances from the six CL-Bench tasks with 97 banking instances from $\tau^3$-Bench. Across four language models and five matched rollouts, Routed Continual Learning raises normalized reward over a single global in-context learning (ICL) history by 15-30% of the maximum attainable normalized reward, achieves higher mean normalized reward than ICL-only clustering, and reduces estimated API cost by 65-72% relative to Global ICL. These results support approaching continual learning as a routing problem that chooses both a learning mechanism and a state cluster rather than committing to one representation globally.
authors: Michael Philip, Mahesh Balakrishnan, David Geraghty, David Mao, Vidhya Venkat, Ilya Mironov
bullets: Addresses the challenge of retaining shared experience across varied future problems without costly global histories or overly lossy compression.
Clusters past trajectories and uses an LLM router to reuse or create clusters based on the problem, memory-system descriptions, and cluster summaries.

papers.abstract: Accurate precipitation forecasting remains elusive as physics-based models struggle to resolve mesoscale convection and machine learning often yields physically inconsistent, blurred results that consistently underestimate extreme events. We present FitzRoy, the first system that simultaneously achieves state-of-the-art predictive skill and physical realism over the continental United States. Through a reinforced diffusion framework, where a conditional discrete diffusion model is refined via reinforcement learning, FitzRoy effectively resolves the long-standing trade-off between pointwise accuracy and structural fidelity. Across lead times up to 24 hours, FitzRoy consistently matches or exceeds state-of-the-art models while preserving structural realism and capturing extreme events. Its low-latency inference further enables deployment in real-time operational settings. In case studies such as the 2025 Texas Hill Country floods and the 2026 Missouri floods, FitzRoy signals record-breaking accumulations that existing models largely missed. By bridging the gap between realism and skill, FitzRoy establishes a new frontier for high-fidelity precipitation forecasting.
authors: Ozan Sener, Anand Avati, David Hafner, Jierui Lin, Laura Manduchi, Xiaoying Pang, Langwen Huang, Torsten Hoefler, Russ Schumacher, Vladlen Koltun
bullets: Addresses blurred, physically inconsistent forecasts and systematic underestimation of precipitation extremes.
Uses a conditional discrete diffusion model refined through reinforcement learning.
Across lead times up to 24 hours in the continental United States, it matches or exceeds state-of-the-art predictive skill while preserving realistic structures.
Low-latency inference supports real-time operational deployment.
Case studies of major Texas and Missouri floods show signals of record-breaking accumulations that existing models largely missed.

figures.caption: Figure 5 Evaluation of forecast realism. (A) Frequency bias as a function of lead time. FitzRoy is essentially unbiased regarding rain vs. no-rain occurrence and reproduces event frequencies accurately, showing only slight overprediction for heavy rain. FitzRoy demonstrates superior frequency bias compared to NBM and ENS-CF, both of which significantly underpredict heavier rainfall events. (B) Calibration curves for FitzRoy and probabilistic baselines at four precipitation thresholds. The x-axis shows forecast probability and the y-axis the observed frequency of events exceeding the threshold. Perfect calibration follows the diagonal; points below (above) indicate overconfidence (underconfidence). Only bins with at least 1,000 samples are shown. FitzRoy is well-calibrated across all intensity thresholds. (C) Top: mean power spectral density of hourly precipitation accumulation as a function of spatial frequency. Bottom: relative difference with respect to MRMS. Curves closer to MRMS indicate better performance. FitzRoy closely matches the MRMS power spectrum, whereas all other methods overpredict power at low spatial frequencies. (D) Hurricane Milton case study (12:00 UTC October 9th, 2024). FitzRoy and HRRR both capture the hurricane structure and eye, whereas all other evaluated methods blur these features. FitzRoy localizes the storm more accurately than HRRR, which misplaces the eye of the hurricane, especially for longer lead times.

Figure 1 Flooding in the Texas Hill Country. (A) 6-hour observed accumulated precipitation from radar between 03:00 and 09:00 UTC on 4 July 2025 around Camp Mystic (center of red box). (B) Area-averaged observed and forecasted accumulations over the red box shown in panel A (Lat: 29.8◦ – 30.2◦, Lon: −99.6◦ – −99.2◦) for different initialization times. (C) 6-hour accumulation forecasts for different initialization times (lead times). While physicsbased systems such as HRRR struggle even at 6-hour lead times, FitzRoy consistently predicts extreme precipitation 19 hours in advance. FitzRoy slightly overpredicts the rain, but for an extreme event this overprediction is preferable to underprediction for emergency alertness. FitzRoy also maintains consistency across initialization times, whereas HRRR degrades as the lead time shortens and the deadly flooding approaches.

Figure 4 Evaluation of deterministic and probabilistic forecast skill via scorecards. (A) Precipitation accumulation. (B) Instantaneous precipitation rate. (C) Probability of rain. Each scorecard displays a collection of metrics over all forecast lead times, where hatched cells indicate statistically not significant differences (two-sided test at a 5% significance level following Hamill (1999)). Across nearly all tasks, metrics, and lead times, FitzRoy matches or outperforms the physics-based and ML baselines within their intended scope of operation.

Figure 2 Missouri flood. (A) 9-hour observed accumulated precipitation from radar between 03:00 and 12:00 UTC on 10 July 2026. (B) Area-averaged observed and forecasted accumulations over the red box shown in panel A (Lat: 37.28◦ – 38.00◦, Lon: −91.48◦ – −90.56◦) for different initialization times. (C) 9-hour accumulation forecasts for different initialization times (lead times). FitzRoy consistently identifies the extreme accumulation magnitude across multiple initialization times, whereas operational baselines exhibit significant underprediction.

papers.abstract: Gardening in the backyard implies living there, while checking into an Airbnb more likely means staying for a few days. Such duration judgments are important for understanding human mobility, travel behavior, and social context. However, duration is rarely stated explicitly in social media posts and must instead be inferred from noisy textual, visual, and contextual cues. In this paper, we investigate whether vision-language models possess such duration commonsense. We create a new corpus of geotagged tweets co-annotated by humans and LLMs to serve as a testbed for this task. We find that state-of-the-art models struggle with duration inference, even when guided by multi-turn Chain-of-Thought prompting. Error analyses further reveal that models often fail to integrate critical contextual information, or they overly rely on prominent visual details while overlooking subtle hashtags and semantic nuances. These findings underscore the significant challenges remaining in context-aware multimodal understanding.
authors: Chenyang Yu, Zhaomin Xiao, Yan Huang, Eduardo Blanco
bullets: Introduces duration commonsense reasoning as a task for interpreting human mobility and social context.
Builds a geotagged-tweet corpus co-annotated by humans and LLMs.
Evaluates vision-language models, including with multi-turn Chain-of-Thought prompting.
Models often miss important context, hashtags, and semantic nuances while overemphasizing salient visual details.
Results highlight persistent challenges in context-aware multimodal understanding.
