papers.abstract: Embodied instruction following in interactive environments requires agents to interpret natural language commands and complete long-horizon tasks. Existing planners either rely on large labeled trajectories, or use few-shot and zero-shot LLM prompting that produces a whole plan in a single serial reasoning process. These approaches depend on linguistic common sense, commit to a plan from the initial instruction, and only update after failures, which weakens robustness and state awareness. We present AtomTree, a hierarchical framework for state-aware task planning with LLMs. AtomTree incrementally builds a tree of subgoals and actions, where the LLM decides at each step, from the current symbolic state, whether to further decompose or to output a grounded low-level action. A lightweight memory module summarizes past outcomes for reuse in later decisions. When a low-level action stalls, AtomTree triggers hierarchical backtracking replanning to return to the parent node and regenerate the subtree plan from the latest state, preventing continued drift along an incorrect trajectory. In zero-shot evaluation on the ALFRED benchmark, AtomTree outperforms prior LLM-based planners. Project page: https://zhaihaotian.github.io/atomtree-website/.
authors: Haotian Zhai, Tianming Sha, Junnan Li
bullets: Addresses the brittleness of one-shot, serial LLM plans for long-horizon interactive tasks.
Builds a hierarchical tree of subgoals and actions, deciding at each step whether to decompose further or issue a grounded low-level action.
Uses symbolic state updates and lightweight memory to inform subsequent planning decisions.
Performs hierarchical backtracking and replanning when an action stalls, regenerating plans from the latest state.
Outperforms prior LLM-based planners in zero-shot evaluation on ALFRED.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of our hierarchical planning framework for embodied instruction following. Given a task instruction and the current visual state, our method recursively decides whether to decompose the current goal into finer-grained subgoals or execute it directly. This process incrementally builds an explicit hierarchical goal tree, shown in the upper-right panel, where higher-level goals are progressively refined into executable actions. In contrast, we compare against two representative paradigms: (1) a fully supervised end-to-end EIF model trained on the full dataset, and (2) an LLM-based method using retrieved few-shot examples. While these baselines may produce incorrect action sequences, our method maintains a structured tree-based plan and performs step-by-step decomposition conditioned on the current state and memory, enabling more accurate long-horizon reasoning and execution.

Fig. 3: Overview of our state-aware decision prompt. The prompt summarizes the role and mission, decision options, input information, available atomic actions, global rules, output format, and a small set of decision-guiding examples. Given the current subgoal together with the current state and memory, the LLM predicts whether to decompose the goal into subtasks or execute it directly.

Fig. 4: Qualitative comparison with and without memory. Without memory, the model predicts an incorrect subgoal after picking up the cleaned lettuce, whereas AtomTree correctly predicts the next subgoal as navigating to the fridge.

Fig. 1: Error analysis on the Valid Seen split of the ALFRED benchmark with respect to ground-truth PDDL plan length, showing that for FLARE, a state-of-the-art few-shot method, incorrect-plan errors dominate overall and become the primary failure mode for long-horizon tasks (PDDL length > 7).
Fig. 5: Comparison between a few-shot baseline and AtomTree on a multi-instance task.

TABLE I: Quantitative comparison on ALFRED [1]. We report SR and GC on four splits: Valid Seen, Valid Unseen, Test Seen, and Test Unseen. We annotate each method by its evaluation setting, publication venue, and whether it is explicitly state- and history-aware. For methods that do not report results on certain splits or metrics, we mark them as “N/A”. Results marked with an asterisk (*) are produced by [13].

TABLE II: Ablation of ATOMTREE on ALFRED validation splits. “Hier.” enables hierarchical planning with Decompose and a subgoal tree. “Memory” adds the state&history memory mt = (St, Ht). “Replan” enables hierarchical backtracking replanning. We report SR on Valid Seen and Valid Unseen.

papers.title: AtomTree: A Hierarchical Framework for State-Aware Embodied Instruction Following with LLMs

papers.abstract: We run Kroko, a 65.7M-parameter streaming Zipformer2 transducer for English, on the ESP32-P4, a microcontroller with two 400 MHz RISC-V cores, a 128-bit SIMD extension (PIE) and 32 MB of PSRAM, but no neural accelerator. Without any training, the encoder's 290 matrices are stored with 2 or 4 bits per weight in Hadamard-rotated groups: the width of each matrix comes from its measured sensitivity, and each matrix is first corrected toward the original model's output, then rounded with GPTQ and a search over the group norms. The released 71 MB of int8 weights become a 26.65 MB file. Activations are int16 between the matrix products and int8 into them. A C engine with hand-written PIE kernels processes each 1.28 s chunk of audio in 0.90 s on both cores, beam search included, and its PC build computes the same bits as the chip, so accuracy is measured on whole test sets. LibriSpeech WER is 4.34% on test-clean and 10.26% on test-other, against 3.94% and 9.17% for the released model; on FLEURS and Common Voice the gap grows to 2.3 and 1.1 points. A GPU simulator shows that the integer arithmetic costs nothing and that the whole gap comes from the weights, and an ablation on all of test-clean shows that GPTQ does most of the work. We also report the port's speed history, from 51.3 s to 0.62 s of encoder time per chunk, each design step measured again in one build, an attempt to reach 16 MB that stopped at 19.63 MB, and what did not work. We did not measure energy. The inference engine, the firmware and the 2/4-bit weights are available at https://github.com/BoumedineBillal/esp32-pie-asr.
authors: Billal Boumedine
bullets: Kroko is deployed on a dual-core 400 MHz RISC-V microcontroller with 32 MB PSRAM and no neural accelerator.
Sensitivity-based 2/4-bit weight quantization uses Hadamard rotation, GPTQ correction, and group-norm search, reducing weights from 71 MB to 26.65 MB.
A hand-optimized C engine with PIE SIMD kernels supports real-time-enough streaming inference, including beam search.
LibriSpeech WER rises from 3.94% to 4.34% on test-clean and from 9.17% to 10.26% on test-other; degradation is larger on FLEURS and Common Voice.
The study finds GPTQ is the main contributor to quantization quality; a 16 MB target was not reached, and energy was not measured.

papers.title: Streaming Speech Recognition on a Microcontroller: a 65.7M-Parameter Transducer in 2 and 4 Bits on the ESP32-P4

papers.abstract: Visual rule reasoning asks whether multimodal models can recover an abstract concept from a few examples. Existing studies either infer rules from visual examples but evaluate only classification or verbalization, or supervise executable generation with rules provided as input. Consequently, the relationship between visual rule understanding and reliable rule instantiation remains insufficiently explored. We present Bongard-Forge100k, a controlled benchmark, together with RuleForge, a backbone-agnostic framework that jointly learns visual rule understanding and rule-conditioned executable generation. The benchmark contains 108,797 problems: 86,000 for training, 19,297 for testing familiar rules, and 3,500 for testing held-out rule compositions. The framework progresses through rule-understanding training, joint understanding and scene-program supervision, and refinement via execution-grounded reinforcement learning with Understanding Replay. Executing generated programs under multiple random seeds provides verifiable feedback on executability, rule satisfaction, diversity, and robustness. With UniLIP as the primary backbone, RuleForge improves multiple-choice accuracy over the base model by 20.93 percentage points on familiar rules and 28.42 percentage points on held-out rule compositions, while increasing scene-level rule satisfaction on familiar rules from 2.91% to 70.99%. Additional experiments on InternVL3.5, Qwen3-VL, and Show-o2 demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed training data and framework across diverse multimodal architectures.
authors: Weifeng Xu, Yaxiong Wang, Zhedong Zheng
bullets: Introduces Bongard-Forge100k, a 108,797-problem benchmark covering familiar rules and held-out rule compositions.
Uses staged training: rule understanding, joint understanding with scene-program supervision, and execution-grounded reinforcement learning with Understanding Replay.
Evaluates generated programs through execution across random seeds for executability, rule satisfaction, diversity, and robustness.
With UniLIP, improves multiple-choice accuracy by 20.93 points on familiar rules and 28.42 points on held-out compositions.
Raises familiar-rule scene satisfaction from 2.91% to 70.99%; results extend across several multimodal backbones.

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in off-road terrain is commonly achieved using hierarchical control and planning architectures that rely on explicit cost maps and one-way information flow from a high-level planner to a low-level controller, decoupling planning from the true execution cost experienced during control. We propose a hierarchical planning and control framework in which information flows bidirectionally, allowing the low-level controller to guide trajectory selection at the planning level. The highest level of the hierarchy is a Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control-style planner that determines optimal trajectories and passes these waypoints to a pretrained low-level reinforcement learning (RL) controller. Rather than drawing from an explicit cost map, our MPPI planner leverages the value function of the RL controller as an implicit cost representation. In this formulation, MPPI serves as a trajectory exploration mechanism, while the low-level controller's value function guides the search. To account for the distribution shift seen by the value function between training and evaluation, we propose an online policy evaluation process that adapts the value function to unseen driving experiences, and we demonstrate this adaptation in unseen off-road simulation environments. We evaluate our approach in a high-fidelity off-road driving simulator across a range of challenging terrain conditions and compare its performance against a baseline MPPI controller. The results demonstrate that our method achieves safer and more effective navigation to goal locations while eliminating the need for explicit cost maps and enabling tighter coupling between planning and control.
authors: Anoushka Alavilli, Raymond Song, Guanya Shi, Jeff Schneider
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between high-level planning and low-level execution in hierarchical off-road navigation.
Uses MPPI to explore trajectories, with the pretrained controller’s value function guiding trajectory selection.
Applies online policy evaluation to adapt the value function to unseen driving experiences and distribution shift.
Evaluated in a high-fidelity off-road simulator across challenging terrains against a baseline MPPI controller.
Reports safer, more effective goal-directed navigation while removing the need for explicit cost maps.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of our value-guided planning framework. We pre-train RL policies to provide both an actor πθ(s) and a value function Vϕ(s). MPPI samples candidate trajectories and evaluates them using a cost that combines goal progress with the negative value estimate, treating −Vϕ(s) as a control-aware cost. The selected trajectory is executed by the policy, and the resulting experience can be used to update the value function online. This enables planning to be guided by the expected performance of the controller without requiring an explicit cost map.

Fig. 3: Comparison of pitch and vertical jerk violations across all 64 evaluation trajectories for the MPPI baseline ((A), (B)), our algorithm ((C), (D)), and our algorithm with online adaptation ((E), (F)). Panels (A), (C), and (E) show pitch violations exceeding 0.4 rad (22.9◦), while (B), (D), and (F) show vertical jerk violations exceeding 10e−2 m/s3. The violations are colored by their severity and are no more than 0.7 rad. and 2 m/s3 for pitch and jerk respectively. The MPPI baseline includes an explicit pitch cost term, whereas our method is trained with a jerk penalty in the reward function. papers.abstract: Human handwriting is produced as an ordered sequence of pen movements, but an offline image keeps only the final ink. Handwriting trajectory recovery aims to restore the ordered stroke points and their pen-up/pen-down transitions. Existing image-trajectory pair datasets are recorded with digitizing tablets under controlled conditions, which limits writer coverage and stylistic diversity. Moreover, there is no benchmark that measures the visual grounding capabilities of general-purpose Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for the stroke trajectory recovery task. In this work, we introduce inkGround, a benchmark for stroke trajectory recovery from full-page, camera-captured handwriting. inkGround pairs 537 page images (~18.7k words, ~163k strokes) with reference trajectories produced by a pretrained offline-to-online model, filtered by OCR agreement, and verified by human raters. Because these references are pseudo-labels that represent one plausible pen trajectory, we also evaluate VLMs on the IAM-OnDB dataset, which provides recorded pen trajectories. We cast the task as text-conditioned point grounding: given a page image and a target word, the model must locate the word and output its ordered stroke points. Outputs are scored by trajectory fidelity (DTW, Chamfer distance), readability of the rendered strokes (Accurate Rate, Correct Rate), and style similarity. We benchmark four open-source and three frontier closed-source VLMs with a shared in-context prompt. Closed-source models, notably Gemini-3.1-Pro, produce legible trajectories close to the reference, and this ranking also holds on IAM-OnDB.
authors: Sidra Hanif
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 537 camera-captured handwriting pages containing about 18.7k words and 163k strokes.
Frames trajectory recovery as text-conditioned point grounding: given a page and target word, predict ordered stroke points.
Uses pseudo-label trajectories filtered by OCR agreement and human verification, with IAM-OnDB providing recorded-trajectory evaluation.
Evaluates trajectory fidelity, rendered-stroke readability, and style similarity across four open-source and three closed-source VLMs.
Closed-source models—especially Gemini-3.1-Pro—generate legible trajectories close to references, with the ranking replicated on IAM-OnDB.

papers.abstract: Clinical practice guidelines encode evidence-based recommendations as conditional decision flows, which makes them a natural source of process supervision for training reasoning models. Two properties of clinical reasoning make this supervision difficult to use. A decision flow consistent with a guideline does not by itself determine the correct answer for a given patient, which we call the path--answer gap, and several valid decision flows can support the same clinical decision, which we call path multiplicity. Current training approaches address parts of this problem. Answer rewards supervise the final decision, and process rewards computed against a reference flow supervise one valid decision flow per case. Supervised fine-tuning on annotated flows teaches guideline-consistent reasoning but constrains the model to one trajectory per case and can reduce answer accuracy. We introduce GUIDER, a method that jointly optimizes a decision flow controller and a reasoning policy. The controller learns to generate plausible decision flows from guideline-derived supervision, and the policy learns to generate a decision flow and a final answer for each patient case. GUIDER computes the process reward for the policy over several controller-generated flows, which accounts for path multiplicity, and gates this reward on answer correctness, which addresses the path--answer gap. Joint training allows the process supervision to evolve with the policy. On MedGUIDE, GUIDER with Qwen3-14B achieves 82.5 weighted accuracy and 73.5 guideline adherence, 3.3 and 3.1 points above the strongest clinical reinforcement learning baseline. With Qwen3-14B and Gemma4-12B backbones, GUIDER also improves over CRPO, MRPO, and FaithMed on the out-of-domain benchmarks AMEGA-LLM, RealMedQA, and CancerGUIDE.
authors: Gaurav Bhatt, Marinka Zitnik
bullets: Clinical guidelines provide process supervision, but valid paths may not uniquely determine answers and multiple paths may support the same decision.
GUIDER jointly trains a decision-flow controller and reasoning policy.
It evaluates policy reasoning over multiple controller-generated flows and gates process rewards on answer correctness.
On MedGUIDE with Qwen3-14B, it achieves 82.5 weighted accuracy and 73.5 guideline adherence, outperforming the strongest reported clinical RL baseline by 3.3 and 3.1 points.
The method also improves over several baselines on the out-of-domain AMEGA-LLM, RealMedQA, and CancerGUIDE benchmarks.

The policy generates its own decision flow and final answer from the patient case. GUIDER computes an answer-gated process reward from the agreement between the policy flow and the controller flows, and it optimizes the policy with GRPO and the controller with guideline supervision in a joint objective.

papers.abstract: Packing a 3D volume into a token sequence is not merely long-sequence modeling. Once the volume is packed, sequence order no longer encodes the geometry of the sample---so a positional mechanism indexed by sequence position can learn the memory layout rather than the object. This is a general failure mode for attention over packed geometric data. We introduce PACK3D, a local-global attention operator that separates memory layout from attention geometry. PACK3D keeps local neighborhood attention exact, compresses only distant context into contiguous 3D block summaries, and indexes every query-key interaction with axial RoPE on true token-grid coordinates rather than packed positions. Because the rotation is applied before a block is summarized, the query-to-summary logit remains a weighted sum of query-relative 3D displacements; compressed global context therefore stays spatially interpretable after packing, instead of collapsing to anonymous pooled content. We measure the failure mode directly. On a controlled synthetic task---train on one packing, change only the memory order of the tokens, hold the physical labeling rule fixed---learned positional embeddings and packed-sequence RoPE solve the training layout perfectly yet collapse under Morton, block-contiguous, and random repacking, while axial grid-coordinate RoPE stays exact throughout. The same coordinate system carries to real data: on Allen WTC-11 hiPSC microscopy, PACK3D improves over a parameter-matched 3D U-Net on the 15-structure joint task and over a matched learned-position local-global baseline, with controls isolating the coordinate system, not encoder capacity, as the source of the gain. A fused Triton implementation matches windowed-attention latency at 65k tokens while supplying the long-range context windowing cannot---so the operator is not only correct but trainable at scale.
authors: Amil Khan, Anantajit Subrahmanya, B. S. Manjunath
bullets: Packed sequence positions can encode memory layout rather than physical object geometry.
PACK3D combines exact local attention with compressed summaries of distant 3D blocks.
Axial RoPE uses true token-grid coordinates, keeping query-to-summary relationships spatially interpretable.
On a controlled repacking task, packed-position methods fail after reordering, while grid-coordinate RoPE remains exact.
On hiPSC microscopy, PACK3D improves over matched 3D U-Net and learned-position baselines; a fused implementation scales to 65k tokens with windowed-attention latency.

papers.selection_reason: Packed 3D attention with axial coordinate RoPE; core technical contribution is efficient local-global attention over geometrically structured 3D volumes.
papers.title: Geometry Matters in Packed 3D Attention

papers.abstract: Streaming federated learning (SFL) allows clients to train a shared model from continuously arriving data without retaining large local datasets. Such streams often exhibit temporal dependence, yet its effect on generalization remains poorly understood. In this paper we study the expected generalization gap of the aggregated model when client data follow Markov processes, using information-theoretic and rate-distortion techniques. Our framework accommodates heterogeneous Markovian dynamics across clients and distinguishes temporal dependence from information acquired during local learning. We establish bounds under cross-entropy loss, specializing them to Linear Next-Token Prediction (LNTP) and Self-Attention Next-Token Prediction (SANTP). These results quantify the effects of client count, communication rounds, sample size, data dimension, mixing time, and context length. In particular, they reveal a communication--generalization tradeoff: although frequent aggregation may help optimization, it can weaken generalization guarantees. They also suggest a potential advantage of distributed over centralized streaming learning under a fixed total data budget. Temporal dependence enters through the square root of the mixing time. By analyzing the history-state process, we obtain refined bounds with improved context-length dependence under suitable mixing conditions. Experiments on GPT-style language-model pretraining with TinyStories and real-world time-series forecasting illustrate how collaboration and communication frequency influence generalization under temporal dependence
authors: Masoud Kavian, Milad Sefidgaran, Youssef Attia El Hili, Malik Tiomoko, Abdellatif Zaidi
bullets: Models heterogeneous client streams as Markov processes and separates temporal dependence from information learned locally.
Uses information-theoretic and rate-distortion analysis to bound cross-entropy generalization, including LNTP and SANTP settings.
Identifies a communication–generalization tradeoff: more frequent aggregation may improve optimization but weaken generalization guarantees.
Bounds depend on client count, communication rounds, sample size, dimension, mixing time, and context length; temporal dependence scales through the square root of mixing time.
Experiments with GPT-style pretraining on TinyStories and real-world time-series forecasting examine collaboration and communication frequency.

papers.abstract: Self-distillation offers a way to improve reasoning models when a suitable external teacher is unavailable. However, common approaches rely on privileged information to construct a stronger self-teacher, limiting their use when only unlabeled prompts are available. In this paper, we introduce Weakening-Induced On-Policy Self-Distillation (WISD), which instead constructs a weaker counterpart of the original model and uses the contrast between the two as a training signal without requiring privileged information. We explore two ways to construct the weaker model: low-bit quantization and magnitude pruning. We evaluate WISD across diverse architectures and scales on mathematical and coding reasoning tasks. Across these benchmarks, quantization and pruning improve average accuracy over the original models by 4.0 and 5.5 percentage points, respectively, achieving state-of-the-art performance even without privileged information. Notably, pruning raises Qwen3.5-4B's accuracy from 57.7% to 70.5% on HMMT 2025 and from 39.1% to 56.7% on LiveCodeBench v6. Quantization raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B's accuracy from 68.5% to 74.6% and from 61.8% to 69.5% on the same benchmarks, respectively. These results establish WISD as a novel and effective self-distillation framework for large reasoning models.
authors: Yecheng Wu, Song Han, Han Cai
bullets: Addresses self-distillation when only unlabeled prompts are available and no stronger teacher can be constructed.
Creates weaker counterparts via low-bit quantization or magnitude pruning, then uses their contrast with the original model as the training signal.
Evaluated across multiple architectures and scales on mathematical and coding reasoning tasks.
Quantization and pruning improve average accuracy by 4.0 and 5.5 percentage points, respectively, and achieve state-of-the-art performance in the reported evaluations.
Reported gains include Qwen3.5-4B improving from 57.7% to 70.5% on HMMT 2025 with pruning, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B improving from 68.5% to 74.6% with quantization.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of WISD. (a) Prior self-distillation. Privileged information c, such as solutions, demonstrations, or feedback, strengthens the original model into a self-teacher. (b) WISD. We instead retain the original model as the stronger member and construct a weaker copy through training-free quantization or pruning. The frozen pair scores the same self-generated trajectories, and its token-level log-probability contrast provides cached supervision for a student initialized from the original model, without privileged information.

Figure 4. Token-level effects of WISD. Original-model trajectories illustrate a coverage check with quantization (a) and a zero-divisor check with pruning (b). Blue and orange indicate increased and decreased target probability relative to the behavior distribution. papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models have increased interest in interaction paradigms for video understanding. The evolution from offline to streaming and proactive interaction has gradually shifted models from passive responders toward more proactive agents that can decide when to answer. However, existing proactive paradigms typically assume that the information required to answer a query is complete, leaving models to only wait or answer. In the real world, however, information is often incomplete due to uncertainty from either the video or the user. In proactive paradigms, such uncertainty can cause the model to wait forever or generate highly hallucinatory responses. We therefore argue that proactive interaction should be redefined with a third action: ask, allowing models to actively ask for missing information. To study when and what models should ask before answering, we introduce AskStream, the first multi-turn benchmark spanning video and user uncertainty for streaming video understanding, with four task categories and eight subtasks. It contains 438 videos with 2,714 manually annotated frame-level time windows across three types: wait, ask, and answer. Across both multiple-choice and open-ended settings, even the strongest model attains only 52.18% on our proposed Ask-F1 metric, highlighting substantial limitations in proactive information seeking under uncertainty.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the memory footprint of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but lowering bit widths while maintaining task performance remains challenging. Existing work has used sensitivity estimates from calibration data to assign bit widths to different model components. However, using task success directly to guide mixed-precision allocation is underexplored because closed-loop evaluations are costly and the effect of quantizing one component depends on the precision of other components. To this end, we propose \textbf{QbD-VLA}, a task-guided mixed-precision quantization method that uses task success from short closed-loop evaluations to assign weight and activation bit widths while accounting for interactions between model components. Experiments covering four VLA models and all four LIBERO suites show strong task performance at average precisions of approximately 4 bits for weights and fewer than 6 bits for activations. On SIMPLER, the gain over uniform quantization is small. On a Franka Research 3 robot arm, simulation-selected allocations show no detected success-rate loss on X-VLA but fail on $\pi_{0.5}$. These findings support using task success to guide mixed-precision VLA quantization, while highlighting the need for real-world evaluation before deployment. Code is available at \href{https://github.com/jiuyixu25/QbD-VLA}{\texttt{github.com/jiuyixu25/QbD-VLA}}.
authors: Jiuyi Xu, Xiao Hu, Meida Chen, Song Wang, Yang Ye, Yangming Shi
bullets: PTQ can reduce VLA memory use, but selecting low bit widths without harming task success is difficult.
QbD-VLA guides per-component weight and activation precision using task success and accounts for interactions between components.
Across four VLA models and all four LIBERO suites, it maintains strong performance at approximately 4-bit weights and fewer than 6-bit activations on average.
On SIMPLER, it provides only a small gain over uniform quantization.
Simulation-selected precisions showed no detected loss for X-VLA on a Franka Research 3 arm but failed on π₀.₅, motivating real-world validation.

papers.abstract: Future planetary rovers will traverse steep, deformable terrain where slip, sinkage, and terrain deformation can threaten mobility. Although simulation can capture some wheel-soil effects, unmodeled deformable-terrain phenomena create sim-to-real gaps requiring deployment-time adaptation. Yet, rover operations leave little room for extensive trial-and-error. We introduce TERRA (Targeted Exploration for Reward-Relevant Adaptation), an online adaptation framework that efficiently seeks deployment data exposing task-relevant model errors and corrects them. TERRA adapts a simulation-trained world model with a reward-weighted prediction loss and trains a loss predictor to estimate where future performance-relevant errors are likely to occur, using this signal to guide exploration during MPC. In simulation, TERRA reaches approximately 90% slope-climbing success within five trials under severe out-of-distribution pretraining conditions, outperforming exploration baselines in reward, completion time, and energy to first success. On the ERNEST rover, TERRA recovers coordinated active-suspension locomotion on a deformable Mars-simulant slope within three to five real-world trials. Project website: https://terra-explore.github.io
authors: Jacob Levy, Arthur Bouton, Tristan D. Hassler, Hari Nayar, David Fridovich-Keil
bullets: Addresses sim-to-real gaps from unmodeled slip, sinkage, and terrain deformation while limiting costly trial-and-error.

In simulation, reaches about 90% slope-climbing success within five trials under severe out-of-distribution conditions.
On the ERNEST rover, restores coordinated active-suspension locomotion on a deformable Mars-simulant slope within three to five trials.

papers.abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), which aligns a student model's token-level distribution with that of its self-teacher prompted by privileged context, has emerged as a promising direction to mitigate reward sparsity in sequence-level post-training paradigms. However, OPSD often fails to achieve continuous performance gains during training. In this paper, we find that the model's limited self-teaching capability underlies this phenomenon by generating unreliable guidance on certain samples. To address this problem, we propose Teacher-Evolution Self-Distillation (TESD), which enables the self-teacher to generate rollouts and receive environmental feedback based on task correctness and context independence. First, using these rewards as training objectives, we perform teacher-oriented optimization to continuously enhance the model's self-teaching capability during distillation. Second, by estimating teacher guidance reliability from these rewards, we apply adaptive student-oriented optimization to down-weight samples with unreliable guidance. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and model scales show that TESD consistently outperforms representative token-level and sequence-level methods, highlighting the necessity of improving supervision quality in OPSD.
authors: Shufan Shen, Zhongni Hou, Chao Bi, Yufei Zhang, Guojun Yin, Shuhui Wang
bullets: OPSD can stagnate because its self-teacher produces unreliable guidance for some samples.
TESD trains the self-teacher with environmental feedback on task correctness and context independence.
It estimates guidance reliability and adaptively down-weights samples with weak supervision.
Experiments across multiple datasets and model scales show consistent gains over representative token- and sequence-level methods.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overall framework of TESD. Given an input query, the student first generates rollouts, which provide the privileged context for the self-teacher. Then, TESD optimizes the student and the self-teacher, respectively. For the self-teacher, it interacts with the environment and learns from the obtained rewards of correctness and independence. For the student, it is supervised by the logits of the self-teacher. The loss value is adaptively weighted by the teacher’s mean reward of the corresponding input query, which estimates the quality of teacher guidance.

papers.abstract: Autonomous far-range rocket landing is a challenging control problem because navigation, descent-rate regulation, attitude management, and fuel use must be coordinated in the presence of uncertain atmospheric and vehicle dynamics. This paper presents a curriculum-driven proximal policy optimization (PPO) framework for three-dimensional rocket landing in a stochastic environment incorporating altitude-dependent aerodynamic drag, wind shear, temporally correlated turbulence, discrete gusts, uncertain propulsion and aerodynamic parameters, thrust-vector misalignment, engine lag, actuator-gain variation, noisy observations, and command latency. Learning is organised into far-range approach, soft descent, and integrated landing stages. Policy transfer, critic warm-up after reward changes, rehearsal of earlier tasks, and progressive expansion of weather severity are used to support learning across these coupled phases. Across 100,000 evaluation episodes, the policy achieves 96,656 successful landings, corresponding to a success rate of 96.656\% and a 95\% Wilson confidence interval of 96.543--96.766\%. Success decreases from 98.84\% under zero-disturbance conditions to 88.07\% in the highest weather-severity band. Successful touchdowns exhibit small miss distances and low residual horizontal and vertical velocities. An exploratory logistic-regression analysis identifies mean wind speed as the strongest measured correlate of success, with initial distance, initial altitude, initial vertical velocity, and wind-shear exponent also associated with outcomes. The results quantify both the effectiveness of the learned policy over the evaluated disturbance distribution and the degradation that occurs under severe compound atmospheric conditions.
authors: Atin Chowdhury, Piyush Joshi
bullets: Addresses coordinated navigation, descent-rate, attitude, and fuel control for far-range landing under stochastic disturbances and model uncertainty.
Uses staged learning for approach, soft descent, and integrated landing, with policy transfer, critic warm-up, rehearsal, and progressively harsher weather.
Evaluated over 100,000 episodes: 96,656 successful landings, with success ranging from 98.84% in calm conditions to 88.07% under the most severe weather.
Successful landings generally have small position errors and low residual horizontal and vertical velocities.
Mean wind speed is the strongest measured correlate of success in an exploratory logistic-regression analysis.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) based on Transformer architectures have achieved remarkable performance across artificial intelligence tasks, but their computational cost remains a major bottleneck. Structured sparsification provides a promising approach to reducing this cost. In particular, $\ell_{1,\infty}$ projections can induce column-wise sparsity in model matrices, but existing proximal methods (Prox) typically require $\mathcal{O}(nm\log(nm))$ operations for matrices in $\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$, limiting their computational and energy efficiency. In this paper, we introduce Two-Stage Clipping (TSC), an efficient structured sparsification operator inspired by bilevel optimization. Rather than solving a bilevel optimization problem in the strict sense, TSC decomposes the computation into two successive stages. First, group-level quantities are projected to allocate the global sparsity budget and identify active groups. Second, the resulting values are used as group-wise clipping thresholds for the matrix coefficients. For square attention matrices ($n \times n$), the complexity of our TSC method is $O(n^2)$, which is linear in the number of matrix coefficients. We establish a theoretical bound on the discrepancy between TSC and the exact proximal projection and show on synthetic data that the additional Euclidean approximation cost remains small in practice. Extensive benchmarks demonstrate substantial runtime improvements over proximal baselines and validate the theoretical norm identities underlying the proposed construction.
authors: Michel Barlaud, Jean-Paul Marmorat
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of exact ℓ₁,∞ proximal projections, which typically require O(nm log(nm)) operations.
Uses two stages: project group-level quantities to allocate sparsity and identify active groups, then clip matrix coefficients using group-wise thresholds.
Runs in O(n²) for square attention matrices, linear in the number of coefficients.
Theoretical analysis bounds its discrepancy from the exact proximal projection, while synthetic experiments find small additional Euclidean cost.
Benchmarks report substantial runtime gains over proximal baselines and support the proposed norm identities.

papers.abstract: Linear attention and state space models (SSMs) offer efficient alternatives to softmax attention by maintaining a fixed-size recurrent state, but this design requires careful management to preserve useful historical associations and limit interference. The delta rule helps reduce interference through correction of the value associated with each key, but it does not explicitly account for how related value features are distributed across the state. We observe that a state $\boldsymbol{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_k\times d_v}$ can be viewed as a bank of $d_k$ addresses storing $d_v$-dimensional values. While a key-side read $\boldsymbol{S}^\top\boldsymbol{k}$ retrieves the value associated with $\boldsymbol{k}$, a value-side read $\boldsymbol{S}\boldsymbol{e}$ aggregates addresses whose stored value features match the selector $\boldsymbol{e}$. Based on this observation, we propose Dual DeltaNet (DDN), which extends Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) with a two-sided delta rule. The key-side delta rule reads with the current key to correct its associated value, while the complementary value-side delta rule reads with selected features of the current value to reorganize the addresses it occupies. We derive a chunkwise parallel training algorithm and a rank-2 recurrence that increases arithmetic intensity during inference. Compared with KDA, GDN-2, and Mamba-3, DDN achieves the strongest overall performance across language modeling, zero-shot downstream tasks, and retrieval, while incurring modest training and inference overhead relative to KDA. Code: https://github.com/ReichtumQian/DualDeltaNet
authors: Yixiao Qian, Yaxin Zhang, Song Chen, Jiaxu Liu, Shengze Cai, Chao Xu
bullets: Targets interference and poor organization in fixed-size recurrent states used by linear attention and SSMs.
Extends Kimi Delta Attention with complementary key-side and value-side delta rules.
Introduces chunkwise parallel training and a rank-2 recurrence for higher inference arithmetic intensity.
Reports strongest overall performance among DDN, KDA, GDN-2, and Mamba-3 across language modeling, zero-shot tasks, and retrieval.
Adds modest training and inference overhead compared with KDA.

papers.abstract: There is a fundamental contradiction between the desire for models that can generalize, and models that can continuously adapt to recent input with changing statistics. These conditions, captured in few-shot and continual learning settings, can bias or disrupt learned representations. This harms generalization to a broader context, leaving the model unable to overcome input variance. This paper proposes a solution based on the Complementary Learning System architecture (CLS), in which a Short-Term Memory (STM) delegates generalization to a slow, statistical Long-Term Memory (LTM). Delegation is achieved by working in a space of robust, generalized perceptions produced by the LTM. With this separation, the STM can focus on memorizing recent input and avoiding interference between memories. We show that on an image classification task, the resulting CLS model is more resistant to forgetting in a domain-incremental continual learning setting than a baseline ResNet LTM, and generalizes more effectively in a few-shot setting than other continual learners. In the continual setting, overall accuracy is slightly worse than existing continual learning models, but with a different mix of performance characteristics. Results analysis suggests that the model is limited by the representations and representational plasticity of the LTM. In future work, we will seek to address this by replaying STM memories to the LTM.
authors: David Rawlinson, Gideon Kowadlo
bullets: Addresses the tension between broad generalization and rapid adaptation to changing input statistics.
Uses a slow Long-Term Memory (LTM) to produce robust perceptions while a Short-Term Memory (STM) memorizes recent inputs with less interference.
On image classification, the model is more resistant to forgetting than a baseline ResNet LTM and generalizes better few-shot than other continual learners.
Overall continual-learning accuracy is slightly below existing continual-learning models, despite a different performance profile.
Performance appears limited by the LTM’s representations and plasticity; replaying STM memories into the LTM is proposed as future work.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Architecture of the proposed CLS model with a sparse, episodic (RL) Short-Term Memory (STM). The STM is an Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C) model. The actor produces a multiplicative bias output which gates the residual stream of the Long-Term Memory (LTM), a four-stage ResNet18 model adapted to CIFAR images. STM input includes previous bias output, post-bias LTM encoding and LTM classification logits. These accumulate in a buffer over each episode; the initial encoding is unbiased. The STM is rewarded for producing bias which improves the accuracy of LTM classification.

Figure 5: Continual learning results, with test set accuracy for each of the four fine-class sets plotted over the three training phases. Results are averaged over the seeds and orderings of fine classes 3, 4 and 5. Top row: Accuracy over the 4 test sets (1 & 2, 3, 4, 5). Middle row: Forgetting of any trained fine classes trained so far. Bottom row: Stability / plasticity tradeoff of each model.

Figure 4: Comparison and ablation STM variants. The RL-STM is compared to some competitive published models (FlyModel, SDMLP) and some simple alternatives such as ablation of various features (linear probe, sparse supervised STM without RL, LTM-only fine-tuning). The Nearest Class Mean (NCM) keeps a running mean of all input samples. The STM variants all consume the 512-dimensional encoding produced by global average pooling of stage 4, which is the input of the LTM’s own dense classifier. Only the RL-STM biases the LTM. Italics describe how each STM learns. The linear probe’s dense layer is initialized from the LTM’s.

Figure 1: Active perception within a Complementary Learning System could allow a STM to learn rapidly without needing to generalize. In this concept, generalization occurs within the LTM, which is manipulated by the STM to emit stable, familiar representations relevant to the task. Using the generalization ability within the LTM, the STM could even immediately reason about completely novel stimuli, if they are expressed in terms the STM can already understand.

Figure 2: The CIFAR-100 dataset has 20 “coarse” classes and 5 “fine” sub-classes of each coarse class, yielding a total of 100 distinct classes. Next, individual pairs of coarse classes are selected for continual and few-shot experiments using the unseen fine classes 3, 4 and 5.

papers.abstract: A memory can be outdated for present-day reasoning yet indispensable for reconstructing the past. Relevance-based retrieval overlooks this tension: semantic relevance, evidence-grounded validity, and query-specific eligibility are distinct. We propose CALM, a conflict-aware lifecycle memory governance framework that decouples persistent memory preservation from query-time admission. CALM converts heterogeneous records into evidence-grounded memory cells, updates validity and lifecycle states using support, conflict, and dependency signals, and admits query-appropriate evidence through training-free or learned gating informed by temporal applicability. Across LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo with Qwen and GPT backbones, CALM outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving the best overall accuracy. Compared with simple filtering and reranking, query-conditioned admission further improves evidence selection. Conflict-blocking and robustness analyses show CALM suppresses erroneous retrieved memories while retaining useful evidence. Historical-reconstruction experiments demonstrate that preserving superseded records supports accurate earlier-state reasoning without compromising current-state answers.
authors: Chang Li, Xianhao Ou, Xinyan Ma, Hao Li, Haoyuan Xu, Jiafeng Liang, Xiaohan Wang, Jiajun Chai, Guojun Yin, Ming Liu
bullets: Separates persistent memory preservation from query-time evidence admission.
Represents heterogeneous records as evidence-grounded memory cells with lifecycle states.
Updates memory using support, conflict, dependency, and temporal-applicability signals.
Query-conditioned admission improves evidence selection over simple filtering and reranking.
Evaluations show strong overall accuracy, conflict suppression, and accurate historical reconstruction without harming current-state answers.

papers.abstract: Large audio language models (LALMs) can process speech directly, but it remains unclear how well they use the non-lexical acoustic information that speech carries. We study this question through pain, using TAME-Pain, which contains pain-neutral Harvard sentences and spoken pain ratings recorded at different self-reported pain levels. We introduce HEAR, a four-stage diagnostic framework that traces pain-related information from the speech signal to the model's prediction, and apply it to seven closed-source and open-weight LALMs. On the Harvard sentences, where pain can only be inferred from the voice, all models perform at chance level, and same-speaker references or few-shot examples improve balanced accuracy by no more than six points. On the spoken ratings, the same models reach 87.5-99.7% balanced accuracy. Layer-wise probing of open-weight LALMs shows that pain can be decoded from early audio representations (74.1% balanced accuracy for binary prediction and 45.0% for three-class severity), but that this information, along with most pain-associated acoustic cues, decreases in deeper layers. In an acoustic perception test, weaker models cannot distinguish even large changes in these cues, whereas stronger models can but still fail to infer pain. Finally, we recover pain-related acoustic cues and directly reinject them as structured text into the prompt, which improves pairwise pain prediction by up to 32 points. These results indicate that current LALMs encode paralinguistic information in early layers that is largely unavailable when the model produces its answer.
authors: Wenqi Li, Xiangjue Dong, Sulaiman Vesal
bullets: On pain-neutral Harvard sentences, where pain is conveyed only through voice, all seven LALMs perform at chance; references and few-shot examples help by at most six balanced-accuracy points.
On spoken pain ratings, models achieve 87.5–99.7% balanced accuracy, suggesting performance depends strongly on task and available linguistic information.
HEAR traces pain information from audio to prediction: pain is decodable in early representations but declines in deeper layers, along with most associated acoustic cues.
Stronger models can perceive large acoustic changes yet still fail to infer pain; reinjecting recovered cues as structured text improves pairwise prediction by up to 32 points.

Table 11: Construction and validation of the audio perturbations. We select ten representative acoustic attributes spanning the four parameter groups across 88 features. Each manipulation aims to shift its target eGeMAPSv02 parameter(s) while leaving parameters of other feature families unchanged (parameters within one family are inherently correlated). Shifts are measured on 24 recordings, each from a different training speaker, as the perturbed recording minus its matching null resynthesis (same tool at zero strength), divided by that parameter’s mean within-speaker SD over the training speakers. Target shift is the median of this shift over the 24 recordings, oriented so that a leading − on a target parameter means it is expected to decrease, and averaged over the target parameters when a cue has several. Range: for each cue and direction, the candidate strength whose Target shift is closest to ±1 SD. A setting passes calibration if |Target shift| ∈ [0.5, 1.5] and none of the 24 recordings fails processing; passing settings are shown in bold, and non-bold settings are excluded. Pairs: test recordings (760 in total, from 10 held-out speakers) for which both perturbed versions of a cue were processed successfully; the effect of each bidirectional cue is estimated from the + versus − version of the same recording. Cues marked † were excluded from the analysis because more than 5% of their 1×/2× pairs showed no achieved change in the target parameter (jitter 10.0%, shimmer 8.9%, breathiness 9.3%). In total we generated 18,240 test-set versions for the 17 passing settings and 7 null resyntheses (4 failed, all Pauses), 2,280 2× WORLD versions, and 4,560 round-trip null resyntheses for the PSOLA and speech-rate cues. a Each sample is multiplied by (e/ẽ)k−1, where e is the smoothed Hilbert envelope, ẽ its median and k the exponent; k > 1 exaggerates and k < 1 flattens loudness fluctuations. b Non-speech stretches detected by WebRTC VAD are resampled to the given multiple of their length; speech is left unchanged. c One of the 24 calibration recordings also failed processing. d 760 minus 4 recordings whose perturbation failed and 1 recording whose + and − versions had identical target values.

papers.abstract: Smart wheelchairs are robotic devices that gather information from the surroundings and allow people to safely drive through various environments. They usually rely on the interpretation of high-level user's intentions, typically decoded through human-robot interface (HRI) or brain-machine interface (BMI). However, navigating in an unknown environment and accurately understanding user commands remain significant challenges. Misinterpretation of commands or the environment can lead to user frustration, distrust of the system, or even unsafe situations. In this paper, we present a novel Multi-Layer Navigation System (MLNS) for a smart wheelchair that enables navigation in unknown environments while interpreting and safely contextualizing user's intentions even in the case of limited and faulty commands. The stack relies on a Virtual Sensors-Driven Potential Fields (ViSPF) method for obstacle detection that accounts for the wheelchair's actual size, a Model Predictive Control (MPC) module for trajectory generation, and an open-vocabulary computer vision algorithm for target identification. Finally, a system based on Priority Queue (PQ) was implemented for target selection. We validated our system on a real smart wheelchair with experiments involving 10 participants without disabilities, including scenarios with faulty input interfaces. The results demonstrate the robustness and effectiveness of our system in real-world environments, proving its potential for practical applications in assistive technologies.
authors: Piero Simonetto, Anna Polato, Francesco Pasti, Muhammad Rameez ur Rahman, Sebastiano Vascon, Nicola Bellotto, Emanuele Menegatti, Stefano Tortora, Luca Tonin
bullets: Addresses unsafe navigation and command misinterpretation in smart wheelchairs with restricted input interfaces.
Combines virtual-sensor-driven potential fields for size-aware obstacle detection, MPC for trajectory generation, and open-vocabulary vision for target identification.
Uses a priority-queue mechanism to select navigation targets and contextualize user intentions.
Validated on a real smart wheelchair with 10 participants, including faulty-interface scenarios, demonstrating robust real-world operation.
Scope: experiments involved participants without disabilities; broader clinical validation is not described.

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement requires models not only to acquire useful training experience, but also to decide when their current experience has ceased to be useful. Existing methods often focus on what experience to generate next, while paying less attention to when fresh experience should be introduced. Many also construct training targets through self-consistency or majority voting, making supervision depend on the model's own uncertain predictions. We address these two questions separately: training dynamics determine when to acquire new experience, while the answers to new tasks remain independently checkable. A-RSI monitors reward variation and accuracy in training logs to refresh a task pool when its learning signal declines, without consulting validation or test scores. A static library of model-authored programs produces multimodal questions and derives their reference answers; we specify the task-generation contract, automatically verify chosen properties of the reward and refresh rules, and separately audit the generated answers. The training loop uses no external training examples or human-written answer labels. On the primary eleven-benchmark suite, A-RSI raises the performance average from 57.77 to 61.05 with 800 fresh tasks.

papers.abstract: Multi-source millimeter-wave (mmWave) observations offer an opportunity to learn human representations reusable across sensing tasks. However, sparse detections and multipath effects make these observations unstable, challenging existing point cloud pretraining methods. We propose PT$^3$, a prototype-guided self-supervised pretraining framework for mmWave human point clouds. PT$^3$ represents local states in spatial regions as sparse compositions of shared prototypes and learns their temporal evolution through autoregressive prediction. Observation consistency further stabilizes representations under radar perturbations. After pretraining on unlabeled sequences from multiple sources, the same frozen encoder supports action classification, dense point generation, joint pose estimation, and future motion prediction on datasets not used for pretraining. Across these tasks, PT$^3$ outperforms the compared pretraining baselines and achieves competitive or superior performance to task-specific models.

bullets: Addresses sparse detections and multipath effects that destabilize mmWave point-cloud representations.

A frozen pretrained encoder supports action classification, dense point generation, joint pose estimation, and future motion prediction across unseen datasets.
Outperforms compared pretraining baselines and is competitive with or better than task-specific models.

papers.abstract: The growing volume of end-of-life products has intensified the need for automated disassembly, yet hook-type connections remain challengin: their orientations vary, they deform under load, and their geometry is hidden, so vision alone cannot identify a feasible non-destructive disassembly direction. This work proposes a constraint-aware reinforcement learning framework that infers feasible extraction directions online from contact forces. The policy is trained in a robot-agnostic, object-centric simulation on a simplified peg-in-hole pair and deployed zero-shot on a physical robot, where it transfers to real connections with unseen, multi-stage constraint structures. Because instantaneous contact forces are noisy and locally ambiguous, the policy is coupled with a particle filter belief that provides the policy with temporally integrated directional information and reduces redundant exploratory motion. The approach is validated on four real-world tasks, from peg-in-hole pairs to the inner propeller and front cover of an end-of-life air-conditioning unit. The full method achieves success rates of 100%, 100%, 90%, and 75% with the highest path efficiency on every task, and raises the success rate on the air-conditioning cover from 45% to 75% relative to a policy trained without the belief. These results indicate that force-driven reinforcement learning can enable disassembly without product-specific models or demonstrations.
authors: Nadeen Elhadad, Takuya Kiyokawa, Kensuke Harada
bullets: Addresses hook connections whose orientations, deformation, and hidden geometry make vision-only disassembly unreliable.

Trained on a simplified peg-in-hole simulation and deployed robot-agnostically without product-specific models or demonstrations.
Validated on four real tasks, achieving success rates of 100%, 100%, 90%, and 75%, with the highest path efficiency in each.
The belief component improved air-conditioning-cover success from 45% to 75% and reduced redundant exploration.

Right: During deployment, a single-system condition is adopted where the gripper and grasped object are assumed to move as a rigid composite body and the wrist-measured forces equal the constraint force on the object [18]. Using proprioceptive information, force sensor data, and particle filter belief specifics, the policy drives a Cartesian impedance controller on the physical robot.

Fig. 2: Training Environment: Simulated contact interaction under misaligned and aligned extraction actions. When the commanded action direction (cyan arrow) deviates from the groundtruth extraction axis (left), the peg engages the surrounding constraint geometry, producing visible contact forces (gold contact markers). On the other hand, when the action direction is more aligned to the groundtruth axis (right), contact decreases until it disappears at complete alignment. This illustrates that contact forces carry direct information about the feasible motion direction, which the proposed method exploits during learning.

papers.abstract: Why do multilingual language models generalize across languages even without shared vocabulary? The Platonic Representation Hypothesis posits that models trained on different data, objectives, and modalities converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. Extending this intuition to representations inside a single multilingual model, we propose the Relational Identifiability Hypothesis: relations in a shared world can promote entity alignment by ruling out alternative cross-lingual correspondences, making corresponding entities more likely to become directly readable without an additional transformation. We test this hypothesis in a controlled bilingual Transformer whose two token-disjoint languages describe the same modular-arithmetic world. We find that the languages can develop a shared answer subspace without aligning corresponding numbers. Cross-lingual alignment emerges selectively when the available relations constrain number correspondences: subtraction makes zero task-level identifiable, inducing selective alignment, while an order-sensitive operation produces broad alignment across numbers. These patterns predict success in zero-shot cross-lingual transfer. Together, our results show that relational structure in a shared world can promote entity alignment and enable transfer.
authors: Frederick Riemenschneider, Anette Frank
bullets: A controlled bilingual Transformer models two token-disjoint languages describing the same modular-arithmetic world.
The languages can share an answer subspace without directly aligning corresponding numbers.
Relations constrain possible cross-lingual correspondences: subtraction selectively aligns zero, while an order-sensitive operation broadly aligns numbers.
The resulting alignment patterns predict successful zero-shot cross-lingual transfer.
The study is limited to a controlled synthetic arithmetic setting.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn to predict representations rather than pixels, offering a compact way to model how visual scenes evolve. We ask whether this predictive objective improves closed-loop control when a vision-language-action (VLA) policy already uses V-JEPA features. We call our JEPA-conditioned flow policy family SaiVLA-JEPA. It combines a vision-language model with a diffusion transformer action expert and receives features from a frozen V-JEPA encoder. Two lightweight auxiliary heads predict future representations during training and are omitted at inference, leaving the action sampler unchanged. We compare policies without JEPA features, with current JEPA conditioning, and with additional future supervision on 10,030 paired LIBERO-Plus episodes. Current JEPA conditioning reaches about 82.5% success versus 71.6% without JEPA, while future supervision provides no detectable aggregate gain at the evaluated training budget. We separately evaluate SaiVLA-JEPA-TCA, which adapts latent context, and SaiVLA-JEPA-TPA, which adapts selected parameters. The context-retry gain is a system-level result under a larger attempt budget; parameter adaptation shows no consistent advantage over the frozen policy and target controls. These results motivate assessing latent-prediction objectives through paired closed-loop rollouts rather than latent loss alone.
authors: Rufeng Xiao (VLA Research Team, Synthoid.ai), Ruihao Xiao (VLA Research Team, Synthoid.ai), Wei Chen (VLA Research Team, Synthoid.ai), Xinhai Sun (VLA Research Team, Synthoid.ai)
bullets: Evaluates whether predicting future latent representations improves closed-loop VLA control.
SaiVLA-JEPA combines a vision-language model, diffusion-transformer action expert, and frozen V-JEPA features.
Two auxiliary future-prediction heads are used only during training and do not alter inference-time action sampling.
On 10,030 paired LIBERO-Plus episodes, current JEPA conditioning achieves about 82.5% success versus 71.6% without JEPA.
Context retry can improve system-level performance under a larger attempt budget, while parameter adaptation shows no consistent advantage.

figures.caption: Figure 1: SaiVLA-JEPA architecture and its FutureJEPA training variant. Current images feed the frozen VJEPA and VLM encoders; projected JEPA tokens join the native prefix and action tokens in the repeated DiT action expert, while VLM features enter through per-block cross-attention and robot state is encoded separately. Four Euler evaluations produce a 16-action chunk. For FutureJEPA, JEPA-token hidden states from the shared DiT trunk feed residual heads at offsets 4 and 16, supervised by detached targets from a frozen V-JEPA encoder. This auxiliary branch is absent at inference. CurrentJEPA omits future supervision; BaseFlow also omits JEPA conditioning.

Figure 2: SaiVLA-JEPA-TCA context pathway. The frozen SaiVLA-JEPA policy applies the context adapter at each of four Euler evaluations using fixed e = [m; u]. After every executed four-action window, a frozen observer computes a latent prediction loss and two gradient steps update only m and u for the next action chunk. The initial attempt uses zero context and defers fitting until it ends. On failure, m is retained with decay or evidence gating while u is cleared. Network weights remain frozen online.
Figure 3: Success and cost under bounded retries. Left: cumulative success with up to five attempts, compared with the one-attempt baseline. Right: mean cumulative environment steps per case.

papers.abstract: Behavior Cloning (BC) of expert controllers for multiscale dynamical systems is challenging: state variables evolving at widely separated timescales induce highly nonlinear couplings that a shared latent space may fail to adequately represent, degrading closed-loop generalization. We propose Structured Representation Learning for Behavior Cloning (SRLBC), an architecture designed to leverage the physical knowledge of multiscale systems in which slow state variables, fast (stiff) state variables, and predictable exogenous inputs evolve at different timescales. On 500 long-horizon roll-outs of a pressurized water reactor (PWR) load-following benchmark -a high-dimensional, stiff industrial system with challenging safety constraints -and across 20 training seeds, separated embeddings systematically outperform shared embedding baselines on cumulative cost, imitation accuracy and constraint satisfaction. The resulting standalone policies approach NMPC closed-loop performance at a computational cost 15 times lower on average. Since standalone policies still leave a few percent of trajectories infeasible, we embed the learned policies in a safety-augmented approximate NMPC framework, in which the optimizer is only called when the predicted input sequence is not certified as safe. This yields controllers still 6.8 times faster than the NMPC controller on average, with a feasibility (i.e., constraint satisfaction) of at least 99.8% for all architectures, SRLBC retaining the lowest closed-loop cost. Under distribution shift, standalone BC policies degrade sharply: SRLBC degrades the least, and once safety-augmented, it retains a feasibility above 98% with the lowest closed-loop cost. Beyond the quantitative results, Jacobian-based sensitivity analysis shows that the resulting controller relies on a sparse and less redundant set of latent features, each attributable to a single group of physical variables, and aligned with the physical timescale decomposition of the system.
authors: Perceval Beja-Battais (CB), Alain Grosset{\^e}te (CB), Nicolas Vayatis (CB)
bullets: Shared latent spaces struggle with nonlinear coupling in multiscale dynamical systems, motivating timescale-aware representation learning.
SRLBC separates embeddings for slow states, fast stiff states, and predictable exogenous inputs.
On a PWR load-following benchmark, separated embeddings improve cumulative cost, imitation accuracy, and constraint satisfaction over shared-embedding baselines.
Standalone SRLBC policies approach NMPC performance at 15× lower average computational cost; safety-augmented policies are 6.8× faster while achieving at least 99.8% feasibility.
Under distribution shift, standalone policies degrade, but SRLBC degrades least and retains over 98% feasibility when safety-augmented.

papers.abstract: Multi-Object Tracking (MOT) requires localizing multiple objects and maintaining their identities over time. Recent query-propagation trackers carry target-specific representations across frames and update them with current-frame image features, yet identity association remains difficult when visually similar targets overlap or cross. During such interactions, current-frame query updates may contain components directed toward nearby active tracks, which may affect identity association in later frames. To investigate this issue, we analyze track-query updates preceding identity switches (IDSWs), where the same target is assigned a different track ID. Our analysis shows that (i) propagated track-query representations change more abruptly before IDSWs, (ii) current-frame updates have larger positive projections along directions toward other active tracks, and (iii) bounding-box intersection over union (IoU) retrieves the counterpart track involved in a subsequent IDSW with high recall when that track remains active before the switch. Motivated by these findings, we propose Test-time Track-Query Calibration (TQC), a training-free and gradient-free method for query-propagation trackers. TQC calibrates the tracker output before propagation using a bounded correction estimated from update components directed toward nearby active tracks. It requires only track-query representations and bounding boxes available during inference, without retraining or architectural modification. Across nine DanceTrack and SportsMOT test settings, TQC improves HOTA and AssA in all settings and IDF1 in eight, with an average HOTA gain of +0.38 and limited inference overhead. Controlled variants on six validation settings further show that TQC's correction direction yields more consistent HOTA improvements than alternative directions with matched correction norms.
authors: Riku Inoue, Shogo Sato, Yu Mitsuzumi, Kazuhiko Murasaki, Tomoyasu Shimada, Takashi Sano
bullets: Problem: Similar targets that overlap or cross can cause track-query updates to absorb information from neighboring tracks, leading to identity switches.

Analysis: Track-query representations change more abruptly before ID switches, with updates showing stronger directional alignment toward other active tracks; IoU often identifies the counterpart track.
Method: TQC applies a bounded, training- and gradient-free correction to tracker outputs before propagation using track-query representations and bounding boxes available at inference.
Results: Across nine DanceTrack and SportsMOT test settings, TQC improves HOTA and AssA in all settings and IDF1 in eight, with an average HOTA gain of +0.38 and limited overhead.
Scope: The method targets query-propagation trackers and relies on nearby active tracks remaining available for calibration.

papers.abstract: Few-shot action recognition (FSAR) requires representations that expose discriminative motion dynamics from only a few labeled videos. Recent trajectory-based methods leverage long-term point tracks for explicit temporal correspondence, but often treat trajectories as carriers of sampled visual features or summarize their motion with compact 2D displacement-based descriptors. We instead view an action as the ordered evolution of 2.5D trajectory states and their local geometric interactions. Based on this view, we introduce GeoTRAM, a geometry-aware trajectory state modeling framework for FSAR. GeoTRAM lifts sparse tracks into 2.5D trajectories, where StateMotion models ordered intra-trajectory state evolution and RelMotion captures state-conditioned local interactions through time-varying relative geometry and motion. Quality-filtered spectral sampling provides more reliable trajectory initialization; complementary semantic, motion, and depth cues are separately refined and preserved for joint spatio-temporal modeling; action-guided reweighting and top-$\rho$ trajectory selection support complementary frame- and trajectory-level matching. Experiments on five FSAR benchmarks demonstrate strong gains on the motion-centric Something-Something benchmarks while maintaining competitive performance on more appearance-driven benchmarks and a favorable accuracy--efficiency trade-off.
authors: Zhiqi Miao, Marko Haralovi\'{c}, Stanislav Levendeev, Sarvesh Angadi, Jannatul Ferdous, Dan-Cristian Ploesteanu, Jiapan Guo, Estefan\'{i}a Talavera
bullets: Targets the challenge of recognizing actions from only a few labeled videos, especially when motion dynamics are discriminative.
Lifts sparse point tracks into 2.5D trajectories and models both ordered intra-trajectory evolution and time-varying inter-trajectory geometry.
Uses quality-filtered spectral sampling, separate semantic/motion/depth refinement, and action-guided trajectory selection for matching.
Shows strong gains on motion-centric Something-Something benchmarks and competitive results on appearance-driven benchmarks.
Reports a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off, with scope spanning five FSAR benchmarks.

Semantic, depth, and motion cues undergo cue-specific temporal refinement before concatenation and joint spatio-temporal modeling. Finally, dual-CLS-guided reweighting suppresses less action-relevant trajectories, followed by the complementary frame-level prototype matching and top-ρ trajectory-level instance matching.

papers.abstract: The large-scale digitisation of medieval manuscripts creates a growing need for automated iconographic indexing. We evaluate two complementary paradigms for this task on 9,735 full-folio images annotated with 2,333 TIMEL concepts: generative Vision-Language Models (VLM) and supervised discriminative classifiers (SDC). The VLM experiments evaluate fine-tuning, structured JSON decoding, taxonomybased candidates generation, and deterministic reranking. The discriminative experiments evaluate flat, hierarchy-aware, and patch-attention heads over a frozen DINOv3 encoder. Our results highlight key functional differences: ML-Decoder (SDC) achieves the strongest overall retrieval performance (precision@1 of 0.696, MRR of 0.806), with loss calibration (Asymmetric Loss) serving as the primary performance lever. While SDCs provide superior precision and reliability within a closed vocabulary, VLMs offer strong semantic generalization and broad taxonomic coverage, particularly through structured JSON targets and verify-calibrate reranking (hierarchical F1 of 0.559). Furthermore, model behavior strongly depends on concept abstraction: SDCs excel at perceptually grounded descriptive concepts, whereas VLMs provide useful hypotheses for complex interpretative scenes. Finally, we find that enforcing explicit hierarchy within model architectures limits coverage compared to spatial feature aggregation. Overall, rather than competing approaches, SDCs and VLMs emerge as complementary components for future hybrid indexing systems combining structured retrieval with exploratory annotation assistance. As a methodological contribution, we define the soft F1 metric to provide a taxonomy-aware evaluation that credits semantically close predictions based on lowest common ancestors.
authors: Vincent Jolivet (ENC, CJM), Lucas Terriel (ENC), Chahan Vidal-Gor{\`e}ne (CJM, ENC)
bullets: Evaluates generative VLMs and supervised discriminative classifiers on 9,735 folio images annotated with 2,333 TIMEL concepts.
ML-Decoder achieves the strongest retrieval performance, with precision@1 of 0.696 and MRR of 0.806; Asymmetric Loss is the main performance lever.
VLMs show broader taxonomic coverage and semantic generalization, especially with structured JSON targets and verify-calibrate reranking.
Classifiers perform best on perceptually grounded concepts, whereas VLMs better support hypotheses for complex interpretative scenes.
The approaches are complementary: the study proposes hybrid systems and introduces taxonomy-aware soft F1 evaluation.

papers.abstract: Complex Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering (TKGQA) involves more than retrieving facts: the timestamp or validity interval of one fact can constrain the search for another, while multiple intervals may jointly determine the answer. Existing single-agent TKGQA methods typically investigate these facts within a single reasoning context, where evidence from different event histories can become interleaved and distractors can misdirect subsequent retrieval. Distributing investigations across agents can separate event-specific evidence into distinct contexts, but effective collaboration must still be learned because question decomposition, subtask investigation, and evidence synthesis are interdependent. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{Co}-Evolving \textbf{S}elf-Play \textbf{T}imeline \textbf{A}gents (CoSTA), which organizes facts into navigable timelines, delegates investigations to workers, and uses a coordinator to synthesize their original timestamped observations. CoSTA initializes a shared policy through role-conditioned distillation and jointly optimizes both roles through co-evolving self-play with final-answer rewards. Across three benchmarks, CoSTA achieves state-of-the-art overall performance, with particularly strong gains on complex multi-fact questions, while its compact variants outperform the evaluated closed-source LLM agents.
authors: Haikun Liu, Zhichao Yan, Shaoru Guo, Jiawei Gu, Victor Gutierrez Basulto, Jiapu Wang, Ru Li

Achieves state-of-the-art overall results across three benchmarks, especially on complex multi-fact questions; compact variants outperform evaluated closed-source LLM agents.
