papers.abstract: Robotic grasping relies on large manually annotated datasets, which are costly to create. We introduce a straight-skeleton-based algorithm for generating two-finger grasp keypoints and identifying regions suitable for stable, feasible grasps. Our automated pipeline produces consistent grasp annotations without human intervention. We also propose the Skeleton-based Generative Grasp Convolutional Neural Network (SkelGG-CNN), a 4-DoF architecture that learns geometric grasp features from skeleton-based guidance. To extend auto-labeling to 6-DoF grasping, we develop a generalized quasi-3D skeletonization algorithm that operates directly on point clouds. Using automatically generated 4-DoF labels, SkelGG-CNN achieves accuracies of 95.42%, 96.55%, and 97.1% on Jacquard V1, Jacquard V2, and Cornell, respectively. On the GraspNet novel split, 6-DoF auto-labeling achieves an average precision of 18.33, comparable to state-of-the-art model-based approaches. In simulation, the 6-DoF method achieves success rates of 98.4% on Dex-Net and 89.1% on EGAD!. Real-world experiments with a Delta parallel robot show success rates of 97.4% on single household objects and 95.0% in cluttered scenes, outperforming state-of-the-art methods without domain adaptation. The 4-DoF pipeline adapts across environments and produces annotations approaching human-level precision, enabling efficient training of lightweight models on small datasets. The generalized 6-DoF method provides scalable, geometry-aware annotations for cluttered 3D scenes.
authors: Ali Sabzejou, Farbod Azimmohseni, Mehdi Tale Masouleh, Ahmad Kalhor
bullets: Generates two-finger grasp keypoints and stable, feasible grasp regions using straight-skeleton geometry.
Introduces SkelGG-CNN, a skeleton-guided 4-DoF model, and a generalized quasi-3D skeletonization method for point-cloud-based 6-DoF labeling.
Reports 4-DoF accuracies of 95.42%–97.1% across Jacquard and Cornell, and 6-DoF average precision of 18.33 on the GraspNet novel split.
Achieves simulated 6-DoF success rates of 98.4% on Dex-Net and 89.1% on EGAD!, with real-robot success rates of 97.4% on single objects and 95.0% in clutter.
The approach supports small-dataset training and cluttered 3D scenes, with scope demonstrated on the reported benchmarks and a Delta robot.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the proposed method. The pipeline begins with the simulation environment, where RGB-D images are captured from a set of 3D meshes sourced from the Dex-Net dataset. The subsequent stages show the details process of the straight skeleton-based grasp pose estimation algorithm. After this process, the generated grasp poses are used to create the SkelGG-CNN model labels. The skeleton heatmap is generated during the polygon offsetting phase of the algorithm, adding geometric features to the model.

(Left) The input object point cloud is partitioned into overlapping horizontal cross-sections (80% overlap) orthogonal to the z-axis. papers.abstract: Search-based machine-learning (ML) agents improve a solution by writing candidate programs, executing them, and keeping the best. Execution gives the search reliable feedback, but a single run can take hours, and most runs end in programs the agent discards. Recent agents try to save these runs by letting a large language model act as a world model that predicts how each program would perform. However, a wrong prediction feeds the search false information. We argue that an agent does not need to predict the outcome of execution, only the decision that execution would support. We propose World Reward Models (WRMs), which learn from real execution results to choose directly which candidate will perform better, without predicting any intermediate outcome. We prove that a selector which predicts execution from the same inputs cannot outperform the best direct selector, that predicted outcomes add an error which can make a likelihood-trained world model prefer the worse program on every instance, and that cross-entropy on executed winners drives a WRM toward the optimum. Our WRM, ForeCritic, adapts a 9B typed decision model to 5k executed program pairs. On 12,438 held-out pairs from 26 ML tasks, it picks the better program 79.4% of the time, while general-purpose LLM judges reach 53--62%, and its probabilities are calibrated. Inside AIDE, ML-Master, and ForeAgent, it cuts mean task time by 4.4--7.5 times while keeping their mean scores within 0.01 or raising them.
authors: Yuxiao Lee, Zherui Yang, Fan Liu, Hao Liu
bullets: Search-based agents waste substantial time executing programs that are ultimately discarded.
WRMs learn from executed comparisons to select the better candidate directly, avoiding error-prone intermediate outcome prediction.
Theoretical results show direct selection can outperform outcome-based world modeling, while winner-based cross-entropy training approaches the optimal selector.
ForeCritic selects the better program 79.4% of the time on 12,438 held-out pairs across 26 ML tasks, versus 53–62% for general-purpose LLM judges.
Integrated into three agents, it reduces mean task time by 4.4–7.5× while maintaining or slightly improving mean scores.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models (UMMs), which can process and generate diverse modalities within a single framework, have recently emerged as a powerful paradigm. However, when these models undergo continual learning on multiple tasks across different modalities, their learning and forgetting dynamics remain poorly understood. In this paper, we systematically investigate how architectural design and adaptation method shape intra-modal learning and cross-modal interference between the generation and understanding sides. Specifically, we report three findings. First, the severity of cross-modal interference decreases with the degree of modality-specific parameter isolation. Second, a within-model asymmetry: the generation side of a UMM is markedly more fragile than its understanding side. Third, what post-training adds is the first to be forgotten: purely post-training capabilities such as personalized generation collapse by 84\% to 90\%, while pretraining capabilities remain stable. Together, these results clarify how parameter isolation and post-training fragility shape UMMs' learning and forgetting dynamics, offering a starting point for developing continually evolving UMMs.
authors: Xinrui Wang, Zhihao Chen, Jia Tang, Alexandra Gomez-Villa, Bartlomiej Twardowski, Joost van de Weijer, Songcan Chen
bullets: Greater modality-specific parameter isolation reduces cross-modal interference.
The generation side is substantially more fragile than the understanding side.
Post-training capabilities, such as personalized generation, are forgotten first, while pretrained capabilities remain stable.
The findings provide design guidance for building continually adapting multimodal models.

papers.abstract: Monitoring a model's chain of thought (CoT) is useful for safety only if the final answer depends on the written steps. Prior measurements use natural tasks where true reasoning is unknown. We measure it against an exact ground truth on a synthetic box-swap task where every intermediate state is known. We replace one step inside a model's own chain with a wrong but valid state and check whether the answer follows the edit. We evaluate 25 open-weight models--Qwen3 (0.6B-14B, base and post-trained), Gemma 3 (1B-12B), Llama 3 (1B-8B), and 8 OLMo 2 checkpoints--on 7,200 items each. We find five results: (1) Reliance rises with size and saturates. In Qwen3, answer reliance rises from 16-18% at 0.6B to 97-100% at 14B; a logistic in log N fits well (R^2 = 0.89), and Gemma 3 and Llama 3 follow this trend. (2) Capability is the main driver. Across all models, reliance and step accuracy correlate at r = 0.99; equally capable models are equally reliant, regardless of family. (3) Size still matters at matched correctness. On problems solved correctly before the edit, reliance increases with size among capable models (rho = 0.80, p = 0.002). (4) Post-training does not change reliance. Base and post-trained Qwen3 differ by at most 0.03 from 4B upward; a large gap at 1.7B matches a large capability gap. (5) No model up to 14B solves the task internally. Without written steps, every capable model is at chance once a problem has four or more swaps. OLMo 2 checkpoints never become capable, making the training-token axis a limitation. On tasks requiring step-by-step computation, scale makes the chain of thought more load-bearing, supporting CoT monitoring in this regime.

bullets: Reliance on edited reasoning steps rises with model size and then saturates, reaching 97–100% for 14B Qwen3 models.

Base and post-trained Qwen3 models show nearly identical reliance from 4B parameters upward.

No tested model internally solves sufficiently complex tasks without written steps; the findings are limited to this synthetic step-by-step setting and do not cover models that remain incapable, such as OLMo 2 checkpoints.

papers.abstract: Humans routinely consume multimodal content, where textual and visual information is naturally interleaved. Although Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) can jointly generate text and images, multimodal interleaved generation remains largely underexplored. Progress in this area is hindered by two key limitations: (1) the lack of well-defined interleaved generation tasks and corresponding training data, and (2) the absence of fine-grained evaluation protocols that can reliably diagnose model performance across different capability dimensions. To this end, we present IntReal, comprising two complementary components: IntReal-100K, a real-world dataset of multimodal interleaved samples spanning four major categories, and the IntReal Evaluation Suite, which evaluates model performance across seven complementary dimensions using specialized expert models, enabling coarse-to-fine diagnosis. Extensive experiments validate our evaluation suite through low inter-metric redundancy (max pairwise absolute Spearman's $\rho \leq 0.42$ ), high agreement with human judgments (83.3% accuracy), and strong consistency across different expert evaluators (Spearman's $\rho > 0.9$ ), supporting the complementarity and reliability of our metrics. By benchmarking four families of UMMs, we show that IntReal Evaluation Suite reveals distinct strengths and weaknesses across models. Post-training experiments demonstrate the utility of IntReal-100K for improving interleaved generation and further show that training unimodal generation can also benefit interleaved generation. These findings suggest that interleaved generation can benefit from modality-specific optimization, rather than requiring joint text-image training at every stage.

Results suggest modality-specific optimization can benefit interleaved generation without joint text-image training at every stage.

papers.abstract: Repeating transformer layers can improve language model performance without adding parameters. However, the added computational depth increases both forward and backward computation costs during training. Training such models requires choosing a backward window that controls how many final layer repetitions retain gradients during backpropagation. Longer windows improve per-token learning efficiency but increase per-update cost, while shorter windows reduce per-update cost but sacrifice per-token efficiency. Understanding which window performs better requires examining different training budgets. Prior work compares backward windows across computational budgets. When training budgets increase, it remains unclear whether the same window continues to perform best. We measure how the relative performance of two windows shifts as training budgets grow. Our method isolates per-token efficiency by training both windows on identical data, and compares complete training recipes at approximately equal training time at each budget. Results show that shorter windows lose much of their advantage as budgets grow. Controlled experiments show that both benefits decrease at larger budgets, with a greater decline in the benefit of extended training. Backward window comparisons depend on the available budget, and the preferred window among the tested candidates can change as the budget grows.
authors: Jiarun Shen, Xiao Li
bullets: Repeating transformer layers improves performance without increasing parameter count but raises training computation costs.
The backward window controls how many final layer repetitions receive gradients, trading per-token efficiency against per-update cost.
The study compares two windows under matched data and approximately equal training time across increasing budgets.
Both windows’ benefits decline at larger budgets, especially the benefit of extended training.

papers.selection_reason: Training looped language models with different backward windows directly concerns LLM architecture and training efficiency.
papers.title: Deeper Backpropagation or More Updates? Training Looped Language Models Across Budgets
papers.tldr: The best backpropagation window for looped language models depends on the available training budget, with shorter windows losing their advantage as budgets increase.

papers.abstract: LLM-guided evolutionary search iteratively selects existing programs, uses LLMs as mutation operators to generate a new program, and evaluates it to guide subsequent search. To preserve diversity and reduce the risk of premature convergence, it often adopts the island model, in which groups of programs, called islands, evolve separately. However, this structure alone does not guarantee distinct search directions, as islands may start from similar programs or converge toward similar solutions during evolution. This suggests that diversity must be considered throughout the search process, from initializing islands with distinct programs to developing island trajectories and sharing discoveries across islands. To this end, we propose HoliDivEvolve , a holistic approach to establishing and effectively utilizing island diversity throughout evolutionary search. Specifically, we introduce diverse initialization to establish different initial programs, trajectory adaptive island selection to allocate computation based on current score, recent growth, and the remaining search budget, and growth adaptive migration to share alternative ideas across islands. Experiments across diverse benchmarks show that HoliDivEvolve achieves competitive performance on most evaluated tasks. We further conduct controlled analyses to examine how our design choices affect search behavior and final performance.
authors: Seockbean Song, Youngsik Yoon, Sungjae Lee, Siwei Wang, Wei Chen, Jungseul Ok
bullets: Island models alone may fail to maintain distinct search directions because islands can begin similarly or converge toward similar solutions.
The approach uses diverse initialization to create distinct starting programs.
Trajectory-adaptive island selection allocates computation using current score, recent growth, and remaining search budget.
Growth-adaptive migration shares alternative discoveries across islands.
Experiments across diverse benchmarks show competitive performance on most evaluated tasks, with controlled analyses of design choices.

papers.abstract: To solve problems in 3D space rather than merely describe images, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) need 3D spatiotemporal reasoning: reconstructing 3D geometry from occluded 2D views, anticipating physical dynamics, and executing precise, closed-loop actions. Prior studies test passive VQA on static images or symbolic planning, requiring no execution or supplying privileged coordinates while ignoring collision, statics, and timing. We introduce SpaceAct, an interactive benchmark evaluating 3D spatiotemporal reasoning via closed-loop physical action and active perception, with SAPA, a Spatiotemporal Active-Probing Agent framework. Built on interlocking bricks and mechanical puzzles, it has 108 verified instances across 36 task families in six categories, without privileged coordinates, and diagnostic modes (+plan, +state, no-camera, blind, L7 levers). In brick-bridging or aperture-threading, models rotate the camera to resolve occlusion, read in-scene rulers, output 6-DoF poses under swept-collision and statics checks, and self-correct via split-screen rollback feedback (dynamic tasks freeze time during deliberation and give five strobe frames). Across 10 frontier MLLMs on the 44 hardest instances, scores span 4.8-79.1 (seven solve at most 27.3% of 6-DoF tasks); for the top three, a reference plan (+plan) closes 44% of the gap while leaving collisions at 5.2 per episode, whereas adding exact 3D state (+state) closes 90% and cuts collisions to 0.5; for four others, +plan lifts the mean score from 10.9 to 35.3 and +state to 81.8; and 46% of failures are collision or observation loops. SpaceAct and SAPA advance evaluation to closed-loop physical interaction, showing that even with a valid plan, MLLMs remain bottlenecked by 3D visual grounding and action refinement, while offering a testbed for active multi-view exploration and explicit 3D grounding.
authors: Chenglong Shi, Zekai Yuan, Yue Song, Jon Pu, Will Wu
bullets: Benchmarks 3D spatiotemporal reasoning through active perception and physical action rather than passive image question answering.
Includes 108 verified brick and mechanical-puzzle instances across 36 task families, with no privileged coordinates and diagnostic settings for planning, state access, vision, and control.
SAPA uses camera rotation, in-scene measurement, 6-DoF action output, collision/statics checks, and feedback-based self-correction.
Across 10 MLLMs, performance ranges from 4.8 to 79.1; many models solve few 6-DoF tasks, and 46% of failures involve collision or observation loops.
Providing exact 3D state greatly improves performance and reduces collisions, while reference plans help less, highlighting 3D grounding as the main bottleneck.

figures.caption: Figure 4: The SpaceAct task suite and the SAPA active-perception agent. (a) The six task categories contain 36 task families and 108 verified instances in total (44 in the main matrix). (b) At each turn, the input comprises actively acquired RGB observations with rulers, task rules, the available tools, and a dynamic memory (a bounded history window plus a persistent note). A single MLLM call per turn jointly performs 3D localization (𝒢vis), physics identification (ℐphys), multi-step planning (𝒫plan), and frame-aware control (ℰctrl), returning a JSON response with a rationale, a memory update (note), and 1–5 tool calls; the four capabilities are a diagnostic decomposition, not four separate calls. The tool calls execute sequentially in swept substeps of at most 0.05 stud or 0.5°, without a motion planner, under collision/topology and static-equilibrium checks, and the simulation clock is frozen while the model deliberates. (c) Observations are RGB images with rulers and no coordinates; dynamic tasks provide five frames from the same viewpoint at 0.25-s intervals. The first violation truncates execution and skips the remaining calls, returning a 1280 × 640 split-screen rollback view (left: the violating contact; right: the last valid state). (d) The diagnostic conditions grouped by the operator of Eq. (3) that they replace or stress.

Figure 2: SpaceAct's four design principles (conceptual illustration). Active 3D grounding: the agent reads in-scene rulers and moves the camera to resolve occlusion, with no privileged coordinates. Physics-constrained action: the full swept motion path is checked for collisions and structures for static equilibrium, without a motion planner. Controlled-time dynamics: simulation time pauses while the model deliberates and during camera actions, and advances only with timed physical actions; five sameview frames expose the motion. Controlled failure diagnosis: split-screen rollback feedback pairs the contact with the last valid state, and separately run +plan and +state conditions isolate the bottleneck.

Figure 3: Inputs of the three controlled-diagnostic conditions (schematic), each run separately on the same instances. All conditions share the RGB observation, task and rules, history, and note; the model generates every action, and all actions run under the same execution protocol. +plan adds a reference high-level plan (turns and regions; distances are left to the model). +state supplies the reference plan as well, plus the coarse layout as text and the exact 3D pose of the payload at every turn.

papers.abstract: When a person declined our robot's invitation to play, Alice turned her shoulder away and said "No worries, it's all good." Only after a brief pause did she drive off. The words and gestures were plausible but their order changed the message. In another episode, Alice informed a host that his visitor had arrived---while the visitor stood right beside him. Both came from a three-year ROS 2 HRI consortium that integrated large language and vision models as they emerged. Today's foundation models give robots broader capabilities to perceive their surroundings, reason about situations and generate behavior. Yet capability alone does not ensure that a changed situation shapes the action that reaches a person. Evidence may never be acquired, or a purpose or constraint may fail to survive planning and execution. A system may even report Success when an action no longer serves its intended purpose. Drawing on the consortium's engineering experience, we develop five design lessons about attention, knowledge, commitments, embodied timing and action authority. We then introduce TRACE, a lightweight review that changes one interaction premise, follows it to a decision or enforcement boundary, and produces an actionable architecture finding. A bounded analysis of a published LLM-generated behavior-tree system illustrates how an available clarification mechanism can go unused. The engineering lesson is to preserve accountability boundaries, not the computational pipelines that once exposed them.
authors: Eliahu Khalastchi (The College of Management Academic Studies)
bullets: Real HRI failures included poorly ordered speech and gestures, and announcing a visitor who was already present.
The authors identify five design lessons: attention, knowledge, commitments, embodied timing, and action authority.
TRACE reviews what happens when one interaction premise changes, tracing its effects to a decision or enforcement boundary.
A bounded analysis shows that an available clarification mechanism in an LLM-generated behavior tree may go unused.
The central engineering lesson is to preserve accountability boundaries rather than merely reusing computational pipelines.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) show strong performance in radiology report generation (RRG) and medical visual question answering (Med-VQA), producing free-form clinical descriptions and answers from medical images. However, they may generate clinically meaningful statements that lack visual evidence or contradict image content. We refer to these errors as visually irrelevant hallucinations and investigate them at the phrase level. We propose CLEAR (Counterfactual Localized Evaluation of Alignment and Response), a model-agnostic post-hoc framework for phrase-level hallucination risk estimation. CLEAR decomposes generated responses into visually assessable clinical phrases. For each phrase, phrase-conditioned grounding identifies a candidate visual region, which is selectively perturbed by a localized counterfactual intervention. CLEAR characterizes the intervention using two complementary auditing cues: response cues, capturing semantic and clinically meaningful changes in the generated response, and alignment cues, measuring changes in image-phrase compatibility. These cues are normalized and jointly modeled to estimate phrase-level hallucination risk. Across four datasets spanning RRG and Med-VQA, CLEAR outperforms state-of-the-art hallucination detection baselines across multiple medical and general-purpose VLMs. On MIMIC-CXR, CLEAR improves AUPRC from 85.10% to 90.23%. Its effectiveness is further validated on a GT-derived controlled VIH benchmark. These results establish visually irrelevant hallucination as an important fine-grained reliability failure mode in medical VLMs and demonstrate the value of model-agnostic visual-support auditing for more trustworthy multimodal clinical generation.
authors: Ke Zou, Nan Zhou, Tao Yang, Meng Liu, Linchao He, Zehui Liao, Ling Huang, Guangren Huang, Yidi Chen, Yi Zhang, Hu Chen, Huazhu Fu
bullets: Medical VLMs can produce clinically meaningful statements that are visually unsupported or contradict the image.
CLEAR is a model-agnostic, post-hoc framework that decomposes outputs into visually assessable phrases.
It grounds each phrase to a candidate region, perturbs that region, and combines response-change and image–phrase alignment cues to estimate hallucination risk.
Across four radiology report generation and Med-VQA datasets, CLEAR outperforms existing detection baselines across multiple VLMs.
On MIMIC-CXR, CLEAR raises AUPRC from 85.10% to 90.23% and is additionally validated on a controlled benchmark.

papers.abstract: Quadrupedal manipulators can extend their workspace through whole-body interaction, but task-planning agents' capabilities remain limited by their available controllers. We present ELEVATE, a framework that uses persistent failures during task-program refinement to identify and acquire missing whole-body control capabilities. When these failures suggest a missing physical capability, a coding agent formulates and iteratively refines a reinforcement-learning problem, specifying behavior-specific rewards, curricula, and termination conditions. Validated controllers are added to the capability library and composed with existing controllers to retry the task. Starting from a single pretrained loco-manipulation controller, ELEVATE autonomously acquires controllers for wall-supported elevation, supported manipulation, and wall descent across a sequence of seven simulation tasks. These controllers are reused in subsequent reaching and object-manipulation tasks. On the five tasks beyond the initial controller's workspace, ELEVATE achieves mean success rates of 98.4%-100% across five independent runs, while coding-agent baselines with a fixed controller library fail to complete these tasks. The synthesized task programs, together with the acquired controllers, also transfer to a physical quadrupedal manipulator without real-robot training or fine-tuning, achieving 18/20 successes in rack retrieval and 16/20 in floor-to-rack placement. Videos and demonstrations are available at https://agentic-quad-elevate.github.io/public/.
authors: Shiqi Liu, Radu Corcodel, Ding Zhao
bullets: Uses persistent task-program failures to detect missing physical capabilities.
A coding agent formulates and iteratively refines reinforcement-learning problems with behavior-specific rewards, curricula, and termination conditions.
Validated controllers for wall-supported elevation, supported manipulation, and wall descent are added to and composed from a capability library.
Across five tasks beyond the initial controller’s workspace, it achieves 98.4%–100% mean success in simulation and transfers without real-robot training or fine-tuning.
On hardware, it succeeds in 18/20 rack-retrieval trials and 16/20 floor-to-rack placement trials.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student using teacher predictions on student-generated responses. Some methods insert teacher-written segments, or bridges, but disagree on how to train on those tokens. We compare no loss, forward KL and reverse KL on identical trajectories using Qwen3-1.7B as student and Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as teacher. We separate gradients by which model wrote each token. Under our short training runs and BF16 inference, pre-specified tests detected no added accuracy benefit from teacher text as context or as a training target. A one-paragraph bridge after the student's first paragraph is only 2.7% of the tokens and contributes a small gradient nearly orthogonal to the student-token gradient. In this main comparison, the three loss treatments gave similar gradient directions and were statistically equivalent in accuracy within a +/-5 percentage-point margin. An exploratory pilot placing the bridge where failed responses disagreed most with the teacher suggested a benefit from teacher-token loss. A pre-specified replication did not confirm this, and fourfold weighting showed no significant accuracy benefit. Two limitations bound these findings. Among the tested amounts of training on fixed responses, gains peaked after four updates before the student increasingly failed to stop generating. None of the tested online training variants met the criteria for stable stopping and improved accuracy. Our evaluations used BF16 inference, which rounds away most of the small weight changes. When evaluated in exact FP32, the tested replication models frequently reached the response-length limit. Our accuracy findings therefore concern BF16 inference; they do not establish that teacher-token supervision is generally unnecessary.
authors: Leran Chen, Zhiyuan Yao, Lingnan Kong
bullets: The study compares no loss, forward KL, and reverse KL for teacher-written bridge tokens on identical student-generated trajectories.

The three loss treatments had similar gradient directions and statistically equivalent accuracy within a ±5 percentage-point margin.
An exploratory disagreement-based bridge placement suggested benefit from teacher-token loss, but replication and fourfold weighting found no significant accuracy gain.
None of the tested online variants achieved both stable stopping and improved accuracy; conclusions are specific to BF16 inference and short training runs.

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling improves large language models through additional computation, but how to adapt the topology of internal computation to individual inputs remains underexplored. Existing approaches largely fix recurrent or parallel architectures during training, or reconfigure frozen models along a single structural axis. We introduce SelfMorph, which makes computational shape an input-dependent inference-time decision. It unifies the original forward path (BASE), serial reuse of a layer span (REPEAT), and local branching and merging of perturbed hidden states (BRANCH) in a unified space parameterized by type, location, and intensity. Since they offer complementary benefits rather than uniform dominance, we use a lightweight selector that reads the backbone's depth-wise hidden state trajectory on the prompt to choose a morphology before response generation. We train the selector by distilling utility-based distribution from offline morphing that jointly account for task performance and computational cost. Evaluated on three LLMs spanning 4B-27B, SelfMorph achieves a 8.06% mean relative improvement on five in-distribution benchmarks and 4.45% on four unseen benchmarks. It achieves the strongest performance in 24 of 27 settings. These findings identify input-adaptive computational topology as a complementary axis of test-time scaling beyond generating more tokens. Our code is available at https://github.com/creator-xi/SelfMorph.

The selector is trained by distilling utility distributions that balance task performance and computational cost.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have spurred growing interest in temporal knowledge graph question answering (TKGQA). Most existing methods rely on semantic retrieval augmented generation (RAG), which suffers from fundamental limitations in complex temporal reasoning. On the one hand, semantic-based RAG methods struggle to capture the multi-hop causal knowledge required for complex temporal reasoning. On the other hand, these methods introduce excessive redundant knowledge, trapping LLMs in spurious reasoning chains that potentially result in erroneous answers. To address these problems, we propose a Temporal Causal Chain-guided RAG (TCC-RAG) to retrieve a concise yet sufficient set of causal knowledge to support complex temporal reasoning. Specifically, we reformulate the temporal knowledge graph into a multi-view causal cue graph, with causal cues inducing connections that explicitly encode temporal evolution and causal dynamics. Based on the causal cue graph, we construct a query-specific temporal causal chain to guide the retrieval process, enabling the model to focus on a concise set of causally relevant knowledge. Finally, we introduce a causal evidence filter to refine the retrieved knowledge, ensuring its causal consistency with the underlying temporal logic of the query. Experiments show that TCC-RAG achieves substantial performance gains of 10.72% and 8.40% on two TKGQA benchmarks, and delivers a remarkable 62.97% improvement for multi-step temporal reasoning.
authors: Xinxun Zhang, Yuxiang Wang, Shanshan Feng, Jun Zhang, Tieyun Qian, Binhang Yuan, Kai Yin, Xiao Yan, Jiawei Jiang
bullets: Targets the limitations of semantic RAG in multi-hop temporal-causal reasoning and its redundant, misleading retrieved knowledge.
Reformulates temporal knowledge graphs as multi-view causal cue graphs encoding temporal evolution and causal dynamics.
Builds query-specific temporal causal chains to guide retrieval toward sufficient, causally relevant knowledge.
Uses a causal evidence filter to enforce consistency with the query’s temporal logic.
Reports performance gains of 10.72% and 8.40% on two TKGQA benchmarks, including a 62.97% improvement in multi-step temporal reasoning.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: The framework of TCC-RAG. (a) Temporal facts are organized into a Temporal Event Graph (TEG) and two temporally sorted indices: the Subject Causal Cue Index (SCCI) and Object Causal Cue Index (OCCI). (b) NER and LLM extraction ground query entities through matching and consistency checking. Relation, cue, and role parsing then guide view routing and temporal chain retrieval. (c) The Causal Evidence Filter removes equivalent duplicates and selects a sufficient subset of query-consistent facts. (d) The LLM reasons over the filtered evidence to generate answers. When structured retrieval yields no facts, semantic retrieval provides fallback candidates that also pass through the filter.

papers.abstract: Sparse-view cone-beam computed tomography is widely used for fast, low-dose volumetric imaging and lesion localization in dentistry and image-guided interventions, but it introduces severe artifacts. Feed-forward Gaussian methods transfer the reconstruction cost to training and decode each coordinate from projection-aligned features and neighboring anchors. However, information from the whole scan is written only when the field is constructed and cannot be retrieved during coordinate decoding, leaving the volume inconsistent within the scan. This is a common limitation of such methods: once the field is fixed, decoding uses only local features and reconstruction quality drops substantially. We propose SparseTokenGS, a Gaussian-based method for sparse-view cone-beam computed tomography reconstruction via a reusable token pool. Anchor Token Fusion and Point-Token Attention query this shared pool at the anchors and at the query coordinates, respectively. The local Gaussian prior is retained, and the volume is reconstructed in one forward pass, without per-scan optimization or a projection-domain loss. On three public chest and dental datasets, SparseTokenGS achieves the highest reconstruction performance among the compared methods. On clinical dental scans, reconstruction from only six projections reaches 29.51 decibels in peak signal-to-noise ratio and a structural similarity of 0.842 against the full-view reference, and off-the-shelf tooth-and-pulp segmentation keeps these structures separable for root-canal localization. Experiments on volcanic rock and chicken show performance after same-object adaptation. A reusable token pool gives feed-forward reconstruction a mechanism that keeps scan-wide context available through decoding and can benefit future rapid clinical lesion localization and analysis. The code is available at: https://github.com/FrankDengAI/SparseTokenGS.
authors: Zihan Deng, Zhenzhen Gong, Yujie Liu, Jiaxin Gong, Dingkun Liu, Kexian Xie, Yixing Huang, Peng Jin, Tianye Niu, Zhisheng Wang, Fenglin Liu, Hongming Shan, Lequan Yu
bullets: Targets severe artifacts in fast, low-dose sparse-view CBCT, where local-only decoding can produce inconsistent volumes.
Uses a reusable token pool queried by Anchor Token Fusion and Point-Token Attention, while retaining a local Gaussian prior.
Reconstructs volumes in one forward pass without per-scan optimization or a projection-domain loss.
Achieves the best reconstruction performance among compared methods on three public chest and dental datasets.
With six projections on clinical dental scans, reaches 29.51 dB PSNR and 0.842 SSIM; tooth and pulp remain separable for root-canal localization.

In (b), each anchor queries the token pool and a zero-initialized residual is added to its local feature. In (c), a coordinate network embeds the query, and the view feature, the neighboring Gaussian feature, and the point-token feature are concatenated and mapped to one intensity.

papers.abstract: 3D reconstruction from single-view sports broadcast is a pivotal capability for automated analytics and immersive AR/VR replays, yet notoriously ill-posed due to difficult-to-calibrate moving cameras and depth ambiguity. Unlike widely studied racket sports, team sports such as volleyball feature unpredictable multi-contact sequences and high altitude jumps. These dynamics categorically invalidate the standard planar projection assumptions relied upon by existing methods. To resolve these limitations without 3D training supervision, we propose a complete, physics-grounded pipeline tailored to monocular broadcast volleyball. First, we include a correction module to the perspective drift induced by ground-plane projection by coupling temporal jump spotting with Newtonian interpolation for 3D player placement. Second, for 3D ball trajectory estimation, we design a dedicated sub-trajectory segmentation architecture alongside a collision-matching algorithm. By anchoring physical equations to reconstructed 3D hand vertices, we lift noisy ball 2D detections into a spatiotemporally coherent 3D scene. Evaluations on multi-camera benchmarks demonstrate our approach significantly reduces 3D spatial drift compared to 2D-reprojection baselines.

Evaluations on multi-camera benchmarks show reduced 3D spatial drift versus 2D-reprojection baselines.

The blue modules highlight the contributions introduced in this paper.

papers.abstract: Discretizing continuous actions into discrete skills using methods like VQ-VAE has emerged as a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation. However, quantization errors yield a suboptimal distribution for the skill prior, degrading its performance. While reinforcement learning offers a path for refinement, its direct application faces unstable encoder updates and a granularity dilemma in importance sampling. To address these challenges, we introduce Cascaded Skills Optimization (CSO), a two-stage post-training framework. First, Rejection-Sampling Supervised Fine-tuning aligns the model's observation-to-skill mapping with the distribution of successful online trajectories via supervised fine-tuning. Second, with the observation encoder frozen, Skills Policy Optimization computes an independent, clipped importance ratio for each complete skill, enabling stable and efficient updates. With a lightweight QueST-style policy, CSO raises overall LIBERO success from 80.1% to 97.5%, improves performance on RoboTwin2.0, and achieves 61.0% success across five physical single-arm tasks. Additional comparisons with FAST, discrete BEAST, and fixed-buffer IQL further validate the effectiveness of our two-stage post-training strategy.
authors: Zhiyuan Xiang, Xiang Deng, Wanjie Tao, Xu Chen, Zhao Jielun, Weili Guan
bullets: Addresses performance degradation from quantization errors in learned skill priors.
Uses rejection-sampling supervised fine-tuning to match observation-to-skill mappings with successful online trajectories.
Freezes the observation encoder and applies clipped, skill-level importance ratios for stable policy optimization.
Raises LIBERO success from 80.1% to 97.5%, improves RoboTwin2.0 performance, and reaches 61.0% success across five physical single-arm tasks.
Evaluations against FAST, discrete BEAST, and fixed-buffer IQL support the effectiveness of the two-stage strategy.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The architecture and data flow of our proposed CSO framework. Stage 1 (R-SFT): The initial policy is executed to collect trajectories, and successful trajectories are stored in a replay buffer. The observation-to-skill policy is then fine-tuned on this curated dataset using a supervised objective; the action tokenizer and decoder remain fixed. Stage 2 (SPO): With the encoders now frozen, the policy collects groups of trajectories. The SPO algorithm then updates the skill prior with a skill-level policy gradient based on terminal group-relative advantages.

papers.abstract: Large language models are typically adapted to a task either by placing knowledge in the input context, which keeps it external and re-encodes it on every call, or by fine-tuning, which internalizes it but demands a costly round of optimization per task. We aim to internalize the knowledge carried by a context directly into model parameters, without per-task optimization and without keeping the context in the input at inference time. To this end, we propose CLIK, a context-conditioned parameter generator that maps a given context to LoRA parameters for internalizing knowledge in a single forward pass through a Transformer encoder with cross-attention, requiring no test-time gradient updates. Once the generated LoRA is inserted into a frozen base model, the model answers downstream queries from the query alone, having internalized the context into its weights rather than re-reading it. Because the adapter depends only on the context, it is generated once and reused for every query on the same document, so the cost of reading that document is amortized across queries. On document question answering, CLIK substantially improves over the no-context base model and outperforms existing hypernetwork-based generators, while remaining behind a base model that reads the context directly, and it carries over to multi-turn dialogue without any multi-turn-specific training. Analysis further shows that the context-dependent part of the generated adapter concentrates in a compact and specific substructure.
authors: Xinhao Zhong, Mengxuan Wu, Chonghua Liao, Linxi Xie, Ruicheng Feng, Yanpei Guo, Hao Tan, Jiaxin Hong, Jason Li, Panpan Zhang, Ziheng Qin, Qinglin Lu, Yuzhang Shang, Tongliang Liu, Damian Borth, Haggai Maron, Yongxiang Hua, Zhixiang Wei, Jian Hu, Yunfei Wu, Xing Sun, Xin Li, Haoyu Cao, Zhangyang Wang, Kai Wang
bullets: Targets the cost of repeatedly encoding long context while avoiding task-specific fine-tuning.
Uses a cross-attentive Transformer encoder to map context directly to LoRA parameters.
Generates the adapter once per document and reuses it across downstream questions and dialogue turns.
Improves substantially over the no-context base model and existing hypernetwork generators, but remains below direct context reading.
Finds that context-specific information is concentrated in a compact substructure of the generated adapter.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of CLIK. A frozen language model encodes the context, and a learned ELMo-style weighting of its all-layer hidden states conditions a trainable generator that produces a context-specific LoRA adapter in a single forward pass. The adapter is injected into the same frozen backbone, which then answers the question from a context-free prompt (the student). We train the parameter generator by distilling an in-context teacher, the identical frozen model that reads context and question together, into this student. The objective is a temperature-scaled KL divergence between the teacher and student next-token distributions over the shared answer tokens. The backbone is frozen and shared across all paths, and only the generator is trainable. Gradients (dashed red) flow back through the injected adapter to the generator alone.

Figure 3 Multi-turn evaluation of CLIK on the SQuAD, ROPES, and DROP datasets, comparing the single-turn setting against two multi-turn scenarios that differ in how conversational state is propagated. Top (Dynamic KV cache): the base model accumulates a KV cache across turns while the LoRA generated from the initial context is kept fixed. Bottom (Dynamic LoRA): the KV cache is discarded and CLIK regenerates the LoRA parameters at each turn from the updated context. Both scenarios improve over the single-turn baseline without any multi-turn-specific training, but neither has a per-turn cost that is independent of the history (Table 7).

Figure 1 Three ways to supply external knowledge to a frozen LLM. Context in Prompt: re-injecting the context as text incurs high token cost. Context in Parameter: fine-tuning each context into a LoRA incurs high computational cost. Context-conditioned Parameter Generator (ours): a generator maps each context to a LoRA in a single forward pass, free of both test-time optimization and context in the input.

Table 1 Main results on the single-hop and multi-hop question-answering benchmarks with Qwen3-4B-Instruct. papers.abstract: Producing long-form videos from narration requires interdependent decisions that remain coherent across shots. Existing agentic editors often use multi-stage workflows driven by general models, leaving the quality-cost trade-off of compact, task-adapted policies unclear. We address this gap with WeVisCut, a long-form script-to-video system that connects tool execution with policy learning. Its agent harness maintains shared production state so that tool feedback informs subsequent decisions and repairs. Because finished videos do not expose these decisions, our four-stage data pipeline combines editing inversion with verified replay to turn recovered editing intent into executable supervision. Applied to 3,750 finished videos, this pipeline yields over 130K training examples. We use this supervision to train a single 9B policy that coordinates production and recovers from failures within the same harness. Moreover, we introduce a 100-task benchmark and five metrics assessing editing quality and delivery reliability. Under a shared tool environment, WeVisCut substantially outperforms its base model and achieves comparable performance to Claude Opus 5 while using nearly 33x fewer generated tokens per successful output minute. It also outperforms task-matched native editors on our proposed metrics.

Introduces a 100-task benchmark with five metrics for editing quality and delivery reliability.
Outperforms its base model and task-matched native editors, matching Claude Opus 5 with nearly 33× fewer generated tokens per successful output minute.

papers.abstract: Reliable box manipulation requires successful placement without damage, which depends on maintaining sufficient contact force without excessive loading. We hypothesize that per-finger force feedback improves manipulation reliability relative to open-loop finger commands. To this end, we present Finger External-Force Estimation from Proprioceptive SignaLs (FEEL), an uncertainty-aware residual method that estimates per-finger external force magnitude from proprioceptive histories. Our method combines a calibrated virtual-spring estimate with a residual distribution predicted by a Mixture Density Network (MDN) and requires no dedicated contact sensors during deployment. The estimated force is used for continuous per-finger adaptation, while predictive uncertainty is evaluated as an empirical signal of ambiguity in proprioceptive force estimation. Across ten fingers and contact forces spanning 0-20 N, our method achieves a mean RMSE of 0.251 N, reducing the error by 92.8% relative to the virtual spring and by 9.4% relative to an end-to-end MDN. In box pick-and-place, force adaptation maintains task success at 10/10 and increases both damage-free outcomes and reliability from 7/10 to 10/10. The project page is available at https://finger-force-estimation.pages.dev/
authors: Junha Cha, Chanwoo Kim, Kisang Park, Yeoncheol Jang, Doyoung Kim, Seungmin Kim, Kyungjae Lee, Sungjoon Choi
bullets: Targets reliable box placement by maintaining sufficient contact force without excessive loading.
Combines a calibrated virtual-spring estimate with an uncertainty-aware Mixture Density Network residual.
Enables continuous per-finger force adaptation without dedicated contact sensors during deployment.
Achieves 0.251 N mean RMSE across ten fingers and 0–20 N contact forces.
Improves box pick-and-place reliability and damage-free outcomes from 7/10 to 10/10.

papers.abstract: While single-view novel view synthesis methods have been dramatically enhanced recently, how to quantify their performance has yet to be standardized. In this work, we demonstrate that an important factor lies in how each method's own reference frame is aligned with the so-called ground-truth pose. Existing methods often rely on test-time optimization of target poses for this alignment, which inherently is ill-posed due to the complexity of the optimization landscape of camera poses vs render accuracy, leading to methods being evaluated at an arbitrary local optimum. Some recognize this limitation and thus rely on 3D reconstructions of entire scenes using training and test views to align poses, which may be infeasible. In this work, instead, we propose to use traditional 2D-to-2D and 2D-to-3D image matching techniques to align 3D reconstructions. We also evaluate only within co-visible regions, between different views, which is the only place where a `correct' ground truth can be defined. Our evaluations show that with proper coordinate alignment, novel-view synthesis methods that use explicit 3D Gaussians achieve the state of the art, despite being previously reported in the literature to be outperformed by pure image-based 2D methods. We further provide a simple baseline that directly utilizes an off-the-shelf video generator and a feed-forward geometry estimator. Our simple baseline is already comparable to state-of-the-art methods specifically trained for novel-view synthesis, without any task-specific training.
authors: Yang-Che Tseng, Erqun Dong, Jeong-gi Kwak, Gopal Sharma, Shakiba Kheradmand, Stephan Garbin, Hossam Isack, Kwang Moo Yi
bullets: Current evaluations can be unreliable because aligning predicted and ground-truth camera frames via test-time pose optimization is ill-posed.
The work aligns reconstructions using traditional 2D-to-2D and 2D-to-3D image matching instead of difficult pose optimization or full-scene reconstruction.
It evaluates only co-visible regions, where a valid ground truth can be defined across views.
Under this protocol, explicit 3D Gaussian methods achieve state-of-the-art results, contrary to some prior reports favoring image-based 2D methods.
A video-generator and feed-forward geometry-estimator baseline is competitive with task-specific methods without task-specific training.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Qualitative results – We show qualitative examples for each dataset under both evaluation resolutions, with the ground-truth target view (co-visibility overlay in blue) on the left. Middle: native-resolution methods, Flash3D [38], ViewCrafter [51], Lyra [3], SHARP [32], and our own baseline (Tab. 1). Right: methods that support the 256 × 256 centre-crop setting, LVSM [18], PF3plat [14], and our baseline (Tab. 2). Both halves show the same scene and held-out target view for each dataset, listed above each row. All methods are shown with our conservative co-visibility overlay. With our enhanced alignment protocol, the actual qualitative performances of Flash3D [38], ViewCrafter [51], and our baseline align well with the quantifications in Tab. 1. Our suggested baseline, while simple, performs on par with Flash3D [38].

Figure 3. Examples of misalignment leading to inaccurate evaluation – We show examples with Flash3D [38] for RealEstate10K (scene 01a5cc, fr. 50) and DTU (scan103, fr. 12), with test-time optimization only, and our proposed protocol. As shown, optimization alone leaves a large pose offset. Combined with the fact that many methods do not mask via co-visibility [5, 6, 18, 48, 51], the PSNR values can be very low, up to a level where it effectively is at a level where two random images are being compared (< 10 dB). With our image-matching-based pre-alignment, on the other hand, images are better aligned, and reasonable PSNR values are extracted. The yellow tint marks the non-co-visible region that our protocol excludes from computing the metrics.

Figure 6. Qualitative effect of generated views – For each scene we show the ground truth and the full init×train factorial of Tab. 3: rows vary the initialization (input view only vs. all generated views) and columns the training supervision. Training on generated views smears fine geometry (top scene) and hallucinates floaters in disocclusions (bottom scene); using them only for initialization stays sharpest. The teal overlay marks pixels outside the co-visible region, excluded from the metric.

Figure 2. Extracting co-visible regions – We show example covisible regions extracted by our protocol. We extract by projecting each pixel back and forth via DUSt3R [44] and checking their relative depths. We make a conservative estimate of co-visible regions to not disadvantage methods that do not extrapolate pixels outside the input view.

Figure 7. ViewCrafter [51] point-cloud conditioning vs. diffusion output. ViewCrafter [51] rasterizes its single-image point cloud from the (canonical) target pose to form the conditioning frame (middle), then a video-diffusion model synthesizes the final view (right). The raster is geometrically and photometrically faithful wherever the single view provides coverage (the speckled regions are sparse splatting where coverage thins); the diffusion model fills the remainder but can hallucinate geometry and drift in color as the viewpoint rotates away from the input. Rows: RealEstate10K (SV), RealEstate10K (VC), DL3DV-10K, DTU, Tanks & Temples (VC), on the same scenes as Fig. 4.

Figure 1. – Evaluation can be misleading due to inaccurate test-time pose alignment – We visualize the error map with the conventional test-time optimization and our proposed protocol (red is higher error, blue is lower). With the same 3D scene reconstructed from the reference view, conventional test-time optimization can leave residual misalignment between the rendered and ground-truth views, leading to large quantitative error. In contrast, our evaluation protocol provides a more robust alignment strategy, enabling more reliable performance measurement.
Figure 5. Example views generated by video models – We show example views generated by video models.

Table 1. Quantitative results – We summarize the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index Metric (SSIM) [45], and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) [52] for each method on our benchmark datasets, with the mean over all datasets reported on the right. Within each group, best results are in bold and second best are underlined. Using test-time optimization only reports wildly different results compared to when our evaluation protocol is used: Flash3D [38] is among the worst performing methods with a naive evaluation but, with better alignment, performs better than DepthSplat, while SHARP [32] leads the test-time-optimization-only group on average—its Gaussians are regressed directly in the input-camera frame, so it needs little alignment to begin with.

Table 2. Quantitative results (256×256 square evaluation) – PSNR, SSIM [45], and LPIPS [52] for the methods that support the square (256×256 centre-crop) setting, under both test-time-optimization-only and our evaluation protocol, with the mean over all datasets reported on the right. Flash3D [38] and ViewCrafter [51] are omitted as they cannot produce a comparable 256×256 cell. PF3plat [14] is evaluated with its RealEstate10K checkpoint on every dataset, as are MVSplat [6] and NoPoSplat [49]. Within each group, best results are in bold and second best are underlined.

Table 3. Ablation on using generated views – We ablate when to use generated views for training our 3D Gaussians. Including generated views for initialization only and training Gaussians only with the real input view gives best results.

papers.abstract: Visual foundation models learn rich pathological morphology but lack explicit concept-level supervision. Vision--language pretraining can provide this supervision but requires costly image--text pairs. Here, we introduce GloSAGE, a semantic self-distillation framework that uses lesion profiles predicted by a pretrained visual teacher to construct structured pathology descriptions. Reliability-guided selection identifies image--text anchors, while Knowledge-Structured Pathology Text Synthesis and Evidence-Guided Negative-pair Construction account for partially observed lesions. Image--text alignment trains projection layers while retaining the frozen visual encoder; an intermediate Semantic Transfer Layer supplies features for downstream tasks. Developed on GloMillion and evaluated across seven glomerulus- and case-level cohorts, GloSAGE supported zero-shot lesion recognition, image--text retrieval, hard-negative discrimination and concept-intervention analyses. It outperformed its source visual model in most lesion-recognition tasks and improved lesion grading, while supporting competitive case-level disease classification, injury grading and baseline renal function estimation. Ablations supported the combined contributions of knowledge-structured text and evidence-guided negatives, and the intermediate transfer layer improved mean lesion-recognition ROC-AUC relative to the complete projection output. A frozen language model conditioned on GloSAGE features generated glomerular descriptions. These findings suggest that teacher-derived lesion profiles can provide annotation-efficient semantic supervision for extending a glomerular visual foundation model.
authors: Qiming He, Jing Li, Zihan Wang, Tian Guan, Yifei Ma, Zimo Zhao, Yanxia Wang, Hongjing Chen, Yexing Zhang, Yizhi Wang, Xinrui Chen, Xitong Ling, Minxi Ouyang, Yujie Xie, Lianghui Zhu, Yiqing Liu, Qingxia Hou, Shuyan Zhao, Xiaoqin Wang, Lili Ma, Qiang Huang, Zhiyuan Shen, Junru Cheng, Siqi Zeng, Chao He, Yonghong He, Zhe Wang
bullets: Addresses the lack of concept-level supervision in visual pathology foundation models without requiring costly image–text pairs.
Uses reliability-guided image–text anchors, knowledge-structured pathology text, and evidence-guided negative pairs to handle partially observed lesions.
Aligns images and text while freezing the visual encoder; an intermediate Semantic Transfer Layer supports downstream tasks.
Evaluated across seven glomerulus- and case-level cohorts for lesion recognition, retrieval, hard-negative discrimination, concept intervention, and clinical prediction.
Improved most lesion-recognition tasks and lesion grading over the source visual model, with competitive case-level performance; ablations supported both structured text and guided negatives.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of GloSAGE. (A) Development of GloSAGE through semantic self-distillation. A pretrained visual teacher predicts lesion profiles for glomerular images in GloMillion, and KEYS converts these profiles into knowledge-structured captions. Paired images and captions undergo image–text contrastive pretraining through PIRA with EDGE-guided negative construction. STL transforms pretrained visual features for downstream tasks. GloSAGE is evaluated across seven cohorts for semantic capabilities, clinical diagnosis, component contributions and language-related extensions. (B) Framework of KEYS, PIRA and EDGE. Reliability-guided selection identifies over 40,000 trustworthy visual–semantic anchors. KEYS transforms their lesion profiles into structured descriptions incorporating lesion hierarchies, subtypes and severity grades. PIRA aligns images encoded by the frozen visual encoder with descriptions encoded by PubMedBERT through trainable projection heads, while EDGE excludes unsupported or contradicted negative pairs. (C) Evaluation of semantic enhancement through zero-shot lesion recognition, bidirectional retrieval, hard-negative discrimination and concept intervention. The upper-right, lower-left, and lower-right panels show the relative reduction in ROC-AUC deficit achieved by GloSAGE compared with other models on PAS, Masson, and PASM stains, respectively. papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are advancing in multimodal understanding and reasoning, accelerating medical model development. Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) uses evidence from the four examinations to determine disease location and nature, differentiate syndromes and guide treatment. This diagnostic process constitutes a complete chain of reasoning. We present Fu-TCM, a multimodal TCM LLM trained on data retained after cleaning and filtering an initial collection of approximately 7.12 million examples derived from classical texts, textbooks, medical images, clinical cases and publicly available datasets. The model was further optimized using Bianzheng-Grounded Policy Optimization (BGPO), which explicitly targets syndrome differentiation through rewards for response format, intermediate TCM reasoning fields and final syndrome predictions. Fu-TCM-27B led all six benchmarks spanning TCM reasoning, text and vision, achieving a macro-average accuracy of 81.01% and surpassing the strongest reference model with complete results across all six benchmarks by 7.13 percentage points. Its largest margin was 11.90 points on Fu-bianzheng. Case-level analyses further showed a positive association between intermediate-field accuracy and final syndrome-selection accuracy in most evaluated models. These findings suggest that TCM syndrome differentiation may be computationally learnable and that structured reasoning supervision can improve performance across TCM tasks.
authors: Jiahang Xie, Tong Jin, Lingfei Wu, Yaping You, Jie Huang, Yuanchang Jin, Weikang Gong, Wei Cheng, Jia You, Pan Sun, Jianfeng Feng, Hongcheng Guo
bullets: Addresses TCM diagnosis, which integrates evidence from four examinations into syndrome differentiation and treatment guidance.
Trained on filtered data from classical texts, textbooks, medical images, clinical cases, and public datasets.
Uses Bianzheng-Grounded Policy Optimization to reward response format, intermediate reasoning fields, and final syndrome predictions.
Fu-TCM-27B achieved a macro-average accuracy of 81.01% across six benchmarks, leading all evaluated benchmarks.
Case analyses found that more accurate intermediate reasoning fields were generally associated with better final syndrome selection.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Fu-TCM framework. a, Processing of multisource traditional Chinese medicine texts, images and clinical cases to construct text-based and image–text question–answer pairs, case-reasoning data and test datasets. b, Two-stage training with TCM domain-specific learning and Bianzheng-Grounded Policy Optimization, using rewards for response format, syndrome prediction and intermediate bianzheng fields to optimize structured bianzheng reasoning. c, Performance comparison between Fu-TCM and leading models across text, vision and TCM reasoning benchmarks. d, Same-question parallel external validation comparing model-only responses, responses from participants answering independently and responses from participants assisted by Fu-TCM.

Figure 2: Benchmark performance of Fu-TCM and reference models. a, Macro-average accuracy across six benchmarks for the eleven models with complete results. b, Paired accuracy differences between FuTCM-27B and the strongest non-Fu-TCM model on each benchmark, with matched-item 95% bootstrap confidence intervals based on 20,000 resamples. c, Accuracy profiles across Fu-bianzheng, Fu-text, Ladder text, Shizhen exam, Fu-vision and Shizhen vision; radar axes denote models and radial distance denotes accuracy.

papers.abstract: Historical experience can guide scientific coding at multiple levels, but task-level retrieval may miss implementation lessons that become relevant during execution. We introduce MUSE, a memory management framework combining multi-level memory with selective runtime injection for scientific coding agents. MUSE builds global, approach-level, and implementation-level memory from historical trajectories. At initialization, the agent receives global memory and problem-matched approach-level memory. During execution, current interactions are used to retrieve implementation-level memory. An LLM gate selects relevant experience and generates specific review advice, or skips injection. Across four benchmarks spanning numerical problem solving, kernel optimization, and scientific software repair, MUSE outperforms retrieval and memory baselines on all evaluation metrics. Ablations support the multi-level design and gated injection, while transfer experiments show that memory remains useful across kernel benchmarks. These results show that multi-level memory and selective runtime injection enable effective reuse of experience in scientific coding. Code is available at https://github.com/hr-jin/MUSE.
authors: Haoran Jin, Defu Lian, Xiting Wang, Hong Xie
bullets: Builds global, approach-level, and implementation-level memories from historical trajectories.
Provides global and problem-matched approach memory at initialization, then retrieves implementation lessons during execution.
Uses an LLM gate to inject relevant review advice or skip unnecessary memory injection.
Outperforms retrieval and memory baselines across four benchmarks covering numerical solving, kernel optimization, and software repair.
Ablations support the multi-level and gated designs; transfer experiments indicate usefulness across kernel benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) is now a common ingredient in language-model pre-training, as it improves downstream performance and enables faster inference through speculative decoding. We identify a flaw in standard MTP training, in which a residual component of the MTP gradient interferes with both next-token and multi-token learning, increasingly so with scale. Specifically, the MTP cross-entropy gradient can be decomposed exactly into a KL self-distillation term that pulls each MTP head toward the model's own next-token prediction (NTP) distribution and improves speculative decoding, and a residual that has a low signal-to-noise ratio and buries the useful KL signal. We introduce the KL gradient-recovery trick: when two distributions share a linear output head, the gradient of their KL divergence can be recovered exactly by combining their cross-entropy gradients through straight-through gradient routing. Unlike minimizing the KL directly, this trick requires no vocabulary-sized logit matrices and is compatible with standard fused cross-entropy kernels. This enables Soft Multi-Token Prediction (Soft-MTP), a one-line code change to MTP that removes the noisy residual and backpropagates only the KL self-distillation signal by reusing the existing NTP and MTP cross-entropy computations. Soft-MTP supports both DeepSeek- and Meta-style MTP, adds no parameters, and incurs no measurable overhead. From 167M to 1.2B parameters, Soft-MTP improves over standard MTP with lower NTP perplexity, faster speculative decoding and higher zero-shot accuracy at every scale, lower MTP perplexity from 689M onward, and stronger math and code reasoning after fine-tuning at 1.2B. Soft-MTP also matches, if not exceeds, direct KL divergence minimization on most metrics. Soft-MTP is, in effect, a free lunch for MTP optimization. Our code can be found at https://github.com/JaydenTeoh/Soft-MTP.
authors: Jayden Teoh
bullets: Standard MTP gradients contain a noisy residual that increasingly interferes with next-token and multi-token learning as models scale.
The authors decompose the gradient into a useful KL self-distillation component and a low-signal residual.
A gradient-recovery trick extracts the KL signal using existing cross-entropy computations and fused kernels, avoiding vocabulary-sized logit matrices.
Soft-MTP is a one-line modification compatible with DeepSeek- and Meta-style MTP, with no added parameters or measurable overhead.
Across 167M–1.2B parameters, it improves perplexity, speculative decoding speed, zero-shot accuracy, and—at 1.2B—math and code reasoning after fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Frontier large language models write correct CUDA kernels for most single-operator benchmark tasks, yet their accuracy collapses on accelerators whose architecture and programming language they have rarely seen. We present a case study of an LLM agent loop built for such accelerators. Our example is the FuriosaAI RNGD NPU, programmed in a recent, sparsely documented Rust DSL, where the loop optimized three Gemma-4-12B decode kernels over 12 days on a shared, scarce device. The loop builds its own target knowledge: it writes and checks a summary of the DSL documentation, measures the chip with microbenchmarks, records compiler-derived legality rules, and revisits this knowledge when the toolchain changes, rechecking rules and measurements where it can. A role-based search over per-kernel Design Trees explores whole-kernel designs and accumulates small accepted changes in the best version of each kernel. Because device time is scarce and readings are noisy, cheap checks screen new designs before any device run, and late in the run a change was accepted only after repeated comparisons with the best kernel on the device. The final kernels reach a 9.293x geomean speedup over the official baseline, each within 1.25x of the cycles needed just to move its weights. Our prompts, profiler and acceptance test are available at https://github.com/bgchun-fs/multi-agent-kernel-gen-loop.
authors: Byonggon Chun
bullets: Targets the challenge of LLM-generated kernels failing on unfamiliar accelerator architectures and languages.
Builds and updates target knowledge from documentation summaries, microbenchmarks, compiler legality rules, and toolchain checks.
Uses role-based search over per-kernel Design Trees, with cheap screening before scarce, noisy device evaluations.
Applies repeated on-device comparisons late in the process to validate accepted changes.
The final kernels are each within 1.25× of the cycles required to move their weights; prompts, profiler, and acceptance test are released publicly.

papers.abstract: Perception tasks for navigation in robotics, including aerial platforms such as drones and autonomous driving systems, are inherently structured. Drone-mounted cameras typically capture sky above, terrain below, and obstacles or man-made structures in between, while driving data often contains organized road layouts, lane markings, and surrounding agents. Motivated by these axis-aligned structural priors, we note that such information is typically more structured than in generic image tasks. We hypothesize that processing information in a quadtree-esque manner can not only model features effectively in a hierarchical manner, but also offers an efficient linear-time alternative to vanilla attention mechanisms, which run in quadratic time. In this paper, we propose Sibling-Selective Quadtree Attention (SSQA), which models image tokens hierarchically as a structured, full quadtree. We show analytical complexity analysis that guarantees linear-time feature modeling, in addition to empirical experiments comparing inference speeds with other popular modeling approaches, such as Mamba 2 and Quadtree Attention. Our results, benchmarked across several tasks, show that we achieve results at least as good, if not notably better, as others at a fraction of the computational costs.
authors: Yufan Chen, Arnav Bali, Angela Liu, Laura Zheng, Ming C. Lin
bullets: Targets structured navigation perception in robotics, including drones and autonomous driving.
Organizes image tokens as a structured full quadtree based on axis-aligned scene priors.
Introduces sibling-selective attention to support hierarchical feature modeling.
Provides analytical guarantees of linear-time complexity instead of quadratic vanilla attention.
Experiments across several tasks report competitive or better results at a fraction of the computational cost, including comparisons with Mamba 2 and Quadtree Attention.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Mean Epoch Wall Times (s) across 50 epochs on IllusionAnimals classification (2242 inputs) on A100 GPU. Despite other methods also modeling attention in linear time, a practical caveat is the lack of compute optimization in practice. As a result, some methods are even slower than vanilla ViT [6] out-of-the-box from official implementations. SSQA is both easy to integrate and requires no additional practical optimizations, our results show that SSQA maintains or even improves performance over other hierarchical modeling baselines.

Fig. 2: Top-Down vs. Bottom-Up Gating; Squares indicate leaf nodes. Our work has a key difference from previous work in hierarchical quadtree-based attention approaches: bottom-up gating. Previous works (a) avoid subdivisions into tokens with smaller granularity if possible by selecting top-k tokens with highest saliency during training. As a result, tokens on the same level outside of top-k saliency neglect hierarchical reasoning, even if there agents present in those patches. For example, in a driving scene, one patch may have a higher density of pedestrians, but it shouldn’t imply less attention on the single agent falling outside of the same patch. In our approach, we model features from bottom-up, ensuring that features are modeled hierarchically across the entire image. Doing so not only improves performance on various benchmarked tasks, but also maintains linear complexity with respect to number of tokens (shown in §III-G).
Fig. 4: Model Efficiency. SSQA is substantially lighter by reducing the number of parameters by nearly 3x and more compute-efficient by up to a factor of 8x for classification test.
Fig. 3: Training Dynamics. SSQA (a) converges faster and (b) reaches target accuracy earlier than the ViT baseline.

TABLE II: Thorough Compute vs. Accuracy for Classification on IllusionAnimals (50 epochs, 2242).

papers.tldr: SSQA uses sibling-selective quadtree attention to hierarchically model structured perception features with linear-time complexity and lower computational cost than standard attention.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires an agent to use past observations without navigation-specific training. We study what information an 8B-scale navigation system should retain and how it should be organized for subsequent decisions. Our agent combines instruction progress, hierarchically compressed observation history anchored to poses, and accumulated geometry in complementary task, temporal, and spatial memories. An 8B observer summarizes observations, and an 8B reasoner uses the memories to select waypoint intents or request additional views, a geometric controller executes the selected targets. A semantic information perspective motivates the distinction between retaining evidence, making it accessible to the reasoner, and acquiring further observations. On R2R-CE val-unseen, the complete system achieves the highest among the evaluated Qwen3-based zero-shot baselines. Removing temporal memory reduces SR and sharply increases average path length from 16.9 to 39.1m, removing the spatial-map and planning component reduces SR as well. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that our zero-shot method achieves higher success rates than the post-trained baseline in both corridor and office environments, suggesting better transfer to the evaluated real-world settings. As a complementary evaluation, LAW2 uses paired instruction interventions to examine behavioral responses, instruction following ability beyond endpoint success. These results support preserving task progress, observation history, and geometry in structured memory for zero-shot navigation with smaller open models.
authors: Yuhang Peng, Zhikai Wang, Ziyi Wang, Jiaru Zhong, Xiaoji Zheng, Jingzhi Huang, Yi Wang, Jiangtao Gong

On R2R-CE val-unseen, the full system outperforms evaluated Qwen3-based zero-shot baselines; removing temporal memory greatly lengthens paths and lowers SR.
Real-world tests on Unitree Go2 show higher success than a post-trained baseline in evaluated corridor and office settings; LAW2 probes instruction-following behavior beyond endpoint success.
