papers.abstract: AI compute is becoming large and fast-changing electrical loads. Its impacts on data center infrastructure and power grids depend not only on total energy consumption, but also on how their power draw moves over sub-second to minute timescales, including peaks, ramps, and synchronized fluctuations across accelerators. Existing energy benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) report aggregate quantities such as joules per token and rarely release the underlying time-series measurements, leaving these power dynamics poorly characterized and difficult to model. We introduce LLM-PowerTrace, an open dataset of time-resolved, per-GPU power traces for LLM fine-tuning and inference, sampled every 100\,ms on varying NVIDIA platforms paired with complete workload and system metadata. For fine-tuning, LLM-PowerTrace profiles open model families spanning a wide range of model sizes and fine-tuning methods, together with controlled sweeps over batch size, sequence length, precision, parallelism, and checkpointing. For inference, it covers variations in concurrency, GPU frequency, KV-cache and weight quantization, prompt and output lengths, and request-arrival patterns. LLM-PowerTrace profiles a set of open model families across a wide range of model sizes, and controlled sweeps over batch size, sequence length, precision, parallelism, and checkpointing for fine-tuning, and it sweeps concurrency, GPU frequency, KV cache and weight quantization, prompt and output lengths, and request arrival patterns for inference. Built upon power traces, we define power-grid-facing metrics as well as AI-compute power\&energy scaling law for extrapolating beyond the measured settings. Together, LLM-PowerTrace provides a dataset foundation for modeling, forecasting, and managing the fast-changing electrical behavior of AI compute.
authors: Jiansheng Wang, Jaskeerat Singh, Haochen Xu, Xinyi Li, Mingyuan Yan, Shaohui Liu, Yuzhuo Li, Yize Chen, Wenqi Cui
bullets: Addresses the gap between aggregate energy benchmarks and missing sub-second-to-minute power dynamics such as peaks, ramps, and synchronized fluctuations.
Provides per-GPU power traces sampled every 100 ms across NVIDIA platforms, with complete workload and system metadata.
Covers broad controlled variations in model size, batch size, sequence length, precision, parallelism, checkpointing, concurrency, frequency, quantization, and request patterns.
Introduces power-grid-facing metrics and an AI-compute power and energy scaling law for extrapolation beyond measured settings.
Supports modeling, forecasting, and management of rapidly changing AI-compute electrical loads.

The panels report request latency, energy per request, energy per token, power distribution, ramping rate, and spectral entropy. It summarizes the effects of the tensor-parallel degree on the six inference metrics (five models on A100, H100, and H200; node power and energy summed over the GPUs of the group; Llama-3.1-70B runs only at TP 4; with capped hosts excluded, TP 1 pools A100 and H200 runs, TP 2 pools H100 and H200 runs, and TP 4 pools all three GPUs, so the pooled trend mixes the TP degree with the platform). Request latency falls from 11.1 s at TP 1 to 4.8 s at TP 2 and is 6.4 s at TP 4, whose group adds the A100 and Llama-3.1-70B, while energy per request and per token stay flat from TP 1 to 2 and double at TP 4, partly because the TP 4 group includes Llama-3.1-70B (Figs. 35a, 35b, 35c). Node power rises from 489 to 1,013 and 1,594 W (Fig. 35d). The ramping rate grows with the degree, from 67 to 119 and 316 W/s, as more GPUs ramp together, while spectral entropy falls from 0.65 to 0.54–0.57 (Figs. 35e, 35f).

Figure 33: [Inference] Complete quantitative comparison across different weight precisions. The panels report request latency, energy per request, energy per token, power distribution, ramping rate, and spectral entropy. It compares BF16, FP8, and GPTQ-INT4 weights across the six metrics (five models on A100 and H200; all H100 weight-precision runs ran with a lowered power limit and are excluded). Quantized weights shorten request latency from 11.2 to 8.1 and 7.5 s and cut energy per request and per token by about 30% (Figs. 33a, 33b, 33c). Mean power falls from 576 to 533 and 505 W, and 95th-percentile power falls more (Fig. 33d). The ramping rate rises from 71 to 88 and 101 W/s, while spectral entropy rises slightly, from 0.59 to 0.65 and 0.64 (Figs. 33e, 33f).

Figure 29: [Inference] Complete quantitative comparison across different GPU platforms. The panels report request latency, energy per request, energy per token, power distribution, ramping rate, and spectral entropy. It compares A100, H100, and H200 (BF16, TP 1, closed loop, pooled over Qwen3-8B and 14B, the only models with an H100 run at the standard power limit; 6, 2, and 6 runs). Request latency falls from 10.1 s on A100 to 5.5 and 4.2 s on H100 and H200, and energy per request and per token fall in the same order (111, 99, and 83 J; 0.22, 0.19, and 0.16 J) (Figs. 29a, 29b, 29c). Mean power rises from 353 W on A100 to 565 and 625 W on H100 and H200, each within a narrow band (Fig. 29d). The ramping rate falls from 94 to 83 and 55 W/s, and spectral entropy from 0.79 to 0.53 and 0.41 (Figs. 29e, 29f).

Figure 30: [Inference] Complete quantitative comparison across different maximum concurrency levels. The panels report request latency, energy per request, energy per token, power distribution, ramping rate, and spectral entropy. It summarizes the effects of the concurrency limit on the six inference metrics (six dense Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B on A100, H100, and H200). Request latency stays near 5–6 s up to 32 concurrent requests and then rises to 21 s at 256, while energy per request falls from 2.0 kJ to 45 J (Figs. 30a, 30b). Energy per token falls about 45-fold, from 3.9 to 0.088 J, as more requests share each decode step (Fig. 30c). Mean power rises from 373 to 573 W, and the pooled band spans the three GPUs: its 95th percentile (near 694 W from 64 requests on) reflects the H100 and H200 runs and its 5th percentile (198 to 396 W) the A100 runs, which reach their 400 W limit at high concurrency (Fig. 30d). The ramping rate peaks at 32 requests (55 W/s) and falls once the GPUs saturate, while spectral entropy rises at high concurrency (Figs. 30e, 30f).

Figure 27: [Inference] Complete quantitative comparison across different model sizes. The panels report request latency, energy per request, energy per token, power distribution, ramping rate, and spectral entropy. It summarizes how the six inference metrics vary with active parameter count (BF16, TP 1, closed loop, pooled over A100, H100, and H200). Request latency and energy per request rise from 5.2 s and 72 J for Qwen3-8B to 18.8 s and 269 J for Qwen3-32B, while the MoE Qwen3-30BA3B (3B active) is slower and costlier than the dense 8B model (Figs. 27a, 27b). Energy per token follows the same order, from 0.14 J for Qwen3-8B to 0.52 J for Qwen3-32B (Fig. 27c). Mean and 95th-percentile power rise only modestly with size, from 493 to 516 W on average (Fig. 27d). The ramping rate falls from 78 to 48 W/s between Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B, with the MoE model (76 W/s) close to Qwen3-8B, while spectral entropy is highest for the MoE model (0.74 against 0.58–0.60) (Figs. 27e, 27f).

Figure 34: [Inference] Complete quantitative comparison across different KV-cache precisions. The panels report request latency, energy per request, energy per token, power distribution, ramping rate, and spectral entropy. It compares BF16 and FP8 (E4M3) KV caches across the six metrics (five models on A100, H100, and H200, BF16 weights). Request latency changes by less than 1%, and energy per request and per token fall by about 2% on average (a median 2.7% and at most 5% across the 13 same-host pairs) (Figs. 34a, 34b, 34c). Mean power falls slightly, from 574 to 559 W (Fig. 34d). The ramping rate rises from 80 to 89 W/s, less than its run-to-run spread, and spectral entropy falls from 0.60 to 0.58 (Figs. 34e, 34f).

Figure 15: [Fine-tuning] Model size. Complete quantitative comparison across different model sizes for fine-tuning tasks. The panels report iteration duration, energy per iteration, energy per token, power distribution, ramping rate, and spectral entropy. It summarizes how the six fine-tuning metrics vary with active parameter count. Mean iteration duration and energy per iteration increase with model size, with a particularly pronounced increase for the largest models (Figs. 15a, 15b). Energy per token exhibits a similar upward trend at larger model sizes, while remaining non-monotonic across intermediate configurations (Fig. 15c). Mean and upper-tail power increase initially before approaching a broad plateau, whereas lower-tail power varies more modestly (Fig. 15d). Ramping rate increases toward medium–large models but remains non-monotonic across configurations, while spectral entropy exhibits no consistent relationship with model size (Figs. 15e, 15f).

Each setting is a separate run; 30 s of each run are shown side by side, separated by grey lines, so the segments are not contiguous in time.

Figure 31: [Inference] Complete quantitative comparison across different Poisson arrival rates. The panels report request latency, energy per request, energy per token, power distribution, ramping rate, and spectral entropy. It summarizes the effects of the arrival rate on the six inference metrics (Qwen3-8B, 14B, and 32B on H200, free-length generation; Qwen3-32B at TP 2). Request latency rises only slightly with rate, from 3.1 to 4.1 s, while energy per request falls from 1.9 kJ to 109 J (Figs. 31a, 31b). Energy per token falls from 4.9 to 0.28 J as idle time is amortized over more requests (Fig. 31c). The 5th-percentile power stays near idle up to 0.5 requests/s (117–128 W on one GPU and 261–270 W for the two-GPU Qwen3-32B node) and rises to 577–638 W on one GPU (1.28 kW for Qwen3-32B) at 8 requests/s, as the GPUs stop draining between requests (Fig. 31d). Figure 36: [Inference] Complete quantitative comparison across different SM clock frequencies. The panels report request latency, energy per request, energy per token, power distribution, ramping rate, and spectral entropy. It summarizes the effects of the locked SM clock on the six inference metrics (Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, and Llama-3.1-8B on one H100, closed loop; the 1980 MHz setting throttles to a median of 1830 MHz). Request latency falls from 14.4 s at 345 MHz to 5.8 and 5.7 s at 1605 and 1980 MHz, while energy per request and per token are lowest at 1200 MHz (66 J and 0.13 J) and rise again at higher clocks (Figs. 36a, 36b, 36c). Mean power rises from 184 to 535 W, with a narrow band at every clock (Fig. 36d). The ramping rate grows at every clock step, from 8 to 68 W/s, while spectral entropy falls from 0.48 to 0.43–0.45 (Figs. 36e, 36f).

Figure 32: [Inference] Complete quantitative comparison across different input/output lengths. The panels report request latency, energy per request, energy per token, power distribution, ramping rate, and spectral entropy. It summarizes the effects of the forced input/output length on the six inference metrics (Qwen3-8B, 14B, and 32B on one H200 with 32 requests in flight). Request latency and energy per request grow mainly with the output length, from 1.7 s and 33 J at 128/128 to 35 s and 753 J at 2048/2048 (Figs. 32a, 32b). Energy per output token is highest for long prompts with short outputs (0.89 J at 2048/128) and 0.26–0.37 J otherwise (Fig. 32c). The 2048-token prompts hold power within a few percent of the 700 W limit, with the 5th percentile at 681 W (Fig. 32d). The same workloads have the smallest ramps (20 W/s against 39–56 W/s) and the highest spectral entropy (Figs. 32e, 32f).

Figure 20: [Fine-tuning] Sequence length. Quantitative comparison across different sequence lengths. The panels report iteration duration, energy per iteration, energy per token, power distribution, ramping rate, and spectral entropy. It summarizes the effects of sequence length on the six fine-tuning metrics. Iteration duration and energy per iteration increase sharply beyond 256 tokens (Figs. 20a, 20b), while energy per token decreases from 16 to 256 tokens before approaching a plateau (Fig. 20c). Mean, 5th-percentile, and 95th-percentile power increase with sequence length, although upper-tail power begins to saturate at the longest sequences (Fig. 20d). Ramping rate shows no clear monotonic trend, while spectral entropy decreases toward 256 tokens before increasing again at longer sequences (Figs. 20e, 20f).

Figure 16: [Fine-tuning] Batch size. Complete quantitative comparison across different batch sizes. The panels report iteration duration, energy per iteration, energy per token, power distribution, ramping rate, and spectral entropy. It summarizes the effects of batch size on the six fine-tuning metrics. Iteration duration and energy per iteration increase with batch size as more samples are processed per optimizer step (Figs. 16a, 16b). In contrast, energy per token generally decreases, indicating that larger batches amortize fixed computational and synchronization overheads over more tokens (Fig. 16c). Mean and 95th-percentile power increase only moderately, while 5th-percentile power rises sharply at small batch sizes before leveling off (Fig. 16d). Ramping rate also increases with batch size, whereas spectral entropy varies non-monotonically and peaks at intermediate batch sizes (Figs. 16e, 16f).

The panels report iteration duration, energy per iteration, energy per token, power distribution, ramping rate, and spectral entropy. papers.selection_reason: Time-resolved GPU power traces and scaling laws for AI compute energy are relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: LLM-PowerTrace: A Dataset of Time-Resolved GPU Power Traces for AI Compute
papers.tldr: LLM-PowerTrace is an open, high-resolution dataset for analyzing and modeling the time-varying GPU power demands of LLM fine-tuning and inference.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) represent images and videos as long visual-token sequences, substantially increasing inference costs. These costs motivate visual-token pruning, whose effectiveness depends on both what signal is used for selection and when that signal becomes available. Our analysis reveals complementary limitations: visual-side [CLS] attention produces scattered, background-biased selections under aggressive compression, while stronger query-conditioned signals become available after substantial computation within the large language model (LLM). This raises a natural question: can structurally coherent, query-aware token selection be performed before consulting the LLM? We therefore propose ST-Pruner (Spectral-Textual Pruner), a training-free framework for pre-LLM visual-token selection. It combines attention-independent spectral saliency with inverted patch-text similarity through parameter-free multiplicative fusion. Across diverse LVLMs, ST-Pruner retains over 95% of full-token performance using at most 11.1% of visual tokens and achieves a 3.2x end-to-end speedup on LLaVA-NeXT. Code is available at https://github.com/sejong-rcv/ST-Pruner.
authors: Intaek Shin, Geuntaek Lim, Sungjune Park, Yukyung Choi
bullets: LVLMs face high inference costs from long visual-token sequences.
Visual [CLS] attention can select scattered, background-biased tokens, while query-aware signals typically require costly LLM computation.
ST-Pruner is training-free and operates before LLM processing.
It fuses attention-independent spectral saliency with inverted patch-text similarity using parameter-free multiplication.
Across diverse LVLMs, it achieves a 3.2× end-to-end speedup on LLaVA-NeXT while retaining over 95% of full-token performance.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of ST-Pruner. Given pre-LLM visual features Z, the spectral branch derives its saliency score from a randomized low-rank SVD, while the semantic branch computes inverted patch–text relevance using a query embedding from the corresponding frozen text encoder of the paired vision–language model. Their parameter-free multiplicative fusion determines the top-K visual tokens, which are retained in their original sequence order before LLM inference. The textual query is independently tokenized for the standard languagemodel input.

papers.title: Don't Ask the LLM: Visual Token Pruning with Spectral Structure and Semantic Relevance

papers.abstract: Language-model answers are often treated as a visible record of the internal decision that produced them. We test this assumption in conflicting-context question answering, where two supplied documents support incompatible answers. A model can process the disagreement and still return a one-sided answer, even under prompts that ask it to disclose conflict. In Qwen 0.8B, hidden source commitment is captured by a residual source-choice direction whose sign tracks which document the answer uses. Sparse middle-layer MLP writers feed the same coordinate, and steering the coordinate changes the chosen source. A transfer run on Gemma 3 1B preserves the source-choice readout and sparse-write bridge under LLM-audited labels. Conflict disclosure follows a different pattern, appearing weaker, later-layer, and only partially steerable. These results support a practical monitoring strategy for retrieval systems that detects silent source commitment with residual readouts and pairs conflict-surfacing prompts with disclosure steering when the model has selected a side under disagreement.
authors: Samuel Dawit Assefa, Jae Won Cho
bullets: In conflicting-context QA, models may choose one document without explicitly disclosing the disagreement.
A residual source-choice direction tracks which source the answer follows in Qwen 0.8B.
Sparse middle-layer MLPs write to this direction, and steering it changes source selection.
The readout and sparse-write mechanism transfer to Gemma 3 1B under LLM-audited labels.
Conflict disclosure is weaker, later-layer, and only partly steerable, motivating combined monitoring and prompting strategies.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates 'hidden source commitment' in LLMs during conflicting-context question answering, proposing methods to detect and steer model behavior based on internal decision directions.
papers.title: Hidden Commitment: When Language Models Silently Pick a Side and How Steering Can Surface It
papers.tldr: Language models can silently commit to one conflicting source, but residual-stream readouts and steering can reveal and influence that hidden choice.

papers.abstract: Compositional diffusion planners have demonstrated remarkable success on long-horizon diffusion planning by sampling short trajectories, namely chunks, and composing them into a long trajectory. However, averaging overlapping chunks can induce the mode-averaging problem, resulting in discontinuous trajectories. Several works aim to address this problem, whereas a non-negligible portion of plans remains infeasible. In this work, we propose Selective Compositional Diffuser (SCD), handling this problem by measuring reachability. To this end, we present a self-supervised learning method for the reachability classifier. This is trained on offline data and generated chunks jointly to address potential distributional mismatch, while reducing the bias inherited from the generated data. Based on this, we construct a graph whose edge costs represent whether consecutive chunks are reachable, and traverse the graph to find effective yet efficient routes. Lastly, we generate bridging trajectories and refine the composed trajectory for smooth transitions. We evaluate our method on OGBench stitching tasks. It practically reduces incompatible mode compositions and the mode-averaging problem compared to the studied baselines. Across tasks, SCD improves success rates, reaching state-of-the-art results on HumanoidMaze-Large and Giant tasks.
authors: Chanyoung Park, Youngjoong Kim, Jaesik Park
bullets: Addresses discontinuities from averaging overlapping chunks and infeasible plans in compositional diffusion planners.
Trains a self-supervised reachability classifier on both offline data and generated chunks to reduce distribution mismatch and bias.
Builds a graph of chunk transitions, searches for efficient reachable routes, then generates bridging trajectories for smooth composition.
On OGBench stitching tasks, reduces incompatible mode compositions and mode averaging compared with studied baselines.

papers.abstract: Pneumonia changes across respiration, inflammation, and organ function, while the measurements that describe it arrive at different times and are often incomplete. We introduce PULMOWORLD, a world model for longitudinal pneumonia dynamics that connects asynchronous state estimation, recursive simulation, and evidence-constrained planning. History-aware filtering separates state propagation from observation-driven correction, so a measurement updates the shared belief only when it is observed. That belief supports recursive forecasts of clinical values and modality representations, and summaries of future prognosis. Cap-MBRL searches imagined continuations inside an authorized action set and replaces a frozen fallback only when a candidate meets the risk budget and a predicted-cost margin. On the pneumonia cohort MASS, recursive forecasts are competitive with task-trained sequence models, and simulated future states retain prognostic information. Trained separately on public MIMIC-IV-CXR chest radiographs and clinical trajectories, this model improves prognostic discrimination over latest-value fusion in development and is competitive on long-horizon error on the locked pneumonia panel. In five known-mechanism MASS-Syn environments, Cap-MBRL lowers selection regret relative to direct fallback execution.
authors: Cheng Tang, Xinyu Zhang, Jiawei Chen, Minghui Zhang, Shaocong Wei, Wei Li, Yuxing Chen, Kongcheng Zhang, Chun-Mei Feng, Nanqing Dong, Xinyuan Zhu, Ziyan Huang, Junjun He, Yirong Chen, Lingtong Huang, Min Cen, Ming Hu
bullets: Addresses longitudinal pneumonia dynamics across respiration, inflammation, and organ function when observations arrive irregularly and may be missing.
Uses history-aware filtering to separate state propagation from observation-based correction, enabling recursive forecasts of clinical values, modality representations, and prognosis.
Cap-MBRL evaluates imagined futures within an authorized action set and replaces a fallback plan only when predicted risk and cost criteria are satisfied.

On MASS and related pneumonia evaluations, forecasts were competitive with sequence models, improved prognostic discrimination over latest-value fusion, and reduced selection regret in five synthetic environments.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) achieve strong image recognition performance, but their self-attention increases quadratically with the number of input tokens and makes them computationally expensive. The standard implementation of ViT models treats all patch tokens with equal importance across every layer of the model. This uniform treatment introduces redundant computation and may reduce the model's focus on the most discriminative object regions. In this paper, we propose ConvRoute-ViT, a convolutional token routing mechanism for efficient vision transformers that performs token reduction through convolutional routing. Our model preserves the most relevant patch tokens according to class-token attention at selected layers, while the remaining tokens are spatially reorganized and compressed into a compact set of convolutional summary tokens. This design reduces the sequence length without completely removing the contextual information of the less informative tokens. By applying the routing process hierarchically, the proposed framework constructs compact and discriminative representations for deeper layers. Experiments on CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet show that ConvRoute-ViT improves computational efficiency while maintaining classification accuracy compared with the base ViT.
authors: Manish Das, Shiv Ram Dubey, Satish Kumar Singh
bullets: Addresses redundant computation from treating all ViT patch tokens equally and the quadratic cost of self-attention.
Uses class-token attention to preserve relevant tokens at selected layers.
Spatially reorganizes and convolves remaining tokens into compact summary tokens rather than discarding them.
Applies routing hierarchically to build compact, discriminative representations in deeper layers.
Experiments on CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet report improved computational efficiency with maintained classification accuracy versus base ViT.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed ConvRoute-ViT architecture. The input image is converted into patch tokens with positional encoding and a CLS token, creating an input size of B×N ×D. After initial transformer processing up to kth transformer layers, the ConvRoute Token Routing Module computes the token importance score and retains the top-R important tokens. The remaining tokens are passed through the ConvRoute Compressor where they are spatially reshaped to generate compact ConvSummary tokens, resulting in B ×M ×D and are processed by transformer layers from k+1→ l. A second ConvRoute Token Routing Module is applied at layer l to further reduce the sequence and is then passed through the subsequent transformer blocks for final classification.

Fig. 2. Attention heatmaps for representative CIFAR-100 samples [24]. Each example consists of three panels arranged from left to right: the input image, the base ViT attention map, and the ConvRoute-ViT attention map.
TABLE III COMPARISON WITH REPRESENTATIVE CNN AND TRANSFORMER BASELINES ON CIFAR-100 AND TINYIMAGENET. RESULTS ARE TAKEN FROM [26], AND MODELS MARKED WITH † ARE IMPLEMENTED FROM SCRATCH.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes ConvRoute-ViT, a convolutional token routing mechanism for Vision Transformers that reduces computational cost by selectively retaining and compressing patch tokens.
papers.title: ConvRoute-ViT: Convolutional Token Routing for Efficient Vision Transformers
papers.tldr: ConvRoute-ViT efficiently reduces ViT token sequences by retaining important patches and compressing the rest into convolutional summary tokens while preserving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting has recently emerged as a promising alternative to per-scene optimization, enabling fast novel view synthesis by predicting Gaussian primitives directly from input images. However, it quickly faces a bottleneck of rendering efficiency while scaling from sparse to dense multi-view inputs, which offer more geometric constraints but produce a rapidly growing set of candidate Gaussians. Existing solutions cannot reliably distinguish redundant primitives, leading to many redundant primitives from repeatedly observed regions and increased rendering cost without much gain in visual quality. We propose BudSplat, a compact feed-forward 3DGS framework that learns to keep the most valuable Gaussians under a limited primitive count. BudSplat has two novel designs. The first is a detail-aware importance score that is extracted from multi-level visual tokens, providing an explicit cue for regions where pruning is likely to harm perceptual quality. The score can be injected into voxel fusion to preserve high-value local contributors during multi-view aggregation. The second is quality-aware Gaussian pruning that selects a compact set of primitives by jointly considering rendering contribution and detail importance. The quality-aware pruning enables local quota redistribution that helps avoid over-allocating primitives to large redundant regions. Experiments on RE10K, DL3DV, and ACID show that BudSplat achieves a favorable trade-off among rendering quality and efficiency.
authors: Muyu Xu, Fangneng Zhan, Yu Wei, Ling Shao, Shijian Lu
bullets: Addresses the rapid growth of redundant Gaussian primitives as the number of input views increases.
Uses multi-level visual tokens to estimate detail-aware importance and preserve regions where pruning could hurt quality.
Introduces quality-aware pruning that jointly considers rendering contribution and visual detail.
Redistributes local primitive quotas to avoid wasting capacity on large, redundant regions.
Experiments on RE10K, DL3DV, and ACID show a favorable quality–efficiency trade-off.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of BudSplat. With dense geometry, confidence maps, and multi-layer tokens as predicted from multi-view RGB images by VGGT, the detail-aware decomposition first extracts residual token cues and predicts patch-level detail scores. The predicted scores are then propagated to the importance-preserving voxel fusion together with confidence and voxel support, retaining important local contributors during aggregation. Finally, the quality-aware pruning ranks the fused Gaussians by opacity, detail importance, and support-aware redundancy correction, followed by patch-level quota redistribution to select a compact set of retained Gaussian for rendering.

Figure 2: Qualitative comparison on challenging low-overlap target views. Red boxes highlight regions where baselines suffer from incomplete Gaussian coverage, blurred local structures, or uneven rendering quality. Our method allocates Gaussian budget more effectively, producing stable renderings and preserving perceptually important details with fewer Gaussians.

Figure 3: Target-view visualization of Gaussian density allocation and RGB rendering before and after pruning. Top row: projected Gaussian density before pruning, after pruning, removed density, and retention ratio. Bottom row: normal RGB rendering before pruning, after pruning, absolute difference, and reference image. The density diagnostic shows that pruning mainly removes redundant Gaussian support from low-frequency and highly overlapped regions, while preserving more support around high-frequency structures. The RGB difference map further shows that the remaining rendering changes are concentrated around edges, boundaries, and fine details rather than smooth regions.

Table 1: Main quantitative comparison under increasing input views. We report PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and the number of rendered Gaussians (#GS). For our method, Oursρ denotes retaining a ρ-fraction of fused Gaussians after pruning. Pink and orange cells indicate the best and second-best results under each dataset and view setting, following the metric direction indicated by the arrows. OOM denotes out-of-memory during inference.

Table 3: Additional main quantitative comparison 20, 24, 48 input views. We report PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and the number of rendered Gaussians (#GS). For our method, Oursρ denotes retaining a ρ-fraction of fused Gaussians after pruning. Pink and orange cells indicate the best and second-best results under each dataset and view setting, following the metric direction indicated by the arrows. papers.title: BudSplat: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting under a Rendering Budget
papers.tldr: BudSplat makes feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting more efficient by retaining the most visually valuable Gaussians under a fixed rendering budget.

papers.abstract: Loss spikes in language model pretraining can waste substantial compute and derail otherwise healthy training runs. A primary driver of these instabilities is the growth and divergence of output logits in the final language modeling (LM) head. In this work, we study a particularly costly form of this instability associated with output logit growth: delayed, terminal divergences that emerge only after prolonged training, which we call time-bomb spikes. We find that these instabilities are preceded by rapidly growing quantization error in the LM head, which eventually culminates in a loss spike. Crucially, reducing numerical precision accelerates time-bomb spikes, while increasing precision improves stability. We then propose a simple yet effective mitigation that replaces AdamW on the LM head with SGD with momentum, suppressing logit growth and improving stability over long training horizons. Finally, we find that existing mitigation techniques from the literature (along with our own) all reduce quantization error, suggesting a shared numerical mechanism behind their effectiveness. Together, our results identify finite precision error as a hidden driver of time-bomb spikes and show that suppressing this error is key to stable long-horizon pretraining.
authors: Zaiqian Chen, Aditya Somasundaram, Sophie Li, Sean McLeish, John Kirchenbauer, Tom Goldstein, Micah Goldblum
bullets: Studies delayed terminal divergences in language-model pretraining, termed “time-bomb spikes.”
Finds that rapidly increasing LM-head quantization error precedes these loss spikes.
Lower numerical precision accelerates instability; higher precision improves stability.
Replacing AdamW with momentum SGD on the LM head suppresses logit growth and improves stability.
Existing mitigations appear to work partly by reducing quantization error, indicating a shared numerical mechanism.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Increasing LM head β1 is more effective than tuning its learning rate alone. Left: Final evaluation loss across trunk learning rates. Head learning rate tuning yields modest gains, while β1 = 0.99 closes much of the gap to LM head SGD-M. Adding µ-centering or z-loss improves some settings, but all AdamW variants diverge or time-bomb at the largest trunk learning rate, whereas SGD-M remains stable. Dashed lines denote tuned head learning rates. Right: output logit norm trajectories, showing how each method constrains LM head growth.

Figure 7: Methods that prevent time-bomb failure suppress quantization error. For 28Mparameter models trained in BF16 mixed at peak LR 0.1, the unmitigated baseline develops timebomb spikes (left) together with orders-of-magnitude growth in logit quantization error (middle) and predictive distribution quantization error (right). All mitigation methods prevent the time bomb and keep both numerical-error metrics bounded across five seeds. Solid lines show medians and faint lines show individual runs. The same effect is more pronounced under BF16 true training; the unmitigated baseline fails catastrophically after significant growth in numerical error (Figure 20).

Figure 1: Reduced precision accelerates time-bomb spikes, while LM head SGD-M prevents them. Lowering LM head precision brings the failure earlier, with BF16 true diverging first, BF16 mixed later, and FP32 remaining stable throughout training (left). Output logit norm grows under every AdamW baseline, including FP32 (middle), but it destabilizes training only in reduced precision, where LM head quantization error grows by orders of magnitude before each failure (right). Quantization error is measured as the RMS difference between native BF16 logits and FP32 logits computed from the same hidden states. Replacing AdamW with SGD-M on the LM head keeps both logit norm and quantization error nearly flat, preventing the time bomb even in BF16 mixed precision. Results are for 28M parameter models trained at peak learning rate 0.1 for ∼28× the Chinchilla optimal token horizon, using AdamW throughout (baselines) or SGD with momentum on the LM head (SGD-M).

Figure 9: Skipping a small fraction of high-loss tokens eliminates loss spikes but hurts convergence. A 162M model trained at the Chinchilla-optimal token budget with peak learning rate 0.15. One run is the baseline; the other skips high-loss tokens identified via a rolling window threshold.

Figure 3: Long horizon training can result in time-bomb instability. Two 404M parameter models train similarly for most of pretraining, but the higher LR run exhibits delayed, unrecoverable loss increases accompanied by accelerating output logit growth.

Figure 14: LM head SGD-M is the only intervention stable across the spike-prone learning rate regime at both model sizes. Final evaluation loss versus peak learning rate for 162M and 404M models. µ-centering and z-loss diverge at some η ∈ [10−1, 3×10−1] at both sizes, and row-centering, while stable at 162M, diverges inconsistently at 404M and is omitted there. LM head SGD-M remains stable throughout and achieves the lowest loss at the high end.

Figure 15: LM head SGD-M also stabilizes training at 1.4B scale and pairs well with Muon. Training loss curves for 1.4B models at peak learning rate η = 0.07 (single seed). Replacing AdamW with SGD-M (β = 0.99) on the LM head reaches a lower final training loss than AdamW, µ-centering, and z-loss, and combining a Muon backbone with LM head SGD-M reaches the lowest loss of any configuration shown.

Figure 16: Time-bomb instability emerges across the long-horizon learning rate sweep alongside accelerating output logit growth. Evaluation loss (left), output logit norm (middle), and output logit mean (right) for 404M-parameter models trained for 96B tokens across peak learning rates from 3× 10−4 to 3× 10−1. Runs train similarly for much of pretraining, while higher-learning rate settings exhibit substantially greater late stage logit norm growth and, in several cases, deterioration in evaluation loss.

Figure 17: Longer training horizons are associated with increasingly severe late stage LM head growth. Evaluation loss (left), output logit norm (middle), and output logit mean (right) for 28M parameter models with parameterized RMSNorm, and peak LR of 0.1 trained with horizons of 4B, 8B, 12B, and 16B tokens. Extending training exposes progressively larger output logit norm growth and late stage loss deterioration, consistent with time-bomb instability becoming more prominent during prolonged training.

Figure 2: Learnable gain parameters in normalization layers stabilize training and can prevent fast loss spikes. Comparing a 162M spiking run with the same seed and configuration only differing in the inclusion of learnable RMSNorm parameters, the parameterized norm configuration exhibits no fast spikes, output logit swings, or large logit norm growth.

Figure 6: Reduced precision in the LM head accelerates time-bomb instability and increases quantization error as logits grow. For 28M parameter models trained at peak LR 0.1, BF16 true runs fail earliest, BF16 mixed runs deteriorate later, and FP32 remains stable across five seeds (left). The same ordering appears in the quantization error between BF16 native and FP32 reference logits (middle) and in the KL divergence between the corresponding predictive distributions (right), indicating that loss spikes coincide with increasingly large finite precision error. Solid lines show the median across seeds and faint lines show individual runs.

Figure 10: A single-token context swap collapses the logit distribution at a spike. Full-vocabulary logits (V = 50,260) at the Rank-1 spike event before (blue) and after (orange) replacing the final context token Command with a comma, with the target token ery held fixed. The standard deviation contracts 17×, from 121.87 to 6.87, recovering the range typical of non-spiking steps.

Figure 13: Parameterized RMSNorms effectively mitigate fast loss spikes. The five parameterized runs are highly consistent and overlap closely, indicating low seed-to-seed variability relative to the parameter-less runs.

Figure 12: Skipping high-loss batches defers rather than eliminates fast spike instability. Following Karpathy (2024), we skip any batch whose loss exceeds 7 standard deviations from a rolling 1000-step window and revert the optimizer state. Reverting to either the previous or second-toprevious optimizer state does not prevent subsequent fluctuations in output logit mean characteristic of spike events.

Figure 20: Methods that prevent time-bomb spikes also suppress quantization error. For 28Mparameter models trained in BF16 true at peak learning rate 0.1, the unmitigated baseline develops severe unrecoverable loss spikes (left) together with orders-of-magnitude growth in logit quantization error (middle) and predictive distribution quantization error (right). µ-centering, z-loss, and LM head SGD-M prevent the time bomb and keep both numerical-error metrics bounded across five seeds. Solid lines show medians and faint lines show individual runs.

Figure 18: Normalized logit error grows as the logit mean becomes large relative to variation across logits. Across BF16 true and BF16 mixed baseline runs, the normalized RMS error between native BF16 logits and FP32 reference logits, RMS(zbf16 − zfp32)/std(zfp32), increases with the relative logit mean, |mean(z)|/std(z). Colors indicate precision, markers indicate peak learning rate, and lines trace individual training trajectories.

Figure 4: SGD-M is competitive in both optimization quality and control of LM head growth. Across trunk learning rates, µ-centering, z-loss, and LM head SGD-M improve stability relative to the AdamW baseline, while differing in both final evaluation loss (left) and the degree of LM head growth suppression (right). Across high learning rates, µ-centering and LM head SGD-M strongly suppress output logit norm growth, whereas the baseline develops the largest late growth and corresponding time-bomb spikes (right). Faint curves show individual learning rates; solid curves and shaded regions show the median and interquartile range across learning rates.
Figure 11: Fast loss spikes coincide with sharp swings in the output logit mean. A spiking 162M run compared with a non-spiking run using the same configuration and differing only in random seed.

Figure 19: Lower precision triggers time-bomb spikes at smaller learning rates. Fraction of seeds exhibiting a time-bomb instability across peak learning rates and numerical precision settings. As precision decreases from FP32 to BF16 mixed to BF16 true, instability emerges at progressively smaller learning rates. A time-bomb is defined as three consecutive post-midpoint evaluations at least 0.01 above the running-best evaluation loss.

Table 2: Learning rate sweep across the spike-prone regime (η ∈ [10−1, 3×10−1]) for 162M and 404M models. Final evaluation loss (↓ lower is better) is reported. † marks runs whose loss spiked during training and did not recover.

Table 1: A single-token context swap collapses the spike. Top-5 predicted tokens at the Rank-1 spike event before and after replacing the final context token Command with a comma. Before the swap, the model assigns extreme logits to unrelated subword tokens; after the swap, the top predictions are ordinary function words with logits in a normal range, and the loss falls from 610.00 to 12.73. denotes a leading space.

Table 3: Tuned SGD-M on the LM head suppresses spikes and remains competitive on evaluation loss. Final evaluation loss and training-loss spike score (defined in Section A.6) at peak learning rate η = 0.15 for 162M and 404M models. Values are mean ± standard error across 5 seeds; bold marks the lowest evaluation loss for each model scale.

papers.tldr: Finite-precision quantization error in the LM head can trigger delayed loss spikes, while higher precision or momentum SGD improves long-horizon training stability.

papers.abstract: Embodied systems can update policies, world models, skills, and executable programs from deployment experience, allowing one interaction to benefit later tasks. When a system also revises and reuses its data-acquisition, feedback, or learning procedures, experience changes the process that produces capability, introducing recursive self-improvement. This paper surveys research in physical AI through the connection between persistent capability and its improvement process. We first explain the functional distinction between learner updates and improvers, then compare policy learning, imagined experience, memory and skill accumulation, and executable harnesses. These approaches connect to revisions of curricula, rewards, and research programs in different ways. Contact validity, recovery, retention, and resource costs determine whether the resulting gains accumulate during continued deployment. An L0-L3 rubric distinguishes task-local adaptation, persistent capability gain, inherited process revision, and verified improver gain. Representative benchmarks and within-study contrasts relate these distinctions to existing results. We further propose common-data and interactive comparisons that evaluate reference and revised improvers from shared learner starts, separating the use of experience from its acquisition. This perspective connects the diverse methods, physical operating conditions, and evaluation evidence, underpinning embodied RSI. A comprehensive list of studies in this survey is available at https://github.com/nkd-lkz/physical-ai-rsi-survey.
authors: Xiaofeng Han, Kaize Luo, Zenghuang Fu, Zichong Zhu, Zhe Feng, Changwei Wang, Rongtao Xu, Weiliang Meng, Xiaopeng Zhang
bullets: Distinguishes ordinary learner updates from improvers that revise data collection, feedback, or learning procedures.
Reviews policy learning, imagined experience, memory and skill accumulation, and executable learning harnesses.
Identifies contact validity, recovery, retention, and resource costs as factors governing whether gains persist during deployment.
Introduces an L0–L3 rubric spanning task-local adaptation to verified improvement of the improver itself.
Proposes common-data and interactive comparisons to separate learning from experience from improving how experience is acquired.

figures.caption: FIGURE 1. Overview of the review framework for recursive self-improvement in physical AI. (a) Conceptual distinctions among programmed robots, learned policies, persistent self-improvement, and recursive improvement. (b) Physical experience and feedback support capability updates, while system-generated process revisions are retained and reused to govern later learning. (c) Persistent artifacts can modify the learner, the improver, or both. (d) The evidence rubric distinguishes task-local adaptation (L0), persistent capability gain (L1), inherited process revision (L2), and verified improver gain (L3). L3 requires greater subsequent gains from shared learner starts under matched resource budgets and independent tests. The levels specify evidence requirements for individual claims. Comparisons are schematic, and robot scenes are illustrative renderings.

FIGURE 3. Evidence requirements across a declared reset boundary. Episode context c, retained learner state x, and improvement procedure ϕ have different persistence roles. L0 describes task-local changes that reset; L1 concerns retained capability gains in later independent attempts. L2 requires a system-generated process revision to be inherited and used in a later learner update. L3 requires greater subsequent gains under shared learner starts, matched resource budgets, and independent tests. The diagrams illustrate the criteria and corresponding evaluation conditions.

FIGURE 5. Four carriers of persistent physical experience. Policy and value updates change parameters and action selection; world models retain predictive structure learned from observed transitions; indexed memory and skill libraries support retrieval and composition; programs and harnesses retain changes to execution logic, illustrated by a recovery branch. Each panel exposes the retained representation and its later use. A program change is classified by its functional role in execution or in producing later updates.

FIGURE 6. Fixed-model planning and model–policy co-improvement. The fixed-model planner evaluates imagined action alternatives and executes a selected action while retaining model parameters. In the coupled loop, real transitions train the model, the updated model generates imagined trajectories for policy learning, and the updated policy collects further physical experience. Solid and dashed paths distinguish physical and model-generated experience. The observed–predicted offset is schematic; coupling alone does not establish inherited revision of the improvement procedure.

FIGURE 2. Information boundaries between physical interaction, learner updates, and improver revision. Observations supply experience for learner updates; system-generated procedure changes are retained and used in later update rounds. Development screening can inform these revisions. A concealed reporting audit evaluates frozen candidates on independent held-out outcomes and supplies no feedback to the updates being assessed. Grids, contact geometry, records, and program differences are schematic representations.

FIGURE 7. Four locations for inherited improver revision. Changes to acquisition alter the selected experience; changes to feedback alter the training signal; changes to learning or search alter the update routine; changes to a development gate alter which candidates are retained. Highlighted differences are accepted, inherited, and used in a later cycle. The rows describe alternative intervention locations. Development-gate revisions remain subject to declared external constraints, while independent reporting tests stay fixed for the comparison.

FIGURE 8. Physical continuity and learning-state retention are separate, coordinated processes. Contact changes or calibration drift can require physical recovery before redeployment. Candidate changes to retained state are checked on earlier and new tasks, then accepted or rolled back to the previous checkpoint. Recovery is not itself a learning update. The resource ledger spans collection, recovery, updating, and verification, including robot time, computation, human effort, and wear or repair.

FIGURE 4. Developmental trajectories of self-improvement in Physical AI. The 46 selected works are grouped by mechanism, with a separate column for recent work. Branches indicate thematic grouping, not causal inheritance or increasing RSI maturity. Intervals have unequal duration; within-period placement follows mechanism. R, S, and D denote reported real-robot, simulated/virtual, and non-embodied settings, not evidence strength. P denotes a project report without an assigned experimental-setting tag. Persistent updates and task gains alone do not establish improver gain.

FIGURE 9. Conceptual physical failure modes. (a) A plausible pose can yield unstable contact, illustrated by contact-normal and tangential-slip directions. (b) Partial observations can produce a false-positive judgment despite an unsuccessful physical outcome. (c) A new-task update can disrupt an earlier skill. (d) Sensor calibration or actuator offsets can change the observation–action mapping. The scenes, state changes, and offsets are illustrative rather than experimental measurements.

FIGURE 11. Common-data and interactive conditions for improver comparison. In the common-data condition, cloned learner starts and identical permitted evidence enter the reference and revised improvers. In the interactive condition, each improver acquires its own evidence under matched starts and resource ceilings. Branch-specific successor learners are assessed by independent held-out tests that provide no update feedback. The two conditions assess evidence use and acquisition plus updating, respectively; report subsequent gain, retention, transfer, and actual costs.

papers.title: Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI: Mechanisms, Evidence, and Evaluation
papers.tldr: This survey frames embodied recursive self-improvement as systems that improve both their capabilities and the processes used to acquire those capabilities, and proposes ways to evaluate it.

papers.abstract: Topology-agnostic motion generation aims to synthesize motions for diverse characters with arbitrary skeletons. Unlike conventional motion generation, which assumes a fixed skeletal template, this setting must handle diverse joint configurations and inconsistent joint semantics across characters. Existing methods address this challenge through dense full-joint modeling, which incurs substantial computational cost and hinders learning transferable motion patterns across diverse skeletal topologies. We present ETA-Motion, a topology-agnostic motion generation framework based on sparse joint learning. Instead of learning motion from all joints, our method uses a compact subset of joints to reduce redundancy and trains the motion generator on the resulting sparse skeleton. To facilitate correspondence across diverse topologies, we introduce semantic joint embeddings that combine textual and visual cues, together with topology-aware training objectives for preserving skeletal structure. Although ETA-Motion is trained only on sparse skeletal observations, it supports full-skeleton motion generation during inference. Experimental results demonstrate that ETA-Motion outperforms existing topology-agnostic baselines while significantly improving efficiency and generalization to unseen motions and unseen topologies.
authors: Seoyoung Hwang, Tae-Kyun Kim
bullets: Targets topology-agnostic motion generation for characters with diverse skeletons and inconsistent joint semantics.
Uses a compact subset of joints to reduce redundancy and computational cost during training.
Combines textual and visual semantic joint embeddings with topology-aware objectives to preserve skeletal structure.
Trained on sparse observations but generates full-skeleton motion at inference.
Reportedly improves efficiency, generalization to unseen motions and topologies, and performance over existing baselines.

papers.abstract: Test-time training (TTT) layers replace the linear fast-weight memory of modern recurrent architectures with a small neural network trained online by gradient descent. This nonlinear memory is more expressive than the linear memories of Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2, but is difficult to parallelize: existing implementations such as TTT-MLP rely on sequential, block-wise weight updates that run several times slower than chunkwise-parallel linear recurrences. Moreover, their block-wise execution only approximates the token-by-token online recurrence, whereas linear recurrences admit an exact chunkwise-parallel evaluation. We introduce ParaTTT (PTTT), an algorithm for parallelizing arbitrarily deep nonlinear memories by iteratively refining estimates of the inner-loop gradient trajectory. Starting from a guess of the hidden-layer gradients, each refinement consists of three chunkwise-parallel passes: a forward pass that evaluates the resulting feature trajectory, an exact gated-delta-rule pass that computes the readout trajectory and its feature gradients, and a backward pass that propagates these gradients into a new estimate. The exact online gradient descent recurrence is a fixed point of the iteration, while decoding requires no refinement iterations. We prove geometric convergence for a two-layer variant under sufficient contraction conditions. In practice, two iterations suffice. With two refinement steps at 4K context, PTTT evaluates the inner-loop trajectory $32\times$ faster than TTT-MLP with the block approximation at matched error, while the full 340M model trains $4.9\times$ faster. Models trained at 340M and 1.3B parameters match or exceed Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2 and remain competitive with same-size Transformers on language-modeling perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, with better recall than the linear recurrences.
authors: Noel Loo, Neehal Tumma, T. Konstantin Rusch, Mathias Lechner, Alexander Amini, Daniela Rus
bullets: TTT layers use more expressive nonlinear memories than linear recurrent alternatives but are difficult and slow to parallelize.
ParaTTT iteratively refines hidden-layer gradient trajectories using three chunkwise-parallel passes: forward, gated-delta readout/gradient computation, and backward propagation.
The exact online gradient-descent recurrence is a fixed point of the refinement process; decoding requires no refinement iterations.
Two refinement steps are typically sufficient; at 4K context, inner-loop evaluation is 32× faster than block-approximated TTT-MLP at matched error, while the full 340M model trains 4.9× faster.
At 340M and 1.3B parameters, models match or exceed Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2, remain competitive with similarly sized Transformers, and show better recall than linear recurrences.

figures.caption: Figure 2: One iteration of ParaTTT; the recurrences are evaluated in chunkwise-parallel form over all T tokens. (1) A parallel forward pass evaluates the hidden layers from the current estimate of their pre-activation gradients. (2) The readout runs exactly on the resulting features and DELTARULEGRAD returns each token’s feature gradient. (3) A parallel backward pass propagates it through the hidden layers using shifted reads of the transposed recurrences (see Step 3 in Section 3.2 for details) and updates the estimate. (4) After N iterations a final forward pass and readout produce the output.

Figure 1: Parallelism and approximation in nonlinear TTT. Each cell represents a hidden preactivation gradient δzt(W) = ∂ℓt/∂zt|W, with the layer index omitted. Columns index tokens; downward steps mark computational dependencies, not approximation error or elapsed time. (a) Exact gradients δz⋆t use the latest online weights W̄t−1, including decay. (b) Block-wise TTT, as used by TTT-MLP (Sun et al., 2025) and Titans (Behrouz et al., 2025b), evaluates gradients at shared block-entry weights Wblk s for s < t ≤ s + b, omitting earlier within-block updates. (c) ParaTTT refines the full gradient trajectory using three chunkwise-parallel passes per round. The block size b and refinement count N control the respective approximations; the exact trajectory is a fixed point of the ParaTTT iteration.

papers.abstract: Offline reinforcement learning seeks to learn decision policies from previously collected data, but deployment environments may differ from the domains in which the data were collected, and logged variables may omit confounders that affected both historical actions and outcomes. We study offline policy learning under the joint challenges of domain discrepancy and unmeasured confounding, where multiple heterogeneous source datasets provide complementary information about a target domain. We develop a causally adjusted transportability framework combining transportability theory with instrumental variables, negative controls, and proxies to identify target-domain causal quantities. For confounded contextual bandits, identification reduces to systems of bridge-function integral equations, enabling minimax estimation from finite samples. Confidence sets for the identified quantities are then used for pessimistic policy optimization, yielding CAT-CCB. We extend the framework to episodic confounded Markov decision processes, where complementary sources identify target reward and transition mechanisms under structural and completeness conditions. Under Gaussian dynamics and linear function approximation, this yields CAT-CMDP. We establish high-probability finite-sample suboptimality guarantees that quantify the effects of approximation, estimation, source-to-target shift, offline coverage, and sample size. For bounded finite-dimensional linear classes, the contextual-bandit guarantee recovers the standard $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(N^{-1/2})$ rate. Numerical experiments support the effectiveness of the framework for learning target-domain policies from heterogeneous confounded data. Together, the results provide a principled approach when no single source dataset suffices for causal identification and policy optimization.
authors: Junyi Liao, Hangqi Ren, Zhuoran Yang
bullets: Addresses offline reinforcement learning with both source-to-target domain discrepancy and unmeasured confounding.
Uses transportability theory with instrumental variables, negative controls, and proxies to identify target-domain causal quantities.
Develops bridge-function integral-equation methods and pessimistic policy optimization for confounded contextual bandits (CAT-CCB).
Extends the framework to episodic confounded MDPs under structural and completeness conditions, including Gaussian linear dynamics (CAT-CMDP).
Provides finite-sample suboptimality guarantees and numerical evidence, with performance depending on approximation, estimation, shift, coverage, and sample size.

papers.tldr: A causal framework enables offline policy learning in a shifted target domain despite unmeasured confounding, by combining information from heterogeneous source datasets.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) requires instruction-consistent planning and reliable execution under collision constraints. Yet many hierarchical approaches optimize the planner while keeping execution fixed. We introduce MATCH, a framework that jointly learns a language-conditioned planner and a goal-conditioned primitive-action executor. An execution-aware topological graph represents start-dependent execution options and integrates executor value estimates with realized outcome memory, enabling the planner to select execution requests and refine their targets through bounded continuous offsets. A transition-aware dense macro reward balances ordered progress along the reference route against execution residual, encouraging executable requests without substituting local success for instruction following. A staged curriculum culminates in synchronized on-policy updates, with the executor learning on planner-generated requests and the planner adapting its requests to the executor's current behavior. With 0.5B parameters, MATCH achieves state-of-the-art performance on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks. Preliminary real-robot deployments further demonstrate its practical potential.
authors: Shuhao Ye, Yufei Wei, Demao Wang, Shichao Zhai, Rong Xiong, Yue Wang
bullets: Targets VLN-CE challenges involving collision-aware execution and instruction-consistent planning.
Uses an execution-aware topological graph combining executor value estimates with realized outcome memory.
Allows the planner to issue execution requests and refine targets through bounded continuous offsets.
Introduces a dense macro reward balancing ordered route progress with execution residual.
Staged curriculum and synchronized on-policy learning couple planner and executor adaptation; reports state-of-the-art results on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, with preliminary real-robot demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Existing code reveals past implementation decisions but rarely explains the reasoning behind them. When coding agents implement new features or modify existing functionality, past decisions may conflict with new task instructions. This raises a fundamental question for agentic software evolution: when multiple implementations satisfy the same functional requirements, how do coding agents decide whether to follow existing code or new task instructions? We investigate this question through bidirectional, controlled experiments in purpose-built repositories, followed by validation in real-world open-source repositories. Our approach isolates three competing sources of guidance: (1) agents' default preferences, (2) repository precedents, and (3) explicit task instructions. We conduct 5,625 trials across four coding agents and six implementation pairs, with validation in four open-source repositories spanning three programming languages. We find that agents share the same default implementation choices, yet overwhelmingly follow repository precedent when it conflicts with those defaults (359/360 trials). Crucially, not all precedents carry equal influence: three supporting local files yield 96% adoption, compared with only 4% for sibling-resource files, and changing file placement alone can shift adoption from 0% to 100% at a fixed example count. When new task intent conflicts with existing code, written priority rules achieve substantially higher success than code examples alone (59/60 versus 38/60 joint successes for two agents on two implementation pairs). The effectiveness of explicit rules also extends to open-source repositories, where a harness-loaded rule raises joint success from 0/120 to 117/120. These findings motivate design-decision traceability that preserves not only implementation choices but also the rationale and priorities that should guide future changes.
authors: Haichao Zhu, Geyang Xu, Zhaorui Yang, Jiyuan Wang, Qian Zhang
bullets: The study separates three influences on agent decisions: default preferences, repository precedents, and explicit task instructions.
Across 5,625 controlled trials, agents followed conflicting repository precedents in 359 of 360 cases, though influence depended strongly on precedent location.
Three supporting local files drove 96% adoption, while sibling-resource files drove only 4%; changing file placement alone shifted adoption from 0% to 100%.
Written priority rules outperformed code examples for resolving conflicts and also improved outcomes in four real-world open-source repositories.
The findings support preserving the rationale and priority of design decisions, not just their resulting code.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates how coding agents balance repository precedents with new task instructions when evolving existing code.
papers.title: Precedent or Intent? What Coding Agents Follow When Evolving Existing Code
papers.tldr: Coding agents usually follow existing repository patterns over their default choices, but explicit priority rules can reliably steer them toward new task intent when precedents conflict.

papers.abstract: Current datasets for text-to-video generation are largely limited to short clips depicting a single event or coarse-grained captions. As a result, they provide limited supervision for modeling long-take temporal dependencies, often leading to temporally inconsistent generations when describing multiple events. In this paper, we introduce MEV, a multi-event video dataset designed for long-take video generation. MEV provides high-quality real-world videos where subjects can perform a sequence of distinct, non-overlapping events, featuring precise temporal boundaries and fine-grained procedural annotations. This event-centric discretization reduces confounding factors and enables models to support temporally localized conditioning and build long-take videos from atomic event units. Furthermore, we introduce a comprehensive annotation pipeline that segments videos into temporally grounded events, and generates structured captions at both the global level and the event level. In addition, under an event-centric evaluation protocol, we conduct multi-event generation experiments by fine-tuning on MEV with temporally grounded event conditioning, leading to improved long-take event transitions and more coherent content. We believe this work provides a publicly available resource for multi-event fine-tuning and event-centric evaluation, together with practical insights into learning from temporally structured video-text data.
authors: Peiyuan Zhu, Shaoan Xie, Yifan Shen, Wen Tian, Zijian Li, Guangyi Chen, Kun Zhang
bullets: Addresses the lack of datasets containing long videos with multiple distinct events and fine-grained temporal supervision.
Provides real-world videos with non-overlapping event sequences, precise temporal boundaries, and procedural annotations.
Introduces global- and event-level structured captions through an event-segmentation annotation pipeline.
Supports temporally localized conditioning and construction of long-take videos from atomic event units.
Fine-tuning with event conditioning improves event transitions and content coherence under an event-centric evaluation protocol.

MEV provides video-level captions at multiple granularities (short/middle/long), complemented by a structured set of global fields (e.g., background, theme, style, shot type, camera movement, lighting, atmosphere, and subject profile). At the event level, each long-take video is temporally segmented into atomic events with precise timestamps under a consistent camera perspective, and each event is annotated with camera-based descriptions, semantic attributes for subset selection or conditional supervision, and VBench-based quality scores assessing generation-relevant video quality across six dimensions.

We evaluate the open-source Wan 2.1-14B [23] and the closed-source Kling 2.6 [64] by concatenating global captions with event-level captions in a single-pass generation manner. Results show that higher caption granularity improves alignment with the Ground Truth video and enhances coverage of sequential events. Wan 2.1 consistently fails to capture some events (e.g., turning off the lamp and lying down), and even the closedsource Kling 2.6 struggles to execute “turning off the lamp”, indicating potential limitations for multi-event video generation.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used for financial guidance, yet little is known about whether their advice changes across social identities in Global South contexts. We introduce the Indian Financial Automated Advice Bias (IFAAB) benchmark, a counterfactual audit dataset of 31,734 GPT-4o-generated financial-advice responses for synthetic Indian personas varying by gender, caste, education, employment, residence, age, and district. Holding the underlying request fixed, we evaluate disparities in LLM-implied wealth, income, savings, projected gains, textual similarity, advice topics, and qualitative bias judgments. In the gender-only audit, male-labelled profiles receive 60.1\% higher initial total resources and 46.8\% higher post-advice total resources than comparable female-labelled profiles; in the caste-augmented audit, the post-advice total-resource gap remains 49.4\%. Adding district information reduces the aggregate post-advice total-resource gender gap to 7.9\%, revealing strong geographic conditioning. Standalone caste comparisons also show systematic stratification: relative to General-category profiles, OBC, SC, and ST profiles receive significantly lower post-advice total resources, respectively. Textual audits show low semantic similarity between paired gendered responses, with an average TF--IDF cosine similarity score of 0.44. Qualitative analysis shows that women are more often steered toward cautious saving, community support, and basic financial literacy, while men receive more growth-oriented advice involving investment, entrepreneurship, and asset accumulation. IFAAB provides a reusable benchmark for evaluating fairness, suitability, and consumer-protection risks in LLM-mediated financial advice, and highlights the need for locally grounded, intersectional evaluation of AI systems in high-stakes economic domains.
authors: Kriti Mahajan

papers.abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) typically mitigates distribution shift by imposing divergence constraints on the action distributions of the learned and behavior policies. However, this paradigm cannot ensure the underlying dynamic consistency structure: even minor action deviations can lead to drastically different transitions, inadvertently driving the agent away from the offline dataset. To address this, we explore policy constraints through their induced state-consequence distributions rather than relying on pure action-distribution matching. Nevertheless, directly enforcing such consequence-aware constraints is computationally intractable without access to the true underlying dynamics model. To bypass this issue, we propose Structural Behavior Regularization (StBR), which replaces the intractable objective with a closed-form latent divergence. Structuring this latent space to reflect transition dynamics renders the latent divergence a theoretically bounded surrogate for the true consequence-distribution divergence. By regularizing the learned policy with this latent divergence, StBR adaptively tightens the behavior constraint in dynamics-sensitive regions, effectively preventing deviations outside the offline dataset. Empirically, we demonstrate that StBR achieves superior performance across diverse offline RL benchmarks.
authors: Wen Jiang, Ke Jiang, Xiaoyang Tan
bullets: Action-distribution constraints may fail when small action changes cause large transition differences and dataset departure.
The method, Structural Behavior Regularization (StBR), uses a closed-form divergence in a dynamics-structured latent space.
This latent divergence provides a theoretically bounded surrogate for the intractable true consequence-distribution divergence.
StBR adaptively tightens constraints in regions sensitive to dynamics, helping keep learned behavior within the offline data distribution.
Experiments report superior performance across diverse offline RL benchmarks.

papers.abstract: We demonstrate the first zero-shot sim-to-real transfer for a surgeon-robot collaboration task in open surgery: retractor take-over. A robot arm takes a retractor from the surgeon's hand and preserves retraction at handoff, using a policy trained only on simulated demonstrations, without human demonstrations or real-world fine-tuning. Imitation learning from real demonstrations is limited by collection and labeling costs, and by performance degradation when the environment changes. Our framework, SimRetract, generates simulated demonstrations designed for transfer: the policy observes masked instrument images and grasp geometry, learns to recover from off-nominal states, and acts with margin for execution drift. Deployed zero-shot, it grasps the retractor in 90% of 50 surgeon-defined phantom presentations and preserves retraction at handoff in 78%. Results on unseen retractors suggest potential for generalization to instruments with similar grasp geometry. Across ten policy configurations and 1,200 simulated and real trials, we localize the sim-to-real gap to components: in simulation, grasp rates across ablations span 80-96%, while on the real robot removing the instrument mask alone drops performance to 22% grasped and 12% held. Transfer-oriented design thus makes zero-shot sim-to-real transfer feasible for a surgical assistance task without human demonstrations. Code is available here: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/simretract-58D2.
authors: Xucheng Wang, Zhizhou Yang, Sung Eun Kim, Romain Hardy, Michael P. Sampson, Aakash Reddy, Ankit Pal, Xiaoman Zhang, Luyang Luo, Pranav Rajpurkar
bullets: Addresses costly real-world demonstration collection and limited robustness to changing surgical environments.
Trains an imitation-learning policy solely on simulated demonstrations using masked instrument images and grasp geometry.
Designs simulations for transfer by including off-nominal recovery and execution-drift margins.
Across 50 surgeon-defined phantom presentations, the robot grasped the retractor in 90% and preserved retraction at handoff in 78%.
Results on unseen retractors indicate potential generalization to instruments with similar grasp geometry; performance depends strongly on instrument masking.

papers.title: SimRetract: Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Robotic Assistance for Retractor Take-Over in Open Surgery

papers.abstract: Mobile manipulator robots rarely reposition their base during manipulation, because doing so requires real-time knowledge of how well the arm can reach its surroundings among obstacles. Reachability maps (RMs) encode this knowledge, but existing methods are slow, coarse (typically 5 cm), or ignore real obstacles. This article asks whether a neural network can predict an obstacle-aware RM at 2 cm resolution from a live depth camera, on embedded hardware, fast enough for online use. We present HERON, a 3D U-Net trained on RMs computed with the GPU-accelerated inverse kinematics of cuRobo, first on synthetic scenes and then on real depth data, and deployed on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT and INT8 quantization. HERON predicts the RM of a 2.56 m cube around the arm in 115 ms on average, for a measured system rate of 8.57 Hz, close to the 10 Hz update rate of the obstacle map, whereas computing the same map with cuRobo takes about 90 min. Against the cuRobo ground truth, 95% of the voxels lie within 1 class out of 51 with the FP32 model and within 3 classes with the INT8 model, with a Pearson correlation of 0.99 and a quadratic weighted kappa above 0.9. Accuracy degrades mainly at the workspace boundaries.

Runs in 115 ms on average (8.57 Hz), compared with about 90 minutes for direct cuRobo computation.

papers.abstract: Language models increasingly create 3D content through code, with practical workflows often relying on editing existing programs rather than regenerating them, for speed and precise control. Such edits require understanding what a program builds and foreseeing how a change reshapes it, yet prior benchmarks mostly evaluate generation or simple edits against a reference. In this paper, we introduce 3DCodeEdit, a benchmark of 2,592 instruction-guided editing tasks over 108 Blender programs that construct objects entirely in code. Its edits range from parameter to structural changes, style redesign, and scene composition, and are judged from renders against human-reviewed checklists. Across 17 models, the average success rate is only 37%, and even the strongest models complete fewer than 60% of structural and style edits. As models become more capable, their failures shift to geometric foresight, where the code runs but builds the wrong shape. We therefore study whether multi-turn feedback can compensate for this missing foresight. Feedback from a separate reviewer model that describes how the renders differ from the request helps most, more than maximum reasoning effort or an agent harness, and can let a 27B model surpass the single-shot rate of a 2.8T-parameter model.
authors: Binjie Wang, Xinran Zhao, Shoubin Yu, Xiang Li, Silong Yong, Chenyang Yang, Tianyu Chen, Ruofei Du, He He, Chen Zhao, Tongshuang Wu
bullets: Introduces 2,592 editing tasks across 108 Blender programs, covering parameter and structural edits, style redesign, and scene composition.
Evaluates 17 models using rendered outputs and human-reviewed checklists rather than code similarity alone.
Average success is 37%; even the strongest models solve fewer than 60% of structural and style edits.
As models improve, failures increasingly involve geometric foresight: executable code that produces the wrong shape.

Reviewer-model feedback describing render discrepancies helps more than additional reasoning effort or an agent harness, enabling a 27B model to exceed a 2.8T-parameter model’s single-shot performance.
