papers.abstract: Fully Sharded Data Parallelism (FSDP2) maintains parameters and gradients as per-parameter tensors, whereas its collective path operates on flat, rank-major buffers. Converting between these layouts copies all-gather outputs into parameter storage and packs gradients into full-group fp32 buffers. Layout conversion alone accounts for 6.4% of step time in Llama-3.1 70B training at 8K tokens per GPU. Communication kernels impose a second cost: a default NCCL reduce-scatter can slow a concurrent GEMM that would otherwise complete in a single wave by 69%. We present TIDE, a set of zero-copy collectives built on public NCCL 2.31+ APIs. TIDE preserves FSDP2's per-parameter storage and compute kernels while folding layout placement into collective addressing. TIDE-AG delivers shards directly to parameter storage using NVSwitch multicast and paced recursive-doubling RDMA, with no SMs used for transport or placement. TIDE-RS consumes per-parameter bf16 gradients directly and reduces them into fp32 shards (a mixed-precision mode that NCCL does not provide) using copy engines and short-lived thread blocks (CTAs) for node-local accumulation and NVSwitch for cross-node reduction. A two-phase pipeline separates gradient reads from network progress; Slot-Reuse optionally stages gradients in vacated all-gather slots. On 64 GPUs, TIDE reduces step time by up to 27.1% relative to Stock FSDP2 and 6.0% relative to FSDP2+SymmMem across Llama-3.1 70B, Wan2.2, and Qwen3-30B-A3B. It reduces reduce-scatter SM time by factors of 12.5-14.5 and cuts interference with concurrent compute by up to an order of magnitude. Its reduce-scatter buffer remains nearly constant from 16 to 64 GPUs at a fixed per-GPU output size, and its peak memory is up to 4.7 GiB below FSDP2+SymmMem's and, with Slot-Reuse on Wan2.2, below Stock FSDP2's.
authors: Zejian Wang, Yifan Zhao, Kaihui Ren, Xiaoling Zhou, Yubin Wang, Chenhao Guan, Lin Zhang, Yufeng Li, Zhikang Mo, Zhuoru Ma, Yingtong Xiong, Jihu Guo, Yiqiao Liao, Chengru Song
bullets: FSDP2’s mismatch between per-parameter tensors and flat rank-major collective buffers causes substantial copying and compute interference.
TIDE folds layout placement into collective addressing while preserving FSDP2 storage and compute kernels.
TIDE-AG uses NVSwitch multicast and paced RDMA; TIDE-RS combines copy engines, CTAs, and NVSwitch for mixed-precision gradient reduction.
On 64 GPUs, TIDE cuts step time by up to 27.1% versus Stock FSDP2 and 6.0% versus FSDP2+SymmMem across three workloads.
It reduces reduce-scatter SM time by 12.5–14.5× and lowers memory usage, with scope focused on public NCCL 2.31+ APIs and the evaluated GPU configurations.

papers.abstract: Walking offers a window into physical function that may support interpretable video-based frailty assessment. We developed silhouette-based "gaitomics" to connect frailty predictions with measurable patterns of body configuration and movement. In 66 older adults assessed using the Fried Frailty Phenotype, standardized silhouettes and gait energy images yielded 90 descriptors of shape, temporal variation, motion, and texture. Minimum redundancy maximum relevance selection using the mutual information difference criterion prioritized informative features while limiting redundancy. Each classifier was evaluated using nested stratified cross-validation with five outer and three inner folds at the participant level, with feature ranking and feature-count selection confined to training partitions. Shapley additive explanations examined contributions to held-out predictions. Bilateral silhouette difference led the aggregate feature-selection rankings for three-class classification and both comparisons involving frail participants. Attribution profiles differed across tasks, with texture and consecutive-frame silhouette differences prominent in three-class classification. Among classifier-specific evaluations, CatBoost achieved the highest mean three-class micro-AUC of 0.647 \pm 0.085. Leading pairwise mean micro-AUCs were 0.833 \pm 0.249 for frail versus nonfrail, 0.765 \pm 0.168 for frail versus prefrail, and 0.554 \pm 0.129 for prefrail versus nonfrail classification. These findings connect model predictions to explicit gait characteristics while revealing task-dependent feature priorities and limited separation of prefrail and nonfrail participants. The framework provides an interpretable basis for further investigation, with larger independent studies needed to establish reliability and clinical relevance.
authors: Laura McDaniel, Ryan Roemmich, Crystal Szczesny, Peter Abadir, Rama Chellappa, Basudha Pal
bullets: Analyzed 90 shape, motion, temporal-variation, and texture descriptors from standardized silhouettes and gait energy images in 66 older adults.
Used mutual-information-based feature selection, participant-level nested cross-validation, and SHAP explanations to link predictions to gait characteristics.

CatBoost achieved a mean three-class micro-AUC of 0.647; frail-versus-nonfrail classification was stronger than prefrail-versus-nonfrail classification.
The study is limited by small sample size and weak prefrail/nonfrail separation; larger independent studies are needed to assess reliability and clinical relevance.

papers.abstract: Robot imitation learning uses demonstrations from operators of varying skill, but selecting training data remains challenging. Existing methods score demonstrations using smoothness, diversity, or estimated influence on policy performance, but differences in selection and evaluation protocols make it difficult to determine whether they outperform simple baselines. We introduce \textbf{CuraEval}, a framework combining mathematical analysis of demonstration scores with controlled comparisons against fixed size-matched random subsets and full-data training on mixed-skill robomimic data using Diffusion Policy and BC-RNN. We show that the evaluated PSD score depends only on episode length and squared position magnitudes, and produces nearly the same ranking as episode length on \textit{square} ($\rho=0.999$). With Diffusion Policy, selecting the shortest 50\% of demonstrations improves \textit{square} success from 70.7\% under random selection to 76.5\%. Compared with random selection, our adapted geometric-entropy LOO selector reduces success at 25\% retention from 94.7\% to 74.0\% on \textit{can} and achieves 41.7\% on \textit{square}, below the mean success rates of all three independently sampled random subsets (59.8--62.5\%). On the same 3 \textit{square} Diffusion Policy training seeds, length-based selection at 75\% retention improves success over full-data training from 76.7\% to 86.7\% under the original protocol, but lowers it from 80.5\% to 79.5\% after checkpoint reporting, rollout count, and evaluation seed change jointly. No evaluated curated condition significantly outperforms full-data training after Holm correction, although confidence intervals still permit useful gains. Code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/CuraEval.
authors: Jiuyi Xu, Meida Chen, Yang Ye, Yangming Shi
bullets: Evaluates demonstration scores on mixed-skill robomimic data using Diffusion Policy and BC-RNN, with size-matched random and full-data baselines.
Finds the PSD score is determined by episode length and squared position magnitudes, ranking nearly identically to episode length on square.
Selecting the shortest 50% improves square success from 70.7% to 76.5% versus random selection under one setup.

After correcting evaluation conditions and multiple comparisons, no curated setting significantly beats full-data training.

papers.abstract: Coding agents are typically provided end-to-end behavioral specifications that the code they produce should satisfy, such as tests and input--output examples. How many such specifications must a developer provide, and which ones, for the agent to produce the developer's intended program? We argue that this cannot be determined a priori, for it depends on the structure of the implementation, which is left to the agent to decide. An agent first commits to a structure---a decomposition into data types, modules, and functions---which fixes a class of candidate programs; behavioral specifications then select a program within that class. A set of tests that suffices for one structure may leave another badly underdetermined, requiring different edge cases or exponentially more examples. Since the structure is chosen by the agent, developers cannot ensure their specification is complete without reverse-engineering it from thousands of lines of generated code. To resolve this, we introduce Skeleton Coding, in which developers jointly specify the structure---in high-level, code-like format---alongside behavioral specifications. Theoretically, we model AI-assisted coding as a control problem, and show that skeletons can reduce exponentially the number of tests developers must supply to steer an agent toward an acceptable program. Empirically, across four models and three benchmarks, the best-performing skeleton specifications reduce mean test error by 48.4% relative to the best end-to-end behavioral specifications. Even when the agent can query a complete reference implementation, adding a skeleton reduces mean test error relatively by up to 27.0%. Skeletons also narrow the average gap between small and large models by about 52.4% while lowering implementation cost by 15--26x, and reduce code erosion by 24.7% on average.
authors: Aditya Golatkar, Alessandro Achille, Renos Zabounidis, Vlad Sobal, Yangruibo Ding, Baishakhi Ray, Jonathan Buck, Guy Van den Broeck, Maryam Fazel, Pietro Perona, Wei Xia, Stefano Soatto
bullets: Behavioral tests alone may be insufficient because their effectiveness depends on the implementation structure chosen by the agent.
Skeletons specify decompositions into data types, modules, and functions, narrowing the candidate-program space before behavioral tests select details.
A control-theoretic analysis shows skeletons can reduce the number of required tests exponentially in some cases.
Across four models and three benchmarks, skeletons reduced mean test error by 48.4% versus the best end-to-end behavioral specifications.
Skeletons also reduced implementation cost, narrowed the small/large-model performance gap, and mitigated code erosion; scope is limited to the evaluated models and benchmarks.

(b) Fixing a skeleton restricts the agent to programs with that skeleton. (c) Each set of end-to-end tests further keeps only the programs that agree with the reference on the tested inputs.

papers.tldr: Skeleton Coding lets developers specify a program’s high-level structure alongside tests, substantially improving coding-agent reliability and reducing specification effort.

papers.abstract: Weight-only, lossy quantization substantially reduces the storage and memory requirements for serving large language models (LLMs), but the growing key-value (KV) cache remains a bottleneck for long-context inference on personal devices. We present Group-Adaptive Additive Codec (GAAC), a lossless KV compression and serving system that exploits exponent redundancy to reduce storage and accelerate attention without introducing KV approximation. GAAC encodes BF16 exponents using calibrated per-channel base-plus-offset codes over contiguous ranges. GAAC adapts code widths across small groups while preserving KV values bit-for-bit. A fused attention kernel reconstructs KV tiles on the fly, avoiding full-cache decompression. Block-wise compression and fixed-capacity slots support incremental cache updates and paged serving. Across five tested models, GAAC achieves 1.405-1.407$\times$ lossless BF16 KV compression. We also study compression performance on low-precision tensors FP8 E4M3 caches ( 1.09-1.14$\times$) and E5M2 caches (1.25-1.30$\times$). On NVIDIA DGX Spark, GAAC accelerates decode attention at a 64K-token context by 1.19-1.27$\times$ and end-to-end W4A16 decode steps by 1.04-1.15$\times$. In serving, it reduces resident KV memory by approximately 26% and increases aggregate throughput by 13-29% under comparable KV-memory budgets. On Apple M4, GAAC achieves 1.02-1.25$\times$ attention speedups, demonstrating portability beyond NVIDIA GPUs.
authors: Yipin Guo, Arun M George, Siddharth Joshi
bullets: Addresses KV-cache growth as a bottleneck for long-context LLM serving on memory- and bandwidth-constrained devices.
Uses adaptive base-plus-offset coding for BF16 exponent groups while preserving KV values bit-for-bit.
Fused attention reconstructs compressed KV tiles on demand, supporting incremental updates and paged serving without full-cache decompression.
Across five models, achieves 1.405–1.407× BF16 KV compression, about 26% lower resident KV memory, and 13–29% higher serving throughput under comparable memory budgets.
Reports attention speedups on NVIDIA DGX Spark and Apple M4, including 1.19–1.27× at 64K-token context on DGX Spark and 1.02–1.25× on M4.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of GAAC. (a) GAAC exploits the concentration of BF16 exponent values in contiguous high-frequency regions. Each group of eight exponents shares a 2-bit tag indicating 3-bit, 4-bit, or raw mode. The sign and mantissa bits of each element are stored unchanged in a single byte. Each code is an offset from a calibrated per-channel base, ci = ei − bw,i. In the illustrated example, one exponent outside the 3-bit window causes the entire group g+1 to use 4-bit mode. Bits per element include the sign-mantissa byte and the mode tag. (b) Compared with standard attention, GAAC reduces KV loading time by reading fewer bytes from the compressed cache, with only a small computational overhead from on-the-fly decompression. o denotes the attention output. Figure 3: System design of GAAC. (a) New tokens are appended to an uncompressed BF16 tail until the block is full. (b) The full block is encoded once. If its compressed size S does not exceed the slot capacity C, it is stored in a compressed slot; otherwise, it remains in BF16 format. (c) The paged KV cache holds compressed and raw finalized blocks in block-table order, followed by the incomplete BF16 tail.

papers.abstract: LLM-based agents now share experiences on social platforms and remember new preferences to enhance their performance. However, existing memory systems contain a vulnerability in role-to-principal attribution that attackers can exploit. We identify Role Grounding Misattribution, in which an attacker-designed interaction causes the victim agent to incorrectly record a preference from the attacker as a preference of the victim's user. Specifically, we are the first to formalize Role Grounding Attack (RGA), an attack model that exploits this vulnerability through nested conversation structures. In the memory formation stage, an experience-sharing post quoting a conversation between the attacker agent and its user is published, which explicitly identifies its publisher. The inner conversation expresses preferences from the user of the attacker agent. When the victim agent remembers preferences from this nested structure, its memory loses the context binding and grounds the attacker's preference to the victim's user instead. In the memory retrieval stage, the misattributed preference persists and influences the victim agent's decisions when it encounters relevant scenarios. We instantiate RGA as tool selection manipulation and privacy leakage. Tool selection manipulation causes a tool-call preference to be misattributed to the victim's user, steering the victim toward an attacker-controlled tool. Privacy leakage extends this by misattributing both a tool-call preference and a task-requirement preference to the victim's user. The victim selects the attacker's tool, then includes sensitive information in tool arguments to satisfy the task requirement. We evaluate RGA across five mainstream memory systems and six language models. Tool manipulation and privacy leakage both achieve high attack success rates. These results call for stronger role grounding.

bullets: Identifies Role Grounding Misattribution as a vulnerability in memory systems’ role-to-principal attribution.
Formalizes RGA through nested conversations embedded in experience-sharing posts.
Demonstrates tool-selection manipulation and privacy leakage as attack scenarios.
Evaluates five mainstream memory systems and six language models, finding high attack success rates for both scenarios.
Calls for stronger role grounding to preserve preference ownership and context.

papers.abstract: Behavior Cloning has demonstrated promising generalization capabilities for robotic manipulation in terrestrial environments. However, marine visual distortions and dynamic currents create a severe domain shift that remains a key bottleneck in adapting generalist architectures to underwater field manipulation. To address this, 1616 episodes of underwater manipulation data were collected in calm and turbulent waters and were used to train 14 generalist Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (DynamicVLA) with varying proprioception observation configurations. Across three tasks on 1260 gradable on-hardware rollouts in a pool, 10 models outperformed the baseline, with the highest-performing model achieving a 93.3% overall success rate, including partial successes. Results are also introduced from a case study evaluating the performance of a single-task Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) and a generalist VLA (SmolVLA) policy for two tasks in marine archaeology and conservation: grasping and mooring. Experiments are performed on an ROV on and around the WWII wreck Coralita X127 and at Manoel Island Marina, Malta. Across 748 collected episodes and 508 gradable on-hardware rollouts, the ACT policy substantially outperformed SmolVLA (47.9% vs. 7.9% pooled success rate), earning a 66.7% success rate on the most successful task at the marine archaeological site. To enable further contributions to embodied intelligence in marine field robotics, the BLUEMBODIED KIT used to collect data, train models, and deploy policies on the ROV has been open sourced.
authors: Greta Perez-Haiek (New York University), Luca Macesanu (New York University), Kevin Angers (New York University), Mohammed Imam (New York University), Timothy Gambin (University of Malta), Christopher Clark (New York University)

In marine archaeology and conservation trials, single-task ACT substantially outperformed generalist SmolVLA (47.9% vs. 7.9% pooled success).
The open-sourced BLUEMBODIED KIT supports underwater data collection, training, and ROV policy deployment.

papers.abstract: Serverless platforms increasingly host machine learning (ML) inference workflows, modeled as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) of interdependent functions. Beyond container startup, each ML node must load libraries, model weights, and CUDA kernels before it can run. These costs accumulate along dependent DAG paths and place initialization on the end-to-end critical path. Existing systems optimize one half of this problem. DAG-agnostic pre-loading prepares nodes the request may never reach, wasting host and GPU memory. DAG-aware serving routes and scales whole functions, leaving the loading stages inside a node untouched. This paper presents GearUp, a serverless DAG inference serving system that removes ML-node loading from the end-to-end critical path at low resource cost. GearUp profiles the loading stages of each node and schedules them inside the slack time the DAG exposes, hiding initialization behind upstream execution. It reuses initialized instances within and across requests to avoid redundant cold starts. A probabilistic, traffic-adaptive keep-alive policy sets how long idle instances are retained, balancing memory cost against cold-start risk under bursty load. On the AMBER Alert and FINRA-ML workflows with NVIDIA L40S GPUs, GearUp reduces median end-to-end latency by 64.5% and 75.9% against SMIless, for median speedups of 3.1x and 10.0x over cold execution. Integrated GPU and host memory allocation fall by up to 83.9% and 94.6% against eager pre-loading in InstaInfer. GearUp achieves 4.2x strong scaling on four workers.

bullets: Targets initialization delays from libraries, model weights, and CUDA kernels on DAG critical paths.

Reuses initialized instances across and within requests to reduce redundant cold starts.
Uses traffic-adaptive probabilistic keep-alive to balance retained-memory cost against cold-start risk.
On two GPU workflows, reduces median end-to-end latency by 64.5% and 75.9% versus SMIless, while cutting memory use by up to 83.9% (GPU) and 94.6% (host) versus eager pre-loading.

papers.abstract: Short video platforms have become a primary channel for black and gray industry operations in internet finance, where inducements such as prompts to like, follow, join private chat groups, or click external links frequently steer users toward fraud. Because such videos are short, dynamic, and often convey intent through fleeting visual cues rather than stable text, a moderation system must guarantee detection recall and localize the offending segment so reviewers inspect only the relevant clip. Existing OCR+LLM pipelines transcribe on-screen text frame by frame and classify the transcript, but exploit only textual information. Many inducements are conveyed through visual cues OCR cannot observe, and keyframe-based localization cannot recover precise temporal boundaries. We explore OCR+MLLM, which augments the text pipeline with a Multimodal Large Language Model, and compare three routes: OCR+LLM, OCR+MLLM, and a large zero-shot MLLM, along detection, latency, token consumption, and deployment complexity. OCR preserves the text signal that guarantees recall, while the MLLM jointly performs OCR-grounded discrimination and temporal grounding, localizing both textual and non-textual inducements. We construct a dataset of 2,419 internet finance short videos (66.49 hours) with 3,194 annotated events across four categories, and study reward design for RL-based grounding under class imbalance. We report two findings: auxiliary reward terms are exploited through reward hacking, and stronger localization rewards degrade class-balanced detection. We therefore design a recall-weighted F2 localization reward with class-balanced resampling. Experiments show OCR+MLLM localizes better than the keyframe OCR+LLM baseline (mIoU 26.52 vs. 14.49) and detects non-textual inducements that text-only pipelines miss, while maintaining 67.0 percent macro recall.

On 2,419 annotated videos, OCR+MLLM raises mIoU to 26.52 versus 14.49 for keyframe OCR+LLM and detects non-textual inducements missed by text-only methods.

papers.abstract: Video understanding keeps moving toward longer recordings, and the longer a recording is, the more questions can be asked about it. But processing it again for every question does not scale, so many systems watch the video once, build a memory, and answer later questions from it. Yet what to remember is decided before anyone knows what will be asked, and whatever is left out cannot be recovered later. Moreover, whether the savings pay off is judged by token counts, which fall when the input gets shorter but not when the model reuses what it has already computed. We present REEL, an evaluation framework that compares three saved representations built from exactly the same observed frames, so that a change in answers can come only from what the system remembered. Text writes a short record of what happened, Visual keeps the encoder outputs, and Prefix State also keeps the language-model prefix. Each is compared with full reprocessing (Frames) by paired correctness changes, cumulative GPU time, and storage size. Across six vision-language models and two benchmarks, Text and Frames differ in correctness on 20\% to 29\% of questions, even when their mean accuracy is almost the same. By contrast, Visual and Prefix State stay much closer to Frames. With unlimited storage, Prefix State is the cheapest in total GPU time among memories that keep almost all of the answers Frames gets right, for every model on both benchmarks. The trade-off is storage: Prefix State keeps up to about 21 GiB per video, whereas Text needs only kilobytes. Reusing computation and discarding information both look like efficiency, but only the second removes evidence that later questions may need, and neither mean accuracy nor token count tells them apart. REEL makes that difference measurable for any system that answers many questions from one saved memory.

papers.abstract: Controllable human motion generation has largely focused on specifying what action should occur or where the body should move. We study a complementary question: can full-body motion be controlled by specifying only when each foot contacts the ground? We introduce StepControl, an autoregressive diffusion model conditioned on a future binary left/right foot-contact schedule, without requiring target root and body poses, or semantic prompts. StepControl represents contact as explicit temporal events and injects them through dedicated cross-attention with classifier-free guidance. We further introduce a stochastic mixture noise schedule and warmup strategy for stable long-horizon autoregressive generation. Experiments show that StepControl follows prescribed contact timing more accurately than adapting existing spatially guided motion generators to contact constraints. It maintains effective contact control over long continuous rollouts and responds to edited schedules such as cadence changes, stop-and-go pauses, limping gaits, and bilateral jumping. Our results show that minimal foot-contact schedules provide an effective and intuitive temporal interface for controllable motion generation.
authors: Hojun Jang, Jinseok Bae, Donggeun Lim, Taesun Kim, Seungbin Jeong, Younghwan Lee, Yong Seok Kim, Young Min Kim
bullets: Addresses motion control without target poses, root trajectories, or semantic action prompts.
Uses an autoregressive diffusion model with dedicated cross-attention for future binary foot-contact events.
Introduces stochastic mixture noise scheduling and warmup for stable long-horizon rollouts.
Accurately follows contact timing and supports edited patterns including cadence changes, pauses, limping, and jumping.
Scope: control is specified temporally through foot contacts rather than detailed spatial or semantic constraints.

papers.abstract: A recurring design choice in building AI systems is whether, when a task is too hard for a model, to expand the model (make it larger, better-prompted, fine-tuned), or to decompose the task (extract the parts that admit a deterministic solution to a host, leaving the model only the irreducibly fuzzy residue). We make three claims. First, that many tasks commonly delegated whole to a model are in fact deterministic tasks with a small generative core. Second, and our central empirical result, that decomposing such a task yields a measurable and desirable property we call parity by construction: on the extracted sub-tasks the model-size performance curve becomes flat, because no model performs them at all. We measure this across nine models spanning a 494M-parameter local checkpoint to a frontier Opus-class model, a thirty-fold parameter range on the local family alone: once the host resolves the context, operation selection scores identically for all nine models and selector resolution for eight of nine, while the one task that does not decompose, labelling, remains sloped across the same range. Because the task leaves the model, a stock checkpoint suffices: no task-specific training and no fine-tuning. Third, that this is a general design discipline, not a domain trick: we show the same move recurring across physics setup, motion retargeting, and object-model editing, and in a Web-CLI tool family (same author, so not an independent replication). We give a method for locating the cut, the construction that makes a cut exist (a deterministic surface and a closed grammar over it), and a way to make the residue safe (resolve the deterministic context; verify the generative output), position the work against neuro-symbolic AI, tool-augmented language models, and generate-and-verify approaches, and are explicit about what is measured (one domain) versus illustrative (the rest).
authors: Tejaswi Gowda
bullets: Many apparently generative tasks contain deterministic sub-tasks that can be extracted and delegated to a host system.
The proposed “parity by construction” makes model performance flat on extracted sub-tasks because the model no longer performs them.
Across nine models, operation selection became identical after deterministic context resolution, and selector resolution matched for eight of nine; labelling remained model-dependent.
The approach uses a deterministic surface, a closed grammar, resolved context, and verification of generative outputs—without task-specific training or fine-tuning.
Examples span physics setup, motion retargeting, object-model editing, and a Web-CLI tool family; only one domain is empirically measured, with others illustrative.

papers.tldr: Decomposing AI tasks so deterministic parts run outside the model can make performance independent of model size while leaving models only a small generative residue.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) treat all context tokens uniformly, lacking explicit separation between executable instructions and passive data. This leads to prompt injection vulnerabilities, ambiguous instruction binding, and unreliable execution control. We present a post-training methodology using LLMON (LLM Object Notation), a framework that enables separating instructions from data and requires explicit identifier-based execution. We construct a large-scale structured training corpus of 4.6B tokens spanning general, RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), and tool-calling data, augmented with distractor-infused variants in which competing instructions and irrelevant data segments are present in context but not referenced. Post-training two Granite-4.1 base models (3B and 8B) through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning, we show that LLMON-structured supervision reduces attack success rates on indirect prompt-injection benchmarks from 53-100% to 0.02-5.6% while preserving general capabilities. We further introduce attention-based interpretability metrics that diagnose failure modes at individual transformer layers for structured inputs, revealing how our approach reshapes internal attention patterns. Our results demonstrate that explicit execution semantics can be taught through standard post-training without architectural modification.
authors: Basel Shbita, Michael Hind, Chad DeLuca, Nathan Fulton, Shubhi Asthana, Farhan Ahmed, Anisa Halimi, Yada Zhu, Mauro Martino, David Cox, Dan Gutfreund
bullets: Addresses prompt injection, ambiguous instruction binding, and unreliable execution control caused by treating all context tokens uniformly.
Uses LLM Object Notation (LLMON) with identifier-based execution and structured training data covering general, RAG, tool-calling, and distractor-infused contexts.
Post-trains 3B and 8B Granite-4.1 models using supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning.
Reduces attack success on indirect prompt-injection benchmarks from 53–100% to 0.02–5.6% while preserving general capabilities.
Introduces attention-based interpretability metrics to analyze layer-level failure modes and changes in attention patterns.

papers.abstract: Deciding which member of an animal group produced a vocalization and where that vocalization was produced are central to studying social communication but are rarely evaluated with physically verified ground truth. Existing resources either localize sounds without identifying the caller, or recognize individuals from isolated vocalizations without reliance on the 3D candidate geometry. We close this gap with V33DA, a dataset-centered multimodal benchmark for spatial vocal attribution in social zebra finches: it comprises 33,625 verified events coupling 5-channel audio with three camera views, calibrated 3D pose for every visible candidate, and per-bird radio telemetry across 10 individuals and three experiments. Caller identity is verified from an on-body accelerometer-derived vibration signal; this channel is withheld from benchmark models and used only by an on-body reference ceiling. Given a detected vocalization and the visible candidate birds, the task is to select the caller. We evaluate it under three regimes: session-disjoint testing on familiar birds from held-out recording dates, held-out-experiment transfer to a new cohort, and leave-one-individual-out evaluation on a bird whose vocalizations are held out from training. Reference methods expose a consistent gap between in-domain accuracy and transfer to unseen individuals: methods that can exploit familiar vocal identity perform well on known callers but degrade sharply on unseen ones, whereas candidate-aware methods preserving explicit spatial reasoning transfer substantially better. The on-body reference stays near-perfect across regimes, confirming the internal consistency of the accelerometer-verified labels. We release V33DA with fixed protocols and code for the evaluated methods, and V33DA++, an unevaluated companion set of verified overlapping-call events and +/-2 s context windows.
authors: Maris Basha, Yuhang Wang, Xiaoran Chen, Longbiao Cheng, Luca Yapura, Anja T. Zai, Mathieu Salzmann, Richard Hahnloser

Evaluates session-disjoint, held-out-experiment, and leave-one-individual-out settings.
Finds that familiar-caller recognition degrades sharply on unseen birds, while candidate-aware spatial methods transfer better; releases V33DA, protocols, code, and V33DA++ context data.

papers.title: Who Called? V33DA: A Physically Verified Multimodal Benchmark for Vocal Attribution in Zebra Finch Groups

papers.abstract: Robot-learning studies often compare position and velocity actions as though each label identified a single experimental treatment, yet the label alone does not determine what the robot executes. Before affecting robot motion, bounded policy output passes through filtering, physical scaling, reference construction, feedback, timing, and effort limits. We study how these omitted properties affect attribution under one shared learner and training budget. Across three contact-rich Factory tasks (PegInsert, GearMesh, and NutThread), we compare five joint-space interfaces, with ten independently trained policies per condition. We first remain within the same position-feedback law and vary the executed interface: substituting only the physical action scale as the directly modified component changes sample-median evaluation success by 0.645-1.000 across tasks, while removing an exponential moving average produces task-dependent changes. We then move to a cross-law comparison and choose a velocity scale that exactly matches the position interface's local raw-torque command gain. This calibration raises the sample median on GearMesh and NutThread, with no median change on PegInsert. Yet clear residual sample-median gaps remain on PegInsert and GearMesh, while the NutThread interval includes zero. Thus, even this explicit equality leaves feedback and held-action dynamics unmatched and does not establish position-velocity trained-outcome equivalence. Action-interface comparisons should therefore report the executed pathway and state the physical quantity they match.
authors: Arshia Sangwan, Zhongyang Zhang
bullets: Studies five joint-space interfaces across three contact-rich Factory tasks using one learner, shared training budget, and ten policies per condition.
Within the same position-feedback law, changing only physical action scale alters median success, while removing smoothing has task-dependent effects.
Calibrating velocity scale to match position-interface local torque gain improves median success on two tasks but not the third.
Residual performance gaps remain, showing that matching one gain does not establish position–velocity equivalence.
Comparisons should report the full executed action pathway and the physical quantity being matched.

papers.abstract: We introduce The Prestige, a video understanding benchmark that probes cognitive visual reasoning through professional magic performances, where deliberate misdirection challenges models to track events and explain unexpected outcomes. The benchmark comprises open-ended questions ranging from temporal and causal understanding to robustness against adversarial questions. Evaluation of leading open-source and proprietary VLMs reveals a substantial gap between even the strongest model and human performance. We also find systematic discrepancies between human and automated grading and identify recurring model failure modes. Ablations further show that models can select correct multiple-choice answers even when they fail to generate correct explanations independently, motivating further investigations into question formats. Together, these findings highlight limitations in both VLM reasoning and its evaluation, underscoring the need for more reliable video understanding models and more rigorous benchmarks.
authors: Shuo Wen, Beixi Du, Edwin Meriaux, Junming Shi, Chloe Si, David Meger, Doina Precup, Gregory Dudek
bullets: Uses professional magic performances and deliberate misdirection to test event tracking and unexpected-outcome explanation.
Covers temporal, causal, and adversarial open-ended questions.
Leading open-source and proprietary VLMs perform well below humans and exhibit recurring reasoning failures.
Models may choose correct multiple-choice answers while failing to generate correct explanations.
Findings expose discrepancies between automated and human grading and motivate more rigorous benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) appear to represent and reason about a large range of phenomena. In particular, recent studies have examined whether LLMs can accurately reason about causation. One of the most commonly used benchmarks for evaluating formal causal reasoning in LLMs is CLadder, a framework for procedural generation of benchmark data sets that was released in 2023. Experiments with CLadder appear to indicate that LLMs can perform formal causal reasoning in a large percentage of generated examples. In this paper, we examine what can be reliably inferred when LLMs perform well on test sets produced by CLadder. We identify several examples of superficial and highly predictive patterns that the CLadder generator embeds in data sets it generates. We find that even simple models such as random forests perform well on CLadder-generated data sets after training on a sample of generated data. We also find that the performance of many commercial LLMs on CLadder test sets is extremely brittle and that removing large sections of the text that are critical for formal causal reasoning has almost no effect on performance. Given these results, the most likely hypothesis for the strong performance of state-of-the-art LLMs on CLadder is that they are exploiting superficial patterns learned from exposure to training data from the generator. Any inference that LLMs are exhibiting more complex causal reasoning must rule out this hypothesis.
authors: Justin Clarke, Isha Karn, Patrick Murray, KJ Hill, David Jensen
bullets: CLadder is a widely used benchmark for formal causal reasoning in LLMs, but its procedural generation introduces highly predictive superficial patterns.
Simple random forests perform well on CLadder data after training on generated examples.
Many commercial LLMs show brittle performance, remaining largely unchanged when text critical to causal reasoning is removed.
The findings suggest that claims of advanced causal reasoning must rule out memorization or exploitation of generator artifacts.

papers.abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Super and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, open and efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer models designed for reasoning, long-context understanding, and agentic workloads. Super is a 120B-parameter, 12B-active multimodal model, while Lightning is a smaller 30B-parameter, 3B-active text model; both designed for efficient deployment. Both models combine large-scale distillation, long-context training, and native speculative decoding, while Super further incorporates Indic continued pretraining and agentic software-engineering mid-training. We develop a comprehensive post-training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RLVR and RLHF), complemented in Super by specialized teacher training and multi- teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). This transforms Super from a text-only base model into a multimodal agent capable of reasoning over text, images, video, and interactive tool environments. We further explore test-time scaling through parallel agent execution and self-verification. Across training and deployment, we jointly optimize capability and efficiency. Indic continued pretraining improves Indian-language benchmarks by up to 9.82 percentage points, while agentic mid-training strengthens software-engineering capabilities and robustness across agent harnesses. The post-trained Super model achieves 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, surpassing Nemotron 3 Ultra despite using approximately 4.6x fewer active parameters. Post-training MTP boosting improves speculative- decoding acceptance length by up to 21.8% under probabilistic draft sampling, while NVFP4 quantization achieves 99.62% median accuracy recovery relative to BF16. Inference optimizations enable up to 4,856 output tokens/s/GPU on GB200 while sustaining at least 50 tokens/s/user.

papers.abstract: Benchmarks such as WildfireSpreadTS (WSTS) have enabled data-driven forecasting of wildfire spread from multimodal satellite time series, but they suffer from limitations: size restricts them to large fires that burn for weeks, and they are from similar environments. We introduce AFSeq, a multimodal dataset of 1,194 recent fire events (2023 to 2026) from 8 different countries across three regions, dominated by the short, small fires that existing benchmarks underrepresent. Our dataset is the largest and most diverse to date for time-series-based wildfire spread prediction. We also introduce UTAE-AR, an extension of a classical U-Net with Temporal Auto Encoder, enhanced with recurrent modules before the decoder. This allows the model to not only predict the next day but the whole sequence in an autoregressive way. Moreover, our model can feed its own predicted fire mask back one day at a time, producing the day-by-day forecasts that single-step models cannot. Our results show that UTAE-AR surpasses state-of-the-art on both WSTS, WSTS+ and AFSeq for next-day accuracy while having 21.5% of their parameters, and being able to predict confidently at a longer horizon.
authors: Jose Guillen, Renzo Zanca, Valentin Barriere
bullets: Introduces AFSeq, a multimodal dataset of 1,194 fire events across 8 countries and 3 regions, emphasizing small and short-lived fires.
Addresses the limited size and environmental diversity of existing benchmarks such as WildfireSpreadTS.
Presents UTAE-AR, a U-Net with temporal encoding and recurrent decoder-side modules for day-by-day sequence forecasting.
The model feeds predicted fire masks back autoregressively to produce multi-day forecasts rather than only next-day predictions.
Reports state-of-the-art next-day accuracy on WSTS, WSTS+, and AFSeq with 21.5% of their parameter count, plus confident longer-horizon forecasts.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in monocular depth estimation have demonstrated highly accurate 3D reconstructions within in-distribution terrestrial domains. This study investigates the efficacy of several state-of-the-art approaches to reconstruct out-of-distribution lunar environments using the NASA Ames Polar Optical Lunar Analog Reconstruction (POLAR) stereo dataset and Apollo 17 surface imagery. By leveraging these datasets, we establish a robust analog-to-field validation pipeline that evaluates quantitative performance against ground-truth physical analogs and qualitative performance against historical field data. Our results indicate that select state-of-the-art techniques can successfully generalize to produce high-fidelity relative 3D reconstructions of the unstructured lunar surface.
authors: Michael W. Lanighan, Kenji Brameld, Seth Gee
bullets: Evaluates monocular depth estimation under a challenging out-of-distribution lunar setting.
Uses the NASA Ames POLAR stereo dataset and Apollo 17 surface imagery.
Introduces an analog-to-field validation pipeline combining quantitative and qualitative evaluation.
Finds that selected methods successfully reconstruct unstructured lunar terrain in relative 3D.
The study focuses on efficacy in lunar environments rather than terrestrial in-distribution performance.

papers.abstract: Physical-layer fingerprinting (PLF) has emerged as a promising authentication approach for Internet of Things devices. However, most PLF systems acquire and process a fixed-length waveform for every authentication query, burdening resource-constrained edge nodes. To address this issue, we propose a progressive-observation PLF method that adapts the waveform length to each query. Specifically, a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) first rejects clearly unknown devices from a short observation. Spectral matching then accepts clearly registered devices from a slightly longer observation. Only ambiguous queries proceed to the same matching on the full-length waveform, reducing both data acquisition and computation. Because fingerprints drift across days, we also design an adaptive calibration algorithm to avoid retraining the CNN. The algorithm realigns the features and decision thresholds using a few current-day references from registered devices. We evaluate the method with 100BASE-TX Ethernet devices of two controller types on held-out days. Compared with fixed-length processing, it keeps the false rejection and false acceptance rates equal or lower for both controller types on both days. It also reduces the waveform data per query by 75.1% and the CPU processing time on a Raspberry Pi 5 by 73.7% on average. With the same monitoring bandwidth, an edge node can therefore serve about four times as many authentication queries.
authors: Chenming Zhang, Jiaxiang Geng, Aiqun Hu, Azzedine Boukerche, Peng Sun
bullets: Targets the fixed-length waveform and resource burden of physical-layer fingerprinting on edge nodes.
Uses a lightweight CNN on short observations, spectral matching on longer ones, and full-length processing only for ambiguous queries.
Introduces adaptive calibration to realign features and thresholds using a few current-day registered-device references, avoiding CNN retraining.
Evaluated on 100BASE-TX devices across held-out days, it achieved equal or lower false rejection and false acceptance rates than fixed-length processing.
Reduced waveform data by 75.1% and Raspberry Pi 5 CPU time by 73.7% on average, enabling about four times as many queries at the same bandwidth.

papers.tldr: A progressive-observation Ethernet fingerprinting system reduces authentication data and computation by adapting waveform length while maintaining or improving error rates under fingerprint drift.

papers.abstract: Traditional computed tomography (CT) can capture paired 3D face and skull geometry, but it remains costly, fixed in location, and exposes patients to radiation. For applications such as remote diagnostics, digital healthcare, forensic identification, missing-person investigation, and archaeological analysis, there is an urgent need for a portable, safe, and accessible solution to capture 3D skull geometry. In this work, we introduce Vision Tomography (VT), a concept and framework capable of reconstructing paired 3D face-skull geometry from various visual modalities, and also enabling joint manipulation of 3D facial and skull geometry. To achieve this, we first construct a dataset of over 200 samples, where each case includes a CT-based skull, a CT-based face, and a high-fidelity textured face scan. Secondly, we propose a novel dense ray matching registration method that ensures topological consistency across face, skull, and their tissue correspondences. Building on this registration, we introduce the 3D Bidirectional Face-Skull Morphable Model (BFSM) as the foundation of Vision Tomography, which enables shape inference between the face and skull through a shared coefficient space, while also modeling tissue thickness variation to support one-to-many facial reconstructions from the same skull, reflecting individual facial changes such as age or body fat. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of Vision Tomography across various forensic and medical applications, including paired 3D face-skull reconstruction from images or sketches and predicting surgical outcomes with joint face-skull editing. Extensive experiments confirm the robustness and accuracy of our method. Vision Tomography is available at https://github.com/wang-zidu/BFSM
authors: Zidu Wang, Meng Xu, Miao Xu, Hengyuan Ma, Jiankuo Zhao, Xutao Li, Zhen Lei, Xiangyu Zhu
bullets: Addresses the need for portable, safe 3D skull capture for medical, forensic, and archaeological applications.
Introduces a dataset with over 200 cases containing CT-derived skulls and faces plus high-fidelity textured face scans.
Uses dense ray matching registration to maintain topological consistency across facial, skull, and tissue correspondences.
Builds a Bidirectional Face-Skull Morphable Model with a shared coefficient space and variable tissue thickness, enabling one-to-many face reconstructions from a skull.
Demonstrates image/sketch-based reconstruction and joint face-skull editing for surgical outcome prediction; experiments report robust and accurate performance.

papers.abstract: Ball bounces and racket hits are the events from which tennis statistics are derived, and on monocular video the two are easy to confuse. We release a benchmark of 345 bounce and hit annotations at frame level on eight clips that mix broadcast, fixed elevated, phone and court-level viewpoints, with a frozen development and test split, a confusion-aware matcher, clip-level bootstrap intervals and a blind second annotation of three clips. On it we score supervised precise spotters with published broadcast weights, two zero-shot vision-language models, and RallyArb, an arbitration layer over a ball track and player poses that fits no parameter on event labels. The supervised spotters score near-perfectly on broadcast footage and almost nothing on phone and court-level footage, where the pooled bounce F1 of E2E-Spot is 0.130. RallyArb keeps a bounce F1 above 0.8 on the three phone and court-level clips, two of which were used to tune it, and finds 8 of 11 bounces on the held-out one, but it places hits too far from the contact frame to match human timing. The vision-language models detect events on every viewpoint and miss the contact frame by about 0.1 s. Fine-tuned leave-one-clip-out from its broadcast weights, the spotter reaches about 0.8 bounce F1 on two phone and court-level clips and stays at 0.2 on a grazing phone angle. The annotations, the evaluator and the frozen predictions of every scored row are released.
authors: David Soeiro-Vuong, Andre-Louis Rochet
bullets: The benchmark contains 345 frame-level bounce and hit annotations across eight clips and four viewpoint types.
Supervised broadcast spotters perform near-perfectly on broadcast footage but fail on unfamiliar views; E2E-Spot’s pooled bounce F1 is 0.130 on phone and court-level clips.
RallyArb combines ball tracking and player poses without fitting event labels, maintaining bounce F1 above 0.8 on three phone/court-level clips, though tuning included two of them.
Vision-language models detect events across viewpoints but miss the contact frame by roughly 0.1 seconds.
The annotations, evaluator, and frozen predictions are released; cross-view generalization remains limited, especially for grazing phone angles and hit timing.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and evaluation of event detection in tennis video across viewpoints contributes to video understanding.
papers.title: Can Event Detectors Leave the Broadcast Camera? Evidence from Tennis
papers.tldr: Broadcast-trained tennis event detectors do not reliably transfer to phone or court-level views, while geometry-based arbitration improves bounce detection but mistimes racket hits.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning holds the promise of robots that learn manipulation skills from interaction alone, without pretrained priors or demonstration data. In practice, on-policy methods such as PPO routinely stall on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks: dense reward shaping carries the policy through stages, yet stitching them together and discovering sparsely rewarded events rarely succeeds. We trace this failure to the missing action discrimination in state-value credit assignment: a state-value critic judges progress only by episode outcomes, so when the policy converges to a partial solution all outcomes coincide, and improvement stops because no action can prove better than another. We therefore extend PPO with an action conditioned value critic which, can compare the executed action with alternatives sampled at the same state and aid the learning signal. Combined with Generalized Advantage Estimation and a bound on exploration noise, we show how the extended algorithm escapes the plateau and completes precise peg insertion within a training budget where PPO with identical exploration fails.
authors: Giovanni Minelli, Giulio Turrisi, Lorenzo Amatucci, Victor Barasuol, Claudio Semini
bullets: On-policy RL methods can stall when dense rewards support partial solutions but fail to encourage rare, precisely sequenced events.
The issue is attributed to state-value credit assignment, which cannot discriminate among actions once outcomes become similar.
The proposed PPO extension compares executed actions with alternatives sampled at the same state using an action-conditioned value critic.
Combined with Generalized Advantage Estimation and bounded exploration noise, it escapes a plateau and completes precise peg insertion where matched-exploration PPO fails.

PPO (blue) stalls mid-task without reaching insertion; PPO+GRPO, using grouprelative action credit (yellow), escapes the plateau and converges to consistent insertion.
Figure 1. Task scene with detail of the contact-rich insertion stage: the peg, grasped and transported, must be aligned with and inserted into a tight-fitting hole.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes an action-conditioned value critic for PPO to escape local minima in contact-rich manipulation, directly relevant to robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Learning from Relative Action Credit for Escaping Local Minima
papers.tldr: An action-conditioned critic helps PPO distinguish better from worse actions and escape plateaus in long-horizon robotic manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Humanoid controllers often require task-specific training despite sharing the need for balance and whole-body coordination. We present Metatron, a promptable whole-body execution layer combining a generative base policy with a programmable skill layer. The base policy receives partial goals, collectively called a prompt, that can combine timed body-part targets, velocity commands, and style cues. It produces diverse whole-body motions consistent with these goals. Training combines motion capture, synthetic recovery trajectories, and retargeted scene-interaction motions. After training, the policy is frozen. Stateful programs called skills express task intent as prompts at each control step, drawing rough geometric sketches that the policy turns into coordinated movement. Skills are ordinary code, refined by coding agents that analyze motion data and fit compact rules without task-specific policy training. On the physical Unitree G1, one frozen checkpoint supports walking, recovery, teleoperated object pickup, and sitting on furniture. Comparative evaluations show higher reaching success and push robustness than the tested reference-tracking pipelines. The same recipe produces climbing and acrobatics on a simulated character. Metatron enables coding agents to turn learned motor capabilities into new skills through code, without further policy training.
authors: Chen Tessler, Yifeng Jiang, Alec Otto, Yi Shi, Umar Iqbal, Gal Chechik, Xue Bin Peng
bullets: Addresses the need for separate training for humanoid tasks requiring balance and whole-body coordination.
Combines a generative base policy with programmable, stateful skills that issue prompts containing body targets, velocity commands, and style cues.
Trains on motion capture, synthetic recovery, and retargeted scene-interaction motions, then freezes the policy.
Demonstrated on a Unitree G1 for walking, recovery, object pickup, and sitting; evaluations report higher reaching success and push robustness than tested reference-tracking pipelines.
Also produces climbing and acrobatics in simulation, while remaining scoped to the demonstrated robot and simulated-character settings.

papers.abstract: Advancing language models for specialized scientific applications requires evaluations of scientific fluency, physical reasoning, and quantitative analyses. Using inertial confinement fusion (ICF) as a test case, we have developed an expert-curated benchmark of 250 questions spanning qualitative reasoning, numerical calculation, symbolic derivation, and equation formulation. Responses have been evaluated using deterministic numerical and symbolic checks together with language-model judges. We compared a variety of out-of-the-box closed-source and open-source large language models with Prospero, a model specialized through combined domain-adaptive pretraining and supervised fine-tuning for ICF. We also conducted initial retrieval-assisted evaluations. Prospero improved its aggregate score by 10.7 percentage points over its base model, with gains across all question types. Frontier models achieved the highest aggregate scores, but critical physics errors persisted, particularly in numerical calculations. We note that domain-specific performance can improve through specialization, but benchmark gains alone do not establish scientific reliability. Retrieval improved performance for a smaller model but yielded no statistically significant improvement for a frontier model. Two scientific stress tests further illustrate useful capabilities and the need for expert assessment of physical assumptions and model validity. Based on these findings, we recommend evaluating existing domain capabilities and retrieval benefits before committing to substantial additional specialization.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) ground language in visual evidence, yet their semantic reasoning can be exploited through transferable black-box adversarial attacks. Existing attacks typically allocate perturbations using surrogate-model saliency, which may not reflect how an unseen MLLM semantically interprets or relies on different image regions. We introduce VISTA (Vulnerability-Informed Semantic Transfer Attacks), a black-box framework that identifies semantically vulnerable visual regions from an MLLM's responses without access to gradients, logits, parameters, or internal representations. VISTA supports two attack settings: (i) VISTA-Proxy, a pure-transfer setting that probes an open-source MLLM and transfers the resulting adversarial examples to unseen commercial MLLMs without querying them; and (ii) VISTA-Victim, a query-assisted setting that probes the target MLLM to capture model-specific semantic vulnerabilities. VISTA builds an Uncertainty-Based Multimodal Behavior (UBMB) map from response drift, conflict, misleading, and semantic shifts, then uses entropy-adaptive Sinkhorn routing and a surrogate ensemble to focus perturbations on vulnerable regions. Across GPT-5, Gemini-3.5-Flash, and Claude Sonnet 4.6, VISTA achieves up to 97 % attack success rate (ASR) while maintaining a Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) above 30 dB. Notably, VISTA-Proxy achieves up to 93 % ASR without querying the final victim, demonstrating that response-derived semantic vulnerability can enable effective transfer across heterogeneous MLLMs.
authors: Ahmed Abdelnaby, Mohamed Elmahallawy
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between surrogate-model saliency and how unseen MLLMs actually interpret visual regions.
Builds an Uncertainty-Based Multimodal Behavior map from response drift, conflict, misleading, and semantic shifts.
Uses entropy-adaptive Sinkhorn routing with a surrogate ensemble to focus perturbations on vulnerable regions.
Supports pure-transfer VISTA-Proxy and query-assisted VISTA-Victim attack settings.
Reports up to 97% ASR with PSNR above 30 dB; VISTA-Proxy reaches up to 93% ASR without querying the final victim across GPT-5, Gemini-3.5-Flash, and Claude Sonnet 4.6.

papers.abstract: Neural representation has emerged as a powerful tool to mitigate the demand for increasingly higher-resolution images. However, a fundamental trade-off remains between structured (e.g., feature grids, which offer spatial consistency) and unstructured (e.g., 2D Gaussians, which adaptively capture local variances) representations. This choice significantly affects how well an algorithm represents an image. Here, we present Gaussian-Grid, a hybrid neural representation that adaptively integrates structured and unstructured primitives. By dynamically partitioning computation between 2D Gaussian distributions and their attached multi-resolution feature grids based on the local frequency content, Gaussian-Grid automatically optimizes its architecture to match the underlying complexity of the target signal. We evaluate our approach using high-resolution natural images and demonstrate its applications as GPU-native dataset storage, showing $1.24$-$2.14\times$ decoding speed improvement and PCIe data traffic reduction of $23\times$-$176\times$ over JPEG + ZIP data archiving. The results show that Gaussian-Grid maintains small memory footprints while achieving high reconstruction fidelity across a variety of datasets.
authors: Anatolii Evdokimov, Stavros Diolatzis, Bingxuan Li, Akshay Jindal, Patsorn Sangkloy, Qi Sun
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between spatially consistent structured grids and locally adaptive unstructured Gaussian representations.

Maintains small memory footprints while providing high-fidelity reconstruction across varied datasets.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can learn to follow execution preferences, such as where to grasp an object or how to move around an obstacle, from demonstrations annotated with preference labels. Providing these annotations for every new task, however, is costly. We study whether learned preference control can transfer to new tasks whose demonstrations contain the desired behaviors but lack preference annotations. We find that a policy trained with preference annotations can follow preferences on a new task before adaptation but achieves limited task success. Fine-tuning on target demonstrations without these annotations improves task success while weakening preference control. Motivated by this finding, we introduce Self-Labeled Preference Transfer (SPT). SPT jointly trains a shared vision-language backbone for preference-conditioned action prediction and preference recognition on annotated source demonstrations. It then freezes the recognizer to preserve its cross-task preference recognition capability and uses it to self-label target demonstrations for policy fine-tuning. Across five types of execution preferences in simulation, the recognizer achieves 96.4% accuracy, and SPT reaches 84.8% preference following and 89.2% task success, compared with 59.4% and 88.0% for naive finetuning. We further extend to multiple preferences, achieving 93.8% preference following compared with 42.5% of baselines. In real-world experiments, SPT increases preference following from 52.5% to 92.5% relative to naive finetuning across two task transfers. These results show that SPT can support preference adaptation across tasks and objects while maintaining success, without additional manual preference annotations.
authors: Kaiwen Hong, Shaoting Peng, Xiangyu Zeng, Pengcheng Wang, Boyuan Tian, Haonan Chen, Yifan Zhu, Yixiao Wang, Katherine Driggs-Campbell
bullets: Preference annotations are costly, and naive fine-tuning on unlabeled target demonstrations improves task success but weakens preference control.
SPT jointly learns preference-conditioned action prediction and preference recognition from annotated source demonstrations.
It freezes the recognizer and uses it to self-label target demonstrations for preference-aware policy fine-tuning.
In simulation, SPT achieves 84.8% preference following and 89.2% task success, outperforming naive fine-tuning on preference following.
Across multiple preferences and two real-world transfers, SPT maintains strong preference following without additional manual annotations.

papers.abstract: We address the task of long-video, camera-controlled generation from a single image. The dominant autoregressive paradigm suffers from two key limitations: (1) error accumulation over time, as distant frames are conditioned on previously generated outputs rather than ground truth, leading to drift; and (2) ambiguity in how to incorporate camera control. Standard solutions to both--such as self-forcing and conditioning on explicit 6-DOF poses--either incur significant computational overhead or produce drifting scene geometries over time. We propose a simple and lightweight framework that combines autoregressive generation (WanAR) with hierarchical long-context denoising (FixAR). To enforce scene geometry remains consistent with input cameras, we draw from feed-forward novel-view synthesis and reformulate video generation as a warping-and-inpainting problem. To mitigate drift, we introduce a hierarchical denoising strategy in which different stages condition on different temporal histories. Specifically, we first generate frames conditioned on the immediate past, and then refine them using a second denoiser conditioned on a temporally subsampled long-range history to enforce global consistency. This fine-to-coarse scheme enables each generated frame to effectively condition on the full temporal context without incurring a prohibitive cost. Experiments on RealEstate10k and DL3DV demonstrate that WanAR+FixAR outperforms prior methods for camera-controlled long-video generation, producing results that are both temporally stable and consistent with input camera trajectories.
authors: Kaihua Chen, Yiming Gong, Deva Ramanan, Tarasha Khurana
bullets: Targets error accumulation and ambiguous camera-control conditioning in long autoregressive video generation.
Recasts generation as a camera-guided warping-and-inpainting problem to preserve scene geometry.
Uses immediate temporal history for initial generation and subsampled long-range history for refinement.
Evaluated on RealEstate10k and DL3DV, where it outperforms prior methods in temporal stability and camera-trajectory consistency.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of WanAR, FixAR, and InterpolatAR. We build upon WAN Team et al. (2025), a video diffusion model, and adapt it for camera-controlled autoregressive video generation in static 3D scenes. All three stages share the same Wan2.1 backbone weights, with a different stage-specific LoRA checkpoint loaded for each stage. At each rollout, we estimate depth using MoGe-2 Wang et al. (2025c) on the input frame (or the last generated frame from the previous rollout), and warp it into future camera poses to provide geometry-aware conditioning for WanAR (top). While WanAR can generate plausible long videos autoregressively, visual drift and artifacts gradually accumulate over multiple rollouts. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a hierarchical denoising framework with a second-stage denoiser, FixAR (middle), which refines temporally subsampled keyframes generated across different rollouts using a broader temporal context. Finally, since FixAR only operates on sparse keyframes, we apply InterpolatAR to synthesize intermediate frames between adjacent refined keyframes (bottom). The entire three-stage pipeline can itself be rolled out autoregressively to further extend the video. This hierarchical fine-to-coarse formulation enables both accurate camera control and temporally stable long-horizon video generation.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on RealEstate10k and DL3DV. We show qualitative results on two test scene from RealEstate10k (top two examples) and DL3DV (bottom two examples) across a range of video generation, and novel-view synthesis baselines. We see that proposed WanAR + FixAR combination of models “renders” the scene using scale-consistent camera poses (as compared to ray encoding in DFoT or Plucker conditioning in LingBot), and show that hierarchical denoising mitigates drift over time which some autoregressive baselines like VMem struggle with. We also note that TrajectoryCrafter, a method designed for novel-view synthesis (in short sequences) is also surprisingly strong at the task of camera-controlled minute-long video generation.

Figure 1: In this work, we consider the problem of camera-controlled video generation. Existing approaches condition on cameras represented as ray encodings or Plucker coordinates, but these learn poses up to a global scale factor. We draw from literature in feed-forward novel-view synthesis that warp given views into future poses and reformulate video generation as video inpainting (left). While this allows for precise camera control, minute-long autoregressive video generation in this setup still suffers from drift and error accumulation over time. We propose a hierarchical denoising scheme (right) that looks at multiple rollouts from the inpainting stage and corrects for long horizon artifacts.

Figure 6: We identify a key limitation of existing camera-conditioned methods. When explicit 6- DOF poses are used as conditioning—e.g., via Plücker coordinates or ray maps Song et al. (2025); Team et al. (2026b)—it is difficult to enforce a consistent scale between the scene and the camera trajectory. As a result, generated videos may exhibit visual inconsistencies (top), reflecting scenes rendered under an arbitrary pose scale. Importantly, standard camera-control metrics Xiao et al. (2025) perform a scale alignment with ground-truth camera poses prior to evaluation. Consequently, even when predicted camera trajectories are incorrect up to a global scale factor, they can still achieve low error (bottom), masking this failure mode. Current methods evaluating performance with the PSNR metric circumvent this issue, as they overfit to the pose distribution in a particular datasets, which indicates their limited generalization to other scene or camera trajectories. In our approach, we mitigate this issue by aligning MoGE depth predictions to ground-truth depth for each rollout, and by adopting a warping-and-inpainting formulation for long-video generation. We also adopt novel-view synthesis protocols for evaluation, and instead benchmark methods for camera-control with the masked PSNR (mPSNR) metric.

Figure 5: Top-k evaluation. We note that generative methods for camera-controlled video generation can produce multi-modal outputs for unseen regions of the scene as camera pans in new direction. We conduct such an evaluation for our method. Our finding is that the performance of our final predictions improves with respect to the ground-truth as more samples are drawn from WanAR (thereby covering the generation of multiple plausible 3D scenes in the future).
Figure 4: Qualitative analysis of hierarchical denoising. WanAR exhibits drift over long rollouts, while FixAR mitigates the drift and cleans up accumulated artifacts.

Table 5: Computational cost comparison with baselines. Runtime and peak GPU memory are measured on 280-frame RealEstate10K videos using a single 80GB H100 GPU. We also report our method at 480× 832× 49 for a resolution-matched comparison.

Table 2: Comparison to state-of-the-art on DL3DV Ling et al. (2024). We compare our method with prior art on the DL3DV dataset which has more challenging camera motion, like sudden translation changes, and 360◦ camera pan. Despite this, our method outperforms baselines by a considerable margin. Once again, mPSNR demonstrates better camera control with our warp-and-inpaint strategy for long video generation.

Table 1: Comparison to state-of-the-art on RealEstate10K Zhou et al. (2018). We compare our hierarchical diffusion strategy to state-of-the-art approaches for long video generation and novelview synthesis of static scenes. Our first finding is that a combination of WanAR + FixAR beats all prior art on RealEstate10K, which we attribute to better camera control in WanAR, and better drift mitigation from FixAR. One surprising finding is that novel-view synthesis approaches like TrajectoryCrafter in fact perform better at this task than many long video generation works. With mPSNR, we show better retention of visible regions particularly driven by precise camera control.

Table 7: Comparison of different geometry estimation methods. We initialize WanAR using the first-frame depth estimated by each method and report performance after one rollout. Results are similar across estimators, indicating limited sensitivity to the choice of depth estimator.

Table 6: Ablation on FixAR keyframe interval and sequence length. We compare 49-frame and 25-frame FixAR variants under different keyframe intervals. The 49-frame model remains stable across its training range, while larger intervals degrade the performance of the 25-frame model.
Table 4: Comparison of different conditioning strategies. The Plucker baseline adds a convolutional adapter to the Wan2.1-14B backbone, and is finetuned on Re10K using the same setup.
Table 3: Quantitative analysis of hierarchical denoising. FixAR improves generation realism and leads to consistent gains across evaluation metrics.

papers.selection_reason: Combines autoregressive generation with hierarchical long-context denoising for camera-controlled video synthesis.
papers.title: Hierarchical Diffusion for Camera-controlled Autoregressive Video Generation
papers.tldr: WanAR+FixAR enables stable, camera-controlled long-video generation from a single image by combining autoregressive synthesis with hierarchical long-context denoising.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a two-stage learning framework for versatile and agile humanoid locomotion that couples online reduced-order model (ROM) reference generation with whole-body tracking control. In the first stage, we train a command-conditioned whole-body reference generator using single rigid body dynamics combined with full humanoid kinematics. In the second stage, the frozen ROM policy is rolled out online to generate references for training a whole-body tracking policy on the full-order dynamics model. Learning a kino-dynamically consistent reference generator in the simplified ROM space enables us to generate references over a broad command space and over multiple locomotion strategies using a single unified framework. We demonstrate the approach on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot, achieving longitudinal velocities from -2.0 m/s to 2.8 m/s, lateral velocities up to +-1.0 m/s, angular velocities up to +-3.0 rad/s, one-legged hopping, and continuous transitions across the commands, all using one unified reference policy and one whole-body tracking policy.
authors: Adrian B. Ghansah, Yujin An, Jeeseop Kim, Soon-Jo Chung
bullets: Addresses broad-command humanoid locomotion across multiple strategies with a single framework.
Trains a command-conditioned reference generator using single rigid body dynamics and full humanoid kinematics.
Rolls out the frozen reduced-order policy online to train a whole-body tracker on full-order dynamics.
Demonstrated on a Unitree G1 with fast multidirectional motion, one-legged hopping, and continuous command transitions.
Reported capabilities include -2.0 to 2.8 m/s longitudinal, ±1.0 m/s lateral, and ±3.0 rad/s angular velocities.

papers.title: FORGE: Feasible Online Reduced-Order Reference Generation and Whole-Body Execution for Agile Humanoid Locomotion
papers.tldr: FORGE combines online reduced-order reference generation with whole-body tracking to enable agile, versatile humanoid locomotion using unified policies.

papers.abstract: LLM-based generative recommendation reads long, text-rich interaction histories but generates only short semantic identifiers (SIDs). This asymmetry makes supervised fine-tuning inefficient: encoding the history is expensive, yet each history usually provides supervision for only one target. We present Merge and Branch (M&B) to reduce input cost and learn more from each encoded history. Merge compresses each historical item's SID and text into a small number of learned tokens. Branch uses the compressed history to predict multiple target SIDs. To share history computation while keeping these targets independent, M&B organizes each example as a shallow, wide tree. We develop tree FlashAttention to execute this layout efficiently, processing the shared history once and propagating gradients from every branch for end-to-end training. A tree-structured key/value cache extends history sharing to constrained decoding. Experiments on public benchmarks show that M&B outperforms strong recommendation baselines while substantially improving training and decoding efficiency.
authors: Yunqin Zhu, Yao Xie
bullets: Addresses the costly encoding of long, text-rich histories when each history typically supervises only one short semantic identifier.
Merge compresses each historical item’s SID and text into a few learned tokens; Branch predicts multiple target SIDs from the shared representation.
Uses a shallow, wide tree with tree FlashAttention to share history computation while keeping target branches independent.
A tree-structured key/value cache extends computation sharing to constrained decoding.
On public benchmarks, it outperforms strong baselines while improving training and decoding efficiency.
