papers.tldr: Merge and Branch improves generative recommendation efficiency by compressing interaction histories and predicting multiple targets through a shared tree structure.

papers.abstract: Implicit neural representation (INR) methods for deformable medical image registration require the network parameters to be optimized for each new image pair, making adaptation speed a practical limitation. This work investigates whether early adaptation can be accelerated using an initialization learned from a collection of previously solved registration tasks. We examine two schemes: Reptile meta-initialization and STRAINER transfer of the shared component of a coordinate network. KAN-IDIR is used as the base INR displacement-field model. Experiments are conducted on OASIS-1, with 364 consecutive pairs used for training and 49 pairs for test-time adaptation. Registration quality is evaluated using mean Dice and HD95, together with the fraction of voxels with a negative Jacobian determinant at iteration 1500. In the configurations studied, both schemes yield higher Dice and lower HD95 at early iterations than random initialization. Reptile numerically outperforms STRAINER under a small iteration budget, although their pretraining budgets are not matched. As the number of iterations increases, the differences between the schemes shrink. STRAINER pretraining takes 39-40 minutes, compared with 44.98 hours for Reptile.
authors: Marat O. Zinovev, Dmitry V. Sorokin
bullets: INR registration must optimize network parameters separately for each new image pair, limiting practical adaptation speed.
The study compares Reptile meta-initialization and STRAINER transfer of a shared coordinate-network component using KAN-IDIR.
On OASIS-1, both methods improve early-iteration Dice and HD95 over random initialization.
Reptile performs better under a small iteration budget, but the gap narrows with more iterations.
Pretraining takes about 39–40 minutes for STRAINER versus 44.98 hours for Reptile; budgets were not matched.

papers.selection_reason: Learned meta-initialization to accelerate per-instance INR adaptation fits test-time learning and deployment-time optimization.
papers.title: Meta-Initialization of Implicit Neural Representations to Accelerate Deformable Medical Image Registration
papers.tldr: Meta-learned initialization accelerates early adaptation of implicit neural networks for deformable medical image registration, with Reptile offering stronger early performance but much higher pretraining cost than STRAINER.

papers.abstract: Time-series data play an important role in various tasks, such as weather forecasting, web traffic analysis, and speech recognition. Recently, pioneering studies have increasingly adopted Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) based encoders to learn time-series representations through latent-space prediction. However, they often overlook the underlying factors governing transitions between time-series observations. In this work, we hypothesize that explicitly modeling the information behind changes in time series can facilitate time-series modeling. Building on this hypothesis, we propose ACTS-WM, a self-supervised latent action-conditioned world model framework for time-series analysis. First, we introduce a latent action modeling approach that infers the underlying information behind time-series transitions as latent actions, without requiring explicit action annotations. We then develop a JEPA-based encoder and an action-conditioned world model to predict target time-series representations conditioned on the learned latent actions and task information. We evaluate ACTS-WM across 4 representative tasks on 22 datasets from diverse domains, covering univariate and multivariate forecasting and classification. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that ACTS-WM can improve downstream performance over pretrained JEPA-based encoders by learning complementary representations.
authors: Chia-Han Kuo, Chengshuai Zhao, Huan Liu, Lo Pang-Yun Ting
bullets: Addresses the limitation of JEPA-based time-series encoders that overlook factors driving transitions between observations.
Infers latent actions self-supervised, without explicit action annotations.
Uses a JEPA encoder and action-conditioned world model to predict target representations using latent actions and task information.
Evaluated on 4 tasks and 22 datasets spanning univariate and multivariate forecasting and classification.
Reports improved downstream performance over pretrained JEPA-based encoders through complementary representations.

papers.abstract: A widely held assumption in knowledge distillation is that teacher and student representations must occupy a compatible or explicitly aligned feature space. We propose RPKD (Random Prototype Knowledge Distillation), which discards this assumption by comparing both networks against a shared bank of randomly initialized, frozen prototype vectors. Alignment is therefore carried out in an external reference space rather than in the teacher's native feature coordinates: the teacher side is projected by fixed random maps that carry no trainable parameters, and only the student adapts. Two branches handle the transfer: a logit branch aligning global prototype similarity distributions and a feature branch matching spatially-resolved prototype activation maps. Both operate within the same fixed prototype space, which can be interpreted as a random feature embedding that approximately preserves inter-sample similarity structure, so the prototype bank and the distillation objective stay unchanged across teacher-student pairs while only the input projections are instantiated per architecture. In low-category settings, decoupling the prototype vocabulary from the task label space yields richer supervision than the label space alone, an advantage absent from logit-based methods, whose supervisory signal collapses as class count shrinks. This advantage is especially relevant in real-world scenarios where the label space is typically constrained. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of RPKD, achieving a maximum gain of +7.98% over OFA on CIFAR-100, +12.44% on ImageNet-100, and +1.28% on ImageNet-1K. Source code is available at https://github.com/HamzaEtcibasi/RPKD
authors: Hamza Etcibasi, Ramazan Gokberk Cinbis
bullets: Uses a frozen bank of randomly initialized prototype vectors as an external reference space.
Combines global prototype-similarity distribution matching with spatial prototype-activation-map matching.
Employs fixed random projections for teacher features while only the student adapts.
The prototype vocabulary is independent of task labels, providing richer supervision in low-category settings.
Reports gains over OFA of up to 7.98% on CIFAR-100, 12.44% on ImageNet-100, and 1.28% on ImageNet-1K.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes RPKD, a knowledge distillation method that discards the need for aligned representations, offering a technique for efficient model compression and transfer.
papers.title: You Don't Need Aligned Representations: Knowledge Distillation via Random Prototype Spaces

papers.abstract: Latent multi-agent systems reduce inference cost by keeping intermediate reasoning and inter-agent communication in continuous representations.\ Reusable skills, however, are commonly supplied as text or stored as layer-wise Key-Value states or skill-specific model parameters, introducing repeated processing or substantial per-skill storage.\ We introduce \textbf{SkillMem}, which represents each reusable skill as a small external latent memory and makes it directly available during latent multi-agent reasoning.\ A role-conditioned cross-attention reader allows the same memory to guide different agents according to their roles and current hidden states.\ We train the skill memories and shared reader through behavioral distillation, matching the change in token predictions induced by a textual skill while keeping the backbone frozen.\ For our experiments, we obtain textual skills from paired successful and failed multi-agent trajectories, although existing skills can also be compiled directly.\ Across six benchmarks and Qwen3 models ranging from 4B to 14B parameters, SkillMem provides strong gains for smaller backbones while preserving efficient latent multi-agent inference across model scales.\ We use the same $8\times256$ memory configuration across all evaluated model scales, requiring 9.6\,KB of skill-specific storage per skill, including its retrieval embedding.\ For a library of 100 skills, SkillMem reduces total storage by more than $38\times$ compared with alternative skill representations and achieves up to a $4.23\times$ end-to-end inference speedup.\ These results show that compact procedural memories can be reused without sacrificing the efficiency of latent multi-agent reasoning.
authors: Yuxuan Zhu, Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri, Pin-Yu Chen, Keerthiram Murugesan
bullets: Addresses the repeated processing and high per-skill storage costs of text, Key-Value, and parameter-based skill representations.
Stores each skill in a small external latent memory accessed through role-conditioned cross-attention.
Trains the memories and shared reader by behavioral distillation while keeping the backbone frozen.
Across six benchmarks and Qwen3 models from 4B to 14B parameters, it provides especially strong gains for smaller models.
Uses 9.6 KB per skill; for 100 skills, it cuts storage by over 38× and delivers up to 4.23× end-to-end speedup.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SkillMem. Reusable textual skills are discovered from paired multi-agent trajectories. Each skill is compiled into a compact latent memory by matching the behavioral effect of skill injection. Figure 3: Behavioral skill distillation. For each skill, agent role, and calibration task, the frozen backbone generates a teacher response with the textual skill included in the role prompt. We score the same response with and without the textual skill to measure its token-level effect. We then replace the skill text with its memory and train the memory and role-conditioned reader to reproduce the skill-supported behavior while preserving the base behavior at positions with limited skill support.

papers.title: SkillMem: Compact External Skill Memory for Latent Multi-Agent Reasoning

papers.abstract: Pre-training foundational models is computationally expensive as models scale. In this work, we introduce Bi-Phase Training (BPT), a parameter-efficient pre-training method that preserves the high-rank learning dynamics observed in full-parameter optimization with substantially reduced trainable parameters. BPT parameterizes each weight update as a composition of constrained high-rank left/right transformations via trainable diagonal matrices and low-rank adapters whose updates are periodically merged into the frozen base weights, resulting in a compounding expansion of accessible directions during training. Across language-model pre-training from scratch (Qwen2.5 models from 100M to 1.5B parameters and OLMo-2-1B) on FineWeb-Edu (10B and 100B tokens), BPT achieves validation perplexity close to full-parameter baselines while using far fewer trainable parameters; e.g., at the 1.5B scale, BPT uses 66% fewer trainable parameters with only a small validation-perplexity gap. Additionally, a comprehensive evaluation across diverse downstream tasks shows that BPT preserves much of the full-parameterized model's downstream performance.
authors: Abel Gurung, Joseph Campbell
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of full-parameter foundational-model pre-training.
Uses constrained high-rank left/right transformations with trainable diagonal matrices and low-rank adapters.
Periodically merges adapter updates into frozen base weights, expanding the directions accessible during training.
Evaluated on Qwen2.5 models from 100M to 1.5B parameters and OLMo-2-1B using FineWeb-Edu.
At 1.5B parameters, reduces trainable parameters by 66% with only a small validation-perplexity gap and preserves much downstream performance.

papers.abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables teams of agents, such as robots and autonomous vehicles, to learn coordinated behavior, but what such teams learn is largely determined by their reward function. Because task success alone provides too little guidance for learning, intermediate rewards are usually designed by hand, and this effort must often be repeated whenever the environment or the team changes. Large language models (LLMs) can automate the effort by writing reward functions as code, yet the resulting rewards are typically designed and tested in a single setting. To enable their reuse across settings, GARDEN (Generalist Autonomous Reward Design through Evidence Navigation) is proposed, in which one reward program is developed for a family of related scenarios and transferred, unchanged, to scenarios that were not available during its design. During development, environment code, training records, and agent behavior are investigated by an LLM reward engineer, and draft rewards are tested in trial training runs, while the learning algorithm and the rule for selecting the final reward are held fixed. On unseen scenarios of the Overcooked and SMAX benchmarks, task returns were increased by 58.2% and 52.5% over the default rewards on two kitchen layouts, and the mean win rate in two combat scenarios was raised from 51.0% to 89.9%. Under matched candidate and probe budgets, this exceeded the 84.2% and 79.2% obtained with fixed diagnostic feedback and Eureka-inspired reward reflection. These results show that a single autonomously engineered reward can be reused effectively across related cooperative scenarios.
authors: Dogan Urgun
bullets: Addresses the repeated manual design of intermediate rewards when environments or agent teams change.
An LLM reward engineer examines environment code, training records, and agent behavior, then tests draft rewards through trial training runs.
The final reward and learning algorithm are selected using fixed procedures, enabling unchanged transfer across scenarios.
On unseen Overcooked and SMAX scenarios, GARDEN substantially improved task returns and win rates over default rewards and outperformed compared reflection-based methods.
The approach is scoped to families of related cooperative scenarios; the abstract does not establish generalization beyond them.

papers.abstract: Key-value (KV) caching is a core mechanism in large language models, where intermediate key and value representations are stored to accelerate autoregressive decoding. As generation length increases, KV cache memory and computation grow linearly, making compression critical for efficient long-output reasoning. Dictionary-based sparse KV compression is appealing because it represents each token's KV states as a sparse combination of learned basis elements (atoms) in a dictionary, preserving token-level structure without enforcing a global low-rank constraint. However, existing dictionary-based methods face two practical limitations during decoding: iterative sparse coding methods such as Orthogonal Matching Pursuit add decoding-time overhead, and static dictionaries may mismatch evolving KV distributions under test-time generation. While adaptive dictionary updates can reduce this mismatch, naive append-only strategies lead to dictionary growth during generation. We propose FAD-KV, a \textbf{F}ast \textbf{A}daptive \textbf{D}ictionary KV caching framework for efficient reasoning decoding. FAD-KV integrates (i) a screening-based sparse coding scheme, where a one-shot Top-\(n\) selection identifies a small candidate pool followed by lightweight coefficient refinement, and (ii) a fixed-size dictionary adaptation mechanism that reuses inactive atoms instead of expanding the dictionary. By controlling both sparse coding cost and adaptive dictionary growth, FAD-KV provides a memory-bounded and computation-efficient KV compression framework for long reasoning workloads. Experiments on reasoning and long-context benchmarks show that FAD-KV achieves a strong quality-efficiency trade-off while avoiding unbounded dictionary growth during decoding.
authors: Yuxuan Zhu, David H. Yang, Parisa Shiravani, Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri, Tejaswini Pedapati, Subhajit Chaudhury, Keerthiram Murugesan, Pin-Yu Chen
bullets: KV cache memory and decoding cost grow linearly with generation length, motivating compression for long reasoning outputs.
It replaces costly iterative sparse coding with one-shot Top-n screening followed by lightweight coefficient refinement.
The dictionary adapts during decoding by reusing inactive atoms rather than expanding indefinitely.
Experiments on reasoning and long-context benchmarks show a strong quality–efficiency trade-off while maintaining bounded dictionary size.

papers.abstract: Real-world forgery is inherently heterogeneous: it manifests not only as digital manipulation but also as physical spoofing, and is carried not only by images but also by videos. Despite substantial progress, a unified anti-forgery foundation model covering such a broad threat spectrum remains absent. In this paper, we present Venus-DefakerOne2, which substantially extends the forensic capability boundary along both the forgery-form and media-type dimensions. Trained on tens of millions of open-source and in-house samples, it incorporates two key designs. Tide-Style-Tuning alternates LoRA and full-parameter fine-tuning to balance computational efficiency, generalization, and hard-sample fitting while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Entropy-based Test Adaptation determines the optimal prediction modality by analyzing prediction entropy. Venus-DefakerOne2 achieves new state-of-the-art performance across a comprehensive suite of benchmarks, including DeepFake faces (96.7%), AI-generated images (93.3%), tampered documents (87.6%), manipulated natural images (89.6%), physical spoofs (93.1%), and AI-generated videos (96.0%). It significantly outperforms both specialized expert models and its predecessor, DefakerOne, establishing itself as a powerful and versatile foundation model for binary-decision forensic tasks.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising paradigm for general-purpose household robotics. However, inference and data-collection strategies that have been deployed in smaller-scale settings do not necessarily generalize to large-scale, diverse task suites. To address this gap, we conduct a systematic, paired evaluation of previously proposed inference and data-collection strategies across all 100 tasks. Our evaluation uses a fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ model based on the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge winner, which achieves a Q-score of 0.39 on the public test set. These results show that proposed strategies do not transfer uniformly to new environments and tasks. Project page, videos, and detailed analysis: https://rubenhammele.github.io/behavior2026
authors: Ruben Hammele, Samira Huber, Mohammad Nazeri, Amirreza Payandeh, Alexandyr T. Card, Aaron Nguyen, Anuj Pokhrel, Daeun Song, Xuesu Xiao, S\"oren Pirk
bullets: Evaluates previously proposed inference and data-collection strategies systematically across all 100 BEHAVIOR-1K tasks.
Uses a fine-tuned π₀.₅ model based on the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge winner.
Reports a Q-score of 0.39 on the public test set.
Finds that strategy effectiveness varies across environments and tasks.
Provides detailed analysis and supplementary materials on the project page.

papers.title: What Actually Matters? A Paired Evaluation of Inference Settings for $\pi_{0.5}$ on BEHAVIOR-1K
papers.tldr: A paired evaluation shows that inference and data-collection strategies for the fine-tuned π₀.₅ VLA do not transfer uniformly across BEHAVIOR-1K’s 100 tasks.

papers.abstract: Many open mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models train with Muon instead of AdamW. Most balance the load with a bias on each expert's routing score, adjusted after every step. Their recipes disagree on whether Muon should also train the router. In models with 55M and 108M active parameters, we measure how the optimizer changes the span of these biases, the largest minus the smallest in a layer. The span grows when all tokens favor the same experts, so it shows how hard a layer is to balance. At learning rates tuned on shorter runs, Muon raised the span of the first MoE layer at every seed, roughly doubling it on average, while the other layers changed much less. The rise came from Muon on the rest of the network, whichever optimizer trained the router. In those runs, the inputs to the first router shared a direction, and soon after the warmup its busiest expert averaged four to seven times its fair share. Over the first 3,000 steps, subtracting the batch mean from these inputs removed this overload while barely changing the loss. On the smaller model, halving Muon's learning rate removed most of the rise and slightly improved the loss. Moving only the router to AdamW made the loads shift more during the warmup and slightly raised the loss, so at this scale the results favor keeping the router on Muon.
authors: Marcos Hernanz
bullets: Muon increased the routing-bias span of the first MoE layer across all seeds, roughly doubling it on average at tuned learning rates.
The effect was driven by Muon applied to the rest of the network, not by the optimizer used for the router.
The first router’s inputs became directionally aligned, causing its busiest expert to receive 4–7× its fair share soon after warmup.
Subtracting the batch mean from router inputs removed the overload over 3,000 steps with little loss change.
For the smaller model, halving Muon’s learning rate reduced the imbalance and slightly improved loss; switching only the router to AdamW was less favorable.

papers.abstract: Spiking reservoir computing combines the training efficiency of fixed recurrent reservoirs with the energy efficiency of event-driven inference, where computation is triggered by sparse spikes rather than executed densely at every timestep. However, existing spiking reservoirs almost exclusively rely on Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons, whose low-pass dynamics limit their ability to distinguish information encoded at different temporal frequencies. We introduce HRF-Res, a liquid state machine in which LIF neurons are replaced by a heterogeneous population of Harmonic Resonate-and-Fire (HRF) neurons. These neurons exhibit intrinsic oscillatory dynamics and selectively respond to input frequencies, enabling the reservoir to capture frequency-specific temporal patterns. The result is more discriminative representations and higher classification accuracy than LIF-based reservoirs, achieved without sacrificing the energy efficiency of spiking computation, with up to 19x lower energy consumption than an equivalent non-spiking oscillatory reservoir. Evaluated on ten benchmarks spanning time series, sequential images, audio spike trains, and neuromorphic vision, HRF-Res achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among spiking reservoir methods. These results demonstrate that introducing frequency-selective dynamics into spiking reservoirs improves representational quality and classification performance while preserving their inherent energy efficiency.
authors: Aurora Micheli, Claudio Gallicchio, Nergis Tomen
bullets: LIF neurons’ low-pass dynamics limit discrimination of frequency-specific temporal patterns.
Replaces LIF neurons with heterogeneous Harmonic Resonate-and-Fire neurons featuring intrinsic oscillations.
Frequency-selective responses produce more discriminative temporal representations.
Achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among spiking reservoir methods across ten diverse benchmarks.
Uses up to 19× less energy than an equivalent non-spiking oscillatory reservoir.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Architecture of our proposed HRF-Res. The external input ut is projected into a LIF encoder population (left, pink) via the fixed matrix U. LIF spikes sLIF t are passed to the HRF oscillatory reservoir (right, blue) via V; each HRF neuron oscillates at its own resonance frequency and feeds spikes sHRF t back to the LIF layer via W. All weights are fixed; only the linear readout r = WoyT + bo is trained.

Figure 2: Band-pass properties of HRF-Res vs. LIF-Res. (A) Fraction of resonant neurons (Q > 0) per dataset. HRF-Res has 4–20× more resonant neurons than LIF-Res, confirming that band-pass dynamics survive in a full spiking reservoir setting. (B) Mean Q-factor among resonant neurons. HRF neurons form sharper band-pass filters on all datasets, with the largest gaps on FordA (4.6 vs. 2.0), DVS Gesture (3.4 vs. 1.4) and SHD (2.5 vs. 0.6). Bars show mean ± std over three seeds.

Figure 3: HRF-Res produces more class-discriminative representations. (A) CKA between temporal mean reservoir states and category labels (mean ± std over three seeds). HRF-Res achieves higher CKA than LIF-Res on all four datasets. (B) Distribution of per-neuron preferred frequencies (log scale). HRF neurons show distributed tuning across a range of frequencies, consistent with a heterogeneous bank of band-pass filters; LIF neurons collapse to the lowest sweep frequency, consistent with pure integration.

papers.abstract: Metis is a bet that better data, better training methods and new architectures can buy what a bigger parameter count cannot, at a fraction of the cost. Metis-1.6 is its latest step: two language models built from scratch by a single researcher, Praxis (2.94B parameters, 0.46B active per pass) and Logos (10.23B parameters, 1.18B active per pass). Both run a hybrid Mamba-2 and attention mixture-of-experts stack twice for every token, so each token gets a second look. Each was trained on 1.02T tokens in total: 804.76B of pretraining, 18B of context extension to 131,072 tokens, and 200B of supervised fine-tuning. Metis-1.6 was never meant to challenge frontier models, and across 40 post-trained benchmarks it mostly does not: Logos averages 52.93, seventh of 17 models in its comparison set and within a point of Qwen3-4B. But it gets there on roughly a twelfth of the median training data of the comparators that disclose it, and with fewer active parameters per token than any model that beats it, which puts it on the Pareto frontier for both. In mathematics it ranks second of 30 models, with 67.50% on AIME 2025 and 63.64% on HMMT February 2026. It is weak at code, instruction following and long context. The rest of the report is the part I found most valuable: what went wrong. The optimizer I configured never ran, and attention trained with AdamW for all of pretraining. A 1.77B-parameter n-gram memory learned to switch itself off. Five fine-tuning choices cost capability. And a length reward under group-mean normalization punished correct solutions for being long once a group's pass rate passed 2/3, a sign inversion I prove and fix with a one-line clamp. I close with the 10B-token ablations behind MoRE (Mixture of Recursive Experts), the looped architecture of Metis-1.7.
authors: Giulianno Vollmer
bullets: Introduces Praxis (2.94B parameters; 0.46B active per pass) and Logos (10.23B; 1.18B active), built from scratch by one researcher.
Uses a hybrid Mamba-2 and attention mixture-of-experts stack applied twice per token, with 1.02T tokens of pretraining, context extension, and supervised fine-tuning.
Logos reaches a 52.93 average across 40 benchmarks, placing seventh of 17 comparison models and on the reported Pareto frontiers for training data and active parameters.
Performs especially well in mathematics, ranking second of 30 models, but is weak at coding, instruction following, and long-context tasks.
Analyzes failures including an unused optimizer, an inactive n-gram memory, costly fine-tuning choices, and a flawed length reward; it also presents ablations for the next architecture, MoRE.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Metis-1.6 on one page, drawn for Logos. (a) Twenty layers, three of them attention, each ending in a mixture-of-experts block. The stack runs twice per token with every weight shared, and a depth memory carries what the first pass wrote down into the second. The n-gram memory that fed layers 2 and 5 during pretraining is drawn as a ghost: the models closed its gates on their own, and I removed it before release (Section 5). (b) Inside a layer, each sub-layer reads from and writes to four residual streams, which are then mixed by a doubly stochastic 4× 4 matrix; a controller that knows the current pass sets all three. papers.abstract: On PushT, our fixed action updater (1,505 parameters) solves 8 of 16 scenes reserved from our configuration selection. The comparison planners perform as follows: Selected Adam (7 tasks solved, total planning and encoding time 218.440s), adapted iCEM (2 tasks solved, total planning and encoding time 49.309s), released LePlanner (16 tasks solved, total planning and encoding time 5.652s). The total planning and encoding time for our action updater is 59.079s. Note that our action updater does not satisfy the task-cost criterion we fixed before evaluation. We also conduct another matched experiment where we only replay the first ten commands in each context and then allow the next solve 4, 8 or 12 updates (subsequent solves all get 8 updates). Among all 16 contexts (8 scene clusters), the 3 budgets get 9, 8 and 7 successes, respectively. Interestingly, the extra updates did not rescue any failing task in this experiment. All the changes in success/failure happen in one scene cluster, where we observe that the extra updates decrease the costs of the selected latent world-model trajectories for our updater, while the tasks that used to be successes become failures. The code, weights, evaluators, execution traces and cost accounting accompany the paper.
authors: Josef Chen
bullets: The study evaluates learned and optimization-based planners across 16 held-out PushT scenes.
The fixed 1,505-parameter action updater solves 8/16 scenes in 59.079s of planning and encoding.
The released LePlanner solves all 16 scenes in 5.652s, outperforming the other reported planners on success and time.
In a matched replay experiment, allowing 4, 8, or 12 updates yields 9, 8, and 7 successes, respectively.
Extra updates lowered selected latent-trajectory costs in one scene cluster but turned prior successes into failures; the updater also did not meet the preregistered task-cost criterion.

papers.abstract: Deepfake detectors routinely achieve high aggregate accuracy while exhibiting substantial demographic disparities in their errors: false-positive rates differ by double digits across gender and skin tone. Most existing remedies require either full retraining with a fairness-aware objective or demographic-annotated training data, both impractical when only a pretrained checkpoint is available, while label-free post-hoc calibrators leave the detector's weights unchanged. We introduce FYC (FPR-disparity Weight Perturbation and Youden Calibration), a two-stage post-hoc method that perturbs a detector's weights under an FPR-disparity criterion, then calibrates a separate decision threshold for each demographic group - requiring no architectural changes and no full retraining. Evaluated against every detector benchmarked on AI-Face v2 across six intersectional gender x skin-tone groups, FYC outperforms the field on 18 of 21 reported fairness and utility metrics, including purpose-built fairness architectures, at a fraction of the training cost. We further identify why the choice of fairness criterion is critical: the original Demographic Parity objective used in prior weight-perturbation work is architecture-dependent and unpredictable, improving two of four evaluated architectures, leaving a third largely unchanged, and substantially degrading the fourth (PG-FDD), with no way to anticipate the outcome for a given checkpoint in advance. Conditioning the same objective on real images only - our FPR-disparity criterion - eliminates this unpredictability, improving fairness and accuracy jointly across all four architectures with no exceptions.
authors: Uzoamaka Ezeakunne, Taiwo Olabamipe, Deevesh Jain, Xiuwen Liu
bullets: Targets demographic disparities in false-positive rates across intersectional gender and skin-tone groups.
Uses two stages: FPR-disparity-guided weight perturbation, then separate Youden-calibrated thresholds per group.
Requires no architectural changes, full retraining, or demographic-annotated training data.
Outperforms benchmarked alternatives on 18 of 21 reported fairness and utility metrics across AI-Face v2 detectors.
Shows that conditioning the fairness objective on real images avoids the architecture-dependent unpredictability of Demographic Parity perturbation.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Method overview. Stage 1 fine-tunes a pretrained detector with a weight-perturbation ascent/descent loop, using FPR-disparity (real images only) as the disparity criterion driving the ascent—the criterion we adopt after diagnosing it as reliable across all four architectures we test, unlike the Demographic Parity alternative (§4.4). Stage 2 applies zero-cost per-group Youden-J calibration (§3.3) on top of the resulting checkpoint, producing the final calibrated model.

Figure 2. Raw (pre-calibration) intersectional FMEO at every Stage 1 epoch, DP vs. FPR-disparity, for all four architectures (50kimage random subsample of the test set, global-Youden threshold recomputed per epoch). DP is stable for Xception and DAG-FDD, spikes once for EfficientNet-B4, and oscillates without converging for PG-FDD; FPR-disparity is stable for all four.

Figure 3. Fairness–utility scatter (AUC vs. Intersectional FMEO). Filled circles = baseline; filled squares = FPR-disparity FYC; hollow diamonds = calibration-only (no weight perturbation). Arrows connect baseline to FYC; ideal direction is lower-right (higher AUC, lower FMEO).

Figure 4. Per-group FPR across the six intersectional groups (Female/Male × Light/Medium/Dark skin tone) for Xception, trainseed 1. Gray = pretrained baseline; red = raw Stage 1 (FPRdisparity, pre-calibration); blue = FYC (Stage 1 + Stage 2). Calibration further reduces FPR for five of six groups; M-Light is the one group where per-group Youden-J raises FPR relative to the raw checkpoint in this particular seed, illustrating the per-seed variance behind Table 3’s 3-seed means.
Table 1. Landscape of fair deepfake detection methods. Labelfree: no demographic labels required at any stage. Weight-free: no model weight updates.

papers.title: FYC: FPR-Disparity Weight Perturbation and Youden Calibration for Fair Deepfake Detection
papers.tldr: FYC improves fairness and accuracy in pretrained deepfake detectors through lightweight weight perturbation followed by demographic-specific threshold calibration, without full retraining or demographic labels.

papers.abstract: Scaling visual reinforcement learning (RL) with GPU-accelerated simulation is computationally expensive due to rendering and visual-policy inference costs. Consequently, two-stage teacher--student distillation is commonly used to train visual policies, but introduces an imitation gap. In this preliminary study, we introduce \echomethod{}, \textbf{a single-stage off-policy RL framework that scales experience collection without proportionally increasing visual computation}. Through \textbf{inverse distillation}, a state-based auxiliary policy imitates the evolving visual policy and collects inexpensive, unrendered experience. Echo leverages this experience for off-policy value learning, directly improving the visual policy through a shared privileged critic. We instantiate \echomethod{} with FastTD3 and evaluate it on three visual control tasks and two dexterous manipulation tasks in Genesis. Relative to \sdpgmethod{} under the evaluated configurations, Echo reduces time to reference returns by an average of \textbf{60\% across the three locomotion tasks} and \textbf{56\% across both hand tasks}, while improving peak mean returns by \textbf{62\% and 12\%}, respectively. Both hand tasks also achieve higher mean returns at matched simulator-transition budgets. These initial results suggest that scaling off-policy experience is a promising approach to efficient direct visual RL.
authors: Gagan Khandate
bullets: Addresses the rendering and visual-policy inference costs of scaling visual RL, while avoiding the imitation gap of teacher–student distillation.
Uses inverse distillation: a state-based policy imitates the evolving visual policy to gather inexpensive unrendered experience.
Applies the experience through off-policy value learning with a shared privileged critic to improve the visual policy.
In Genesis experiments, Echo reached reference returns 60% faster on locomotion and 56% faster on dexterous manipulation tasks than the evaluated baseline.
Peak mean returns improved by 62% on locomotion and 12% on hand tasks; results are preliminary and limited to five tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Scaling visual RL with off-policy auxiliary experience. A state-based imitator collects unrendered transitions, while a small rendered subset supplies visual-policy experience. Both streams train a privileged critic that directly improves the visual policy.

Both policies maintain object grasp throughout the episodes. Rollouts are generated using earlier checkpoints than those evaluated in Figure 4 and are illustrative rather than representative of aggregate success rates.

Episode returns as a function of wall-clock training time (top, excluding evaluation) and total simulator transitions (bottom, including auxiliary interactions). Solid lines and shaded bands indicate mean and sample standard deviation across three seeds, respectively; faint lines show individual runs. Reference hyperparameters are in Appendix C; the Ant baseline qualification is in Appendix D.

Figure 4: Visual dexterous manipulation in Genesis. All runs use a three-hour training budget. Solid lines and shaded bands indicate mean and sample standard deviation across three seeds, respectively; faint lines show individual runs. Curves are linearly interpolated over the common support of all six runs. Differences in initial returns arise from shaped rewards and policy initialization.

Figure 2: Two key ideas in Echo. (1) Imitate the visual policy: a state-based imitator matches noise-free visual actions with stopped gradients. (2) Update the visual policy with the shared critic: both experience streams train the critic, whose action gradient improves the visual policy while critic parameters remain fixed. The imitator’s EMA copy supplies TD continuation actions without successor images (dashed purple). Gray arrows denote experience flow.

Figure 6: Inverse distillation and critic-gradient diagnostics. (Top) Online imitation loss (teal, solid) and post-update EMA action error (purple, dashed) on fresh visual-policy states, averaged over 60-second intervals. (Middle and bottom) Critic action-gradient dot product and cosine similarity between visual-policy and imitator actions on paired rendered replay states, measured in separate diagnostic runs. Lines and shaded bands show mean and sample standard deviation across three seeds; faint lines show individual runs.

papers.abstract: Modern automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems have achieved remarkable accuracy by scaling model depth and capacity, but at the cost of increased memory, energy, and computational demands. On edge devices where ASR is often most needed, such as watches and glasses, deploying such large models is infeasible due to extremely constrained resources. This raises a fundamental question: can we achieve high representational power in deep ASR models without scaling up parameterization? In this work, we revisit the role of depth and identify layer wise representational dynamics, in which most layers learn functionally similar transformations. Motivated by this insight, we propose a block-recurrent ASR architecture that replaces parameterized depth with a small set of recurrent blocks, each consisting of weight-shared layers, thereby preserving effective depth while drastically reducing model size. Through representation-guided grouping and knowledge distillation, block-recurrent models retain the accuracy of large reference models while using an order of magnitude fewer parameters. Across Open ASR Leaderboard benchmarks, a model with only two shared blocks recovers 97.4% of the accuracy of large models on average. The compact backbone further enables efficient on-device personalization through lightweight MoE-LoRA adaptation, allowing user-specific models to match or surpass the accuracy of general-purpose ASR systems with significantly lower inference cost. By reusing weights across recurrent steps, the proposed architecture reduces memory-access overhead and inference energy consumption. Together, these results show that high quality ASR can be achieved without large parameterization, and that structured recurrence provides a principled path towards ultra-compressed, energy-efficient, and personalized speech recognition on the edge.
authors: Chen Feng, Tianyi Xu, Ramchalam Kinattinkara Ramakrishnan, Yicheng Lin, Shaojie Zhuo, Zhaocong Yuan, Chenzheng Su, Xiaopeng Zhang
bullets: Targets the memory, energy, and compute constraints that make large ASR models impractical on edge devices.
Finds that many ASR layers learn functionally similar transformations, motivating shared recurrent blocks.
Uses representation-guided grouping and knowledge distillation to preserve effective depth with fewer parameters.
A two-block model recovers 97.4% of large-model accuracy on average across Open ASR Leaderboard benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a large language model (LLM) answer questions by retrieving relevant passages from a large corpus. However, RAG struggles with multi-hop questions, which require chaining facts spread across several documents through intermediate entities that the question never mentions. Graph-based RAG methods retrieve once from the entities a question names and so rarely recover the full evidence chain. Iterative RAG methods recover it step by step, but their accuracy is limited by the many tasks they ask the LLM to perform, such as planning the sub-questions, deciding their dependencies, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known. We propose DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework built on three components. First, DeFT-RAG generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the sub-questions answered so far with their answers (QA pairs). Each sub-question names every entity it asks about, which removes the need to plan, track dependencies or rewrite, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time. Second, DeFT-RAG moves the remaining LLM work outside the LLM: rule-based updates to a QA table that keeps track of what is known, and yes/no decisions made by a fine-tuned lightweight decision model. Third, DeFT-RAG caches the QA pairs and reuses an answer when a later question asks a sub-question with the same meaning. On MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines with both gpt-4o-mini and Qwen3.6 as the backbone, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method. With a QA cache shared across 1,000 MuSiQue questions, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, which reduces LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy.
authors: Dingyi Kang, Bingzhe Li
bullets: Targets multi-hop RAG failures where evidence spans documents connected through unstated intermediate entities.
Generates one self-contained sub-question at a time, using prior question–answer pairs to name all relevant entities.
Uses rule-based QA-table updates and a fine-tuned lightweight decision model to move bookkeeping and yes/no decisions outside the LLM.
Caches semantically equivalent sub-question answers; on 1,000 MuSiQue questions, this served 23.1% of sub-questions from cache and reduced LLM calls by 12.9% without reducing accuracy.
Achieved the best accuracy among 13 baselines on MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and HotpotQA with both tested backbones, while using fewer input tokens than other iterative methods.

papers.abstract: Event cameras, spiking cochleas and similar sensors emit asynchronous events, yet most learning systems first bin them into frames or packets, so the output depends on how the stream was sliced. Networks whose state is updated exactly at every event and evolves in closed form between events are invariant to this slicing. We ask what more makes the output (i) independent of the processing order of simultaneous events and (ii) continuous in the time stamps, even when two events cross in time, while (iii) staying sensitive to temporal order. For arbitrary nonlinear event models we prove that (i) and (ii) are each equivalent to pairwise commutation of the event updates, and that once updates commute, all order dependence comes from their non-commutation with the inter-event dynamics and vanishes linearly in the time lag. This identifies a class of time-mediated non-commutative (TM) models and yields a resolution-robustness bound for any model. We construct the minimal TM layer, a learnable, provably Lipschitz generalization of the Hassenstein-Reichardt correlator; prove that no single additive layer can uniformly represent ordered pair interactions, whereas a three-dimensional TM state can; show that each TM layer adds two levels of temporal nesting versus one for additive layers; and give a single-layer higher-order construction (TM-k) and a stacking rule preserving all three properties. We instantiate these results as the Clock-Free Event (CFE) layer, linear in the number of events, give a topology-free variant for temporal point processes with closed-form likelihoods, and specify a preregistered clock-robustness protocol with a physical-time threat model for spike-retiming attacks. In preliminary development-set experiments, the TM state beats an otherwise identical additive state by 3.5-9.1 points on DVS128 Gesture and by 24.5 and 30.6 points on SHD and Speech Commands.
authors: Han Wang, Jingyuan Bao, Juntao Wu, Saiao Zhou, Yuman Nie
bullets: Event updates that commute are necessary and sufficient for invariance to simultaneous-event order and continuity under timestamp crossings.
The proposed time-mediated non-commutative (TM) models retain temporal-order sensitivity through interactions with inter-event dynamics.
The minimal TM layer is learnable, provably Lipschitz, and can represent ordered pair interactions that a single additive layer cannot.
The Clock-Free Event (CFE) layer scales linearly with event count; a topology-free variant supports temporal point processes with closed-form likelihoods.
Preliminary development-set results report gains over an otherwise identical additive state on DVS128 Gesture, SHD, and Speech Commands.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Clocked versus clock-free processing. Top: binned pipelines slice the event stream into frames of width ∆; the input tensor depends on ∆ and on the phase of the grid, and moving one event across a bin edge by an arbitrarily small ε changes a count (Theorem 11). Bottom: a CFE network updates its state exactly at every event (jumps, coloured by event type) and evolves it in closed form between events (blue); queries (♦) can be placed at arbitrary times, and the result does not depend on how the stream is cut into packets (Theorem 3). Right: output of a single site as two events of types a and b cross in time, computed from the model equations with illustrative parameters. A gated update (SEL) jumps at the crossing and returns two different values at an exact tie, depending on the processing order; the TM layer is continuous and still distinguishes the two orders. Tie invariance and crossing continuity are each equivalent to commuting jumps (Theorem 5), and order information then enters only through the non-commutation of the jumps with the drift (Theorem 8).

Figure 2: The CFE network. An event stream (top left; ON and OFF events of a schematic rotating gesture), or a sampled signal converted into events by a send-on-delta encoder (bottom left, Theorem 22), drives the CFE layer. The sensor is tiled into sites; an event (red pixel) applies a jump to the state of every site in its 3×3 neighbourhood, with a letter given by its polarity and relative offset, and every site state drifts in closed form between events. TM site: events write the fast trace u and, through the mark-dependent gate gc(m)Rc, read the delayed trace s into the accumulator v; no event writes a coordinate that events read, so all jumps commute (Theorem 7). Exact parallel scan: each event acts as an affine map, so the states are computed exactly by a segmented parallel scan, and tie groups may be processed in any order. Queries read the site states x(Tq) at arbitrary times; a readout shared by all arms (signed-log normalization with raw features, convolution over the site grid, anchor-based pooling, a memory across queries and a linear layer) gives a prediction at every query. For event sequences without topology, an intensity head with a closed-form compensator gives the exact likelihood (Theorem 23). Bar heights are schematic.

Figure 3: State difference when two events of different types swap places at lag δ (FP64). TM and NS change linearly in δ , below the Lipschitz bound of Theorem 14. Selective updates jump by a constant amount at every lag, as Theorem 6 predicts.
Figure 4: DVS128 Gesture, folds 0 and 2 (198 calibration clips): accuracy against observation window for TM, NS and the stateless arm (ZERO). The benefit of the ordered state is largest early.

Table 1: Properties of event-model families under exact computation, for generic parameters. (P) partition invariance; (T) tie invariance; (C) continuity in the time stamps across crossings; (O2) ordered pair interactions within one layer. Justifications are in Section A.13.
Table 2: Numerical checks of the theory (FP64, seed 23).

Table 3: DVS128 Gesture, development folds: correct clips at the 200/400/600/800 ms prefixes. V1: 8×8-pixel sites; V2: 4×4-pixel sites with augmentation. “Best unordered” is the better of NS and ZERO at each prefix.

Table 5: SHD validation accuracy (%) of TM variants.

papers.title: Learning Without Clocks: Partition-Invariant Neural Network
papers.tldr: A theory and neural architecture for processing asynchronous events without clock-dependent binning while preserving temporal order and robustness to timing changes.

papers.abstract: Robots, autonomous vehicles, and consumer 360{\deg} cameras use fisheye lenses for wide fields of view (FoVs). Simulation-ready digital twins require photorealistic rendering across the full FoV and an aligned collision mesh. However, prior fisheye Gaussian Splatting methods only rasterize up to 180{\deg} and do not produce meshes, while Gaussian surface reconstruction methods assume pinhole training images. We present GOFish, the first 3D Gaussian Splatting surface reconstruction method to train directly on fisheye images, rasterize FoVs beyond 180{\deg}, and extract an aligned mesh from the same scene. Calibrated densification recovers the surface across the entire FoV, while Calibrated Mip Filtering and Wide-Angle Appearance Modeling keep pixel blur and lens falloff out of the scene and mesh. Across the 200{\deg} FIORD and 205{\deg} FullCircle benchmarks, GOFish improves PSNR over the best prior method by 2.28 and 1.97 dB, respectively. It also outperforms fisheye rendering baselines within their own FoVs and achieves the highest mesh F-score on FIORD and the main ScanNet++ set. Together, the Gaussian scene and mesh form a LiDAR-free, simulation-ready digital twin that renders in real time, ray traces the full FoV, and provides collision geometry.
authors: Allen Tu, Meher Gitika Karumuri, Shifan Zhu, Hailing Wang, Yen-Liang Lin, David Held, Matthias Zwicker, Tom Goldstein
bullets: Addresses fisheye reconstruction beyond 180° while producing collision-ready geometry.
Uses calibrated densification for full-FoV surface recovery.
Applies calibrated mip filtering and wide-angle appearance modeling to separate blur and lens falloff from the scene and mesh.
Improves PSNR over the best prior method by 2.28 dB on FIORD and 1.97 dB on FullCircle.
Achieves the highest reported mesh F-score on FIORD and the main ScanNet++ set, while supporting real-time rendering and full-FoV ray tracing.

papers.abstract: Humans navigate their environment based on their vision system, anticipating how the ground will respond before committing to a step. Self-supervised learning could provide legged robots the same ability, but the supervisory signal is typically chosen on intuition, and its effect on what the model learns is rarely examined. We present Terrain-Aware COntact Supervision (TACOS), which proposes a meaningful and consistent footstep instability score, based on the residual of a factor graph in legged state estimation. It projects the continuous score into preceding images to supervise a dense visual predictor. We propose two variants, a hard score that exploits hindsight and a causal soft score available immediately. Both metrics are compared against state-of-the-art alternatives in two independent evaluations that share no data or labels. On 1716 manually annotated contacts, both variants outperform every evaluated alternative at detecting instability and ranking its severity, improving pooled severity ranking by 28 % over the strongest baseline. On three outdoor test runs, our metric also trains the most accurate visual predictor, improving rank correlation by 58 % over the strongest alternative, and by a further 25 % when supplemented with onboard context. In a real-world experiment over a 50 m forest trajectory, the trained predictor handles non-geometric terrain properties such as mud and vegetation, while stepping around geometric obstacles like fallen branches. Code is available for reproducibility at https://github.com/norlab-ulaval/TACOS.
authors: Jean-Michel Fortin, William Larriv\'ee-Hardy, Gabriel Jeanson, Olivier Gamache, Daniele De Martini, Fran\c{c}ois Pomerleau, Philippe Gigu\`ere
bullets: Defines a consistent footstep instability score from the residual of a legged-robot factor graph.
Projects the score into preceding camera images to train a dense visual instability predictor.
Provides a hindsight-based hard score and an immediately available causal soft score.
Both variants outperform evaluated alternatives for detecting and ranking contact instability; the best predictor improves rank correlation further with onboard context.
In a 50 m forest test, the predictor responds to mud and vegetation while avoiding geometric obstacles such as fallen branches.

papers.abstract: Recent work has hypothesised that large language models may represent some concepts as multi-dimensional manifolds instead of single directions. Using these manifolds to interpret or steer representations often assumes that moving along them corresponds to a continuous change in the represented concept. In this work, we test this continuous manifold assumption on the prototypical weekday manifold. Despite its striking circular geometry, we find that the weekday representations behave more like seven discrete states arranged in a circle than a continuous ring. First, we show that local sensitivity has seven minima aligned with the weekdays, producing a step-like mapping between representation and behaviour under on-manifold steering. Second, we test whether any concepts are represented along the manifold outside the seven discrete states, and find neither time of day, uncertainty, nor natural text populate the intermediate space. Together, these results challenge the continuous interpretation of the weekday manifold and motivate testing whether movement along other representation manifolds correspond to meaningful changes in model representations and behaviour.
authors: Diksha Gupta, Rieke Fruengel, Stefan Heimersheim
bullets: Tests the assumption that representation manifolds encode concepts through continuous movement.
Finds seven local-sensitivity minima aligned with weekdays and step-like steering behavior.
Finds no evidence that time of day, uncertainty, or natural text occupy intermediate positions.
Challenges continuous interpretations of representation manifolds and calls for broader validation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Time-of-day variation along the weekday ring is small and not causal (A) Clocktime variation lies primarily along PC1, while weekday identity is captured mainly by PC2 and PC3. We show the top three principal components of weekday-token activations for prompts of the form “It was {time} on {day}.” (B) Time-of-day modifiers produce small (but systematic) angular shifts within the weekday plane, comparable in magnitude to those induced by non-temporal controls. Shifts are measured relative to each weekday centroid in the PC2–PC3 plane. Points show the mean across seven weekdays ± 1 s.e.m. (C) Steering along the ring has almost no effect on the predicted hour, whereas steering along the off-ring component of the observed “late–early” displacement shifts predictions by one to two hours. The horizontal axis specifies the fraction of a weekday interval traversed along the ring. At each steering amount and layer, the off-ring late– early intervention (brown) and random orthogonal control (green) are matched in ℓ2 norm to the along-ring intervention (black). Curves show mean changes in predicted hour ± 95% confidence intervals.

papers.abstract: Language model assistants sometimes change a correct answer when the user suggests a wrong one. The behavior, called sycophancy, is usually attributed to preference-based post-training, yet early measurements found it in pretrained models. We ask where it comes from by measuring it at every available stage of training: 13 open checkpoints from 5 lineages, from base model through supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization to release. We separate how far an injected claim moves a model's answer from how firmly the answer was held, and vary who makes the claim, how reliable they are said to be, and how strongly they make it. Two sycophancy behaviors with different origins emerge, and both replicate across datasets. Deference to a claim in the prompt is already present in every base model, which ranks sources in the same order as its post-trained descendants. Capitulation in conversation, dropping a stated answer when the user objects, is largely absent from base models and present in every post-trained checkpoint. When the objection names an alternative, most post-trained models give up firmly held answers as often as loosely held ones. We discuss the implications of these measurements for evaluating sycophancy and approaches for addressing each behavior.
authors: Jiarui Yao, Shweta Parihar, Nghia Tuan Bui, Guergana K Savova, Lijing Wang
bullets: The study evaluates 13 checkpoints across five open-model lineages, spanning base models through supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, and release.
It distinguishes how much a suggested claim shifts an answer from how strongly the original answer was held.
Deference to claims in prompts appears in every base model and preserves the same source-ranking pattern seen after post-training.
Capitulation—abandoning an answer after a user objects—is largely absent in base models but present in all post-trained checkpoints.
Both behaviors replicate across datasets, motivating separate evaluation and mitigation strategies.

papers.abstract: Efficient communication remains a major bottleneck in large language model multiagent systems. Latent communication reduces repeated natural-language exchange by transferring internal model states between agents, but these transfers remain costly and are typically designed around conventional KV-cache representations. We address this problem from two complementary perspectives. We introduce SelectKV, a boundary-aware method that selectively communicates KV states while protecting inherited context, and HyLaMAS, which extends latent collaboration to hybrid linear-attention models by communicating both KV caches and recurrent states through a shared workspace. Across six benchmarks, SelectKV reduces communicated KV positions and logical KV payload by 9.7-9.9%, with accuracy unchanged on two benchmarks, within one percentage point on three, and six points lower on HumanEval+. Across Qwen3.5 model scales, HyLaMAS reduces decoded output tokens by 53-80% and achieves 1.16-2.78x speedups relative to text-based multi-agent communication. Together, these independently evaluated methods represent two complementary approaches to efficient latent-state communication across conventional Transformer and hybrid model architectures.
authors: Miles Liao, Aaron Smieszek, Yuhao Ge
bullets: Efficient communication is a bottleneck in large language model multi-agent systems.
SelectKV selectively communicates KV-cache states while protecting inherited context, reducing communicated KV positions and payload by 9.7–9.9%.
HyLaMAS enables hybrid linear-attention agents to share both KV caches and recurrent states through a common workspace.
Across six benchmarks, SelectKV largely preserves accuracy, though it performs six points lower on HumanEval+.
HyLaMAS reduces decoded tokens by 53–80% and yields 1.16–2.78× speedups versus text-based communication across Qwen3.5 scales.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding is used to reduce the inference cost of language models. One-step diffusion drafters propose a block of multiple tokens in parallel, reducing the sequential cost of speculative decoding. On-policy distillation trains these drafters using verifier feedback on their own proposals. However, parallel drafting makes this feedback difficult to use: the drafter predicts each token without observing the preceding tokens sampled within the same block, while the verifier conditions its prediction on those tokens. Different sampled prefixes therefore give different verifier targets for the same drafter prediction. We show that distilling against these targets separately can suppress tokens that are plausible after some prefixes but unlikely after others, harming draft acceptance. We explain the effects of this mismatch and introduce Multi-Draft On-Policy Distillation (MDraft), a new parallel drafter distillation method which samples several draft blocks from the same context and aggregates the verifier's full-vocabulary conditionals across their prefixes. We use all the drafts to collect information from the verifier, allowing support from alternative prefixes to influence the training target. The resulting algorithm improves the acceptance length of a parallel drafter beyond the level of pre-training, and alleviates the effects of the distributional mismatch. MDraft changes only training, retaining the drafter's architecture and inference procedure, allowing the resulting drafter to be used as-is in place of the pretrained checkpoint. Experiments on a suite of mathematical, coding, and conversational tasks show longer accepted drafts than prior distillation methods.
authors: Petr Molodyk, Yuchen Zhu, Jaemoo Choi, Molei Tao, Yongxin Chen
bullets: Parallel drafters make on-policy distillation difficult because verifier targets depend on sampled within-block prefixes that the drafter does not observe.
Training separately on these inconsistent targets can suppress tokens that are plausible under alternative prefixes, reducing draft acceptance.
MDraft samples multiple draft blocks from the same context and aggregates the verifier’s full-vocabulary conditionals across their prefixes.
The method improves accepted draft length beyond pre-training and outperforms prior distillation methods across mathematical, coding, and conversational tasks.
It changes only training, preserving the drafter architecture and inference procedure.

papers.abstract: Large language models are pretrained on vast, uncurated corpora scraped from the public web. This creates a security risk from attackers who plant poisoned content in the pretraining data. We show for the first time that such poisoning can plant a remote code execution backdoor in an agent, causing it to execute attacker-chosen commands on the user's machine. To measure the threat end to end, we pretrain Qwen3 models from scratch at sizes 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B, and then post-train each into a CLI agent using a clean pipeline. Poisoning only 0.1% of the pretraining corpus with our new poison design implants the backdoor: the deployed agent executes the malicious command when the trigger is present while behaving normally on clean inputs. The attack success rate (ASR) increases with model scale, with the 4B model reaching roughly 92% ASR at a 0.1% poison rate and staying positive even when the poisoning rate drops to 0.0005%. Our code is available at https://github.com/safety-research/agentic-backdoor.
authors: Xinyan Hu, Pingbang Hu, Chloe Loughridge, Xuanli He, Nicholas Carlini, Matthew Jagielski, Javier Rando, Yiming Zhang

Poisoning 0.1% of pretraining data produced the backdoor; the 4B model reached roughly 92% attack success and remained vulnerable at 0.0005% poisoning.
The study measures the threat end to end, from pretraining through deployment, with code released publicly.

papers.abstract: Many uses of language models end in a typed decision: a choice among a closed set of options, whose probabilities code can act on. Reading those probabilities from one forward pass is fast but often wrong on decisions that take several steps, such as arithmetic, counting, and date comparison. Letting the model think first fixes most of these errors, but costs seconds per decision instead of milliseconds. To pay for thinking only where it helps, ThinkJev builds a fast and a slow system from one open hybrid-thinking model that can answer directly or after a thought. System 1 reads the model's probabilities for the option letters when it answers directly; System 2 reads the same letters after the model has thought on the same cached prompt, so escalating repeats no work and both systems give probabilities over the same options. Because the letters can be read after any number of thought tokens, one sampled thought also gives the answer under every thinking budget. Without training, ThinkJev lets System 1 answer alone only where a statistical test on labeled dev data guarantees that its accepted answers stay under a target error rate. At a 5% target, Qwen3.5-27B answers 24.5% of 8359 test decisions this way with a realized error of 3.9% (Qwen3.5-4B and 9B: 6.5% and 0.0%). For the rest, stopping each thought as soon as its answer is confident reaches 81.6% accuracy, against 82.7% for always thinking, with 72% of the thought tokens. Choosing when to think from System 1's confidence alone saves less, because the decisions System 1 is least sure of are often not the ones thinking fixes. On the public items of JevBench, an independent benchmark of typed-decision services, Qwen3.5-27B thinks on 29.4% and is not distinguishable in accuracy from the two thinking APIs listed (exploratory). Code and data generators are available at https://github.com/ding-xiaolu/ThinkJev.
authors: Xiaolu Ding, Kai Yang, Dongdong Liu
bullets: Targets typed decisions where direct one-pass probabilities can fail on multi-step tasks.
Builds fast and slow systems from one hybrid-thinking model, using the same option probabilities before or after reasoning.
A single sampled thought supports answers at every thinking-token budget, enabling adaptive stopping without repeated work.
On 8,359 test decisions, Qwen3.5-27B safely answered 24.5% directly at a 5% error target; adaptive reasoning reached 81.6% accuracy versus 82.7% for always thinking using 72% of thought tokens.
Performance depends on labeled development data for error control; confidence alone is a weaker escalation signal, and the JevBench comparison is exploratory.

figures.caption: Figure 2: ThinkJev on one decision: the same answer slots read twice after one processed prompt prefix. Otherwise the model thinks, continuing on the original cache, and the same slots are read after the first t thought tokens (checkpoints not to scale). The three policies of Sections 3.5 and 3.6 (direct answers under an error guarantee, the gate, and the anytime policy) differ only in how τ is chosen and where an escalated decision stops thinking.

Top: System 1, the direct answer, gives calibrated option probabilities; its confidence is below the threshold τ chosen on dev, so the model thinks. Bottom: one sampled thought, with the same answer slots read after its first t tokens (each read calibrated with its own temperature; checkpoints not drawn to scale). Each read is the answer under a thinking budget of t, so the policy can stop at the first confident one. Right: accuracy at each budget over all test decisions, with System 1 at t = 0. The example was chosen for illustration and is not typical; all values are generated from the released outputs (example.tex).

papers.abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer scalable capacity for Web applications, but uneven routing creates computation and communication bottlenecks. Existing placement and replication methods redistribute this workload, yet additional expert copies compete with token-related buffers for limited GPU memory. We present LRMoE, a memory-aware MoE training system that jointly recalibrates backward demand and balances the retained workload. During forward execution, it plans retention quotas and expert placement under resource constraints while preserving all routed computations. During backpropagation, a load recalibration metric estimates each token-expert pair's contribution to the expert update and selects pairs within these quotas. A capacity-aware routing algorithm distributes retained pairs among eligible instances of their original experts. Physical compaction then forms smaller communication payloads and variable-size grouped GEMMs, reducing backward traffic, computation, and execution-buffer demand. Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and GLM4.5-106B-A12B show that LRMoE reduces cumulative MoE-layer training time to fixed-loss targets by 21.2-44.8% relative to SYMI.

Compacts retained pairs into smaller communication payloads and variable-size grouped GEMMs.
On Qwen3-30B-A3B and GLM4.5-106B-A12B, reduces cumulative MoE-layer training time to fixed-loss targets by 21.2–44.8% versus SYMI.

papers.abstract: Spectral compression reduces the storage and scoring costs of dense retrieval by projecting embeddings onto a smaller principal subspace. However, its corpus-derived weighting rules tie all retained directions to a shared spectral trend, without directly accounting for their individual contributions to relevance. To address this, we propose Relevance-Guided Residual Calibration (RRC), a closed-form method for refining spectral weights using relevance judgments. RRC estimates margin-based weights from the means and variances of positive--negative score contributions along each retained direction. It retains directions with positive estimated weights, decomposes their log weights into a fitted power-law trend and a residual, and adds the residual to the compressor's log weights on this support. This allows relevance judgments to adjust individual directions while preserving the compressor's overall spectral trend. RRC applies to PCA, Whitening, and SpecTemp, and incorporates the corrections into the existing transformation shared by documents and queries, without iterative model training or an additional inference stage. Experiments with three encoders on nine datasets covering conventional and reasoning-intensive retrieval show that SpecTemp + RRC achieves the highest mean effectiveness among tested compressors on the BEIR group and BRIGHT at every target dimension. On the five evaluated BRIGHT datasets, it improves over SpecTemp by an average of 2.34 nDCG@10 points at 768 dimensions. The gains also persist under scalar and product quantization, improving the trade-off between per-document storage and retrieval effectiveness. Our code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/rrc-spectral-compression-B5CE/
authors: Yongkang Li, Panagiotis Eustratiadis, Evangelos Kanoulas

Applies to PCA, Whitening, and SpecTemp through the existing shared document/query transformation.
Across three encoders and nine datasets, SpecTemp + RRC had the highest mean effectiveness among tested compressors at every target dimension on BEIR and BRIGHT.
On five BRIGHT datasets at 768 dimensions, RRC improved over SpecTemp by an average of 2.34 nDCG@10 points, with gains persisting under scalar and product quantization.

papers.abstract: Language models do not merely memorize facts; they absorb rhetorical strategies from pretraining data, including the human tendency to reason by analogy. We ask: is this absorbed capability geometrically accessible before any instruction tuning, and what determines whether it can be activated at inference time? We extract an "Analogy Vector" from the residual stream via difference-in-means and show it enables steerable explanation style across seven instruction-tuned models (Gemma-2, Llama-3.1, Qwen-2.5; 2B-32B), improving harmonic mean from 3.22 to 3.94 (+22%) for Gemma-2-9B-IT on 300 held-out test prompts. A small human validation study confirms the LLM judge on Analogy Quality. Our central finding, from seven matched base-instruct pairs, is a gradient of behavioral accessibility: the analogy direction exists in every base model, but its behavioral accessibility under linear intervention scales continuously with instruction exposure during training. Gemma-2 base models (strict pretraining/IT separation) show flat steering landscapes: present but behaviorally inert. Qwen-2.5 base models (instruction data woven into pretraining) are already partially accessible before any explicit fine-tuning; base-instruct cosine similarity of the analogy vector reaches 0.94-0.97 for Qwen versus 0.37-0.66 for Gemma, providing geometric corroboration of the behavioral gradient. This challenges the binary "base vs instruct" framing: the relevant variable is how much instruction exposure a model has received across its full training pipeline. We position activation steering as a complementary interpretability tool that reveals how instruction exposure organizes rhetorical knowledge in activation space.
authors: Shengjie Xu
bullets: An analogy direction is present in every tested base model, but its behavioral accessibility varies continuously with instruction exposure.
A residual-stream difference-in-means vector enables steerable analogy-based explanations across seven instruction-tuned models.

Qwen base models showed partial accessibility before explicit fine-tuning, while Gemma base models’ directions were largely behaviorally inert.
The findings challenge a binary base-versus-instruct distinction and frame activation steering as a tool for studying rhetorical knowledge in activation space.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly become important tools for science, education, medicine, and professional work. Despite their apparent simplicity from the user's perspective, effective and responsible use requires an understanding of how these systems work, what their limitations are, and how their outputs should be evaluated. I wrote this document as a basis for my lecture on LLM in the master in artificial intelligence in medicine at the university of Turin, Italy. This book provides a practical and accessible introduction to LLMs for scientists and professionals. It explains the fundamental ideas behind tokenisation, embeddings, training, inference, context windows, prompting, and instruction hierarchies, while deliberately avoiding mathematical detail. Particular attention is given to the limitations of LLM-generated answers, including hallucinations, uncertainty, reproducibility, bias, and the need for systematic verification and human oversight. The book also discusses privacy, governance, security, and the responsible handling of personal and sensitive information. More advanced topics include Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), retrieval quality, chunking, embeddings, vector search, agents, tools, and workflows. A substantial practical exercise guides the reader through running a local LLM with Ollama and Open WebUI and using it to interact with a collection of scientific papers. The exercise emphasizes evidence retrieval, source verification, uncertainty, disagreement between studies, and the distinction between plausible language and scientifically supported conclusions. No programming knowledge is required.
authors: Umberto Michelucci
bullets: Explains tokenisation, embeddings, training, inference, context windows, prompting, and instruction hierarchies without mathematical detail.

papers.abstract: Despite their strong performance, large language models remain highly sensitive to prompt formulation. This issue is typically addressed at inference-time through manual prompt optimization, which introduces overhead and lacks scalability. Conversely, we focus on train-time approaches that build prompt robustness into the model during instruction tuning. A common strategy is to mix multiple paraphrases of each prompt into training. We demonstrate that across trainable parameters, the per-paraphrasing gradients interfere, with 57% exhibiting sign conflicts and the naive gradient average discarding approximately a fifth of the magnitude. Therefore, we develop two gradient-merging methods, Prompt-TIES and Prompt-DARE, that address this interference by leveraging interference-resolution operators from model and gradient merging and applying them to prompt gradients. In this study, we compare the efficacy of our methods to increase model robustness to train-time robustness methods spanning all three established classes: data construction, consistency regularization, and contrastive alignment. The evaluation is conducted across four models from two families at two scales. We observe the interaction between prompt phrasing and the specific examples accounts for 54% of per-example variability on average, and exceeds 70% on tasks such as ANLI and WiC. The gradient-merging methods directly improve this local robustness and nearly halve per-example variance on fully fine-tuned models at little cost to overall accuracy. The other train-time methods enhance raw performance, but fail to improve per-example variance reliably. Code: https://github.com/FSadrieh/prompt-agnostic-llms. Model checkpoints: https://huggingface.co/prompt-agnostic-language-models.
authors: Frederic Sadrieh
bullets: Prompt sensitivity is usually addressed with manual inference-time prompt optimization, which is costly and difficult to scale.

Prompt-TIES and Prompt-DARE adapt gradient-merging operators to combine prompt gradients and improve robustness.
Across four models from two families and two scales, prompt phrasing and example choice explain 54% of per-example variability on average, exceeding 70% on ANLI and WiC.
The proposed methods nearly halve per-example variance for fully fine-tuned models with little overall-accuracy cost, whereas other train-time methods do not reliably reduce variance.
